### Why grouping dense Boolean IDs only partly speeds up scope undo

The Boolean IDs retire in reverse creation order. The delayed activity queue stores variables in priority order. In a two-iteration audit, all 250 proposed contiguous removals failed the delayed queue's suffix check. Repeated scans inspected 16,500 candidate variables. In nine paired samples, the unbounded scan raised undo from **57,417 to 347,555 instructions per scoped pop**. Limiting the scan to eight variables still cost 116,424, against 57,485 in that run's control. A valid dense ID interval gives no guarantee about where its members sit in the heap. [Audit and scoped phase counters](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/nov24-boolean-retirement-trials.tar.xz)

Keeping the actual deletion order while releasing surviving arena references together reduced undo to **46,777 instructions**, against **19,657** in C++. The whole pop fell from 203,439 to 190,457 instructions, versus 144,725 in C++. The fastest instruction-count prototype bypassed an error return after a heap preflight. It remains experimental. A simpler single-reference change preserved the general deletion routine and measured 54,161 instructions in undo. Each phase used nine paired 1,500-pop samples with empty brackets subtracted. The existing variable-level counter and queue-matched benchmark can distinguish future heap improvements from moving work into the next variable allocation. [Variable measurement driver](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/variables.py) · [All alternatives and observations](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/nov24-boolean-retirement-trials.tar.xz)

### What costs three times as much on repeated incremental checks

The two engines made the same search decisions and quantifier instantiations through the first **32 checks** of both ticket queries and toy consensus. The numeric query also matched on decisions, equalities, conflicts and resource steps. With that search held constant, the g3 solver call cost **3.16×** Z3 on ticket 127, **3.33×** on ticket 290, **2.73×** on the numeric query and **3.43×** on toy consensus. These are instructions per extra check. Each cell is the median of five paired differences between 32 and four checks, divided by 28. ### Owning a rename map once in the shared Ivy frontend

When GoIvy renamed a clause, it built a substitution map and then copied every entry into the annotation. The clause operation now gives its newly allocated map directly to the built-in annotation. Public callers can still mutate the map they pass to `Rename` without affecting the annotation. Custom annotation implementations receive their usual `Rename` call. This improves the same frontend used by both solvers. [GoIvy implementation, tests and benchmark](https://github.com/glycerine/ivy/commit/10d7568c5) · [Raw measurements and release controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-goivy-clause-renaming.tar.xz)

| Names renamed | Previous | Changed | Bytes per rename, previous → changed |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1,199 ns | 722 ns | 824 → 488 |
| 16 | 4,113 ns | 2,310 ns | 2,632 → 1,392 |
| 128 | 24,069 ns | 12,425 ns | 19,272 → 9,712 |

Each cell is the median of 17 alternating runs of 10,000 renames. In separate heap measurements, complete Hermes testing allocated about **1.59 GB less** on the g3 frontend path and **1.58 GB less** on the linked Z3 path. Full Apple saved approximately **0.80 GB** on each backend. These are cumulative Go heap allocations across a run. The linked solver's native heap is outside the Go counters. [Per-process allocation and collection counts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-goivy-clause-renaming.tar.xz)

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple `ord_live.ivy`, all isolates | 767.48 | **756.96** | 1,041.66 | **1,030.83** |
| Hermes testing, 6,338 checks | 1,082.04 | **1,064.02** | 1,222.69 | **1,202.76** |

The table uses three complete before/after runs per cell on a pinned CPU. The long runs overlapped other work, so these comparisons use retired instructions. Ordinary Hermes had seven quiet rotations with medians of **7.850 → 7.837 s** on g3 and **6.861 s** on linked Z3 with the new frontend. Each backend reproduced the expected status and both output streams on **228 specs**, including 91 expected failures. The full GoIvy release test suite passed. The rfn2 trace matched across 2,334,030,415 bytes and Paxos matched all 27,855 reference lines. ### Keeping quantifier-instance cache storage local to a solver

Each check cleared its quantifier-instance cache by dropping the lookup table, tuple records and reference storage. The next check allocated all three again. Commit `17110e632` releases the AST owners in their original order, clears the table and reuses bounded capacity in that solver. A solver that never instantiates a quantifier allocates no table. A drop in occupancy also releases excess capacity after a large batch. [Implementation](smtcore/cached_var_subst.go) · [Peak-capacity and failure tests](smtcore/cached_var_subst_ownership_regression_test.go)

| Distinct tuples between resets | g3 before, ns/tuple | g3 after, ns/tuple | In-tree Z3, ns/tuple | Go heap bytes/tuple, before → after |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 2,432 | **2,131** | 769 | 391 → **107** |
| 64 | 2,157 | **1,918** | 800 | 385 → **98** |
| 256 | 1,991 | **1,799** | 796 | 346 → **86** |
| 1,024 | 2,084 | **1,830** | 829 | 444 → **96** |

The Go and C++ fixtures instantiate the same quantified DAG with the same tuple sequence. Every request must miss, and the last result must equal the independently constructed DAG. Each cell is the median of 21 rotating runs of 65,536 tuples per width on CPU 45. Across all four widths together, eleven hardware-counter rotations measured **5.767 → 5.233 billion instructions** for g3 and **2.339 billion** for Z3. In a separate g3 recording, 37% of the remaining sampled instructions fell under application construction. C++ also spends about a third of its smaller instruction budget constructing applications. The source comparison points to per-application cost and substitution traversal as the next questions in this fixture. [Go benchmark](smtcore/smt_quantifier_substitution_benchmark_test.go) · [C++ benchmark](../src/test/perf/quantifier_instance_batches.cpp) · [Raw runs, profiles and capacity trials](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-quantifier-instance-batches.tar.xz)

The cache change alone saved little across complete specs. Four pinned instruction-count rotations measured **88.51 → 88.27 billion** on TLB, **58.67 → 58.34 billion** on ordinary Hermes and **127.29 → 127.28 billion** on Apple dramc_nb2. Linked Z3 used 65.56, 50.17 and 140.11 billion respectively. All 228 verifier cases, including 91 expected failures, produced matching status and output. The 1,799 shell controls matched outcomes, the packaged datalog timeout returned the expected result on both versions, the rfn2 trace matched byte-for-byte, and all 27,855 Paxos lines matched. [Per-workload measurements and release controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-quantifier-instance-batches.tar.xz)

### Where the extra first-push instructions go

TLB still makes 58 physical first pushes on **each** backend. A first push preprocesses the assertions accumulated by a fresh solver before it opens its first scope. Across those pushes the whole boundary cost **17.41 billion instructions in g3 and 5.92 billion in linked Z3**. Hybrid reliable broadcast cost 1.63 / 0.54 billion across 34 pushes and Flash cost 1.08 / 0.35 billion across 28. On today's Apple rfn2 path, g3 avoided all ten first pushes still made by linked Z3. TLB is a better case for studying the remaining per-push cost. [Whole-push counters and solver-configuration census](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-first-push-and-rewrite-trials.tar.xz)

| TLB first-push pass | g3, billion instructions | Linked Z3, billion instructions | g3 excess, billions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Propagate values | 3.310 | 0.874 | **2.436** |
| Infer quantifier patterns | 2.577 | 0.609 | **1.967** |
| Maximize BV sharing, including its follow-up reduction | 2.606 | 0.707 | **1.899** |
| Convert to negation normal form | 1.193 | 0.324 | 0.869 |
| Reduce asserted formulas | 1.165 | 0.702 | 0.463 |
| Find macros | 1.893 | 1.612 | 0.281 |
| Refine injectivity | 0.072 | 0.009 | 0.063 |

The first three passes account for **6.30 billion**, about **55%** of the measured 11.49-billion gap. Each of the three ran 58 times on both backends. Z3 also ran the explicit macro and reduction passes twice per push where g3 ran them once. The table sums each pass over all 58 pushes within a verification, then takes the median of five rotations. Each bracket counts user instructions on the thread executing the pass, subtracts its own empty measurement, and must fall inside the first-push interval on the same thread. The whole-push observations used a separate build. All four specs reproduced both reference streams and the expected exit status on every run. [Portable measurement driver](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/first_pass_instructions.py) · [Native counter](../src/test/perf/asserted_pass_interval.h) · [Per-pass measurements and stack samples](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-matched-first-pass-instructions.tar.xz)

A second set of five TLB pairs measured the inner loops at `fda3f51b7`. Inferring patterns on the pending formulas used **2.509 / 0.605 billion** (g3 / Z3), accounting for 98% of the whole pattern-pass gap in that build. In value propagation, the forward sweep used **1.164 / 0.317 billion** and the reverse sweep **1.151 / 0.310 billion**. Both include inserting substitutions. For BV sharing, the loop itself used **0.998 / 0.235 billion**, while the whole pass used **2.585 / 0.708 billion**. About 59% of that pass's excess lies outside the BV loop, which is followed by ordinary theory reduction. Skipping every BV rewrite would still leave the larger part of this gap. [Five pairs with nested intervals for each of four specs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-matched-first-pass-instructions.tar.xz)

Two potential shortcuts had much smaller ceilings. Across complete TLB, 5,477 solver reconfigurations used a total of 0.368 billion instructions. In a separate root census the rewriter made 452,533 calls and took 5,110,791 steps. Unchanged roots with an empty substitution accounted for 2,551,559 steps, but only 21,865 steps repeated a result in the same solver, pass, mode and substitution epoch. Reusing results by manager and root alone would have contradicted 529 observed results even with the elimination mode included. Moving goal simplification ahead of the existing verification proof path raised ordinary Hermes from 58.24 to 63.82 billion instructions. [Configurations, roots and order trials](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-first-push-and-rewrite-trials.tar.xz)

To reproduce the pass measurements, supply the stdout and stderr of a reference run in the reference directory. Use the same spelling of the input path because GoIvy prints it in diagnostics. Ordinary source builds contain no observers. The optional `--detail` switch adds the inner formula loops and the two directions of propagation.

### Reusing ownership of unchanged assertions

On complete TLB, **25,502 of 31,235** preprocessing batches returned precisely the expressions and proofs that the solver already held. The old publication code released and reacquired every row. Commits `9c7b15de7` and `fda3f51b7` leave the common prefix in place. When the two lists have the same length, they also keep the common suffix. New references are acquired only across the changed middle. A failed acquisition restores the prior ordered rows. Repeated expressions, changed proofs, growth, shrinkage, a stale middle proof and successful retry have focused tests. All retained references belong to the same solver and arena. [Production implementation](smtcore/smt_asserted_macros.go) · [Rollback and ownership tests](smtcore/smt_asserted_publication_test.go)

| Rows | Difference between successive batches | g3 before, ns/op | g3 after, ns/op | In-tree Z3, ns/op |

| 8 | First row | 313 | 88 | 29 |
| 128 | Identical | 4,584 | 318 | 458 |
| 128 | First row | 4,482 | 462 | 458 |
| 1,024 | Identical | 36,088 | **2,457** | 3,724 |
| 1,024 | First row | 36,086 | **3,126** | 3,693 |
| 1,024 | Last row | 36,085 | **2,482** | 3,708 |

These are medians of 21 rotating three-engine measurements on CPU 44, each doing 3,000 publications. Both fixtures keep both input batches alive and check every final row. With a first-row difference they fell from 546,024 to 53,056. On eight rows with one difference, Z3 retains a roughly threefold lead. Run the Go benchmark with `go test ./smtcore -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkSMTAssertedBatchReplacement$' -cpu=1 -benchtime=3000x -benchmem`. Three complete rotations measured **88.60 → 88.63 billion instructions** on TLB (linked Z3 65.76), **58.62 → 58.79** on ordinary Hermes (50.17), and **11.87 → 11.78** on Apple rfn2 (49.11). The previous column uses the same frontend and the g3 solver immediately before the two ownership changes. The replacement loop's order-of-magnitude improvement addresses a small fraction of those workloads. The complete 228-case verifier corpus matched stdout, stderr and exit status, including 91 expected nonzero exits. ### Which general rewrites are worth pursuing

The largest measured first-push costs are common to several specs. Flash and hybrid reliable broadcast both spend about four times Z3's instructions on pattern inference and on value propagation. On TLB, direct classification of flat uninterpreted applications found two independent singleton triggers in 28,302 calls out of 31,533. The observer compared the number, term identity and order of the predicted triggers with the regular pattern collector. A bounded fast path still saved only about one billion complete-run instructions on TLB. The trigger collector is a candidate for reducing per-node cost across the remaining cases. The higher ceiling lies in skipping whole traversals that an earlier pass has already done. That requires matching the mutation, cache and resource state when validating a shortcut. [Flat-trigger predictions and verified checkout comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)

A different experiment factored shared branches of nested conditional terms while simplifying temporary verification assertions. I independently checked 118 saved rewrite-equivalence queries with the in-tree and installed Z3. Both returned UNSAT on every query. Applying the rewrite to compound Boolean or datatype branches throughout the verifier improved ordinary Hermes, but increased the complete Raft no-assume experiment from 19.77 to 22.78 billion instructions. Restricting candidates to ground shared branches made raftok substantially worse. Equivalent formulas can select a different search and satisfying model. [Projected-model checks, equivalence queries and policies tested](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-first-push-and-rewrite-trials.tar.xz)

A bounded scan of the first assertion batch offered a more selective policy. Enabling factoring after observing a datatype application among the first 256 distinct nodes took ordinary Hermes from **57.87 to 51.16 billion instructions**, while the Raft no-assume control measured **19.11 → 19.15 billion**. Enabling it unconditionally in that same comparison took Raft to 22.03 billion. All 228 verifier corpus cases matched under the bounded policy. A datatype elsewhere in the batch is an empirical predictor of search behavior. Four follow-ups tested for datatype terms specifically at the shared branch, its operands, the condition, or the surrounding branches. On ordinary Hermes these took **66.77–67.02 billion**, versus **59.02** for their control and **52.00** for batch-level selection. Looking only at the local term failed to predict the beneficial search change. [Conditional policies, executable build metadata and corpus](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)

During these experiments GoIvy changed its dependency to published g3 v0.2.13. Three exploratory checker comparisons linked that module and missed local source overlays. Their end-to-end numbers were discarded. The replacements in the archives explicitly select the two local modules and retain each binary's dependency metadata. The independent Go and C++ microbenchmarks build directly from the source tree. The permanent pass-measurement driver creates a private Go workspace for this purpose. [Verified verifier builds and replacement runs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)

On a separate CPU, five alternating quiet rotations on ordinary Hermes measured **7.310 s** on current g3, **6.585 s** with experimental datatype-guided factoring and **6.406 s** on linked Z3. The prototype recovered about four fifths of the elapsed-time gap, leaving it 2.8% slower than Z3. The CPU had to deliver at least 95% occupancy and its sibling had to remain at least 95% idle. Three per-goal instruction-count pairs measured **6.34 billion fewer instructions inside the 959 physical solver checks** with the prototype. In each pair, all 8,364 recorded batch, condition, phase and result rows matched. Three checks accounted for 2.98 billion of the saving across batch 10 condition 70, batch 14 condition 69, and batch 5 condition 69. This is a candidate for the incremental verification path. The retained solver still uses the original search policy. [All timing attempts, both long holdouts and 228 corpus results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)

An attempted shortcut for BV sharing showed why eliminating unchanged traversals needs more than expression equality. On TLB, a bounded structural scan predicted an unchanged term 40,576 times. The actual traversal returned that term 40,575 times and exhausted a resource limit once. Both disputed cases on dramc_nb2 and the disputed toy-consensus case also exited at their resource limits. The structural scan would have returned success. A complete-verifier prototype using this shortcut raised toy consensus from 2.99 to 5.33 billion instructions and Raft no-assume-test from 22.31 to 30.33 billion. Restricting it to calls without an active step limit recovered the Raft regression but left the toy regression; requiring an unlimited arena budget as well brought toy consensus back to its control. The safer next experiment is to reduce cost *within* each existing traversal step while preserving its cache effects, ownership and cancellation checks. [Original failing terms, output values, limits and crossover trials](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)

I would prioritize three further measurements from this frontier.

1. **TLB first push.** Bracket the common application visitor and the result-cache operations within both propagation sweeps and the ordinary reduction after BV sharing. Compare instructions per visited application and per cache hit. Retain the exact visit, cancellation and ownership sequence in the first prototype. The three leading passes account for 6.30 billion excess instructions. The nested counters distinguish the shared theory-rewrite work from the trigger collector. [Matched pass counters and leaf samples](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-matched-first-pass-instructions.tar.xz)
2. **Ordinary Hermes.** Replay batch/condition pairs 10/70, 14/69 and 5/69 with the same base assertions. Compare instantiated quantifiers, conflicts and selected conditional terms. These three account for 47% of the improvement inside physical checks. The independent Raft no-assume case and the long Hermes variant distinguish a general search improvement from an input-sensitive heuristic. [Per-goal counters, local-term policies and holdouts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)
3. **Repeated incremental checks.** Use the 32-check toy-consensus replay as the general-rewriter control. Both engines make 89,761 theory reducer calls per added check. A narrower prototype for atomic arithmetic bounds reduced the whole-shell slope from 1,666 to 1,602 million instructions, versus 471 million in Z3. Check the resource-limit and failure path before adopting it. The larger opportunity is lowering the cost of repeated theory applications across several operators. [Matched operation boundaries](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-incremental-replay-profiles.tar.xz) · [Bound-shape experiments](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewriter-holdout-experiments.tar.xz)


### Which quantifiers drive the Hermes search

Ordinary Hermes runs 2,575 verification conditions. Across three runs the g3 frontend reached the scoped solver for 959 of them. Within those scopes 457 succeeded in the proof helper, 469 went through the observed general solver call, and 33 went directly to the first check of a new batch. On the 469 observed calls, shared-branch conditional factoring reduced materialized quantifier instances from 181,590 to 145,785 and conflicts from 1,836 to 1,692. The native statistics hook covers all 2,575 calls on its frontend path. The table compares matching batch and goal positions. [Per-check statistics, observation counts and build metadata](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-quantifier-candidates.tar.xz)

| Ordinary Hermes goal | g3 candidates / instances | Conditional prototype | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Batch 5, goal 69 | 29,757 / 4,411 | 2,014 / 931 | 2,102 / 881 |
| Batch 10, goal 70 | 107,005 / 12,512 | 64,774 / 8,809 | 88,100 / 11,934 |
| Batch 14, goal 69 | 37,591 / 4,794 | 6,315 / 1,371 | 9,320 / 1,667 |

The instrumented Go and C++ queues classified every candidate as already satisfied, reduced to true, or materialized as a lemma. All counts and their generation distributions repeated in two complete runs per backend and were independently reproduced with the portable driver. On goal 5/69 a single five-variable rule about timestamps and versions generated **16,162 candidates in g3, 634 with conditional factoring and 654 in Z3**. On goal 10/70 the same rule generated 67,956 / 29,516 / 44,637 candidates. On 14/69 it generated 24,591 / 3,162 / 5,345. In all three engines the inferred trigger for this rule has the same shape. Three applications of the timestamp/version relation cover all five variables, but one application shares no variable with either of the other two. This allows the matcher to combine two independent groups. The body also contains a successor relation that connects the groups. Conditional factoring changes which ground terms and assignments reach this trigger. The counts alone do not identify which earlier assignment caused the search to diverge. ### Connecting disjoint quantifier triggers

On ordinary Hermes, the verifier previously inferred the three-term trigger `R(x,a), R(y,b), R(x,c)` for a five-variable rule. Matching a value for `(y,b)` left every match for `(x,a,c)` available. The rule's body also mentions `S(b,a)`. Requiring a match for that term lets the eager matcher discard unrelated pairs before it constructs instances. The implementation looks for a term that connects the most disjoint groups and resolves ties in favor of a declaration occurring in fewer candidate terms. It uses the filtered candidates of the current quantifier and its bound variables. The solver registers the original trigger for a later matching round. Explicit triggers keep their original terms and order. [Candidate selection](ast/pattern/connected_multi_pattern.go) · [Incremental verifier configuration](smtcore/smt_asserted_patterns.go)

| Complete ordinary Hermes, seven qualifying rotations | Previous g3 | g3 `d9d52ea74` | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Median elapsed | 7.722 s | **5.006 s** | 6.791 s |
| Median retired user instructions | 59.09 billion | **35.97 billion** | 50.14 billion |

g3 finished first in all seven qualifying rotations. Each rotation used one physical core for all three binaries with at least 95% process occupancy and at least 95% idle time on its SMT sibling. Three additional attempts failed the timing criteria. A separate three-rotation instruction panel measured 1.579 → **0.774 billion** on the independent `test/fba.ivy` specification, versus 0.978 billion for linked Z3. TLB measured 88.58 → 88.44 billion, versus 65.59 billion for Z3. On Apple rfn2 the figures were 11.75 → 11.76 billion, versus 49.05 billion. These measurements used GoIvy `3d552b46c` with a private local dependency override. The 2,334,030,415-byte Apple rfn2 trace matched byte for byte, as did all 27,855 lines on the Paxos trace comparison. Focused tests passed in release, checked and debug configurations. ### The cost of the same rewriter operation in Go and C++

During value propagation on TLB’s 58 first pushes, the two engines visited the same number of expressions and processed the same number of application frames. g3 spent about **5.2× as many instructions processing an application**. Its two cache operations also cost more at almost identical call counts. Flash and hybrid reliable broadcast independently reproduced the application-processing gap. [Per-push raw counts, calibration and summaries](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-rewriter-operation-costs.tar.xz)

| TLB value propagation | g3 calls | Z3 calls | g3 instructions per sampled call | Z3 instructions per sampled call |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Visit an expression | 898,606 | 898,606 | 818 | 121 |
| Process an application frame | 961,604 | 961,604 | 2,011 | 385 |
| Look up a rewrite result | 861,963 | 861,971 | 132 | 20 |
| Insert a rewrite result | 418,504 | 418,508 | 723 | 133 |

The table uses the median of five within-run means on g3 `b7caff4fa` and the Z3 library linked to GoIvy `3d552b46c`. Each binary measured one operation at one of every 67 calls and subtracted its own empty sampling cost. Five offsets covered different calls. These are inclusive measurements. Processing a frame can visit a child and insert a result, so summing the four rows would count some work twice. A separate build on the preceding g3 revision gave 1,987 versus 385 instructions per application. On Flash the portable driver measured 2,404 versus 443 across 43,012 calls on both engines. On hybrid it measured 2,201 versus 402 across 67,557 calls on both. [Matched measurements and both builds](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-rewriter-operation-costs.tar.xz)

An independent observer recorded what the cache actually stored. During TLB value propagation **418,201 of 418,504 insertions mapped an expression to itself**. Every insertion was fresh. Of 837,008 lookup misses in allocated caches, 418,504 immediately repeated the preceding miss on the same key. Among the caches released inside this phase, 79,296 held only identity mappings, comprising 401,346 entries. Every one of those nodes had enough external references to survive release. During BV sharing all 403,615 insertions were identity mappings. This suggests testing a smaller representation for short lists of unchanged nodes and measuring the effect on complete verification. The tests must preserve reference counts during rewriting, the order of any actual destruction, eviction behavior and interrupted cleanup. [Cache contents and lifetime observations](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-rewriter-operation-costs.tar.xz)

To repeat a measurement, supply a reference directory with the expected stdout and stderr and run the driver once per operation. For TLB use `--expect-exit 1` to include the two expected proof failures. The driver creates its own Go workspace, links the local g3 checkout, and instruments the in-tree objects used by GoIvy. For cache operations it wraps the actual functions in the linked archive. It verifies both output streams and the exit status in every observation run. [Benchmark driver](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/rewriter_call_cost.py) · [Go meter](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/rewriter_call_meter.go.txt) · [Native meter](../src/test/perf/ivy_rewriter_call_cost.h)

```sh
python3 perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/rewriter_call_cost.py \
  --goivy /path/to/ivy/goivy --spec /path/to/examples/liveness/tlb.ivy \
  --reference /tmp/tlb-reference --expect-exit 1 --abc /path/to/abc \
  --cpu 2 --operation app --rounds 5 --output /tmp/tlb-app-cost
```

### Using E-matching for private refutation attempts

A verification batch can try proving a goal with a subset of its premises in a private solver. A contradiction there proves the full problem inconsistent. A satisfying interpretation of the subset leaves the original goal open. The private solver previously spent substantial time finding such interpretations and discarded them. Commit `b7caff4fa` selects E-matching alone for eligible reusable refutation attempts. The original solver retains its normal search and model construction whenever the private attempt returns inconclusive. [Search policy](api/api_proof_plan_context.go) · [Private and original solver regression](api/api_proof_plan_quantifiers_test.go)

| Complete verifier, median billions of retired user instructions | Previous g3 | Current g3 | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Ticket protocol | 4.628 | **3.762** | 1.473 |
| Apple cf_live | 41.874 | **39.135** | 54.744 |
| Ordinary Hermes | 36.115 | **35.411** | 50.129 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 10.685 | **10.389** | 5.885 |
| ARM rules 3 | 4.527 | **4.439** | 2.211 |
| TLB | 88.556 | **87.902** | 65.622 |
| Apple dramc_nb2 | 126.941 | **125.694** | 139.582 |
| Apple rfn2 | **11.816** | 11.897 | 49.154 |
| raftok | **17.848** | 18.190 | 19.704 |

The panel used the same GoIvy frontend, inputs and CPU within each of three rotations. Separate elapsed-time runs rotated the three engines together and required 95% process occupancy and 95% idle time on the sibling hardware thread throughout each run. Seven qualifying ticket medians were **0.702 / 0.573 / 0.252 s** for previous g3, current g3 and linked Z3. The corresponding cf_live medians were **5.621 / 5.237 / 10.331 s**. All 228 verifier compatibility cases reproduced their expected exit and both output streams, including 91 cases with expected verification failures. Checked, debug and release focused tests passed. The Apple rfn2 trace matched across 2,334,030,415 bytes, as did the complete 27,855-line Paxos output. [Individual measurements, corpus comparisons and trace checks](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-private-refutation-search.tar.xz)

On ticket, the three wide searches with satisfiable premises fell from **707 million to 53 million instructions** inside the private check. All six wide searches that established a contradiction still succeeded. On cf_live, all 22 successful wide refutations survived, while eleven other attempts fell from **3.135 billion to 724 million** check instructions. A width-two native finite-domain replay found a model for all three ticket subsets and ten of the eleven cf_live subsets. Width three yielded models for all eleven. Those models independently explain why a contradiction search could stop early. [Per-plan components, SMT inputs and 1,104 model experiments](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-private-refutation-search.tar.xz)

In five ten-iteration Go benchmark samples, the median satisfying ticket fixture went from **53.46 to 4.29 ms**, 7,287,232 to 1,192,647 bytes and **50,526 to 6,176 allocations** per attempt. The contradiction fixture measured 2.56 / 2.57 ms and 3,922 / 3,836 allocations. Each measured iteration used the same public verification-batch lifecycle as the verifier. In a separate policy experiment, eliminating every wide attempt raised whole Apple `ord_live2.ivy` from 1.193 to 1.291 trillion instructions. A fixed 12,000-step limit raised it to 1.300 trillion. Keeping the wide searches with the retained E-matching policy used 1.157 trillion. Expensive refutations still pay for themselves on that input. ### When preprocessing fewer premises pays for a second solver

On ordinary Hermes, the old wide private search proved 153 of 166 goals. Together those attempts retired **5.02 billion instructions**. Each omitted fewer than 220 conjuncts. Sending these goals through the existing narrower searches and incremental solver reduced complete verification from **5.107 to 4.413 seconds**, versus **6.879 seconds** for linked Z3. A successful private proof can still cost more than the solver work it saves. On Apple rfn2 the observed wide attempt omitted at least 220 conjuncts and established a contradiction. [Per-attempt selections, costs and whole-verifier measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-wide-premise-selection.tar.xz)

Commit `37a8cf71d` applies the existing 220-conjunct maximum in both directions. A reusable wide refutation can select at most 220 conjuncts and must omit at least 220. Selection can stop as soon as the included count exceeds the applicable maximum. The existing bounded narrow searches and the full source solver can still decide the goal. The threshold controls speculative work and has no role in the validity of a returned proof. The test covers both sides of the 219/220 omission boundary. [Selection and search](api/api_verification_goal.go) · [Boundary tests and captured benchmark](api/api_verification_goal_test.go)

| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1.575 | **1.453** | 0.923 | 10.414 / **9.577** / 5.889 |
| Ticket protocol | 0.565 | **0.530** | 0.251 | 3.738 / **3.496** / 1.470 |

Elapsed figures are medians of seven complete rotating triplets on an idle physical core. Each successful run had at least 95% process occupancy and 95% idle time on the sibling hardware thread. Apple rfn2 measured 11.814 → 11.891 billion and toy consensus 2.800 → 2.807 billion. ### Which reductions cost more during TLB's first push

Both engines called the core theory reducer about **584,500 times** during first-push value propagation on TLB. They also processed exactly 209,317 variables. The Go cost per call is higher for the shared operations. Disjunction and negation account for much of the Boolean work at this boundary. [All per-push counts, sampled rules, calibrations and sources](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-reduction-rule-costs.tar.xz)

| Value propagation, 58 first pushes | g3 calls | Linked Z3 calls | g3 instructions per sampled call | Z3 instructions per sampled call |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Core theory reduction | 584,509 | 584,512 | 977 | 98 |
| Check for a substitution | 898,606 | 898,606 | 161 | 52 |
| Process a variable | 209,317 | 209,317 | 208 | 26 |
| Process a constant | 59,760 | 59,763 | 398 | 71 |
| Check for constant folding | 125,768 | 731,036 | 78 | 10 |

The constant-folding rows count different amounts of work. Go filters by child position before entering the measured function. Five alternating offsets per engine measured each operation in a separate build. Probe placement affects generated code. For example, sampling the outer Go theory reducer gave 886 instructions per call, while sampling its inner method in a different binary gave 977. Those values cannot be subtracted to calculate wrapper overhead. [Portable Go and in-tree C++ measurement driver](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/rewriter_call_cost.py)

A further seven-offset experiment classified sampled calls by operator **after** the ending counter read. Each engine also ran an empty function with the same argument types, sampling arrangement and input. Subtracting its cost gave **1,174 / 84** instructions for negation, **2,119 / 362** for disjunction and **324 / 7** for an uninterpreted function, in g3 / Z3 order. The TLB recordings contained 19,717 / 19,704 negation samples, 9,321 / 9,321 disjunction samples and 28,820 / 28,855 uninterpreted-function samples. The uninterpreted case is particularly simple in the native code. A family-ID load and branch return a failed reduction immediately. The Go path calls an AST-manager accessor before returning the same result. The measurements include the generated code around that call. Whole-verifier measurements are necessary to establish the benefit of changing it. [Per-rule ranges, matched empty-function runs and both observers](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-reduction-rule-costs.tar.xz)

### Theory reduction with the hardware probes outside the loop

A two-argument uninterpreted function takes **110 g3 instructions and 25 native instructions** to reject in a direct call to the theory reducer. A Boolean equivalence between distinct atoms takes **2,635 and 223**. Both implementations leave the expression alone in each of those cases. This independently confirms a per-call cost even when both solvers receive exactly the same operator and arguments. [Go fixture](ast/rewriter/th_rewriter_benchmark_test.go) · [In-tree Z3 fixture](../src/test/perf/theory_reduction.cpp)

| User instructions per call, after empty-call subtraction | g3 | Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Uninterpreted function of two atoms | 110 | 25 |
| Negation of an atom | 897 | 104 |
| Double negation, returning the atom | 794 | 115 |
| Disjunction of distinct atoms | 1,464 | 312 |
| Disjunction of an atom with itself, returning the atom | 1,573 | 293 |
| Equivalence of distinct atoms | 2,635 | 223 |

Each of seven rounds on CPU 33 ran fresh processes at 200,000 and 1,200,000 calls. The difference in process instructions divided by one million estimates the cost of one more iteration. Each table entry is the median paired difference between that slope and the slope of an empty callee with the same signature. The empty loops themselves cost about 43 instructions in Go and 13 in C++. All 336 readings ran without counter multiplexing. Both fixtures check the final reduction status and the identity of the returned expression. These direct loops reuse the operands and work outside the full traversal. The first-push samples above capture the actual mix of operands and execution paths. [Every process measurement](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/nov24-direct-reduction.csv.gz)

### Retiring runs of scoped Boolean variables

Commit `0ec8f45c4` reduces the cost of unwinding a run of Boolean variables whose expressions survive the pop. The previous path visited both queue owners and shortened five dense slices for each variable. The new path validates the two queues once, releases the surviving applications, erases the exact descending sequence of queue members, and shortens the slices once. When at most one member survives a heap erase, the final heap order is already determined. With multiple survivors the heap performs the normal sifts, including tie handling. The arena retains ownership of all expressions and queues within their solver. [Trail retirement](smtcore/smt_internalizer_state.go) · [Activity heap](util/heap/heap.go) · [Arena reference release](ast/ast_core_accessors.go)

| Median elapsed per pop, 10,000 pops per run | Previous g3 | Current g3 | Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scoped atoms, original Go Make fixture | 12.680 µs | **11.467 µs** | |
| Scoped atoms, delayed activity queue on both engines | 17.540 µs | **13.978 µs** | 12.742 µs |
| Surviving atoms, original Go Make fixture | 353 ns | 359 ns | |
| Surviving atoms, delayed activity queue on both engines | 298 ns | 312 ns | 479 ns |

The native fixture always enables the delayed queue. Each median contains nine complete rotations on one physical core per rotation, with at least 95% occupancy and an idle sibling for at least 95% of every execution. One incomplete attempt was excluded. The benchmark checks the restored atoms and clauses outside the timed pop. Nine separate alternating invocations of the literal Make targets measured `ScopedAtoms` at 11.812 µs for `make bench` and 14.305 µs for `make cppbench`; these runs shared the machine with other experiments. [Go fixtures](smtcore/smt_hotpath_benchmark_test.go) · [Quiet comparison](perf/scope_restoration/quiet.py) · [Make-target driver](perf/scope_restoration/make_targets.py)

| Queue-enabled scoped pop, solver-thread instructions | Previous g3 | Current g3 | Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Undo core trail | 57,507 | **26,064** | 19,694 |
| Restore learned clauses | 108,264 | 107,590 | 89,254 |
| Pop relevance marks and owners | 19,536 | 19,524 | 8,073 |
| Complete pop | 203,388 | **170,598** | 144,762 |

Each cell is the median of nine independently bracketed runs with 1,500 counted pops. Empty intervals took 54 instructions in g3 and 37 in Z3. Core-trail undo accounts for 31,443 of the 32,790 instructions saved per pop. In a second experiment with an empty interval at each individual source boundary, publishing one Boolean variable took 299 instructions in Go and 222 in C++. The queue callbacks within publication took 191 and 91. Filtering the Go pending-relevance notifications took 7,576 instructions per pop. The C++ relevance propagator has no corresponding notification list. These nested intervals identify the next measurements and overlap their parents. [Phase driver](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/measure.py) · [Per-operation counters](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/restoration.py)

Reference lifetime determines how much a pop can batch. With 8,192 Boolean variables, eleven quiet paired samples measured 216.0 → **124.7 µs** when all expressions survived and 292.4 → **278.3 µs** when every 29th expression lost its last owner. All-last-reference pops cost 1.626 → **1.680 ms** and alternating last references cost 0.994 → **1.085 ms**. An earlier unbounded scan took approximately 26.6 ms on the all-last case because each scalar release retried nearly the whole remaining trail. The retained implementation examines 16 entries at a time and spaces new probes 16 trail entries apart. It stops before a destructor, score-cache update, indexed equality or non-Boolean trail entry requires ordinary processing. [Lifetime benchmark](smtcore/smt_scoped_ref_lifetime_benchmark_test.go) · [Interruption and cached-score tests](smtcore/smt_scoped_boolean_retirement_test.go)

All 228 compatibility cases matched the expected exit and both output streams, including 91 expected failures. Apple rfn2's 26 checks reproduced the 2,334,030,415-byte trace. All 27,855 normalized Paxos output lines matched. The heap tests compare exact entries, inverse indices and iterator epochs over 350 randomized layouts. Release tests passed for the three affected packages, along with focused checked and debug tests. Five independent-process worker measurements gave 52,918 → 52,917 idle bytes per solver at 1,024 solvers × 128 atoms and 782,850 → 782,853 at 48 × 2,048. The paired TLB verifier runs stayed around 86.6 billion instructions. The demonstrated speedup applies to scoped Boolean retirement. ### Retiring pending relevance notifications

Scope pop unmarks a trail of expressions and releases their references. A separate notification queue makes the newly marked expressions available to callers. Every new mark after the last queue filter or drain appends the same expression to both lists. Commit `b3d94b979` uses this shared suffix to remove pending notifications that the pop just retired. Older queue entries are checked against their current relevance. Duplicate notifications retain their original order. A callback can drain the queue or reactivate a mark, and a refused reference release can interrupt the pop. These paths recheck membership. The solver keeps two scalar fields for this bookkeeping. [Implementation and retry path](smtcore/smt_relevancy.go) · [12,000 randomized operations and callback controls](smtcore/smt_relevancy_retirement_test.go)

| 128 atoms, 64 clauses | g3 before | g3 after | In-tree Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Instructions in scoped relevance pop | 19,514 | **12,262** | 8,073 |
| Instructions in complete scoped pop | 171,786 | **163,743** | 144,762 |
| Scoped pop with delayed queue | 13.927 µs | **13.571 µs** | 12.608 µs |
| Scoped pop in original Go Make fixture | 11.462 µs | **11.299 µs** | |
| Surviving atoms with delayed queue | 314 ns | **291 ns** | 481 ns |

Each instruction reading brackets 1,500 timed pops on the solver thread, with nine rotations per engine. The corresponding empty brackets cost 54 instructions in g3 and 37 in Z3. Elapsed medians use nine complete rotations of 10,000 pops per engine. One partial rotation failed the quiet-core check and was excluded from all three elapsed columns. [All measurements, including incomplete attempts](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/nov24-pending-relevance.tar.xz) · [Quiet benchmark driver](perf/scope_restoration/quiet.py)

A separate audit tested each candidate removal against the full live mark table. On TLB it confirmed 90,690 eligible entries out of 90,930 notifications examined across the complete verification. On ARM rules the count was 3,516 of 3,518, on ordinary Hermes 19,801 of 19,819, and on Apple rfn2 148 of 151. These totals explain why a 37% reduction in relevance-pop instructions has little effect on complete verification time. Every one of the 228 corpus processes matched its reference exit and both output streams. The 2,334,030,415-byte rfn2 trace and all 27,855 normalized Paxos output lines matched. Release, checked and debug relevance tests passed. [Audit and compatibility results](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/nov24-pending-relevance.tar.xz)

### Where TLB spends its extra instructions

TLB has 18,953 verification conditions. At g3 `86413f90a`, general search ran on 2,218 of them. The matching check calls cost g3 **33.00 billion instructions** and linked Z3 **10.78 billion**. g3 made fewer decisions, found fewer conflicts and instantiated fewer quantifiers. Another 16,221 conditions went through the incremental push and were proved by an existing g3 helper. Their check calls cost **3.45 billion** in g3 and **24.87 billion** in Z3. Aggregating these two populations hides the cost of general search. [Matched-condition analysis](perf/ivy_apple/incremental_cost/matched_check_groups.py) · [Per-condition counters, source streams and reproduction commands](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

| Matched TLB conditions reaching general search | g3 | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Quantifier instances | 161,559 | 165,083 |
| Decisions | 52,480 | 59,558 |
| Conflicts | 5,888 | 6,003 |
| Boolean variables created | 292,618 | 293,976 |
| Propagations | 194,744 | 202,285 |

The instruction readings bracket the frontend's check call on its solver thread. Each g3 reading includes the attempted private proof and subsequent general check. Separate runs collect each general solver's statistics. The join verifies every condition identity and result before aggregating. There were 456 successful g3 proofs before the first push and 58 direct first checks. Both engines reported 18,951 UNSAT and two SAT results. At the earlier checkpoint, the corresponding 2,195 general checks cost 34.14 versus 10.69 billion instructions. [Raw readings and both checkpoints](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

Commit `86413f90a` limits a second private search after a definition-only search has already tried the same goal. Extra constraints can still discharge the goal when the combined selection fits 32 premises. Apple rfn2's useful wide proof remains available when the first search found no definitions. On four complete TLB rotations, the change reduced median whole-process instructions from **86.46 to 83.99 billion**. On five Apple cf_live rotations it reduced them from **38.94 to 37.58 billion**. A captured TLB goal with one selected definition and 78 wider premises went from 13.81 to 5.08 ms per private attempt. The original wide attempt proved that goal, and the new schedule leaves it for the complete solver. On a captured cf_live goal with 31 definitions and 197 wider premises, both private attempts were inconclusive and the time fell from 40.69 to 14.18 ms. These benchmark medians use nine samples of 15 iterations on a shared host. All 228 compatibility cases matched their expected exit and both streams, along with the enabled rfn2 trace and normalized Paxos output. [Benchmark, boundary and fallback tests](api/api_verification_goal_test.go) · [Full-run and allocation measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

### Reusing ground instances across sibling verification conditions

For each ground goal, I substituted up to three constants of each uninterpreted sort occurring in that goal into universal premises, limiting each premise to 32 tuples. Each instance follows from the submitted premise in every source model. A ground UNSAT result therefore proves the goal, while SAT or UNKNOWN leaves the original solver responsible for the decision. Grouping goals with the same constants allowed one incremental replay per group. The in-tree Z3 executable proved **1,852 of 2,225** selected TLB checks on these ground subsets. The remaining 373 were SAT on the subset. Independent replay from the captured assertion stream reproduced every outcome. The median UNSAT core used **5 assertions** on the 1,852 successes. The median available ground set across the selected checks had 744 assertions. [Portable ground replay](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/ground_subset_replay.py) · [Selected conditions, complete source stream and core sizes](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

| Complete TLB, median of five rotations | Baseline g3, billion instructions | Prototype g3, billion | Linked Z3, billion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Private ground SMT solver, starting after a constant set repeats | 87.16 | 88.74 | 65.62 |
| Incremental Boolean solver, one temporary goal assumption per check | 84.66 | **73.60** | 65.65 |

The first prototype discharged 1,613 additional checks. Its general searches fell from 30.19 to 9.31 billion instructions, but pushing private scopes took 11.42 billion, installing instances took 5.41 billion and the private checks took another 4.17 billion. The Boolean prototype retained its ground terms and clause IDs in one verification batch. It installed consequences of the permanent premises and used a temporary assumption for each goal. Of 1,886 attempts, 1,620 succeeded. The median trial added six clauses to the installed formula. The Boolean experiment uses a later baseline containing the bounded second-search change. Seven complete quiet-core rotations measured **11.89 s** for that baseline, **10.20 s** for the Boolean prototype and **9.89 s** for linked Z3. [Individual checks, quiet timings and prototypes](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

The Boolean projection represents equal terms by equal bit patterns and constrains applications of the same function to agree on equal arguments. A sort with many source values needs codes only for the ground terms in the projection. Classes can be numbered by their first representative, which bounds the bits needed by each successive term. These codes do not constrain the size of the source domain. Across 8,640 generated goals with changing premise sets, the incremental Boolean solver produced 4,648 refutations. Every one was UNSAT in the in-tree native solver. Native returned SAT on 3,855 goals and UNKNOWN on none. Installing the remaining Boolean clauses still took 5.7–6.1 billion instructions on TLB. Reducing clauses before installation and measuring how many sibling checks amortize setup are the next experiments. [Finite-domain model generator, oracle results and phase brackets](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-tlb-matched-search.tar.xz)

### November 24. Reusing ground instances across long verification batches

On TLB, the experimental Go backend completed all 18,953 checks in **8.38 s**, compared with **11.37 s** at g3 `86413f90a` and **9.63 s** with linked Z3. These are medians from seven complete comparisons. Each comparison ran the engines successively on one physical core, required at least 95% solver CPU occupancy and 95% sibling idle time, and compared exit status and both output streams. A separate seven-round comparison reproduced the result at 8.35 s for the prototype and 9.48 s for Z3. The experiment used the existing arena and one logical Go processor. [Per-run times, outputs checked, and source overlays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-batch-admission.tar.xz)

The previous prototype installed every Boolean clause in a private SAT solver. The faster version propagates units implied by shared premises first. It discards satisfied clauses, removes false literals, and creates SAT variables only for the remaining clauses and the current assumption. When later instances imply permanent units, it passes those units on to the SAT solver. Each sibling goal is a temporary assumption. Satisfiable and inconclusive answers fall through to g3's ordinary solver. A change in the premise list starts a new projection. [Encoding, propagation and SAT installation](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-batch-admission.tar.xz)

| Complete verification | g3 before | Start after 12 observed proof calls | Start when frontend expects ≥48 goals | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TLB | 84.62 | 63.57 | **63.23** | 65.65 |
| Apple `cf_live` | 37.66 | 40.09 | 37.70 | 54.85 |
| Apple `dramc_nb2` | 124.42 | 128.04 | 124.69 | 139.97 |
| Apple `rfn2` | 11.78 | 11.76 | 11.81 | 49.07 |

Entries are median **billions of retired user instructions for the entire process**, five runs per engine and input. GoIvy knows the number of sibling conditions before the first check. Giving that count to the proof batch avoided paying setup on short Apple batches. Seven of 228 corpus entries had any batch of at least 48 goals. A second check in the prototype required 192 flat universal premises. Both conditions describe the available reuse and apply independently of the specification's name. All 228 runs reproduced the reference exit and output bytes, including runs with counterexamples. [Batch-size census, full corpus comparisons and counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-batch-admission.tar.xz)

Two simpler encodings also beat linked Z3 on TLB. Equality atoms with explicit triangle constraints for the first eight terms of each sort took 8.51 s in the first comparison. Treating each distinct pair as an independent Boolean equality and keeping function congruence took 8.61 s in the second. Omitting transitivity weakens the private refutation but every source model still satisfies the projected constraints. On 8,640 generated goals with three successive premise lists, ordinal encoding proved 4,646 goals, the triangle version 4,638, and independent pairs 4,577. Native Z3 agreed on every refutation and returned SAT on 3,855 goals. These are experimental results. Release work includes exercising private-budget exhaustion, bounding memory per active solver, and repeating the measurements through the ordinary GoIvy API. [Oracle inputs, answers, and complete timings](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-batch-admission.tar.xz)

All 16 event counts agreed on each of eight inputs. On the eight-hole input both inspected **116,394,977 long-clause watches**, skipped 55,684,132 using a true blocking literal, inspected 299,444,198 candidate replacement literals and moved 48,167,205 watches. | Forced chain, clauses up to three literals | 0.221 | 0.227 | 0.060 |
| Planted model, five literals per clause | 0.338 | 0.324 | 0.099 |

The previous Go clause view returned two slices. Every literal access chose between bytes in the arena and words in a separate wide allocation. Both allocations now use the same little-endian layout. The checked list owner, slot generation and iterator lifetime are preserved. Giving both sizes the same layout alone reduced the eight-hole count to **44.79 billion**. Three independent instruction profiles per engine attributed **49.31 billion** instructions to the previous Go propagation loop and its callees, **32.08 billion** to the current loop and **7.45 billion** to the native loop. Current Go spent about **7.06 billion** resolving arena clauses, **4.45 billion** scanning for replacements and **4.24 billion** appending moved watches. Native clause lookup accounted for about **0.14 billion**. An experimental directory of per-clause byte slices reduced the combined prototype from 37.84 to 33.09 billion at the cost of a second directory containing Go pointers. Encoding each watch in eight bytes initially made the search slower. Carrying its existing encoded clause identity directly through a move lowered the corresponding 36.54-billion baseline to 35.51 billion. That prototype retains historical identities until close. The next storage experiment should measure the memory cost of resolving a live clause once while preserving generation checks and prompt release. ### November 24 — Removing quadratic growth from the byte arena

Growing an arena to 16,384 simultaneously live 256-byte allocations took **90.63 ms**. With commit `af3f04978` it takes **2.73 ms**, a 33.1× speedup. Each of those allocations needs a dedicated chunk. The old allocator searched from slot zero for every new chunk, even when all previous slots were occupied. Growing to *n* chunks therefore inspected *n(n−1)/2* occupied slots. The arena now counts vacant slots and remembers where a search can start. With zero vacancies it appends immediately. When a chunk is released it moves the search start back if needed, preserving reuse of the lowest available slot. The two counters occupy eight bytes per arena. [Arena implementation](arena/small_bytes.go) · [Failure, reuse and reset regression](arena/small_bytes_chunk_directory_test.go)

| DIMACS clause width | Live clauses | Previous g3 | g3 with the directory change | In-tree Z3 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 16,384 | 0.400 | 0.400 | 0.130 |
| 64 | 4,096 | 0.421 | 0.354 | 0.125 |
| 64 | 16,384 | 2.467 | 1.393 | 0.484 |
| 64 | 65,536 | 22.729 | 5.554 | 1.921 |
| 64 | 131,072 | 79.774 | 11.096 | 3.836 |
| 64 | 262,144 | 297.179 | **22.125** | 7.667 |

The table gives median billions of retired user instructions for complete solver processes, including parsing, clause creation, search and writing the model. Each rotation used the same generated clause stream and CPU for all three engines. The largest input had two rotations and the others had three. Every run reported 1,025 decisions, zero conflicts and the requested clause count. The driver checked every distinct printed model against every input clause. Smaller 16-literal clauses share a chunk and showed no measurable benefit at the tested population. [Portable DIMACS benchmark](perf/ivy_raft/wide_clauses.py) · [Raw measurements, allocator variants and corpus](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-chunk-directory.tar.xz)

Reuse also improved. In a population of 16,384 chunks, freeing and refilling 64 scattered holes fell from **381.1 to 32.7 µs**. Refilling 64 holes at the tail fell from **791.9 to 13.7 µs**. An in-place min-heap brought scattered refill down to 18.5 µs, with similar dense growth and a slightly slower tail refill. The simpler two-counter implementation preserves allocation order and changes the search state only after a successful reservation. These are medians of five pinned microbenchmark runs. The TLB, Ticket, hybrid broadcast and ARM verification controls moved by at most 1.1% in either direction. The exact release reproduced the reference exit and both output streams on all 228 GoIvy corpus cases, including 91 expected nonzero exits. [Allocator benchmark](arena/small_bytes_chunk_benchmark_test.go) · [Individual samples](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-chunk-directory.tar.xz)

### Limiting decision depth inside a private ground proof

Bounding a private SAT search at 256 decision levels reduced work on both full Apple specifications, TLB and Hermes testing. A private ground problem retains only selected consequences of the original assertions. UNSAT proves the goal, while SAT still requires the ordinary quantified solver. The resource limit alone had allowed expensive searches for assignments that could never discharge the original goal. Commit `11b33ad26` returns control to the quantified solver when that private search reaches the depth limit. Each worker owns its search state. [Private solver call](api/api_ground_instances.go) · [Decision-boundary tests](sat/sat_solver_decision_depth_test.go)

| Entire Apple `ord_live.ivy` | 788.04 | **732.15** | 1,031.90 |
| Entire Apple `ord_live2.ivy` | 1,303.61 | **1,239.75** | 1,961.20 |
| Hermes testing | 1,106.44 | **1,064.45** | 1,203.72 |
| Ordinary Raft | 22.22 | 22.20 | 214.57 |
| Apple `dramc_nb2` | 124.25 | 124.57 | 140.17 |
| Apple `rfn2` | 11.77 | 11.83 | 49.10 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 9.55 | 9.58 | **5.89** |

Values are median billions of whole-process retired user instructions. TLB and `rfn2` have five rotations, and the other displayed workloads have three. Every engine reproduced the expected exit and both output streams on each measured workload. Seven separately timed quiet-core rotations put TLB at **9.006 s before, 8.759 s after and 10.075 s on linked Z3**. The 228-input corpus included 91 expected nonzero exits. Native Z3 confirmed all 4,646 private refutations among 8,640 generated goals. The median additional live heap per loaded worker was 877,541 bytes. Enabled `rfn2` tracing matched across 2,334,030,415 bytes, and the normalized Paxos replay matched across 27,855 lines. [All eleven verifier comparisons, timing attempts, depth trials and controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-private-decision-depth.tar.xz)

### Skipping writes when a sorted base clause survives intact

On clauses of width 64, scanning the sorted literals once for assignments, duplicate variables and out-of-range variables cut the median from 1.937 to 1.475 billion instructions over 65,536 clauses. The old path wrote each surviving literal back to the same slot. Commit `57aeffa91` lets the SAT solver consume the slice directly when all variables are distinct and unassigned at the base scope. Clauses that need simplification still use the existing routine. The focused differential test compares the output buffer as well as the result across 81 assignments and five clause shapes. [Clause normalization](sat/sat_solver_clause_core.go) · [Differential test](sat/sat_solver_mutable_span_test.go)

| Literals per clause | Clauses | g3 before | g3 after | In-tree Z3 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 16,384 | 185 | 157 | **130** |
| 32 | 16,384 | 278 | **221** | 245 |
| 64 | 65,536 | 1,937 | **1,475** | 1,921 |
| 128 | 8,192 | 427 | **313** | 481 |
| 256 | 4,096 | 406 | **292** | 483 |
| 512 | 4,096 | 780 | **552** | 970 |

Values are median millions of whole-process retired user instructions across three rotations. Seven separately timed quiet-core rotations measured **0.432 s** on g3 and **0.476 s** on Z3 for 131,072 clauses of width 64. At width 512 with 16,384 clauses the medians were **0.259 s** and **0.518 s**. Z3 still finished first at widths 16 and 32 in the timing series. On the harder eight-hole pigeonhole search, g3 used 36.33 billion instructions versus Z3's 8.05 billion. Four complete verifier workloads changed by at most 1% in either direction. All 228 corpus comparisons matched the reference, including 91 expected nonzero exits. [Raw counts, timing triples, trial overlays and controls](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-base-clause-scan.tar.xz)

### Replaying the six private enumeration searches that exhausted their budget

The complete `ord_live2` run discharged 748 of its 754 private enumeration queries. Replaying the six other queries with their original solver histories reproduced all six misses at the production budget of six million resource units. Starting each terminal query on a fresh solver proved one. Keeping the same budget and supplying an independently checked sufficient subset of the premises proved **all six**. This distinguishes two costs that a general optimization must address. Identifying sufficient premises can change the search substantially, and finding them must cost less than the fallback proof it avoids. [Replay benchmark](api/api_enumeration_search_benchmark_test.go) · [Six solver histories and core inputs](api/test_vectors/apple_enumeration_search.json.gz)

| Query | Checks in captured solver lifetime | Original conjuncts | Sufficient conjuncts | g3 with a fresh solver and all premises | g3 with sufficient premises |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 58 | 740 | 129 | Budget exhausted | Proved |
| 2 | 57 | 740 | 163 | Budget exhausted | Proved |
| 3 | 58 | 694 | 123 | Budget exhausted | Proved |
| 4 | 36 | 954 | 119 | Budget exhausted | Proved |
| 5 | 9 | 954 | 103 | Proved | Proved |
| 6 | 13 | 954 | 206 | Budget exhausted | Proved |

In-tree Z3 identified each sufficient set from individually named conjuncts. A second invocation read the selected conjuncts as ordinary assertions and confirmed UNSAT. Even on those subsets, five of six g3 queries exhausted a one-million-unit budget. Ranking premises by shared rare symbols missed all six at that budget. Z3 found models for all six selections of 64 ranked conjuncts, demonstrating that those selections discarded needed information. Reusing the exact conjuncts from earlier cores also missed all six at six million units. Pooling cores from all five *other* difficult queries, including later queries, rescued two. The capture and replay offer a way to test general premise selection independently of frontend costs. Core identities are used only in the benchmark. [Raw solver regimes, extraction, native checks, transfer experiments and reproduction commands](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-enumeration-replay.tar.xz)

### What still costs three times as much when both solvers follow the same search?

On three captured Apple enumeration queries, g3 executed **2.91–3.13×** as many instructions as in-tree Z3. On all six sufficient premise sets, both solvers completed the proof with identical search counters and g3 executed **3.43–3.53×** as many instructions. These are standalone solver processes reading identical SMT-LIB. Across 105 paired measurements on 18 inputs, the two solvers agreed on every reported integer search statistic, including decisions, conflicts, propagations, resource counts and quantifier instantiations. The pairs included 23 UNSAT, 24 SAT and 58 budget-limited UNKNOWN results across four solver configurations. [Standalone comparison benchmark](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/enumeration_budget.py)

| Terminal query, full premises | Quantifier instances | Decisions | Conflicts | g3 billion instructions | Z3 billion instructions | g3/Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 129,420 | 21,613 | 143 | 29.42 | 9.49 | 3.10× |
| 3 | 74,669 | 12,449 | 152 | 24.86 | 8.53 | 2.91× |
| 6 | 138,649 | 16,553 | 182 | 30.12 | 9.61 | 3.13× |

The table uses three rotating, CPU-pinned process measurements per engine at six million resource units. All three full queries exhausted that budget. With sufficient premises, query 1 finished in 2,190,289 resource units and used 10.58 versus 3.00 billion instructions. Query 6 finished in 2,468,846 units and used 13.23 versus 3.81 billion. These ratios describe retired user instructions. The host also ran other work during measurement.

| Sampled instructions in billions, g3 / Z3 | Query 1 | Query 3 | Query 6 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Processing a quantifier-queue entry | 14.81 / 4.94 | 10.57 / 3.67 | 19.92 / 6.24 |
| ↳ Checking whether the instance is already satisfied | 3.55 / 1.96 | 3.28 / 1.91 | 3.86 / 1.79 |
| ↳ Substituting the bound variables | 2.42 / 0.94 | 1.18 / 0.44 | 3.74 / 1.37 |
| ↳ Rewriting the instantiated body | 3.32 / 0.74 | 2.42 / 0.50 | 5.00 / 1.34 |
| ↳ Internalizing the resulting assertion | 3.77 / 0.91 | 2.70 / 0.62 | 5.36 / 1.23 |
| Counterexample search during model checking | 8.74 / 2.43 | 7.53 / 1.98 | 1.29 / 0.38 |

The queue accounts for **50%, 42% and 67%** of excess instructions respectively, using the two whole-process totals as the denominator. The four indented rows are portions of that queue work. Counterexample search can itself run a solver, so its row can overlap the queue. Counts are three-run medians from hardware instruction samples with Go frame pointers and native DWARF stacks. Inlining and truncated stacks limit attribution. [Go instance construction](smtcore/smt_qi_instance.go) · [C++ instance construction](../src/smt/qi_queue.cpp)

Two experiments narrow the implementation choices. Fusing the internalization and literal lookup of asserted disjuncts saved about 0.2–0.4 billion instructions on the hard queries. That addresses only a small part of internalization. A more promising opportunity is repeated rewriting. On query 1, 84,619 of 131,061 rewrites revisited an input whose previous rewrite had left it unchanged. Every one of those inputs again rewrote to itself. Those calls consumed 64% of the rewriter loop iterations. The corresponding shares were 63% on query 3 and 32% on query 6. A bounded 4,096-entry table indexed by AST slot identified 40%, 44% and 17% of all iterations, respectively. These are measured opportunities. Solver-local reuse still needs to preserve substitution changes, cache and reference lifetimes, proof dependencies, cancellation and resource-budget boundaries. [Raw counters, profiles, trial implementations and stack analysis](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-enumeration-matched-search.tar.xz)

### Can repeated quantifier rewrites reuse their old resource charge?

**The same AST can rewrite to itself twice and consume a different number of resource units each time.** I recorded the result, rewriter loop count and resource increment on each instance rewrite in three full queries and their independently sufficient premise sets. A 16,384-entry solver-local table indexed by slot compared the complete handle, including its generation. Every identity hit returned the original AST again. The resource increment differed on 16–32% of the hits, depending on the input. Replaying the previous charge could change when a budget-limited search stops. [Six captured inputs, raw counts and standalone replay driver](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewrite-resource-replay.tar.xz)

| Query | Identity hits in full query | Hits with different charge | Identity hits in sufficient set | Hits with different charge |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 77,515 | 14,272 | 15,894 | 3,655 |
| 3 | 47,345 | 8,959 | 13,179 | 4,223 |
| 6 | 46,520 | 7,467 | 17,621 | 4,139 |

Clearing the table at search initialization and every decision-scope push or pop left **zero hits on all six inputs**. That version paid for maintaining the table without avoiding a rewrite. A second experiment inspected descendants through depth 12. All observed repeated identity roots contained only uninterpreted terms and basic Boolean operations within the inspected depth. None of the inspected nodes had a substitution mapping.

I also tried checking whether small AND/OR argument lists already satisfied the normalizer's constraints. This runs inside the existing rewriter and leaves child traversal and its resource accounting intact. Across 90 rotating process measurements, four versions reproduced every integer search statistic on all six queries. The version checking slices of up to eight arguments reduced median instructions from 29.52 to 29.10 billion on full query 1, 24.95 to 24.62 on query 3, and 30.11 to 29.65 on query 6. A 1–2% reduction leaves most of the gap measured above. I kept these as benchmark overlays. A larger rewriter gain would require reducing the cost of the traversal itself while preserving its cache and budget behavior. [Implementations, per-run counters and reproduction instructions](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-rewrite-resource-replay.tar.xz)

### How much work buys another proof on a wider set of original premises?

I captured all 33 additional premise sets that a selective second search tried during a complete run of Apple `ord_live2`. Each contains the original goal and a subset of the original positive conjuncts. In-tree Z3 independently found **30 UNSAT and three SAT**. The live g3 experiment proved 18 with a 20,000-unit private search. Each UNSAT subset is sufficient to refute its full input. The three SAT subsets show why the checker must continue with the remaining premises after an inconclusive attempt. [Exact SMT-LIB inputs, batch and goal numbers, and oracle answers](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-selected-premise-replay.tar.xz)

| Fresh standalone configuration | Resource limit | Refutations in both solvers, of 30 | g3 billion instructions | Z3 billion instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Macro finder on, model-based instantiation off | 20,000 | 10 | 5.42 | 2.70 |
| Same settings | 50,000 | 26 | 6.66 | 3.02 |
| Same settings | 250,000 | 30 | 10.54 | 4.05 |
| Macro finder off, model-based instantiation on | 20,000 | 18 | 5.57 | 2.70 |
| Same settings | 50,000 | 27 | 6.84 | 3.02 |
| Same settings | 100,000 | 30 | 8.08 | 3.32 |

Each cost sums one CPU-pinned process per input and includes parsing and startup. Across **495 paired comparisons** (33 inputs, three solver configurations and five budgets), g3 and Z3 matched on answer, decisions, conflicts, quantifier instantiations and resource count. The live private solver translates into a reusable manager and charges that work to its own budget. Those differences matter even at the same nominal limit. With macro finding enabled and a 250,000-unit budget, g3 proved all 30 refutable selections in the live checker as well. [Standalone comparison driver](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/selected_premise_budget.py)

Completing more private proofs does not by itself establish a verification speedup. A separate pair of full `ord_live2` runs with per-goal counters found that all 18 goals newly refuted by the 20,000-unit selection had already avoided a subsequent check in the baseline. The largest measured saving came later. Batch 14, goal 110 used **117.65 → 28.38 billion** instructions inside the GoIvy check call, although that goal never attempted the wider selection. Across the spec, early proof attempts rose from 595.44 to 627.24 billion, while the subsequent check calls fell from 573.45 to 425.81 billion. Comparing earlier proof histories and varying the source arena's initial numbering can distinguish a reusable gain from sensitivity to search order. The wider selection remains experimental.

### Arena allocation generations and SAT watch relocation

The hard eight-hole pigeonhole formula lets us compare the cost of the same Boolean search. Both solvers take 31,417 decisions and encounter 25,200 conflicts on the original ordering. Two independent changes reduce the cost per search in g3. [Reproducible input and search-counter checks](perf/ivy_raft/watch_propagation.py)

| Change tested | g3 before, billion instructions | g3 after | In-tree Z3 | g3 before, seconds | g3 after | Z3, seconds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Store generation in the arena allocation descriptor | 36.32 | 34.56 | 8.05 | 4.121 | 4.069 | 1.395 |
| Append a relocated clause watch to its existing backing | 34.57 | 32.02 | 8.05 | 4.056 | 3.775 | 1.411 |

Instruction counts are medians of three rotating pinned runs per executable. Each elapsed-time cell is the median from a separate set of seven accepted rotations. Every process occupied its CPU for at least 95% of wall time while its hardware sibling was at least 95% idle. Each line has its own before measurement. The 3.775-second result is still 2.67 times Z3's elapsed time. [Arena measurements](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-arena-generation.tar.xz) · [SAT watch measurements](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-sat-watch-relocation.tar.xz)

**Arena borrowing.** The four-word allocation descriptor now holds the slot generation. A borrow verifies the generation against the descriptor that already locates the bytes. Freeing a block obtains its size class from the owning chunk. Ten million 32-byte borrows took 1.178 → 0.888 billion user instructions and 8.143 → 5.929 ns per operation. For 256-byte blocks the measurements were 1.182 → 0.892 billion and 9.190 → 7.066 ns per operation. All 28 runs reported zero allocations. Across eleven complete Ivy workloads, median instruction changes ranged from a 0.4% decrease to a 0.5% increase. [Implementation](arena/small_bytes.go) · [Stale-reference tests and benchmark](arena/small_bytes_word_test.go)

**SAT watch relocation.** While propagating a literal with tracing and extensions inactive, the solver can borrow the watch directory. For each moved clause it checks the destination owner, bounds, liveness and generation. A destination with spare capacity can accept the watch immediately. Growth still invalidates the old iterator backing. The four eight-hole input orderings used **7.4%, 7.4%, 3.9% and 7.4% fewer instructions**. All search counters matched the native solver on every ordering. Caching a location inside the watch instead raised the original search from 34.61 to 36.74–37.46 billion instructions in the prototype measurements. [Propagation](sat/sat_solver_propagation.go) · [Recycled destination regression](sat/sat_solver_propagation_test.go) · [Raw prototype comparisons](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-sat-watch-relocation.tar.xz)

The benefit depends on the workload. Fifteen more rotations of a three-literal SAT propagation chain gave 220.11 → 220.72 million instructions under ordinary GC and 165.82 → 167.02 million with GC disabled. Across five whole Ivy workloads the instruction change ranged from −0.2% to +0.6%. Both production changes reproduced the saved output, diagnostics and exit status for all 228 held-out Ivy cases, including 91 expected nonzero exits. Each generated SAT model was checked against every input clause. [Eight SAT inputs, controls and whole-verifier results](perf/ivy_raft/nov24-sat-watch-relocation.tar.xz)
