### Reusing a refuted conjunct across ARM verification goals

On the complete `test/arm_rules3.ivy` spec, g3 took **0.551 s** after the change, down from **0.669 s**. Linked Z3 took **0.366 s**. These are medians from seven rotating comparisons of the same frontend on one physical core. The new g3 took 17.6% less wall time and still took 1.51× as long as Z3. The five separate hardware-counter rotations below include startup, translation and all 115 printed verification passes. [Raw measurements, trace comparisons and reproduction instructions](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-refuted-conjuncts.tar.xz)

| Complete ARM rules spec | Previous g3 | g3 at `5ffad336a` | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Median wall time on a quiet core, seconds | 0.669 | 0.551 | 0.366 |
| Median retired user instructions, billions | 4.365 | 3.570 | 2.193 |

Five goals shared the same implication. Under identical premises, an earlier check had proved `P` impossible. A later goal required both `P` and `¬Q`, so it was already refuted. Three of these opportunities arose after the frontend had pushed the goal. They were 18–20 entries apart in a history of whole goals. Enlarging the exact-match history to 128 entries still missed them. Keeping eight previously refuted signed expressions separately captured the gain. Capacities one, two and four all missed it. A retained expression carries its manager, arena slot and generation. Changing any premise clears the history. [Observed formula shapes and history-size trials](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-refuted-conjuncts.tar.xz)

The solver examines at most 32 AST nodes in a lookup. The history record grew from 176 to 400 bytes on amd64 and is allocated on first use by an eligible solver. The focused benchmark measured 5.35 ns for an exact repeat, 95.1 ns for a negated implication containing a refuted conjunct and 45.8 ns for an independent goal. All three allocated zero bytes per lookup. A four-assignment Boolean truth table checks the direction of implication, and the public API test obtains a satisfiable result after changing the premises. [Tests and Go benchmark](api/api_order_recent_test.go)

All 228 compatibility cases matched the recorded exit status, stdout and stderr, including 91 expected failures. Trace-enabled builds matched on all 2,334,030,415 compared bytes for Apple `rfn2`. The normalized Paxos `log3` comparison matched all 27,855 lines. Independent timing on the preceding candidate measured 0.669 s → 0.556 s on ARM. In the three-rotation hardware panel, the changes on Ticket, ordinary Hermes, Raft, TLB and both Apple `rfn2` and `dramc_nb2` were each below 1% in either direction. The measured benefit so far is on ARM. [Validation and per-run results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-refuted-conjuncts.tar.xz)

### How much of the matched-search gap comes from individual AST and literal lookups?

Across 396 process runs, g3 and in-tree Z3 reproduced the same answers and reported integer search statistics for each of six Apple inputs. Three included every premise and ran to their six-million-resource limit. Three contained sufficient premise sets and finished UNSAT. The table gives the median billions of user instructions over three rotations within each experiment. Each column pairs its own baseline and prototype. [Standalone inputs, Go overlays, replay driver and raw counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-quantifier-hot-paths.tar.xz)

| Full query | Quantifier candidate operands and congruence lookup | Probe the canonical AST table before allocating a temporary node | Reuse literal information during internalization | In-tree Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 29.43 → 28.80 | 29.54 → 29.49 | 29.55 → 28.88 | 9.46 |
| 3 | 25.02 → 24.40 | 25.03 → 24.91 | 25.01 → 24.61 | 8.50 |
| 6 | 30.13 → 29.44 | 30.08 → 29.99 | 30.16 → 29.34 | 9.56 |

The first prototype retained a reference to the arena record holding each compiled operand's reference count, reused an equality declaration and used the existing congruence bucket directly. The stored reference costs eight bytes per compiled operand. The second prototype checked a short hash tag and consulted the full canonical table after a hint miss, before constructing a temporary application. Its saving was below 0.8% on every input. The third prototype combined stack storage for short argument lists, lookup of existing signed literals, direct watch registration, short-clause sorting and a fast path for existing expression records. Even its largest reduction was 2.7%. These experiments account for a small fraction of the 2.9–3.5× general-solver gap. They remain reproducible overlays. [Individual contributions and instructions for rerunning the comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-quantifier-hot-paths.tar.xz)

### Can Boolean guards eliminate the expensive enumeration searches?

On the nine-check history ending at Apple goal 110, folding seven Boolean literals already asserted by the premises let g3 finish the last proof within six million resource units. The entire history used **105.8 billion instructions**, down from **144.9 billion** with the original formulas and the twelve-million terminal allowance needed to finish. On the thirteen-check history ending at goal 132, the same transformation raised the cost of a completed proof from **56.7 to 73.8 billion**. These are single pinned process counts per input and budget. They exclude the offline cost of finding the guards. [Inputs, per-run counters and replay driver](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-enumeration-boolean-guards.tar.xz)

| Captured history | Original formulas | Fold directly asserted literals | Fold literals forced by the propositional premises |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, 58 checks | Exhausted at 12M | Exhausted at 12M | Exhausted at 12M |
| 2, 57 checks | Proved at 12M | Proved at 12M | Exhausted on check 44 |
| 3, 58 checks | Proved at 12M | Proved at 6M | Proved at 6M |
| 4, 36 checks | Proved at 12M | Proved at 12M | Exhausted at 12M |
| 5, 9 checks | Proved at 12M | Proved at 6M | Proved at 12M |
| 6, 13 checks | Proved at 12M | Proved at 12M | Proved at 12M |

The table shows the smaller successful terminal allowance of the two tested, 6M and 12M. Earlier checks always received 6M. The propositional experiment asked in-tree Z3 which nullary Boolean symbols must have a fixed truth value even when quantified formulas are relaxed. This can remove a guarded branch before quantifier search. In a fresh process on query 5, substituting the 32 values forced by the premises gave both engines UNSAT in **5,208,979 resource units**. Including the goal established 48 values, but both engines then exhausted the allowance. This difference in search order also appeared between fresh and incremental checks. [All 120 paired-engine observations and 36 incremental replays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-enumeration-boolean-guards.tar.xz)

I also split on one or two remaining guard symbols and divided six million resource units equally among the two or four subproblems. A refutation requires every branch to finish UNSAT. For query 5, three of four branches finished and one exhausted its budget. None of the six full inputs gained a complete refutation under any tested split. Each of the six deliberately weakened inputs retained a satisfiable branch under every split. I kept the transformed inputs and replay tools for evaluating search changes. The mixed incremental results favor the existing production policy. [Per-branch results for both shells](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-enumeration-boolean-guards.tar.xz)

### Do native finite datatypes or bit vectors make the hard enumeration proofs cheaper?

Giving each Apple enumeration its own SMT datatype reduced the cost of a fresh goal 110 from 29.32 to 21.20 billion g3 instructions. Both searches exhausted six million resource units. On the actual nine-check history leading to that goal, the datatype version exhausted the budget on the **first** sibling. ### Translating ASTs between independent solver arenas

Translating a 1,024-leaf Boolean tree now takes **1.48 ms and 71 Go allocations**, down from **3.91 ms and 12,515 allocations**. When four related trees share the translation cache, the median falls from **2.60 to 0.88 ms**. In-tree Z3 took **0.33 and 0.23 ms** in those two cases. Each figure is the median of eleven rotating measurements on the same logical CPU with 24 translations per process and case. Other workloads were active on the host. [All 198 measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ast-translation.csv)

The old Go translator built a full source-node map, a visited set, a postorder list and a separate map of translated handles. Z3 carries each translated child to its parent on a result stack. The Go implementation now uses that traversal with a second slice for source children. Application arguments, declaration domains and quantifier patterns come directly from the completed children's positions. Each manager keeps its own arena. At 1,024 leaves this reduced allocated bytes per translation from 2,867,085 to 167,276 with a reset before each tree, and from 1,858,904 to 111,956 with reuse. The regression tests translate a 1,536-level shared DAG with both cache lifetimes and retry after injected destination allocation failures. [Go implementation](ast/ast_translation.go) · [Regression tests](ast/ast_translation_shared_test.go) · [C++ traversal](../src/ast/ast_translation.cpp)

The translation speedup has a smaller effect on full verification. In three pinned rotations, ordinary Hermes used 30.70 → 30.64 billion instructions, hybrid broadcast 9.58 → 9.54 billion and Apple rfn2 11.79 → 11.79 billion. Those runs have identical proof outcomes. The Go and C++ benchmarks use the same four trees, creation order and cache-reset schedule. [Go benchmark](ast/ast_translation_siblings_benchmark_test.go) · [Native benchmark](../src/test/perf/ast_translation_siblings.cpp)

From the Go module directory, with this fork's release static library in the build directory, run the two benchmarks with the same CPU affinity.

```sh
taskset -c 17 go test ./ast -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkASTTranslationSiblings$' -benchtime=24x -cpu=1
g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -D_MP_INTERNAL -DNDEBUG -D_EXTERNAL_RELEASE -D_AMD64_ \
  -D_USE_THREAD_LOCAL -D_LINUX_ -msse2 -fopenmp -I../src \
  ../src/test/perf/ast_translation_siblings.cpp ../build/libz3.a -lpthread -lrt -o /tmp/z3-translation
taskset -c 17 /tmp/z3-translation 24
```

### Reusing quantified applications across sibling goals

Ordinary Hermes took **4.13 s** with the new ground-instance pool, down from **4.49 s**. These are medians of seven rotating whole-verifier runs on CPU 0. Every accepted process occupied the CPU at least 95% of the time with its sibling thread at least 95% idle. Separate five-run instruction medians fell from **30.65 to 27.46 billion**. The two g3 builds used GoIvy `832e392ef`. The archived linked Z3 control took 7.08 s and used an earlier frontend build. An independent three-round comparison that includes the AST translation change measured **30.64 → 27.13 billion** for the application change alone. [Timings, process counters and validation data](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-application-instances.tar.xz)

| Complete verification | Previous g3, billion instructions | With application matching | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Hermes RMW | 30.65 | 27.46 | −10.4% |
| Raft without assumptions, test specification | 22.02 | 21.26 | −3.5% |
| Test liveness 2 | 2.62 | 2.51 | −4.2% |
| Hybrid broadcast | 9.47 | 9.30 | −1.8% |
| TLB | 60.21 | 60.16 | −0.1% |
| Flash 2 | 6.68 | 6.76 | +1.2% |
| ARM rules 3 | 3.54 | 3.55 | +0.3% |

The pool instantiates a universal premise when a ground application supplies a correctly sorted term for every binder. An instance can introduce terms that match another premise. With recursion disabled, ordinary Hermes used 30.30 billion instructions in the ablation series. Allowing up to 8 new instances per goal used 28.42 billion, and allowing 32 used 27.48 billion. An instrumented build avoided 89 of 1,331 calls to the concrete solver on Hermes. Other goals finished earlier inside the private proof path. The complete original Apple, Apple 2, sys_live and longer Hermes testing runs changed by less than 0.3% in a separate two-round panel. [Instantiation](api/internal/order/ground_application_instances.go) · [Ablations and whole-run controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-application-instances.tar.xz)

Commit `ba98b3ada` enables this path for batches of at least 24 goals with 3–191 eligible universal premises. Each solver owns its pool. Only permanent ground facts and complete instances enter the shared clause list. Each sibling contributes a temporary assumption. Unit propagation can prove a contradiction, and an inconclusive result returns to the existing verification methods. The mixed-sort regression reverses binder order, changes the base, cancels a check and asks for opposite sibling goals. The complete 228-specification corpus matched the reference stdout, stderr and exit status, including 91 expected nonzero exits. The trace comparison matched 2,334,030,415 bytes on Apple rfn2 and all 27,855 normalized Paxos lines. [API tests and worker benchmark](api/api_ground_application_instances_test.go) · [Native oracle and corpus results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-application-instances.tar.xz)

The native oracle checked 8,640 goals under three successive premise lists. The private method proved 2,051, all of which native Z3 found UNSAT. The oracle included 3,855 SAT checks and no UNKNOWN results. Three unmodified Hermes batches added 123 native UNSAT controls. The private method alone proved 63/73, 9/25 and 21/25. With 32 independent solvers, each pool retained approximately 197, 407 and 185 KiB respectively above its loaded source solver. Closing the pools returned measured live heap to within tens of bytes per solver of baseline. To reproduce the lifetime measurement, run `go test -tags=xtrace_off ./api -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkGroundApplicationWorkerMemory$' -benchtime=1x -cpu=1`. The archive includes a standalone driver for rerunning both the native and Go oracles. [Fixtures, commands and raw heap readings](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-ground-application-instances.tar.xz)

### Does cheaper Boolean rewriting close the matched-search gap?

Boolean equivalence of two distinct atoms fell from **2,678 to 587 instructions per reduction** when a prototype classified both operands directly from their arena records. In-tree Z3 used **236**. On three complete Apple searches with identical decisions, conflicts, quantifier instances and resource charges across engines, the combined Boolean shortcut saved **0.2–0.4%** of the g3 process. This narrows the search for a larger gain to work that occurs more often in those queries. [Portable experiments, solver inputs and per-run counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-boolean-operand-search.tar.xz)

| Reduction in the core theory rewriter | g3 | g3 prototype | In-tree Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| NOT of an atom | 940 | 429 | 117 |
| Double negation | 837 | 615 | 128 |
| OR of two atoms | 1,507 | 604 | 325 |
| OR of a repeated atom | 1,616 | 767 | 306 |
| Equivalence of two atoms | 2,678 | 587 | 236 |
| Uninterpreted function control | 153 | 153 | 38 |

Each cell is the median slope in retired user instructions over five rotating pairs of 80,000 and 400,000 operations. An exact differential test covers 66,048 combinations of operands, operators and options. Its first run caught a shortcut that simplified `true = (not true)` to canonical false. The ordinary reducer returns the existing right operand at that stage. The corrected prototype preserved every result handle, rewrite status and local-context charge in the test. [Go benchmark](ast/rewriter/th_rewriter_benchmark_test.go) · [C++ benchmark](../src/test/perf/theory_reduction.cpp) · [Differential test and patches](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-boolean-operand-search.tar.xz)

Across three whole-verifier rotations, the combined shortcut took TLB from 60.22 to 59.79 billion instructions, hybrid broadcast from 9.40 to 9.32 billion, Hermes from 27.02 to 26.98 billion and ARM from 3.56 to 3.60 billion. All 135 verifier runs reproduced their reference output and exit. The table-driven shortcut remains an experiment. A separate change that uses already-compiled ground substitution plans under a sufficiently large resource allowance saved more on the same standalone Apple queries. Its three full-query medians were 29.56 → 29.01, 25.04 → 24.70 and 30.05 → 29.31 billion instructions. In-tree Z3 used 9.46, 8.50 and 9.56 billion. Every reported integer search statistic matched on all six inputs, including the three UNSAT premise subsets. ### Quantifier substitution under a finite search budget

A finite resource limit used to force every quantifier substitution through the ordinary AST traversal. The compiled substitution plan already knows how to reconstruct a ground instance, and charges exactly two polls per application. A plan contains at most 384 nodes. When 768 or more steps remain, it can finish within the limit. Near exhaustion g3 uses the ordinary traversal, preserving the point at which an interrupted substitution stops. Plans belong to one solver and continue to use its arena. [Implementation](ast/rewriter/ground_instance.go) · [Budget-boundary tests](ast/rewriter/ground_instance_test.go)

| Workload | Previous g3 | g3 with bounded plan reuse | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Quantifier stream, finite budget, instructions per instance | 28,967 | 19,229 | −33.6% |
| Same stream, unbounded, instructions per instance | 19,176 | 19,174 | <0.1% |
| Complete Apple ord_live, billion instructions | 726.79 | 725.30 | −0.2% |
| Complete Apple ord_live2, billion instructions | 1,045.75 | 1,024.85 | −2.0% |
| Apple ord_live2 sys_live isolate, billion instructions | 925.84 | 906.52 | −2.1% |

The stream results are medians of seven rotating instruction-count slopes. The verifier figures average two runs per build in reversed order. The complete ord_live2 saving was **20.90 billion instructions**. On all six saved solver histories, every sibling verdict and resource increment agreed between the two builds at terminal budgets of 6, 9 and 12 million steps, for **693 paired checks**. All 228 compatibility cases matched their reference output and exit, including 91 expected failures. The host ran concurrent work during the instruction measurements. [Go benchmarks](smtcore/smt_quantifier_substitution_benchmark_test.go) · [Every measured count, focused test and portable replay](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-bounded-ground-substitution.tar.xz)

### Internalizing a deep assertion in a solver with thousands of existing Boolean variables

For assertions deeper than 1,024 nodes, g3 built a map of **every live Boolean variable** before sorting the assertion's dependencies. Z3 consults its Boolean-variable index when the traversal reaches a term. g3 now uses its solver-local, generation-checked expression index the same way. The benchmark asserts a 1,025-application chain once, creates unrelated Boolean variables, then repeatedly pushes, asserts one more application of the same function and pops. Both solvers verify that the extension retires and the shared chain survives. [Go implementation](smtcore/smt_internalizer.go) · [Go benchmark](smtcore/smt_deep_assertion_benchmark_test.go) · [C++ benchmark](../src/test/perf/deep_shared_assertion.cpp)

| Unrelated live Booleans | Previous g3, instructions per scope | Indexed g3 | In-tree Z3 | Go allocation per scope, before → after |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,151,295 | 93,153 | 18,978 | 108,960 → 456 bytes |
| 1,024 | 2,123,894 | 93,865 | 18,993 | 218,176 → 456 bytes |
| 16,384 | 14,840,026 | 91,573 | 18,908 | 1,747,200 → 456 bytes |

At 16,384 unrelated variables the scope required **162× fewer instructions**. g3 still spent 4.8× as many instructions as Z3 on the operation. Medians use five rotating, two-size process measurements. The scope includes assertion, push and pop. A CPU profile of indexed g3 at the smallest size attributed 66% of samples to retiring relevance notifications on pop. Fourteen complete GoIvy invocations, including both Apple specifications, Hermes, Raft and TLB, recorded **zero assertions over the depth threshold**. This change addresses deep incremental SMT inputs. The separate Apple substitution result above measures an optimization exercised by the verifiers. [Raw counters, threshold coverage and reproducible comparison](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-deep-assertion-scaling.tar.xz)

### What remained on the deep-assertion solver thread

The scope-pop profile led to a second full-population scan. If base relevance notifications stayed pending, each sibling pop rechecked every surviving notification even when it retired only one new mark. g3 now keeps the surviving queue when it can account for every removal and knows the queued expressions are distinct. Marking an already-relevant member of an equality class forces the earlier notifications to be rechecked. A callback can drain the queue or reinstate a mark, and a failed reference release can interrupt a pop. These cases retain the full membership check when necessary. [Implementation](smtcore/smt_relevancy.go) · [Regression tests](smtcore/smt_relevancy_retirement_test.go)

| Unrelated Booleans | Indexed g3 before the queue change | g3 with both changes | In-tree Z3 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 95,035 | 21,590 | 18,978 |
| 1,024 | 94,773 | 21,115 | 18,994 |
| 16,384 | 92,835 | 17,502 | 18,909 |

Cells are median **solver-thread user instructions per push/assert/pop**, with 8,000 scopes per bracket and nine rotating measurements per engine. At 16,384 unrelated Booleans, g3 used 7.4% fewer instructions than native Z3 on the solver thread. At the two smaller populations it used 11–14% more. Process-level measurements independently put g3 at 18,541–20,553 instructions per scope. On a quiet core, g3 took **2.394 µs** and Z3 **1.552 µs** per scope with 16,384 unrelated Booleans. At zero unrelated Booleans the elapsed times were 2.544 and 1.549 µs. These are medians of seven rotating pairs of 400,000 operations. The 14 Ivy runs had no surviving notification prefix on this path. These figures describe the deep incremental SMT workload. [Go and C++ measurements, runnable comparison and coverage](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-relevance-notification-survivors.tar.xz)

An early prototype assumed that applications always marked an expression once. The randomized reference filter caught a stale pending notification at operation 649. With explicit duplicate detection, the final implementation matched the independent reference after **12,288,000 operations**. All 228 verification cases matched their expected exit, stdout and stderr. [Differential oracle, focused tests and corpus results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-relevance-notification-survivors.tar.xz)

### Can explicit model-table counterexamples rescue the expensive Apple searches?

The model checker can sometimes identify a concrete tuple at which a quantified premise fails in the candidate model. Installing that tuple as a quantifier instance changes the next search. On Apple history 1, installing a unique tuple only during the terminal check turned a twelve-million-step miss into a proof, at **100.69 billion instructions** for the 58-check history. On history 2 the same policy lost a previously successful proof. Collecting two tuples similarly rescued history 1 and lost history 6. The two packaged replays verify every recorded model-table counter along with the outcome. [Policies, 288 solver histories and reproduction driver](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-model-table-witnesses.tar.xz)

| Whole verifier, billion instructions | Previous g3 | First explicit tuple | Unique tuple | Check the evaluated body |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Apple ord_live2 | 1,046.8 | 1,122.6 | 1,258.3 | 1,277.7 |
| Its sys_live isolate | 926.4 | 889.2 | 1,078.3 | 1,092.7 |
| Apple ord_live | 727.4 | 736.4 | 727.0 | 729.5 |
| Issue 73 | 155.1 | 149.5 | 151.5 | 156.4 |

The first-tuple policy saved 37.2 billion instructions on sys_live and cost 75.8 billion on its complete spec. These are whole-process medians across two rotations on the long Apple runs and three on Issue 73. All 90 complete verification runs across seven workloads matched the reference exit and output. The measured policies remain experimental. A production policy would need evidence that the earlier witness saves enough later search under the same sequence of sibling goals. [Per-run counters and implementation patches](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-model-table-witnesses.tar.xz)

### Where the shorter Ivy proofs still spend more than Z3

On Ticket, g3 spent **2.102 billion solver-thread instructions** inside concrete checks versus **0.599 billion** for linked Z3. Its pushes cost 0.450 billion versus 0.144 billion. The early proof attempts cost g3 another 0.469 billion. On hybrid reliable broadcast, the corresponding check costs were 5.124 and 2.687 billion, with pushes at 1.721 and 0.545 billion. Both engines ran through the same GoIvy frontend at `832e392ef`. The figures are medians of three complete invocations per engine, summing each stage within a run. These four boundaries do not account for the whole process. In particular, native base assertions cost 0.236 billion on Ticket and 0.943 billion on hybrid, while g3 spent 0.017 and 0.059 billion there. [Per-call counts for 16 complete verifications](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-preprocessing.tar.xz)

The final query in several expensive batches reduces to true. Proving the permanent assumptions inconsistent is the actual work. For three Ticket queries, an independently verified native unsatisfiable core contained 50 of 112, 51 of 103, and 45 of 107 input rows. On a fresh g3 CLI, adding context simplification before SMT lowered the cost from **879 to 259**, **548 to 363**, and **482 to 205** million process instructions. Removing the permanent premises made all three queries satisfiable. Across 27 captured queries, two satisfiable liveness cases exhausted the four-million-step limit in context simplification on both engines. [Original inputs, cores, satisfiable controls, tactic commands and replay](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-preprocessing.tar.xz)

| Whole verifier, billion process instructions | Ordinary g3 | Separate context, bounded simplification | Same manager, bounded simplification |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

| ARM rules | 3.61 / 3.60 | 6.17 | 6.11 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 9.38 / 9.36 | 9.76 | 9.78 |

The two ordinary-g3 values are the independent controls for their respective trials. After the ordinary early proof failed on a final true condition, the experiment gave the tactic 250,000 steps. A successful proof finished the condition immediately. Other outcomes returned to the existing incremental solver. Reusing the original manager removed the need to translate the assertions but left a net regression on all three verifiers. Grouping all assertions into one conjunction on that manager brought Ticket to 3.93 billion. All **324 complete runs** across the two experiments matched the reference exit and diagnostic output. The shortcut stays out of the verifier. The results favor reducing the cost of the existing incremental check over adding a second speculative check for this class of goals. ### Repeated wide applications in quantifier pattern inference

When a conjunction mentions the same application many times, both original collectors can queue every occurrence before the first one finishes. Each queued copy then walks all the application's children again. A conjunction of width N that alternates two N-argument applications has only 3N argument edges, yet the repeated visits do work proportional to N². g3 now reuses the completed collector entry for an application of arity eight or greater at binder depth zero. Each occurrence takes and releases its original temporary reference. Debugging, tracing, and injected allocation failures follow the full original traversal. The cache belongs to a single collection call. [Collector](ast/pattern/collect.go) · [Go benchmark](ast/pattern/shared_applications_benchmark_test.go) · [In-tree C++ benchmark](../src/test/perf/pattern_shared_applications.cpp)

| Width | Previous g3 instructions | Current g3 instructions | Native Z3 instructions | Previous g3 / current g3 / Z3 time |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 544,008 | 172,429 | 85,370 | 49.70 / 17.24 / 5.96 µs |
| 128 | 25,881,559 | 1,079,808 | 3,084,473 | 2,164.59 / 96.93 / 212.35 µs |
| 512 | 407,323,866 | 4,127,664 | 45,647,198 | 33,516.59 / 370.36 / 3,162.27 µs |

At width 512 g3 used **98.7× fewer instructions** than before and completed inference **8.54× faster than Z3** on a quiet core. At width 16, Z3 still finished 2.89× faster. The benchmarks check that both engines infer the same two ordered patterns. Instruction counts are medians of seven long-minus-short slopes. Elapsed times are medians of seven rotating triples that met the CPU and sibling-idle criteria. At width 512 the Go benchmark fell from 4,494,068 to 234,548 bytes per inference. [Raw counts, quiet timings and runnable comparison](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-shared-application-patterns.tar.xz)

Seventeen complete Ivy verifications had **zero completed cache revisits** among 4,702 visits to applications at or above the arity threshold. The measured gain applies to heavily shared SMT inputs. The Ticket, Raft and Apple runs spent their time elsewhere. The collector matched its original traversal on candidate identity, order, binding sets and sizes in **10,000 generated DAG queries**. All 228 compatibility cases matched their expected output and exit. [Coverage by workload and arity, differential test and full results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-shared-application-patterns.tar.xz)

### Ground proofs for terminal Ticket, hybrid broadcast and ARM checks

All three terminal Ticket checks could be refuted by finite ground instances once a second pass could use witnesses produced by the first. For example, an existential witness that depends on a ticket can provide a thread term to another universal premise. Restricting both passes to constants missed the first two proofs. The experiment preserved the argument dependencies of existential witnesses and accepted only contradictions. Independent runs through g3 and the in-tree Z3 verified the resulting ground problems. Two satisfiable liveness controls stayed satisfiable. [Replay driver, inputs, transformed formulas and counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-instances.tar.xz)

| Captured check | Distinct ground assertions | Assertions in native core | g3 on all assertions, M instructions | g3 on core, M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ticket batch 6 | 5,139 | 68 | 1,663 | 65 |
| Ticket batch 7 | 5,046 | 72 | 1,630 | 66 |
| Ticket batch 8 | 5,064 | 68 | 1,612 | 61 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast batch 23 | 1,300 | 32 | 516 | 52 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast batch 35 | 1,394 | 39 | 558 | 57 |
| ARM batch 7 | 19,453 | 30 | 4,827 | 60 |

Each core was recovered from a separate native run with named assertions and then checked independently without names. In every row, removing the core produced SAT in both engines. Taking the same number of assertions from the beginning also produced SAT. Counts include startup, parsing, solving and teardown in a fresh CLI. They exclude construction of the candidate input and the search that selected the native core. The original quantified Ticket checks cost roughly 0.48–0.88 billion instructions, so enumerating the full ground sets already costs more than ordinary search. [Named cores, complements, equal-sized prefixes and primary results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-instances.tar.xz)

Selecting rows from a candidate model recovered smaller proofs without consulting a core. On Ticket batch 6, one policy asserted 537 of 5,139 rows, but took 22 checks and 55,216 formula evaluations. It spent 2.38 billion instructions against 1.75 billion for asserting everything through the same Go API. On ARM, the best of six policies took 3.67 billion against 4.72 billion for the eager ground checker. Both were substantially more expensive than the original 0.87-billion-instruction quantified check. Quantifier miniscoping also had mixed effects. It reduced Ticket batch 6 from 877 to 461 million instructions, but raised batch 7 from 523 to 1,227 million. These results favor choosing bindings while matching the original premises, before generating and parsing thousands of candidate formulas. None of these offline policies ships in the verifier. [Go model-guided checker, emitted subsets and all 27 quantified comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-instances.tar.xz)

| Liveness 2 | 0.368 | 0.361 | 0.263 | 2.501 → 2.429 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1.244 | 1.238 | 0.819 | 9.374 → 9.325 |
| Apple cf_live | 4.846 | 4.767 | 10.095 | 37.303 → 36.571 |

Times are medians of five rotating runs per engine and workload. Each accepted run matched exit status and both output streams, had at least 95% CPU occupancy, and ran with its SMT sibling at least 95% idle. Retired user instructions came from five separate pairs with the same frontend and one pinned logical CPU per workload. For the other five workloads in the instruction study, Ticket moved from 3.508 to 3.513 billion, Flash 2 from 6.856 to 6.836, Raft without assumptions from 21.254 to 21.059, rfn2 from 11.770 to 11.672, and TLB from 60.245 to 60.184. The 228-case output comparison included 91 expected verification failures. [Measurement driver](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/rotating_verification.py) · [All observations and corpus comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-observed-ground-splits.tar.xz)

Unit propagation can leave a three-literal clause with one false literal and two unassigned variables. The new search picks one of those variables, propagates each sign in turn, and accepts a refutation only if both signs conflict. Each choice inspects up to 128 trail positions and clause occurrences and the search goes at most four decisions deep. Both signs restore the solver's previous permanent assignments, including on exhaustion of the private resource allowance. The randomized test checks every claimed refutation against exhaustive Boolean models across 36,864 incremental queries. For all 51 captured successes, the in-tree native solver verified that the base alone was satisfiable, adding the signed goal was unsatisfiable, and adding its opposite was satisfiable. Two of those real captures run directly as allocation-reporting Go benchmarks. On alternating bit, a refutation takes 138 charged steps and zero allocations. Propagation alone spends 32 steps and leaves the goal open. On Hermes the corresponding counts are 262 and 10, also with zero allocations. [Tests](api/internal/order/ground_instance_split_test.go) · [Benchmarks](api/internal/order/ground_instance_split_benchmark_test.go)

The timing of a proof matters to later incremental checks. In the first prototype, splitting on every eligible residual refuted 93 of 251 residual calls in alternating bit and 105 of 599 in Hermes. The same policy made ARM slower. We tried all 32 subsets of its five successful early refutations, then measured five selections by solver phase. Enabling just batch 6 goal 2 increased the total measured solver-thread work by 1.24 billion instructions across the complete run. Enabling just goal 1 added 0.63 billion. The concrete checks the fast proof bypasses change later search. The released policy lets the first two proof attempts in each batch follow their established paths. This recovered the ARM regression while retaining the alternating-bit improvement. The residual instruction gap on Ticket and ARM warrants a separate experiment on terminal quantified checks. [Policy and batch warmup](api/api_order_abstraction.go) · [Subset and phase measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-observed-ground-splits.tar.xz)

## November 24 — where a faster standalone Ticket proof spends its savings

Three captured Ticket goals took **138, 127 and 130 million retired instructions** to refute in a standalone Go prototype. It starts with the original quantified SMT-LIB, uses g3's NNF transformation and arena, and instantiates universals with terms observed in the same predicate argument positions. A second pass can use witnesses produced by the first. It encodes the resulting ground problem directly as clauses for g3's SAT solver. On 480 generated satisfiable inputs with explicit finite models, both term-selection policies preserved all 480. On 160 inputs with independent quantified contradictions, the two policies found 292 of the 320 possible refutations. A satisfiable weakening leaves the original problem open. [Go prototypes, fixtures, control generator and all results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-boolean-encoding.tar.xz)

The same algorithm proved **all four terminal goals** inside the real Ticket verifier. Complete-process cost still moved from **3.512 to 3.520 billion instructions** over five rotations. Instrumenting three independent rotations showed where the time went. In the table, columns are median millions of retired instructions on the solver thread. The prototype runs after g3's existing early proof attempt, so each successful trial still incurs that earlier cost. The native column uses the same GoIvy frontend linked to this fork's Z3. [Per-operation counters and verifier integration patch](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-boolean-encoding.tar.xz)

| Ticket batch | Existing g3 early attempt | Existing g3 push | Existing g3 check | New ground attempt | Z3 push | Z3 check |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 6 | 80 | 52 | 38 | 138 | 18 | 11 |
| 7 | 76 | 65 | 100 | 115 | 19 | 37 |
| 8 | 72 | 56 | 41 | 123 | 19 | 12 |
| 9 | 82 | 67 | 17 | 122 | 20 | 6 |

Across those four attempts, installing the clauses in the SAT solver took **157 million instructions**, building ground instances took **123 million**, and SAT search took **84 million**. Normalizing the quantified input took 24 million, and copying it into the private context took 13 million. The experiment also separates text parsing from solver costs. Given precomputed ground instances of Ticket batch 6, constructing their shared DAG took roughly 29 million instructions. Eliminating text parsing alone still left the complete ground SMT run above one billion. A sparse Boolean encoding with direct congruence implications reduced that precomputed run to 209 million. Its input already contains the instances, so this last figure excludes the cost of choosing or generating them. [Independent DAG, clause-encoding and original-input benchmarks](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-boolean-encoding.tar.xz)

The complete verifier rejected this prototype as a general optimization. With the same configuration, ARM rose from 3.575 to 3.718 billion instructions and Hybrid from 9.312 to 9.635 billion. Alternating bit improved from 3.311 to 3.245 billion. A separate measurement inside the original early prover located **262 million instructions in four unsuccessful mixed ground/quantified searches on Ticket**. All four then paid for the ordinary incremental solver. Other workloads, including Apple rfn2, obtained real proofs from that same search. Measuring how much of the original problem the private search removes is a lower-cost next experiment than installing another solver behind it. [Fourteen complete verifier phase comparisons and individual early-search measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-boolean-encoding.tar.xz)

## November 24 — avoiding duplicated search on large premise sets

The alternating-bit verifier fell from **0.481 to 0.429 seconds** and Ticket from **0.510 to 0.476 seconds** when g3 sent nearly complete premise sets directly to its ordinary solver after an inconclusive ground check. The rule applies to constant-true goals, where the solver is trying to show that the premises themselves conflict. If at least 64 conjuncts qualify for the private search, g3 first checks their ground consequences. When that check is inconclusive and at least three quarters of the original conjuncts remain, it skips the second, mixed ground/quantified search. This uses the premise counts already available in each solver. [Production change](api/api_short_premises.go) · [Raw results and experimental policies](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-short-premise-reduction.tar.xz)

| Complete verifier | Previous g3, s | Current g3, s | Linked Z3, s | Previous → current g3, billion instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Alternating-bit protocol | 0.481 | 0.429 | 0.310 | 3.311 → 2.931 |
| Ticket protocol | 0.510 | 0.476 | 0.239 | 3.502 → 3.227 |
| ARM rules 3 | 0.509 | 0.504 | 0.342 | 3.541 → 3.507 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1.337 | 1.321 | 0.884 | 9.358 → 9.199 |
| Liveness 2 | 0.341 | 0.328 | 0.249 | 2.415 → 2.342 |
| Toy consensus | 0.406 | 0.405 | 0.407 | 2.803 → 2.818 |
| Apple rfn2 | 1.608 | 1.643 | 11.586 | 11.763 → 11.738 |
| Nested Ticket | 0.515 | 0.504 | 0.345 | — |

Times are medians of seven accepted runs per engine on a pinned CPU. Instruction counts are medians of five separate pairs. All 228 compatibility cases matched the reference exit status and both output streams, including 91 expected verification failures. In a broader trial that suppressed mixed searches on small sets too, toy consensus rose from 2.80 to 3.90 billion instructions. Several of its successful private checks use fewer than 40 conjuncts. On Apple rfn2, two successful mixed searches retained 122 of 244 conjuncts and 151 of 272. Both still qualify under the released rule. The complete isolate measured 11.763 → 11.738 billion instructions. Dramc_nb2 measured 123.771 → 123.842 billion. [Policy trials, full verifier counts and compatibility results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-short-premise-reduction.tar.xz)

The allocation-reporting Go benchmarks replay Ticket batch 6 and alternating-bit batch 10 with their original premises and signed goal. Each check still requires the concrete fallback. Including the private attempt, Ticket fell from **242 to 170 million instructions per operation** and alternating bit from **173 to 106 million**. The concrete-only controls took about 150 and 88 million respectively on both builds. These figures subtract the instruction count of a one-iteration process from a five-iteration process and divide by four, taking the median of five such pairs. Both g3 and this fork's native Z3 independently verified the two fixtures as UNSAT. ### How many Boolean decisions do the Ticket refutations need?

The three standalone Ticket residuals closed after **2, 3 and 12 branching decisions**. A bounded DPLL search watches two literals per clause, tries a variable occurring with both signs in short unresolved clauses, and reports a proof only when both branches lead to conflict. It can run directly on the clauses produced by the private projection. This reduced the complete standalone checks from **141 to 76**, **128 to 73** and **131 to 79 million instructions**, respectively. Only 6, 6 and 10 million of the new totals went into DPLL itself. The measurements include selecting and instantiating quantified premises from the original SMT-LIB. [Executable Go studies, source inputs, counters and differential controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-propagation.tar.xz)

For 12,000 independently generated small CNFs, exhaustive enumeration found 3,836 satisfiable and 8,164 unsatisfiable. All four search configurations agreed with exhaustive enumeration on every case. On quantified inputs with known interpretations, two encodings preserved all 960 satisfiable trials and refuted 272 of 320 contradictory trials. The remaining 48 went back to the caller. Directional gate encoding and eliminating pure literals can reduce the installed formula further. For Ticket batch 6 those two changes reduced unassigned clauses from 7,272 to 5,160. [Generators, controls and individual clause counts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-propagation.tar.xz)

In five complete GoIvy rotations, trying this refutation when the released premise rule declined a second mixed search took Ticket from **3.314 to 3.105 billion instructions**. Hermes went from 26.564 to 26.390 billion. However, alternating bit rose from 2.943 to 3.118 billion, Hybrid from 9.216 to 9.411, and nested Ticket from 3.507 to 3.633. These are comparisons with the release in `5f9a22b74`. The DPLL code stays in the benchmark archive. An improvement across workloads would have to reduce the cost of generating instances on inconclusive attempts. Faster SAT search alone has little room left on the three successful Ticket checks. [Verifier overlays and per-workload comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-terminal-ground-propagation.tar.xz)

### Scope restoration cost as the number of atoms grows

A queue-enabled search backtrack over four scoped atoms costs approximately 8,000 retired user instructions in both engines. At 128 atoms, g3 uses 12% more. At 2,048 atoms it uses 28% more. When the atoms survive the backtrack, both implementations largely avoid work proportional to the number of learned clauses. The widest surviving case took 2,343 instructions in g3 and 3,695 in Z3.

| Scoped atoms | Learned clauses | g3 instructions per pop | Z3 instructions per pop | g3 instructions restoring clauses | Z3 instructions restoring clauses |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 2 | 7,992 | 7,985 | 3,188 | 2,824 |
| 32 | 16 | 40,397 | 38,060 | 25,701 | 22,273 |
| 128 | 64 | 162,087 | 144,731 | 107,025 | 89,218 |
| 512 | 256 | 675,968 | 570,955 | 437,867 | 357,208 |
| 2,048 | 1,024 | 2,917,718 | 2,275,017 | 1,843,646 | 1,429,722 |
| 4,096 | 2,048 | 5,684,534 | 4,611,889 | 3,674,046 | 2,860,505 |

At 2,048 atoms, restoring clauses accounts for about 414,000 of the 643,000 extra instructions. Undoing the core trail costs another 153,000 extra and retiring relevance costs 67,000 extra. Each phase was measured on its own run. This makes restoring clauses the first place to profile at larger widths, particularly the cost of re-creating Boolean variables as the literals are rebound.

For each width, the g3 and in-tree Z3 fixtures preserve the same ternary learned clauses and validate every restored literal and clause identity. The table gives the median solver-thread instruction count per call minus the engine's median empty measurement. Five rounds rotated width and engine order on CPU 13. Eight warm-up pops preceded each measurement. Fixture setup, validation, and outer-scope cleanup were outside the counters. Reproduce with `python3 perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/widths.py --cpu 13 --output /tmp/new-scope-widths`. [Benchmark driver](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/widths.py) · [All 770 phase measurements](perf/scope_restoration/pop_phases/nov24-width-instructions.csv)

### Can matching known literals avoid most quantified instances?

On four captured Ivy goals, matching quantified predicate arguments against ground literals cut the instructions needed for an independent refutation by 3.7–5.6×. The positional strategy tries combinations of observed ground arguments. The alternative first selects ground predicates with the required declaration and sign, then unifies their arguments with the quantified pattern. Each accepted substitution produces an instance of the original universal. If the bounded search runs out of instances or decisions, the caller still has to solve the original query.

| Captured goal | Positional selection, millions of instructions | Literal matching, millions of instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hermes batch 7, goal 1 | 323.60 | 88.18 |
| Hybrid broadcast batch 32, goal 1 | 415.83 | 82.15 |
| Liveness 2 batch 12, goal 1 | 255.65 | 45.25 |
| Ticket batch 5, goal 1 | 213.27 | 49.27 |

Each cell is the lowest median of two complete processes among configurations that proved that goal. These figures describe attainable standalone costs with settings selected after measurement. The sweep covered 27 original captures, seven selection strategies and five parameter settings. Three other Ticket goals exposed a limit of matching known literals. The positional strategy proved them in 76, 73 and 77 million instructions. None of the signed strategies proved them within its budget. Four signed configurations also ran on 1,280 generated quantified formulas each. Every configuration left all 960 formulas with explicit models unrefuted and proved all 320 explicit contradictions. [Archived Go checker, original goals, generators and all measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-signed-ground-instances.tar.xz)

The complete incremental verifier already closes many of these goals cheaply. An observer measured literal matching on every nontrivial goal and then let the existing verifier make its original decision. The last column sums the existing early proof, push and check instructions on exactly those goals where the observer returned a proof. The figures are medians of three complete runs. They do not quantify any change in later incremental solver state that would result from skipping a successful check.

| Spec | Goals proved / attempted | Matching cost on successes, billions | Matching cost on misses, billions | Existing solver work on the successes, billions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hermes | 2,033 / 2,570 | 90.36 | 42.56 | 5.63 |
| Ticket | 166 / 280 | 6.21 | 9.74 | 0.47 |
| Hybrid broadcast | 434 / 837 | 17.02 | 29.14 | 1.25 |
| ARM rules 3 | 38 / 114 | 0.41 | 6.68 | 0.004 |

Four rotations of nine configurations on 14 complete verifier workloads produced 504 matching exit codes and transcripts. Trying the observed-literal strategy at a terminal goal raised Hybrid from 9.186 to 9.516 billion instructions, Ticket from 3.267 to 3.478 billion and ARM from 3.468 to 3.570 billion. The matcher stays in the study archive. The larger opportunity would be to share the cost of normalizing and indexing premises across sibling goals in a single solver. On Hermes, a fresh matcher spent 16× the existing work even on the goals it proved. Any shared implementation has to pay for both rebuilding at changed premises and discarding goal-dependent facts. [Verifier overlays, per-goal counters and reproducible smoke test](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-signed-ground-instances.tar.xz)

### Bounding the memory held by a returned quantifier fingerprint

A fingerprint records that a solver has already tried a quantifier with a particular tuple of enodes. Previously each returned record pointed to the previous record in its hash bucket. Keeping the newest result after resetting its set could keep the entire chain alive. The set now owns the collision links as integer positions. The returned result owns its binding arguments, with common widths allocated together with the record. Equality still compares the exact quantifier handle and every enode pointer.

| Heap measurement across 64 independent workers | Previous | Current |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 256 live tuples per worker, 1 or 2 bindings, bytes per tuple | 114 | 91 |
| 256 live tuples per worker, 5 or 6 bindings, bytes per tuple | 162 | 123 |
| 256 live tuples per worker, 8 bindings, bytes per tuple | 178 | 139 |
| After reset, one result from a 256-entry collision chain, bytes per worker | 24,576 | 64 |
| After scope pop, reusable table and one 2-binding result, bytes per worker | 4,728 | 6,984 |

The medians cover five reversed-order pairs of fresh processes and a full garbage collection at each lifetime boundary. The collision row deliberately gives 256 distinct enodes the same owner. It demonstrates a worst-case lifetime dependency. An empty table kept for reuse after pop costs 2,256 additional bytes per worker in the two-binding case because its insertion-order entries also hold the links. Reset releases that storage. [Go benchmark](smtcore/smt_fingerprint_tuple_memory_benchmark_test.go) · [Worker measurements and alternative table layouts](perf/ivy_apple/fingerprints/nov24-fingerprint-records.tar.xz)

The complete Apple ord_live2 verification inserted 16,156,819 tuples, including 11,965,402 with two bindings. Its busiest table held 38,576 live tuples, of which 31,495 had two bindings. Ordinary Hermes inserted 104,056 five-binding tuples. Across five complete Hermes runs, cumulative process allocation fell from 1,443.06 to 1,435.28 MB and the allocation count fell by 104,156. TLB allocation fell from 2,990.97 to 2,981.28 MB. rfn2, which inserted only 720 tuples, measured 889.12 and 889.21 MB. [Per-set census and complete verifier counters](perf/ivy_apple/fingerprints/nov24-fingerprint-records.tar.xz)

All 228 compatibility cases matched the reference status and both output streams. The six standalone Apple queries also preserved their reported search statistics. In three full, budget-limited queries, g3 measured 29.03, 24.73 and 29.38 billion instructions with the new layout, compared with 29.12, 24.74 and 29.44 billion previously. In-tree Z3 used 9.46, 8.50 and 9.56 billion. Fingerprint storage accounts for little of that threefold instruction difference. [Exact tuple, scope, collision and ownership tests](smtcore/fingerprints_test.go) · [Three-way solver comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/fingerprints/nov24-fingerprint-records.tar.xz)

Restoring a scoped Boolean variable inserts it back into the case-split activity heap. At 2,048 variables this insertion path used **206,916 more instructions per pop in g3** than in in-tree Z3. That accounts for 50% of the independently measured 413,924-instruction gap in restoring all learned clauses, or 32% of the 642,701-instruction gap in the complete scope pop. At 4,096 variables the insertion difference was 415,240 instructions, again about half the clause-restoration gap. ### How overflow pages affect memory after most clauses are retired

With 4,096 scoped variables, grouping short overflow clauses in pages of sixteen reduced allocations per complete round from **8,100 to 2,640** and allocated bytes from **552,386 to 435,732**. The median complete pop nevertheless rose from **5.64 to 5.85 million solver-thread instructions** across seven rotations. More importantly for independent workers, the benefit depended on which clauses survived. [Storage alternatives, allocation counts and hardware measurements](perf/scope_restoration/saved_clause_atoms/nov24-overflow-lifetimes.tar.xz)

| Layout | All live, bytes per clause | 64 adjacent survivors, bytes per worker | 64 spaced survivors, bytes per worker | Idle pool, bytes per worker |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Current independent overflow buffers | 236.3 | 17,760 | 17,856 | 2,400 |
| One allocation per short overflow buffer | 236.3 | 17,760 | 17,376 | 2,400 |
| Additional 4-clause pages | 197.0 | 15,072 | 25,280 | 2,624 |
| Additional 16-clause pages | 181.5 | 14,016 | 47,616 | 3,008 |
| Replace final resident page with a 16-clause page | 181.5 | 13,424 | 47,616 | 2,416 |
| Single word per saved slot/generation and trailing sign bits | 221.5 | 16,896 | 16,576 | 2,560 |

The fixture holds 1,024 three-literal clauses in each of 32 independent workers. It retains the last 64 clauses or every sixteenth clause, then collects the heap before and after retiring those survivors. A single survivor keeps its entire overflow page reachable. This accounts for the **2.67×** sparse-retention cost of the 16-slot layout. Packing the slot and generation into one word improved both survivor arrangements, but changed complete-pop instructions from 5.17 to 5.25 million at width 4,096 in its own seven-round comparison. [Go benchmark](smtcore/smt_clause_atom_memory_benchmark_test.go) · [Per-worker results](perf/scope_restoration/saved_clause_atoms/nov24-overflow-lifetimes.tar.xz)

The real verifiers rarely needed short overflow storage. Across all nine instrumented workloads, only the complete Apple `ord_live2` used it, with **25 short overflow allocations, 2,718 resident short allocations and 1,901 longer allocations**. Complete Apple `ord_live` made 1,164 resident short allocations and 561 longer ones. Ordinary Hermes made 188 and six. The page alternatives therefore stay in the benchmark archive. For the wide-scope fixture, the lower-risk follow-up is to reduce work per restored variable and per saved reference. [Per-workload allocation histograms and replay](perf/scope_restoration/saved_clause_atoms/nov24-overflow-lifetimes.tar.xz)


### Sharing ground proofs across successive verification conditions

A fresh matcher on ordinary Hermes spent **59.41 billion solver-thread instructions constructing ground instances**, 14.51 billion normalizing premises, 12.54 billion translating ASTs, and 8.76 billion creating contexts. Reusing the normalized premises, compiled clauses and watch lists within each solver brought the total cost of trying a proof on all eligible Hermes goals to **2.085 billion instructions** with goal-directed instantiation. Reading conjuncts directly from the source AST lowered that to **0.605 billion**, with somewhat different proof coverage. Each query discarded its temporary assumptions. [Fresh construction costs and shared-proof implementations](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-shared-ground-matching.tar.xz)

### Polynomial cancellation and bound recognition on the same search

On Toy Consensus query 18, g3 spent **63.93 million instructions** cancelling monomials per extra incremental check. Z3 spent **7.46 million** on the same 10,174 calls. The check repeated one verification condition in an existing solver. Both engines produced the same verdict and the same decisions, conflicts, equalities, quantifier instantiations and resource count through repetition 32. Five alternating pairs measured four and 32 repetitions. Each entry is the median paired difference divided by 28. [Raw solver-thread counters, source instrumentation and replay](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-arithmetic-comparison-stages.tar.xz)

| Operation | Toy calls per check, both engines | Toy g3 / Z3, million instructions | Numeric 012725 g3 / Z3, million instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Rewrite an inequality | 7,153 | 144.35 / 19.92 | 2.563 / 0.353 |
| Cancel monomials from two sides | 10,174 | 63.93 / 7.46 | 1.187 / 0.141 |
| Recognize a bound | 19,508 | 38.72 / 4.78 | 1.558 / 0.182 |
| Compute the coefficient GCD | 8,465 | 16.01 / 1.44 | 0.901 / 0.075 |
| Recognize a negative polynomial | 8,465 | 20.02 / 3.23 | 0.306 / 0.018 |

The cancellation and coefficient routines also run for arithmetic equalities. The rows have overlapping callers and cannot be added to obtain total inequality cost. Cancellation took about 6,284 instructions per call in g3 and 734 in Z3 on Toy. The C++ routine borrows the children of a sum and marks products by AST identity. The Go routine materializes the children, uses maps for common products, and revisits terms to obtain coefficients. For Ticket query 127 all five stages had zero incremental calls. Optimizing them can help Toy without addressing Ticket's replay gap. [Native cancellation](../src/ast/rewriter/poly_rewriter_def.h) · [Go cancellation](ast/rewriter/arith_polynomial.go) · [Measurements on four inputs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-arithmetic-comparison-stages.tar.xz)

Seven g3 prototypes tested cheaper operator reads and early recognition of already normalized integer bounds. All produced the original g3 output on 7,408 simplifications under four parameter configurations. The combined shortcut reduced **whole-shell** instructions per extra Toy check from **1,666.05 to 1,641.35 million**. Linked to GoIvy, it took 11.76 versus 11.70 billion instructions on the complete Apple rfn2 isolate, 26.42 versus 26.67 billion on ordinary Hermes, and 3.28 versus 3.24 billion on Ticket. Across 120 complete verifier runs, exit status and diagnostics matched. These shortcuts remain experimental. Monomial cancellation is a better target for reducing the cost of the calls that still execute. [Prototype patches, simplification corpus, search counters and complete verifiers](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov24-arithmetic-comparison-stages.tar.xz)

### How much memory an idle solver kept after popping equality-graph nodes

With 2,048 distinct binary applications and 128 survivors, an idle g3 solver kept **741,123 additional heap bytes** after popping the temporary scope. Clearing each successfully retired node's slot in the internalizer stack reduced that to **188,163 bytes**. The old stack had the correct length and the congruence table returned the correct answers. Go's collector could still reach the retired nodes through the stack's backing array. The difference is exactly **288 bytes for each of the 1,920 retired nodes**. The fix preserves stack capacity and keeps the slot available to retry if unregistering the node fails. [Production change](smtcore/smt_internalizer_state.go) · [Regression test](smtcore/smt_equality_undo_test.go)

| Applications at peak / surviving after pop | Old idle bytes per solver | Clear popped node slots | Old idle bytes with label changes¹ | Clear popped label records¹ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 / 2 | 11,775 | 3,135 | 14,079 | 5,439 |
| 256 / 16 | 96,825 | 27,705 | 115,257 | 46,137 |
| 2,048 / 128 | 741,123 | 188,163 | 872,195 | 319,235 |

¹ The label experiment already includes the node-stack fix in both columns. E-matching can record a node's label hash and the labels on its class root so that a pop can restore both. Those records held a second pointer to the same deleted node. Clearing the restored suffix releases it. The two savings describe different workloads and should be counted once per retired node. Seven rotating fresh-process measurements used eight independent solver states, rooted input terms and a collection before measurement, at peak occupancy and after pop. Peak memory for the 2,048 case was 771,843 bytes per solver without label changes and 902,915 with them. Neither fix changed peak memory or allocations during that benchmark. [Go worker benchmarks](smtcore/smt_cg_scope_memory_benchmark_test.go) · [Label trail](smtcore/smt_enode_trail.go) · [All samples](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-congruence-scope-memory.tar.xz)

Real verification workloads varied substantially. On ordinary Hermes, 1,112 of 2,159 post-pop snapshots at or below the base level found a deleted node reachable through an old label record. The maximum was five unique nodes in one snapshot. Hybrid had 617 affected snapshots out of 1,552, with at most three nodes. ARM, TLB and rfn2 had none at those boundaries. The worker fixture deliberately exercises far more labelled retirements. Across six complete verifiers, the median instruction change for clearing the node stack ranged from about −0.3% to +0.7%. The independent label-trail comparison ranged from about −1.0% to +0.4%. The measured benefit is in idle heap size. [Per-solver census and complete verifier counters](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-congruence-scope-memory.tar.xz)

Small-table alternatives had a different tradeoff. Separating the probe index into 32-bit slots reduced a table holding 2,048 signatures from 98,304 to 73,728 live bytes. Rebuilding that table as it emptied reduced its one-in-sixteen survivor footprint to 17,664 bytes. In the full unlabelled fixture, trimming the existing table during node retirement reduced idle memory from 188,163 to 96,387 bytes after the stack fix, but required additional allocations to rebuild it. The production changes clear retired references. Table shrinking remains an experiment for solvers that stay sparse after a large scope. Across all five comparison matrices, 684 complete verifier runs matched reference exit status and both output streams, and 630 bounded Apple replays matched verdicts and search counters. [Alternative layouts, heap measurements and portable replay](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-congruence-scope-memory.tar.xz)

### Creating and deleting equality-graph nodes

A binary application now takes **195.1 ns** to create and delete in g3, down from **232.2 ns**. The matching operation takes **30.38 ns** in this fork of Z3. All three retain the same arguments, add the new node to each child's parent list, remove it, and verify the final parent counts. Seven rotating triples used the same physical core within each triple, 1.8 million iterations per process, at least 95% idle on the sibling hardware thread, and at least 95% process occupancy. [Go benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_creation_benchmark_test.go) · [C++ benchmark](../src/test/perf/enode_creation.cpp) · [Raw timings, rejected attempts and reproduction](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-construction.tar.xz)

| Children | Previous g3, ns/op | Current g3, ns/op | Native Z3, ns/op | Instructions/op, previous g3 / current g3 / Z3 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 161.5 | 125.1 | 27.28 | 1,751 / 1,385 / 235 |
| 2 | 232.2 | 195.1 | 30.38 | 2,573 / 2,198 / 303 |
| 4 | 271.9 | 233.1 | 33.93 | 3,180 / 2,787 / 353 |
| 16 | 732.6 | 598.7 | 67.45 | 8,809 / 8,386 / 677 |

The Go constructor now reads the application header once for its kind, declaration, family, operation and arity. Placing the justification's two one-byte fields together reduced the equality justification from 32 to 24 bytes. Reordering the node fields reduced the header from 264 to 240 bytes, crossing from Go's 288-byte to its 240-byte allocation class. Z3 uses a 120-byte header, an eight-byte equality justification and trailing child pointers backed by its region. The binary Go fixture allocates **256 bytes in two allocations** per operation. Native requests 136 bytes from its region. In the eight-solver benchmark with 2,048 applications and 128 permanent survivors, the peak increase above the loaded base fell from **771,843 to 679,683 bytes per solver**. [Node representation and constructor](smtcore/smt_enode_core.go) · [Scope memory benchmark](smtcore/smt_cg_scope_memory_benchmark_test.go) · [Seven layouts and all measurements](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-construction.tar.xz)

The instruction counts subtract a 24,000-iteration process from a 300,000-iteration process and divide by 276,000. They include Go allocation and collection. Three independent profiles at a 3,000,017-instruction sampling interval recorded no kernel throttling or lost events. On the binary fixture, the Go runtime accounted for **50% of leaf samples** after the change. With sixteen children it accounted for 31%. Deleting the node accounted for another 15% at that width and looking up the arena byte descriptor for 9%. Allocating short child arrays and nodes together saved one allocation at arities one through four, but raised the binary instruction count from 2,198 to 2,380. This makes solver-local node allocation and avoiding repeated descriptor lookup stronger follow-ups than coupling each short array to its parent object. Any chunk allocation also has to account for the memory held by an externally retained node after a scope pop. [Profiles, allocator variants and build overlays](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-construction.tar.xz)

Across the six complete verifiers, the production layout and header changes moved median whole-process instructions by **−0.47% to +0.11%**. Ticket measured 3.214 → 3.199 billion, rfn2 11.781 → 11.742 billion, and TLB 60.076 → 60.144 billion. All 210 runs across the seven Go configurations matched their reference transcript and exit. All 144 standalone Apple runs across Go and Z3 agreed on verdict and the four recorded search counters for each input. The production build also matched the reference exit and both output streams on all 228 compatibility cases. Node creation remains a sizeable isolated gap. Its share of these complete verifications limits the speedup from this change. [Verifier, standalone solver and compatibility results](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-construction.tar.xz)

### Where the extra bytes go in the equality graph

Commit `d30f79e40` reduces the amd64 g3 enode from **240 to 208 bytes**. Its stored equality reason now matches Z3 at eight bytes. Five paired rotations measured 11.778 → 11.696 billion instructions for rfn2, 60.057 → 60.000 billion for TLB, and 26.481 → 26.497 billion for ordinary Hermes. Across all six complete specifications the change ranged from −0.7% to +0.4%. The reproducible benefit is lower live memory. [Go layout](smtcore/smt_enode_core.go) · [Native layout](../src/smt/smt_enode.h) · [Compiled field offsets and raw measurements](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

| Bytes in one enode header on amd64 | Previous g3 | Current g3 | In-tree Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| AST owner, declaration and cached operation data | 48 | 48 | 8 |
| Child array descriptor | 24 | 24 | 0 |
| Parent vector descriptor | 24 | 24 | 8 |
| Disequality index on the node | 24 | 8 | 0 |
| Equality reason on a proof edge | 24 | 8 | 8 |
| Remaining fields, edge target and padding | 96 | 96 | 96 |
| **Header total** | **240** | **208** | **120** |

Z3's application pointer leads to its declaration. Go stores the manager pointer, two 16-byte arena handles, the family and the operation kind. Each handle contains an owner identity, slot and generation. Z3 stores the child pointers immediately after the header. Both engines pay for the child pointers. The 24 bytes in the Go row are the slice's pointer, length and capacity. Z3 places its parent vector's metadata in the allocated backing block. These differences account for the remaining 88 bytes including the eight-byte pointer to g3's optional disequality index. [Go AST handle](ast/ast_core_storage.go) · [In-tree native enode](../src/smt/smt_enode.h) · [Release compiler layouts](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

The public equality justification remains a 24-byte comparable value. Storing a transitivity edge packs its reason into one garbage-collected pointer. Axiom and congruence use stable tokens, equations reuse the solver's literal cells, and object reasons keep the typed proof object alive. Reversing the proof tree carries that word unchanged. The new tests force collections after the creating frame returns, reverse the path twice, and look up positive, negative, detached and typed-nil reasons. The release passed ordinary, checked, debug/trace and pointer-checked focused runs. All 228 compatibility cases matched their reference exits, stdout and stderr. [Reason encoding](smtcore/smt_justification_refs.go) · [Proof-edge regression](smtcore/smt_conflict_antecedents_test.go)

| Incremental live bytes per solver, 512 binary applications | Previous | Current | Bytes saved |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No optional fields populated | 191,111 | 174,727 | 16,384 |
| Sparse mix | 192,097 | 176,985 | 15,112 |
| Every pair equal with a literal reason | 212,091 | 197,771 | 14,320 |
| Every pair disequal | 212,859 | 208,763 | 4,096 |
| Every node has a theory variable | 191,099 | 174,715 | 16,384 |
| Even mix of equal, disequal and theory-bound pairs | 209,771 | 199,531 | 10,240 |

Each observation held eight independent solvers live, forced garbage collection and subtracted the permanent fixture. The table gives medians across nine new processes per engine and population. Separate calibrated scope runs gave 7,867 → 7,686 instructions per temporary application at width 2,048. Z3 used 917. Shrinking the node recovers little of that execution gap. [Field population benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_field_memory_benchmark_test.go) · [Go scoped batch](smtcore/smt_enode_scope_batch_benchmark_test.go) · [Matched native batch](../src/test/perf/enode_scope_batch.cpp) · [Raw rotations](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

An instrumented solver counted live fields before scope pops and during search. On complete Apple `ord_live2`, the largest sampled graph had **22,785 nodes, 200 distinct declarations, 18,847 nodes with no parents, 6,184 proof edges and 47 nodes with a disequality list**. Ordinary Apple had 139 populated disequality lists among 11,206 nodes. The largest rfn2 graph had 2,352 nodes, 217 declarations and no populated disequality lists. These snapshots explain why moving the disequality header out of every node pays off and make shared declaration metadata worth testing. The archive gives the sampling points and growth thresholds. [Field census from nine complete verification workloads and six standalone replays](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

Parent vectors need a different treatment. Giving each node a nullable pointer to a slice header reduced the mixed field fixture from 199,531 to 192,107 bytes per solver, yet increased a chain's live memory from 182,395 to 198,779 bytes. Giving a small parent vector a single typed backing allocation held chain memory level, reduced the fork fixture by 2,040 bytes, and raised scoped work from 7,650 to 7,928 instructions per temporary node. Moving theory variables out of line reduced the logical node from 208 to 200 bytes. Both sizes use the same Go allocator class, and the all-theory fixture paid 8,192 extra bytes per solver. The shipped layout keeps the parent slice and the first theory variable in the node. [Parent-shape benchmark](smtcore/smt_parent_shape_benchmark_test.go) · [Five parent layouts and six optional-field layouts](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

Other records have different costs. Go and native Z3 both use 4 bytes per literal, 16 per Boolean variable including its 8-byte reason, and 16 for the first theory-variable list cell. The g3 watch-list header occupies 40 bytes versus 8, the fingerprint 48 versus 24, and the SMT clause header **120 versus 8**. Z3 adds literals, activity, atom pointers, proof and deletion callback fields according to the clause's contents. At the largest sampled clause population in Apple `ord_live2`, 26,914 of 54,968 concrete clauses had a justification and none had a deletion callback. This calls for tests with both empty and populated proof fields and measurements of whole live clauses. [g3 clause header](smtcore/smt_clause.go) · [Native clause sizing](../src/smt/smt_clause.h) · [Matched compiled sizes and field census](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-enode-fields.tar.xz)

### Enode deletion preserves parent and declaration order on scope-pop retries

Three reproducible failures occurred during the memory-layout work. A direct enode deletion panicked on an already retired child. A refused scope pop removed earlier parent occurrences before detecting a missing occurrence, preventing retry. A public borrowed enode registered after an owned application of the same declaration also prevented that application’s scope from popping. Commits `c8bdbb2f4` and `1911b04a8` cover all three paths. An earlier construction fix in `7fc72b85b` validates every child lookup before publishing any parent link. [Deletion and retry tests](smtcore/smt_enode_deletion_retry_test.go) · [Borrowed-registration regression](smtcore/smt_borrowed_declaration_test.go)

On a healthy graph, deleting the tail occurrence needs no extra storage. If an occurrence lies in the middle, g3 records its original position. A later refusal restores the previous positions, including duplicates. The declaration index also retains the order of surviving borrowed nodes. Ordinary solver-owned nodes still retire from the tail. [Deletion implementation](smtcore/smt_enode_aux.go) · [Scope pop](smtcore/smt_internalizer_state.go)

### Building declaration indexes when a solver first reads them

Commit `eab0ce237` removes two eager per-declaration indexes from solvers that never query them. The checker and model finder can request every registered enode for a function. The matching interpreter needs only applications with arguments that are eligible for matching. The first reader builds its index from the existing registration order. Subsequent insertions and scope pops maintain each index that has a reader. A checker that borrows nodes or changes internalizers preserves the order across owners. The in-tree C++ matcher indexes a vector by declaration ID. Its entry contains only matching applications. [Go checker](smtcore/smt_checker.go) · [C++ context](../src/smt/smt_context.h)

### Shrinking the concrete clause header from 120 to 64 bytes

Every g3 clause used to carry two Go interfaces for its justification and deletion handler, two pointers for saved atoms and several words of lemma bookkeeping. Ordinary auxiliary clauses use none of them. Commit `5ea5bf703` gives the clause an optional attachment for the two interfaces and an optional block for the lemma and atom state. Small learned clauses share one allocation with their activity block and literals. The C++ allocator places the used data directly after an eight-byte header and allocates optional words only when the clause requires them. ### Where the complete Ticket and hybrid verifiers spend their instructions

Across nine complete Ticket runs, g3 produced 9,667 instruction samples and linked Z3 produced 4,387. The g3 quantifier propagation stack contained 4,321 samples. Of those, 3,841 passed through the instantiation queue. Across the whole process, 2,486 samples passed through instance materialization and internalization and 2,474 through the general rewriter. These last two counts overlap because materialization calls the rewriter. Both engines used the same GoIvy frontend at `832e392ef`. ### An eight-byte directory entry for each auxiliary and learned clause

Z3 keeps one clause pointer in each of its two directories. g3 used to copy an 80-byte record containing a pointer, a literal slice header, proof and owner information, and scope-cleanup state into each directory. Commit `b836f6052` stores one typed Go pointer per entry. The 64-byte clause header records the original width of a short clause and the progress of watch removal. Clauses that actually need a proof, owner or separately allocated literal array retain that information until the entry retires. This preserves the registered literals when a caller shortens a clause, the public snapshot during an interrupted pop, and the ability to resume cleanup. [Directory operations](smtcore/smt_concrete_clause_record.go) · [Scope and public-view tests](smtcore/smt_closed_clause_widths_test.go)

A Raft replay reached the same state in both engines with **7,559 concrete clauses and 5,740 enodes**. The old Go directories occupied **708,560 bytes**, the new ones **66,680**, and the two Z3 vectors **65,488**. Capacity growth explains the remaining differences between equal-width entries. Five Go observations per layout matched the phase, both watch counts, auxiliary and learned counts, proof and saved-atom counts, and watch-directory length at the selected native position. The whole Go process used 22.91 → 22.26 MiB after forced collection at that point.
