### Reusing registered children during ordinary term internalization

A new binary term can reach the equality graph with both operands already registered. g3 used to internalize each operand again, look up its enode in the constructor and reread the parent's kind and declaration. Commit `c059bebf5` carries the header and resolved children through this path. An operand qualifies when its enode is live, non-Boolean and its declaration family has no active theory. A theory can change the solver during a callback. In that case the internalizer resolves the children again and checks the active sort theory separately for each callback. The tests exercise a theory replacing itself and a registered child that still needs its theory variable. [Internalizer](smtcore/smt_internalizer.go) · [Callback regressions](smtcore/smt_term_sort_callbacks_test.go)

| Applications per scope | Previous g3 instructions per new enode | With resolved operands | In-tree Z3 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 | 5,654 | 4,418 | 979 |
| 256 | 5,911 | 4,577 | 907 |
| 2,048 | 6,493 | 5,165 | 917 |

The fixture pushes a scope, internalizes the applications and pops. One in sixteen already belongs to the outer scope. Each cell is a median of seven paired high-minus-low process instruction counts divided by the difference in newly created enodes. At width 2,048 the change saves 20.5% and leaves a **5.63×** gap to Z3. The public enode constructor by itself measured 1,054 → 1,077 instructions for a constant, 1,604 → 1,617 for a binary application and 3,381 → 3,379 for eight operands. The saving comes from the work that the internalizer can avoid upstream. [Go scope benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_scope_batch_benchmark_test.go) · [C++ scope benchmark](../src/test/perf/enode_scope_batch.cpp) · [Public constructor benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_creation_benchmark_test.go)

The change moved whole-verifier instructions between −0.20% on Hermes and +0.97% on ARM across four rotations of six specs. Each of the 228 corpus outcomes matched. Six standalone SMT cases also retained the same answers, decisions, conflicts, quantifier instantiations and resource counts as Z3. These results establish a scoped-term improvement and give no evidence of a comparable speedup on a complete verification. [Release measurements, inputs and replay](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-ordinary-term-inputs.tar.xz)

A separate experiment put immutable declaration metadata behind one shared pointer. With 512 applications of a single declaration the live solver heap fell from 171,269 to 163,101 bytes. With 512 distinct declarations it **increased** from 402,457 to 406,553 bytes. The 2,048-application scope took 5,284 instructions per enode against 5,085 for its contemporary control. A bounded per-solver declaration cache took 5,243. Both representations remain experimental. A retained pointer costs memory for each distinct declaration and adds a load when the constructor needs its metadata. [Declaration population fixture](smtcore/smt_declaration_population_benchmark_test.go) · [Source variants and raw counts](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-ordinary-term-inputs.tar.xz)

### Validating a public expression and locating the scope-construction gap

Two public entry points could index a different manager’s arena or read a retired slot. Commit `4052fd136` checks the owner, bounds, liveness and generation before reading an expression for `Internalize` or `NewSMTEnode`. For a cached application, the same slot supplies both the node header and the Boolean sort predicate. Repeatedly internalizing a previously bound gate took **309 → 283 instructions**, an equality-graph term **313 → 287**, and a negated gate **625 → 574**. Constructing a public binary enode took **1,619 → 1,590** instructions. A version that factored all header and sort paths through separate helpers took 363 instructions for the gate. The shipping build passed all 228 compatibility cases. Whole-verifier instruction changes across six specs ranged from −0.50% to +0.33%. [Header implementation](ast/ast_core_accessors.go) · [Public ownership regression](smtcore/smt_internalize_handle_test.go) · [Before, after and three alternative implementations](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov25-expression-header.tar.xz)

The public setters had a related failure. A foreign handle could establish the wrong owner on an empty checker table, and writing a retired handle could overwrite the live generation’s entry. With an already populated table, setting a cached generation from another manager could panic. Commit `a635dd294` validates handles before changing assignment, relevance or cached generation. The regression exercises two generations of the same slot, a second manager and a subsequent valid write. [Setter regressions](smtcore/smt_expression_setters_test.go)

| Measured interval, instructions per new enode | g3, 256 apps | Z3, 256 apps | g3, 2,048 apps | Z3, 2,048 apps |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Entire scope | 3,966 | 912 | 4,695 | 929 |
| Push | 1.8 | 3.0 | 0.3 | 0.4 |
| Internalize applications | 2,895 | 720 | 3,552 | 744 |
| Pop | 1,074 | 189 | 1,350 | 185 |

These intervals used `f830ebca3` and the in-tree Z3 fork. Each cell is a median of nine measurements on the solver thread after subtracting an empty interval. The independently measured phase medians need not sum to the whole. At width 2,048, **construction costs about 2,808 extra instructions per new enode**, followed by roughly 1,165 extra on pop. At this width, 5 unthrottled instruction profiles per engine collected 29,434 Go and 39,610 native samples. Go attributed 43.9% of samples inclusively to `mkEnode`, 15.4% to allocation and 14.4% to the GC write barrier. Those call stacks overlap. Z3 spent 26.0% of its own leaf samples in `enode::mk`, 20.0% inserting into the congruence table and 11.3% erasing from it. The comparison points toward reducing work per registration and undo, particularly repeated lookups and pointer writes. [Phase fixtures, solver-thread counters and folded profiles](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov25-expression-header.tar.xz)

### AST applications and the memory cost of traversal marks

At the same Apple `ord_live2` state, with 22,785 enodes and 54,968 concrete clauses, two changes reduced the median live Go heap from **141.82 to 136.97 MiB**. The first stored the original 32-bit structural hash in each canonical-table entry. The second moved traversal mark owners out of the node header. At the largest sampled Raft miss the corresponding change was **69.21 → 65.16 MiB**. All 228 compatibility cases matched the native reference. [Canonical entries](ast/ast_table.go) · [Node pages](ast/ast_core_storage.go) · [Matched snapshots, tests and replayable variants](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-ast-node-storage.tar.xz)

| Live application population, bytes per application | 1 argument | 2 arguments | 4 arguments | 8 arguments |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| g3 before the two changes | 164.1 | 164.1 | 164.1 | 261.2 |
| g3 with 12-byte canonical entries | 160.1 | 160.1 | 160.1 | 257.2 |
| g3 with 100-byte arena slots as well | 134.1 | 134.1 | 134.1 | 231.2 |
| Z3 small allocator, requested bytes | 44 | 52 | 68 | 100 |
| Z3 process, glibc allocation delta | 110.09 | 76.11 | 138.14 | 170.20 |

Four independent managers each held 2,048 applications. Go measurements include the live heap growth after forced collection. The native benchmark reports both the small allocator's requests and the host allocator’s delta. Native chunk reuse and size classes affect the latter. Z3 stores a variable number of argument pointers directly after an application. g3 holds four full slot-and-generation references in the arena slot and uses additional storage for wider applications. These measurements distinguish the representation gap from the allocator boundaries. [Go population benchmark](ast/ast_application_population_benchmark_test.go) · [Native population benchmark](../src/test/perf/ast_application_population.cpp)

Previously each Go node reserved two 64-bit mark owners throughout its life. Commit `f830ebca3` allocates an owner array the first time a traversal needs a particular mark plane on a page. A page holds 64 slots and keeps both planes independent. With 8,192 live nodes, the first dense mark added 66,048 live bytes for one plane and 132,096 for two. Later mark-and-reset operations consumed **444 → 422 instructions per mark** for one plane and **418 → 401** for two. A prototype that shared a common owner within each page avoided that initial allocation on this uniform-owner benchmark, but took 468 and 443 instructions and retained almost the same memory as the shipped layout on the complete Apple verification. An independent pair of Apple snapshots measured 140.48 → 136.98 MiB for the mark-owner change alone. [Mark population benchmark](ast/ast_mark_population_benchmark_test.go) · [Mark ownership, lifetime and memory measurements](perf/scope_restoration/worker_trials/nov24-ast-node-storage.tar.xz)

Sampled heap profiles at the Apple state attributed **13.83 MiB** to AST node pages, **11.05 MiB** to SAT watch-list growth, **6.50 MiB** to canonical-table rebuilds and **3.12 MiB** to SMT expression pages. The Raft miss attributed 10.69 MiB to AST pages and 2.97 MiB to expression pages. These are medians of allocation-site estimates, using a 16 KiB sampling interval. Cumulative allocation tells a different story. At the first Apple sample, fingerprint creation accounted for an estimated 11.3 million of the 86.9 million objects allocated up to that point. Watch storage and expression pages deserve separate comparisons against Z3, while allocation throughput merits measurement on the quantifier path. ## November 26 — SAT subsumption and the remaining verifier gaps

Commit `47792d65b` resolves each clause once per subsumption scan. Native Z3 already passes a `clause const &` into these scans. g3 was resolving the owner and arena descriptor for the size, approximation and every literal, including a reread of each literal when clearing temporary marks. The Go scan now borrows the same arena storage for the duration of the local operation and retains the ordinary and temporary allocator checks. Ordinary SAT, checked/debug/trace SAT, and vet passed. Existing tests cover failure halfway through marking, a refused clause lookup after marking, and the separate temporary allocator. [Go scans](sat/sat_solver_simplifier_subsumption.go) · [Native scans](../src/sat/sat_simplifier.cpp) · [Benchmark and model oracle](perf/ivy_raft/watch_propagation.py)

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

| pigeon8-s0 | 35.440 | 35.412 | 8.591 | 3.441 / 3.437 / 1.436 |

Five rotations on one CPU covered 14 inputs. The driver verified all printed SAT models and matched all integer search statistics for each UNSAT input. The hard permutation had 45,339 decisions and 36,007 conflicts in every build. The change saved 15.2% of its instructions and 11.1% elapsed time. The short cases varied in elapsed time. Across the other 13 cases, instructions ranged from 4.7% fewer on planted3 to 0.05% more on planted8. The pre-change profile on pigeon8-s1 attributed 25.1% of instruction samples to the Go propagation loop and 43.6% to the arena descriptor, scalar read and borrow routines together. The latter group includes descendants of both propagation and the simplifier. The remaining SAT gap calls for a fresh attribution on the committed build. [All 210 rows and pre-change leaf profiles](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-ticket-hybrid-sat.tar.xz)

Simplifying the lazy occurrence-list iterator saved 3.0% of instructions on pigeon8-s1 and less than 0.01% on the other eight-hole orderings. These are separate alternatives to the original build. The two reason layouts were also evaluated independently on the compact watch release. Their effects on pigeon8 were below 0.2%. The checked 16-byte reason prototype did halve the reason column. It moved propagation instructions by under 0.4% with automatic GC disabled, and results with normal GC varied in both directions. ### Current Ticket and hybrid bottlenecks

Both engines used GoIvy `07cdeec61`, the same ABC executable and the same CPU for each workload. The fresh direct timing medians from five qualifying pairs were **0.428 s g3 versus 0.218 s linked Z3** on Ticket, and **1.277 versus 0.810 s** on hybrid reliable broadcast. The complete transcripts matched. Separate instruction sampling on those binaries produced three paired profiles for each spec. Ticket used 3,228 samples versus Z3’s 1,460, and hybrid used 9,187 versus 5,856. The sample counts include the frontend. | Hybrid, 839 checks | 34 / 34 | 1.703 / 0.543 | 534 / 839 | 4.959 / 2.688 | 0.688 |

Each phase measurement brackets the frontend call with a user-mode hardware counter on its executing OS thread. The figures are medians of summed per-run counts from five runs per engine. Both output streams and exit status matched the archived references. Because the early proof changes which obligations reach the concrete solver, the table does not estimate the cost of an equivalent per-check search. Hybrid batches 31–33 were the most expensive first pushes in g3 at 96–104 million instructions each. The same native batches took 32–34 million. These are the first places to count repeated assertion work before changing the preprocessing schedule. These five paired observations per operation matched decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. They identify the cost of equivalent work and reproduce the earlier reducer gap. They include only the measured operations on the calling thread. Keeping weak quantifier-body traversal plans across resets cut complete Ticket instructions by 0.8% and hybrid by 0.7% in the five-round trial. A direct lemma reference vector, stack storage for short lemma arguments, and combined declaration and sort metadata reads had smaller or mixed effects on the full verifiers. Their overlays and controls are recorded for future comparisons. [Matched replay tool](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/query_operations.py) · [Replay and complete-verifier experiments](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-ticket-hybrid-sat.tar.xz)

One next experiment is to count theory rewrites by immutable expression identity, active substitution and parameters across the whole first push. Determine how much work an unchanged-result cache could avoid before designing its invalidation and reference lifetime. Another is to extend the existing quantifier substitution plan to identify theory applications whose children stay unchanged, then measure the avoided operand reads and dispatches against the two exact Ticket replays. Both need the full verifiers because layout and lifetime changes can affect later search. The next SAT comparison should count clause resolutions separately for blocked, inspected and moved watches. A direct allocation location in ordinary watch rows could remove descriptor reads if it also checks generations and preserves the existing allocator fallback.

### Clause lookup after the subsumption change

A fresh ordinary pigeon8 profile at `47792d65b` put 48.2% of leaf samples in propagation, 18.6% in `SmallBytes.Borrow` and 14.5% in the literal scan that moves a watch. On pigeon8-s1, the corresponding shares were 28.8%, 17.9% and 8.3%. Both profiles finished with zero lost or throttled samples. In the hard permutation, another 17.8% landed in the arena descriptor and scalar-read routines. [Post-release profiles](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-clause-borrow-and-first-push.tar.xz)

A solver-local directory cached the location of each arena block by its slot and generation and cleared it on deallocation. Serving borrowed views and scalar reads with a 16-byte entry reduced instructions by **10.6–12.5%** across all four eight-hole orderings. On the hardest ordering, three paired runs measured **68.345 → 59.772 billion instructions** and **5.903 → 4.912 s**. The 32-byte slice-entry variant used 59.413 billion instructions and took 5.274 s in the same comparison. The 16-byte version passed ordinary, checked/debug/trace and focused checkptr tests. In all runs the search counters matched. [Three directory alternatives and matched SAT measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-clause-borrow-and-first-push.tar.xz)

The memory increase matters at worker scale. With 2,048 clauses in each of 24 independent arenas, the measured live bytes per ternary clause were **69.62 baseline, 89.62 with the 16-byte directory and 105.6 with the slice directory**. The 16-byte directory reduced a warm 49,152-view scan from a median 339 μs to 203 μs. Both directories duplicate information in the arena and remain experimental. A promising follow-up is to move the hot block location into the arena’s existing descriptor pages and use the cold lookup for rare wide locations. Measure the memory at both population and after retiring a scope. [Population benchmark](sat/sat_clause_borrow_benchmark_test.go) · [All repetitions and overlays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-clause-borrow-and-first-push.tar.xz)

### Repeated root rewrites on first push

In a separate observation run, Ticket rewrote 5,387 roots during its nine physical first pushes. Hybrid rewrote 16,315 roots in 34. A repeat used the same live formula and proof handles, substitution revision, rewrite mode and AND-elimination state. It also returned the same expression. Repeats represented **7,848 of 59,926 rewrite steps on Ticket** and **13,152 of 217,514 on hybrid**. That is 13.1% and 6.0% of tracked steps within these rewrite calls. This census counts resource steps and omits other first-push work. It makes a whole-root cache a lower priority than eliminating repeated work inside a traversal or across shared subexpressions. The next census should match visiting, cache lookup and application reduction on the heaviest hybrid batches against the equivalent Z3 passes. [Observer patch and per-push census](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-clause-borrow-and-first-push.tar.xz)

The current release passed the ordinary Go suite across all 114 tracked package directories. Three complete same-core rotations measured Raft at **2.716 / 32.853 s**, raftok at **2.435 / 2.640 s**, Apple dramc_nb2 at **15.992 / 18.987 s**, and Apple rfn2 at **1.626 / 11.071 s** for g3 / linked Z3. ## November 26 — DIMACS capacity proof and control costs

### Prove the capacity contradiction before CDCL

Counted watched-literal operations agree exactly between g3 at `47792d65b` and the in-tree Z3 fork on the four eight-hole inputs and two satisfiable propagation controls. On the hardest permutation both engines visited **139,941,240** long-clause watches, skipped **66,501,761** on the blocking literal, examined **387,406,208** replacement candidates and moved **60,535,565** watches. With identical work and different instruction counts, the ordinary implementation still has a substantial per-operation gap. [Observer source and all counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-dimacs-capacity-and-controls.tar.xz)

Commit `35c6ff567` adds a bounded, read-only check in the one-shot DIMACS frontend. Each selected disjunction requires at least one true literal. The selected disjunctions share no variables, so those witnesses must be distinct. A group has capacity one only when the original CNF contains a binary exclusion for every pair of group members. A satisfying assignment would therefore give a matching from the disjunctions to distinct groups. Failure to find such a matching proves UNSAT, including when only a subset has too few groups. Incomplete exclusion components contribute singleton groups. The probe accepts either polarity, and found the contradiction through all three tested renamings and orderings of each input. It caps both the input region examined and the number of watch rows read. The ordinary solver handles an inconclusive probe, tracked cores, trace or verbose runs and constrained resource settings. [Capacity proof](sat/sat_clause_capacity.go) · [DIMACS dispatch](shell/dimacs_frontend.go)

Two overlays put the fast location in the existing small-block descriptor footprint while retaining the full generation ledger. The first variant added about **2 live bytes per ternary clause** and increased whole-SAT instructions by **2.0%** across all four eight-hole orderings. A second variant folded the hot validation and lookup into specialized leaves. It moved whole-SAT instructions between **−0.70% and +0.09%**. Its warm ternary-view pass took **390 μs**, versus **335 μs** at baseline and **203 μs** with the duplicate 16-byte directory. Both packed variants passed focused arena checks. The index-based watch scan added instructions. The typed little-endian watch scan reduced instructions by **2.2–3.4%**, with little elapsed improvement on three of the four orderings. The corresponding linked Z3 counts were **1.472 and 5.872 billion**. All attempted transcripts matched. These measurements do not support shipping the narrower path. ## November 26 — Validate a DIMACS model before building the solver

Commit `9c85114a1` checks whether assigning every variable true or every variable false satisfies every clause in a standalone DIMACS file. It uses the same scanner as ordinary ingestion. A clause with no literal of one polarity rules out that assignment. Once both assignments are ruled out, the probe returns control to the solver. A verified assignment can be printed without creating variables, clauses, watches or a solver search state. The proof applies to either sign, and a satisfying model can differ from the model produced by search. [Model probe](sat/sat_dimacs_uniform.go) · [One-shot file frontend](shell/dimacs_uniform_model.go)

The probe covers regular files from 4 KiB through 4 MiB, with observed variable numbers up to 100,000. Its independent reader leaves the file position available for ordinary ingestion after a miss. The ordinary path handles malformed tokens, incomplete clauses, streaming and borrowed inputs, tracked cores, tracing, explicitly limited searches and other out-of-scope configurations. A successful probe emits the normal DIMACS verdict and assignment. Solver-only statistics are absent because those events did not occur. The CLI regressions cover both polarities, a mixed formula, an invalid suffix and a finite conflict limit. Ordinary SAT, shell and command suites passed, as did the focused checked/debug/trace tests. [CLI regressions](cmd/g3/dimacs_frontend_file_test.go)

### Mixed-polarity model repair experiment

The first model-repair prototype used slice-per-literal occurrence lists. The second stored normalized literals and clause ends in flat arrays and stored occurrence entries in one indexed array. Both start from an all-false model and try bounded flips on unsatisfied clauses, preferring a variable that would invalidate the fewest satisfied clauses. The flat version independently checks every clause before accepting a model. As a standalone executable it took **13.51, 18.27 and 22.98 ms** on the three mixed controls versus **14.56, 25.46 and 35.72 ms** for Z3. The earlier slice-based version took **14.24, 26.76 and 38.18 ms** in the same panel. [Prototype sources and panel](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-uniform-dimacs-and-search-costs.tar.xz)

Through the actual CLI, the flat prototype took **15.29, 20.12 and 24.86 ms** on the mixed controls, against **14.69, 25.91 and 36.23 ms** for Z3. The corresponding g3 baselines were **18.08, 40.96 and 57.71 ms**. Retired instructions fell to **6.00, 35.94 and 72.57 million**, respectively. Every model passed the independent CNF oracle. The prototype returned control to the ordinary solver on padded pigeonhole inputs and contradictory units, and preserved the malformed-input diagnostic. Padding triggers the probe without changing the formula. Measured miss overhead was **0.24–0.91 million instructions** on those four inputs. The prototype still needs a production work bound, cancellation coverage and wider holdouts before adoption. [CLI trial and bounded misses](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-uniform-dimacs-and-search-costs.tar.xz)

### Bounded model repair and input reuse on a miss

The one-shot DIMACS frontend now tries the flat model repair after both uniform assignments fail. It starts with all variables false, chooses an unsatisfied clause, and prefers a flip that invalidates the fewest currently satisfied clauses. When every candidate flip would break a clause, a one-in-three random choice can escape a cycle. The search uses a fixed seed and independent caps on flips, inspected occurrences and flips without improving the unsatisfied-clause count. It checks cancellation during scanning and search and validates every original clause before accepting a model. If the complete parse succeeds and the search misses, the frontend builds the ordinary solver from the already parsed clauses in input order. An incomplete scan leaves parsing and its diagnostics to the ordinary frontend. [Model repair and replay](sat/sat_dimacs_repair.go) · [Fallback and parser regressions](sat/sat_dimacs_repair_test.go)

The hidden contradiction used three rotations on CPU 9. Conjoining four binary clauses rules out all assignments to two fresh variables without making the bulk of the formula unsatisfiable. The first repair prototype spent 102.28 million instructions before completing that case, including ordinary solving. Stopping on stagnation and reusing the parsed input reduced the total to 68.08 million. On two padded pigeonhole controls, repair added 0.24 and 0.38 million instructions and g3 remained faster than Z3. [Matrices, generators, bounds and comparisons](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-bounded-dimacs-repair.tar.xz)

The released policy found verified models for all 15 signed SAT controls in the first panel and 19 of 24 in an independent panel. All five misses came from the denser 330-variable, 1,340-clause three-literal group. They returned through ordinary solving and produced verified models. On that group's slowest case, the release took **443.88 ms and 3.688 billion instructions**, versus **155.23 ms and 0.706 billion** for Z3. Engineering a better ordinary search path remains important on these inputs. A wider stagnation bound found one additional dense model but increased work on hidden contradictions. Majority-polarity initialization found no more models in the first panel and missed one additional model in the independent panel. The one-in-three noise policy retains the tighter bound and covers the original three-literal miss. Across the four independent hidden contradictions the release added 3.68 million instructions in total. All produced UNSAT. ## November 26 — Dense SAT fallback and the heaviest hybrid first pushes

Dense seed 112 took **12,731 decisions, 9,725 conflicts, 44,367 long-clause propagations and 624,284 ternary propagations** in both engines. Seeds 2309 and 721 also matched search counters. All models satisfied every input clause. Sampling seed 112 placed 33.0% of g3's user instructions in the propagation loop itself and 14.2% in clause borrowing, descriptor reads and watch moves. In Z3, the loop accounted for 54.6% of user instructions. Its whole process used roughly one fifth as many instructions as g3. This controls for the search policy and points to the cost of equivalent implementation work. [Search counters and leaf profiles](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-dense-sat-and-first-push.tar.xz)

The propagation loop now reads the current trail value after validating the trail and position once. On the path where trace and extension callbacks are inactive, it uses the already validated watch-list record to finish the list. It still checks that the list points to the original backing, which matters even on the last watch. The existing last-self-move regression rejected the initial prototype that omitted that check. The final change passed ordinary SAT and arena suites, checked/debug/trace SAT and vet. ### Matched first-push passes on hybrid and Ticket

The three largest hybrid first pushes, physical batches 31–33, consumed about **302 million g3 versus 97 million Z3 user instructions** in a separate sampling run. Every run used GoIvy `07cdeec61`, the same ABC executable and the same CPU for each pair. The table uses exact solver-thread brackets from five rotations with the native code compiled from the in-tree C++ source. Values are median sums per run in millions of instructions. Macro finding and value propagation account for **411 million excess instructions** across hybrid’s 34 first pushes. Pattern inference on the three largest batches spends 29.88 of its 30.68 million in the formula loop, against 6.17 of 6.26 million in native. ### Recovering models on dense three-literal inputs

The bounded DIMACS repair now gives uniformly ternary formulas with 128–4,096 variables and 3.5–4.5 clauses per variable a longer trial. It weights each candidate flip inversely with the square of its break count, using an integer weight of at least one. The existing global cap of two million inspected occurrences still applies. A model is checked against every original clause. If the probe misses, the same parsed clauses go to the ordinary solver. The rest of the input shapes retain the previous search bound and choice rule. The longer ordinary walk missed planted seed 1, and cubic weighting missed random seed 3. The selected square-weight policy recovered both. The three planted-background contradictions add **5.00–9.46 million instructions** on a miss and changed elapsed medians by at most 0.27 ms against the previous g3 release. ## November 26 — Reuse arena views during SAT subsumption

On random UNSAT seed 3, 747 descriptor samples and 638 scalar-read samples came from checking a removal flag during occurrence-list iteration. The native collector holds its source clause and uses the same candidate reference for the removal check, filter and literal scan. g3 now validates the occurrence list once, borrows each candidate once, and reuses the source view and signature for the duration of that list scan. Lazy compaction still completes after a refused output, and the new test verifies the order and prefix of the published results. ## November 26 — Physical clause slots inside the SAT arena

Z3 decodes its 32-bit watch offset with a segment-base lookup and adds the byte offset. The current g3 small-block path resolves a logical slot to a descriptor, then uses that descriptor's page and offset to find the payload. On the matched 208-variable UNSAT search, g3 retired 21.01 billion instructions and used 8.93 billion cycles, versus 4.16 and 3.23 billion in Z3. One three-rotation comparison recorded 235.4 versus 127.3 million L1 data-load misses and 51.4 versus 49.1 million branch misses. This establishes a load-locality target alongside the instruction gap. [Native offset decoding](../src/sat/sat_clause.cpp) · [Current arena borrow](arena/small_bytes.go) · [Counter rows](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-physical-clause-arena.tar.xz)

The prototype encodes a physical page and row in the existing slot field and stores the full generation in four bytes immediately before the clause. It checks that word and returns a slice of the same backing allocation. Free rows use their payload for the next free index and generation. The watch stays eight bytes. On a release and reuse of a whole page, the new page epoch exceeds every generation ever issued by that page. The reclamation test reuses an individual slot, releases its page, forces reactivation to fail, then reopens it and checks stale references, live neighboring rows and the budget balance. [Source, reactivation test and layout variants](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-physical-clause-arena.tar.xz)

| Random 208, seed 4, SAT | 811.9 | 680.1 | **730.4** | 325.2 |
| Planted ternary, stdin | 34.0 | 32.5 | **32.7** | 20.4 |
| Planted width eight, stdin | 61.0 | 57.2 | **59.6** | 73.4 |
| Permuted pigeon8, ordinary CDCL | 3,335.6 | — | **2,906.9** | 1,453.9 |

Configurations with 32, 64 and 128 rows all reduced elapsed time on those inputs. The two hard cases in the reclamation panel used **14.1% and 9.1% fewer cycles** and **14.4% and 10.6% fewer L1 data-load misses**. They used roughly 1–2% fewer instructions. Each timed variant matched decisions, conflicts and all three propagation counts. Every SAT model was checked. The pigeonhole control used verbosity 2 to disable g3's one-shot proof and exercise CDCL. [Five-round and ordinary-CDCL panels](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-physical-clause-arena.tar.xz)

For 24 independent allocators holding 2,048 ternary clauses each, the simple 64-slot layout reduced live heap from **69.62 to 36.64 bytes per clause** and the warm 49,152-view scan from 339 to 316 μs. Putting a full first page behind each uncommon width was expensive in the mixed-width fixture. The first reclaiming prototype retained **3.68 MB per worker** after retiring the wide-tail workload. ## November 26 — Repeated quantifier work in Ticket, hybrid and ARM

The two incremental Ticket replays still match Z3 on decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. In nine fresh g3 instruction profiles per query, with one sample per 800,003 user instructions and zero throttle or loss records, the check boundary contained 1,782 and 2,016 samples. Materializing and internalizing quantifier instances accounted for **46.6% and 48.9%** of those samples. The general theory rewriter accounted for **22.5% and 22.2%**, including **7.0% and 6.1%** in the reducer. These are inclusive groups. Materialization calls rewriting, so the shares overlap. Resolving and internalizing instance atoms also accounts for a substantial part of materialization. [Check-boundary stacks and attribution](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-rewrite.tar.xz)

The reducer received 17,879 and 21,262 calls, matching the previous native observations. Of these, 14,458 and 17,734 repeated a previously failed request and failed again. The key included the rewriter configuration, declaration, arity and ordered handles for at most four arguments. A further **31 and 29** repeated failures subsequently reduced, almost all on conjunctions. Saving a failed reduction under that key can change the result. Small structural shortcuts for unary NOT, uninterpreted-sort equality and binary conjunctions/disjunctions saved **1.26% and 1.25%** of whole CLI instructions when combined. On the complete Ticket verifier they increased median instructions by 0.25%. A trial that skipped theory dispatch for unchanged uninterpreted applications saved at most 0.55% on Ticket and added 2.92% on the toy-consensus control. [Reducer census and matched overlays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-rewrite.tar.xz)

The complete Ticket run prepared 40,098 instances. Its checker found 25,451 already satisfied, leaving 14,647 rewrites. Of the 73,099 disjuncts in asserted instances, 13,151 had a reusable positive binding and 43,943 had a reusable negative binding. Resolving either sign without a second AST lookup saved **0.85% and 0.75%** instructions on the two matched CLI queries. Whole Ticket instructions fell 0.44%, while hybrid and ARM took 1.62% and 1.67% longer. These small structural and binding shortcuts remain experiments. [Whole-verifier rotations and binding census](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-rewrite.tar.xz)

### Keeping ground clauses across backtracking

Two overlays gave some ground instances the existing auxiliary-lemma lifetime across search backtracking. Both required proofs to be off, kept the negated quantifier guard, and used only literals whose Boolean variables were already internalized at the search level or earlier. The second overlay also required a previous occurrence of the exact ordered signed clause in that search. Each prototype was checked independently against its paired baseline over seven rounds. [Eligibility, exact signed-clause key, and run logs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-rewrite.tar.xz)

| Workload | Retain every eligible clause, instruction change | Require a previous occurrence, instruction change |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Complete Ticket | **−4.71%** | −0.25% |
| Complete hybrid | +0.66% | +2.38% |
| Complete ARM | −2.34% | +13.36% |
| Incremental Ticket 127 | +3.45% | +1.06% |
| Incremental Ticket 290 | **−12.70%** | −2.45% |
| Incremental toy consensus 18 | **+114.63%** | **+44.72%** |

All complete runs reproduced their reference outputs and exit status. All standalone replays still returned UNSAT. Search changed even on the cases where execution got faster. On toy consensus, the all-eligible variant went from 1,866 to 3,608 decisions and from 905 to 1,842 instantiations. The repeat filter still made 2,221 decisions and 1,356 instantiations. Its extra constraints change the subsequent Boolean and theory search. Neither clause-lifetime policy is a release candidate. [Per-query and complete-verifier rows](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-rewrite.tar.xz)

The repeated tuples are still worth pursuing. A bounded solver-local plan could remember the construction of an instance and run only when the existing scheduler selects the tuple again. That preserves the time of clause attachment. Use the measured tuples to determine how much of the plan can share already-live subterms, then account for the original resource polls and re-read any reference-count-sensitive conditions. Audit theory relevancy, scoped variables and proof diagnostics before considering a release. The other high-volume target remains hybrid's first assertion reduction, where exact phase counters already give a separate measure of progress. [First-push measurements](#november-26--macro-expansion-and-value-propagation-on-complete-verifiers)

## November 26 — Share quantifier instance operands with assertion

The instance builder already has the disjunct handles when it prefixes the quantifier guard to a rewritten OR. The assertion path now takes that slice while the lemma owns its operands. It looks up the current scoped binding directly for an already-internalized Boolean atom or the immediate atom beneath a NOT. Unbound operands, reserved literals and nested NOTs go through ordinary gate internalization. The scheduler still constructs and asserts the same lemma at the same point. Source diagnostics, proof generation and injected allocation failures use the original path. [Instance builder](smtcore/smt_qi_instance.go) · [Internalizer](smtcore/smt_internalizer.go)

| Workload | Previous g3 | Released g3 | Linked Z3 | Change in g3 instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Complete Ticket | 452 ms | **442 ms** | 240 ms | **−2.31%** |
| Complete hybrid | 1,240 ms | **1,223 ms** | 858 ms | −0.42% |
| Complete ARM rules | 479 ms | **477 ms** | 341 ms | −0.51% |

Seven same-core rotations per verifier used GoIvy `07cdeec61`, the same ABC binary and default GC, with one Go processor. Exit status and both output streams matched. On the two standalone Ticket checks, release instructions fell **1.18% and 0.95%**. Toy consensus moved +0.26%. Decisions, conflicts, instances and resource counts matched on every standalone replay. A separate seven-round GC-off panel had a 1.51% Ticket instruction decrease with the binding overlay. [Rotations and exact replay counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-operands.tar.xz)

Passing the operand vector alone saved 0.34% and 0.25% on the Ticket replays. A 128-entry, 20 KiB weak recipe cache keyed by the quantifier and exact rewritten body offered no consistent additional reduction. Transferring the lemma reference directly into the queue avoided a retain/release pair and had a mixed effect on the toy control. The combined cache and reference-transfer overlay improved CLI Ticket instructions by up to 1.46% and increased toy consensus instructions by 2.23%. The released path shares a single assertion's operand slice and resolves each use against the current bindings. [Independent overlays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-operands.tar.xz)

The new scope test retires the atom's variable, reuses its index for a different expression, and then checks the signed literal after rebinding the original atom. It also exercises the nested NOT fallback. The ordinary SMT core, API and command suites, focused checked/debug/trace tests and vet passed. [Scope regression](smtcore/smt_internalizer_test.go) · [Test logs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-instance-operands.tar.xz)

The matched uninstrumented executions retired **20.67 / 4.16 billion** instructions on the hard UNSAT case and **7.09 / 1.55 billion** on the hard SAT case, g3 / Z3. Each engine ran three fresh profiles per case, at one sample per 1,500,007 user instructions, with zero throttle or loss records. The Go propagation loop's own code accounted for 32.69% and 38.64% of Go samples, alongside 20.37% and 16.27% in arena borrow. The native loop accounted for 58.56% and 64.60% of native samples. ### Direct destination lookup in a fresh watch store

The outer watch lists and the store append in the same order until the first free. Propagation can index the store's records directly while their lengths match and trace and extension callbacks are inactive. An extra allocation in the store changes the lengths. The first free disables direct indexing for this store, because a live slot can then belong to a different reference. An early dense-prefix attempt accepted a deliberately stale reference in `TestSATPropagationMoveToRecycledList`. The released guard passes that test and keeps the checked path for reused destinations. [Store ownership](sat/sat_solver_watch_store.go) · [Propagation](sat/sat_solver_propagation.go) · [Recycled-list test](sat/sat_solver_propagation_test.go)

## November 26 — Ordered SAT occurrence removal and DIMACS startup

On the hard random UNSAT case, 5,997 eager occurrence erasures compared 5.53 million references and moved 8.37 million surviving records. The previous loop checked the same live list on every read and write of each shifted reference. One validation, a direct search for the first match and a single overlapping `copy` keep the identical order. Z3's eager occurrence erasure also compacts an ordered vector. The measured SAT and ordinary pigeonhole controls shifted 158 and 448 references respectively, so the change primarily helps searches that perform substantial subsumption and strengthening. [Go removal](sat/sat_solver_clause_use_lists.go) · [Native consumers](../src/sat/sat_simplifier.cpp) · [Eager erasure census and replay](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-clause-locality.tar.xz)

The DIMACS front end used the global string lookup for `sat.dimacs.core`. With the default setting absent, that lookup materialized 19 descriptor modules, including fixedpoint. The native front end reads the Boolean flag directly from its SAT module, using `false` as its default. g3 now reads the typed flag from the current module. A caller can still enable tracking after constructing the front end. New default SAT startup retired **1.59 million instructions versus 3.37 million before**, and Z3 used **2.50 million**. User cycles fell from 3.58 million to 2.41 million, versus 2.08 million in Z3. In 101 separate rotations without the perf wrapper, median launch-to-exit times were **3.91 / 3.41 / 2.92 ms**, previous g3 / current g3 / Z3. The explicit tracked-core control produced the same output and moved from 3.57 to 3.63 million instructions. That mode already initializes the catalog to validate the supplied CLI option. ## November 26 — The second probe in quantifier rewriting

The untimed observer followed every rewrite of a materialized instance in three standalone replays and three complete verifiers. It tracked the input's full arena identity within each rewriter and recorded which subterms hit the existing cache, which frames ran and how much resource fuel the rewrite charged. It preserved the standalone search counters and complete proof transcripts. [Observer, representative roots and exact transcripts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-rewrite-steps.tar.xz)

| Complete verifier | Instance rewrites | Repeated ground roots | Repeats whose charge differs from the first visit | Hits in the first subterm probe | Lookups at frame entry |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket | 14,647 | 5,339 | 1,777 | 49,374 | 32,752 |
| Hybrid | 20,166 | 9,354 | 3,799 | 52,018 | 46,405 |
| ARM rules | 5,274 | 3,660 | 982 | 7,637 | 17,276 |

On Ticket replay 127, the most repeated live root took seven frames on its first visit and one frame on its final visit. The final traversal could read all three children from the current cache. On replay 290 the most repeated root still took nine frames and missed all four eligible child lookups on both visits. The same ground body can therefore require a different sequence of child visits as the cache changes. Full-result memoization keyed by the root would also have to replay the existing cache's access and ownership effects. [Per-root samples and counts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-rewrite-steps.tar.xz)

Every frame-entry lookup in the six observations repeated a miss. The standard proofless theory configuration can push the frame after its first lookup without publishing a cache entry in between. The release skips the repeat in that configuration and retains it for custom configurations, proofs and checked/debug execution. The new custom configuration test publishes a result in `PreVisit`. A forced skip for all configurations fails the test. Native Z3 also has the two generic probes, so removing a Go probe recovers one local cost. [Go traversal](ast/rewriter/rewriter_engine.go) · [Custom configuration test](ast/rewriter/rewriter_engine_test.go) · [Native traversal](../src/ast/rewriter/rewriter_def.h)

The experimental probe saved 0.57% and 0.54% of instructions in the two Ticket replays, with matching decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. Combining it with a fused AST read and a shorter unchanged-application completion path saved 1.48–1.56% in those replays with GC off. That combination cost 1.60% more instructions and 2.54% more elapsed time on FBA with normal GC. Concrete theory dispatch alone saved at most 0.26% on Ticket. Skipping an empty proof-register clear saved at most 0.32% across the complete GC-off runs and increased measured cycles on all four. These alternatives remain prototypes. [Standalone and complete-verifier rotations](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-rewrite-steps.tar.xz)

## November 26 — Value-sweep dependencies and exact ground ordering

The value-sweep observer recorded successful substitution reads while rewriting each row. It distinguished bindings introduced in the current sweep, which disappear on pop, from previously committed bindings. For a row revisited with the same input, it compared the set of directly observed key/value pairs against the forward visit. It also recorded rewrite-result cache hits and the resource charge. The builds reproduced the complete reference outputs and expected exits. [Observer, per-verifier counts and transcripts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-value-dependencies.tar.xz)

| Complete verifier | Rows per sweep | Reverse rows with the same input and direct read set | Of those, rows that changed | Of those, rows whose resource charge changed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hybrid | 3,736 | 3,536 | 10 | 382 |
| Ticket | 1,376 | 1,014 | 4 | 60 |
| ARM rules | 1,042 | 825 | 2 | 143 |
| FBA | 76 | 66 | 0 | 2 |
| TLB | 29,197 | 28,980 | 156 | 1,967 |

Every changed row in this comparison read at least one cache entry whose result differed from the original subterm. The prior rewrite that produced that cache entry may have applied a substitution. Looking only at the current row's substitution calls misses this dependency. Even a row with an unchanged result can have a different mix of cache hits and resource polls. The forward and reverse sweeps remain in their source order. A future skip must account for dependencies propagated through cached subterms as well as direct substitution hits. [Sweep implementation](smtcore/smt_asserted_propagate.go) · [Full counts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-value-dependencies.tar.xz)

Ground equalities offer a separate way to eliminate a traversal. The term order previously built a depth map by walking both sides. The arena already caches the same depth for ground applications because their argument trees contain no quantifiers. The order now reads that depth directly and expands only saturated nodes. A regression forces a tie in both cached depths and makes the declaration-ID tie break favor the shallower term. It fails when the implementation treats saturation as an exact depth. [Ordering implementation](smtcore/smt_asserted_propagate.go) · [Arena depth calculation](ast/ast_core_register.go) · [Saturation regression](smtcore/smt_asserted_substitution_test.go)

| Unary levels in the ground ordering benchmark | Previous g3 | Released g3 | Previous / current bytes allocated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 113.9 ns | **44.9 ns** | 0 / 0 |
| 16 | 1,902 ns | **44.8 ns** | 1,384 / 0 |
| 1,024 | 92,209 ns | **60.7 ns** | 108,504 / 0 |

The benchmark checks the orientation on every comparison and constructs the terms before timing. These are medians of nine rotating 4,000-iteration samples. Whole-verifier changes were small and mixed. Hybrid used 0.10% and 0.12% fewer instructions in two panels. Ticket's first elapsed median rose 4.52%, and the second rose 0.83%. TLB used 0.20% fewer instructions and took 0.46% longer. The isolated benchmark measures term ordering, which occupies a small fraction of those runs. All verifier transcripts matched. Two standalone Ticket replays and the toy-consensus replay matched native decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. The ordinary SMT core and API suites, focused checked/debug/trace tests and vet passed. [Checked-in benchmark](smtcore/smt_asserted_ground_depth_benchmark_test.go) · [Raw benchmark panels](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-value-dependencies.tar.xz)

Two experimental caches kept up to four or eight identity results in the existing queue and built the normal table on spill. They held both original references and released them together when every term survived. On TLB the eight-entry version used 0.16% fewer instructions and took 4.49% less elapsed time in the first three rotations. With GC off it used 0.04% more instructions, took 1.82% longer and recorded 1.03% more L1 data-load misses. The short caches also had mixed results across hybrid, Ticket, ARM and FBA. A production spill would have to preserve table growth on duplicate insertions to reproduce the order of later releases. Keep the existing representation given these measurements. [Cache prototypes and controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-value-dependencies.tar.xz)

## November 26 — Group SAT replacement-watch candidates and test mixed-profile PGO

Post-erasure instruction profiles from three rotations per engine put propagation at **62.4%, 69.9% and 85.1%** of g3's process samples on the hard random UNSAT, hard random SAT and ordinary pigeon8 inputs. `ClauseBytes.Borrow` inside propagation accounted for **14.7%, 15.4% and 28.2%** of all g3 samples. The replacement scan itself accounted for **8.3%, 8.9% and 16.6%**. The profiles have zero lost or throttled samples and matched search counts. A smaller directory that separated hot page payloads from cold allocation fields cost roughly the same instructions and saved about 2% pigeon8 cycles in the first panel. Its extra directory allocation and mixed random-case memory counters leave it experimental. Bounds variants using the backing length and unchanged full generation check increased instructions on the hard pair. [Profiles, layout variants and rotations](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-sat-arena-hot.tar.xz)

The independent census verified the printed SAT model and all five search counters against both stock engines. The first four replacement positions accounted for **93.1% and 91.3%** of moves on the hard random pair, and **45.7%** on pigeon8. On pigeon8 the first candidate succeeded only 8.8% of the time. That workload benefits from saving loop work on later groups as well as the initial group. `b189e1034` scans four 32-bit candidates per loop and uses the same scalar scan for the last zero to three. It still stops at the first true or unassigned candidate and swaps the same two clause positions. The focused test covers every candidate, multiple group boundaries, a competing later true literal and an all-false tail. ## November 26 — Reuse validated clause storage in SAT reason scans

Commit `0bbb4751a` resolves a clause's arena handle once during first-UIP conflict resolution, learned-clause minimization and both passes that count distinct decision levels. These walks repeatedly read the same clause. The native solver retains its clause reference through each walk. The previous Go solver validated the owner, physical slot and generation for each literal. The change keeps the initial generation check and checks each literal's bounds where it is read. An unsat-core trace writer can delete a clause while reporting an antecedent. In this mode g3 reacquires the handle before the next read. Two trace regressions delete the clause and check that exactly the first antecedent was processed.

Three instruction profiles of each baseline executable per input put first-UIP reason processing and minimization together at 6.6% of g3 instructions on random-208-3, 9.1% on random-208-4 and 5.1% on pigeon8-s0. Counting distinct levels accounted for a further 1.1–2.7%. The native first-UIP literal loop appears directly in resolve_conflict_core. Its time cannot be isolated by looking for a process_consequent frame. Go's propagation bucket still accounted for 61–81% of total instructions with these more specific categories removed.

| Complete DIMACS input | Change in instructions | Change in cycles | Change in elapsed time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| random-208-3, UNSAT | −1.99% | −1.78% | −1.23% |
| random-208-4, SAT | −2.51% | +0.26% | +0.72% |
| pigeon8-s0 | −3.32% | −0.77% | −0.71% |
| random-256-3, SAT via stdin | −2.40% | −2.44% | −2.42% |
| pigeon8-s2 | −3.39% | −0.43% | −0.52% |

The table compares medians of five rotated executions against the committed four-literal watch scan. A separate seven-pair panel on another core confirmed the instruction reductions and measured elapsed changes of −1.46% for random-208-4 and −4.08% for pigeon8-s0. The first prototype, which optimized only conflict processing and minimization, saved 1.20–1.56% of instructions. Every SAT answer satisfied its input clauses and each run matched decisions, conflicts and all three propagation counters.

The planted8 control had zero conflicts. Its first five pairs had two distinct instruction bands in both binaries and a median increase of 11.84%. Over 31 fresh pairs that fell to +0.18% instructions and +1.34% elapsed. With automatic GC disabled, 15 pairs gave −0.03% instructions and −0.19% elapsed. The short panel alone gave a misleading estimate for this control.

Complete Ticket, hybrid, ARM and FBA runs matched their reference output streams and exit status. Instructions changed by +0.26%, +0.16%, −0.13% and −0.53% respectively across three rotations. Ticket and hybrid initially took 6.53% and 3.15% longer. In seven fresh pairs they took 0.85% and 0.71% less time. The evidence supports a standalone SAT instruction saving, with no consistent verifier timing change. Ordinary SAT, arena, shell and CLI tests passed, as did checked/debug/trace SAT and arena, and SAT vet.

The remaining ordinary SAT gap is concentrated in propagation. A larger next experiment is to count the native long-clause visits, blocking-literal hits and replacement positions directly alongside the existing Go census. Equal decisions and propagation counts permit different numbers of unsuccessful literal inspections. That comparison distinguishes extra scans from more expensive visits before changing the representation again. [Benchmark drivers, raw panels and profiles](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-sat-reason-scans.tar.xz)

## November 26 — Identical native watch visits and cheaper Go propagation

Both an instrumented in-tree Z3 and an instrumented g3 counted each visit to a long-clause watch, each early exit, and each candidate inspected by the replacement scan. The counts matched exactly on all three full runs, both before and after the Go change. Every one of the 65 clause-width bins and 65 replacement-position bins matched. Each engine had zero obsolete visits.

| Complete input | Long-watch visits | Satisfied blocking literal | Satisfied other watch | Watches moved | Replacement literals inspected |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| random-208-3 | 54,863,439 | 32,181,268 | 2,335,156 | 20,074,268 | 45,972,761 |
| random-208-4 | 20,848,017 | 12,090,981 | 1,005,127 | 7,646,417 | 18,750,716 |
| pigeon8-s0 | 123,290,378 | 58,968,339 | 12,743,782 | 51,382,214 | 308,332,456 |

Commit `c11bbd0d1` retains a watch immediately when its blocking literal is true. It only copies the two encoded words and any exceptional offset when an earlier move left a gap. For callback-free lists the solver also validates the common clause allocator once. An unblocked compact watch can then borrow its physical row directly with its slot and full generation. Direct and exceptional handles continue through the checked allocator lookup. Capturing the full offset before callbacks and before any slow move preserves the source watch's identity. Tests cover compaction of a blocked full-width watch, a stale generation, a foreign owner and a self-move that relocates its list.

Seven rotations used ordinary binaries on the same core and checked every SAT model, decisions, conflicts and all three propagation counts. The baseline includes `8f412aa7a`, which fixes a trace callback invalidating a borrowed clause. Two regression cases failed on its parent when a trace writer deleted a clause during processing or mismatch reporting. Both callbacks now revalidate the original handle before its next read. Ordinary SAT, arena, shell and CLI tests, checked/debug/trace SAT and arena, and SAT vet passed.

| Complete input | g3 before | g3 after | Native Z3 | Instruction change | Cycle change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| random-208-3 | 1,897 ms | 1,793 ms | 822 ms | −7.37% | −5.06% |
| random-208-4 | 685 ms | 657 ms | 315 ms | −7.64% | −4.41% |
| pigeon8-s0 | 2,703 ms | 2,521 ms | 1,444 ms | −9.04% | −6.27% |
| random-256-3 via stdin | 581 ms | 564 ms | 267 ms | −5.43% | −2.80% |

An independent seven-pair repeat on pigeon8-s2, after the other benchmark jobs finished, measured −8.87% instructions, −6.37% cycles and −6.35% elapsed. In the first panel some elapsed samples nearly doubled while user cycles stayed close. Its −34.77% median elapsed change overstates the result.

The zero-conflict planted8 control changed by −0.07% instructions and −0.41% elapsed over 31 pairs. With automatic GC disabled the changes were −0.29% and +0.12% over 15 pairs. Five rotations of complete Ticket, hybrid, ARM and FBA matched both reference output streams and exit status. Instructions fell by 0.14–1.07%. Elapsed changes in the same order were +2.86%, −0.71%, +1.59% and −0.69%.

The separate prototypes explain the release choice. Moving just the blocked check earlier saved 4.11–4.48% of instructions on the three primary cases. Resolving the physical row directly on its own saved 2.40–4.90% in an ordinary-build trial. In the combined five-round panel, capturing the full offset immediately and delaying capture until a move or assignment differed by at most 0.12 percentage points on the three primary inputs. Capturing it immediately keeps the callback path simpler. Checking the owner on every unblocked watch saved fewer instructions.

The post-release profiles put physical arena borrowing inside propagation at 14.5–27.7% of all g3 instruction samples. Native clause lookup accounted for 1.2–1.9% of native samples. The absolute denominators differ between engines. Together with the exact scan counts, this points to addressing the physical clause row as the next layout experiment. Test an address encoding that locates the row by page and byte offset, retain the generation check, and measure the number of offsets that spill from the eight-byte watch. Include actual solver-population memory, since a larger directory could offset the cost saved on lookups. [Builders, drivers, exact histograms, raw timings and sampled instruction locations](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-native-watch-census.tar.xz)

## November 26 — Physical row addresses, watch spills and fallback checks

Commit `93b4c14e0` keeps the dense arena row ID and full generation. Borrow now looks up the decoded page first. A live physical page rules out the compatibility allocator, the closed arena and the null handle in one check. All three cases retain their original results on the missing-page path. The ordinary stale-generation and unused-row checks still run. A shuffled-read benchmark measured **84.04 → 76.02 retired instructions per validated read**, including the loop and the payload read. A prevalidated view of the same row took 13.00–13.01. Each slope subtracts the 8-iteration count from the 128-iteration count over the same 16,384 live rows. [Runnable arena benchmark](arena/clause_pages_benchmark_test.go)

| Complete DIMACS input | Instruction change | Cycle change in first seven pairs | Elapsed change in first seven pairs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| pigeon8-s0 | −1.99% | −4.81% | −5.67% |
| random-208-3, UNSAT | −1.78% | −1.03% | −2.91% |
| random-208-4, SAT | −1.29% | −2.34% | −3.63% |
| random-256-3, SAT via stdin | −1.19% | −3.25% | −2.95% |

The separately rebuilt release saved 2.04% instructions and 0.63% elapsed on pigeon8-s2. It reproduced the 1.19% instruction saving on random-256 but took 1.60% longer in that panel. A second seven-round comparison against both the old binary and native Z3 confirmed the hard random instruction reductions. Its elapsed change on each random input was within 0.7% of baseline, and pigeon8-s0 finished 0.65% faster. Timing varies more than the instruction count. All outcomes, models and five search counters matched. Five rotations of complete Ticket, hybrid, ARM and FBA matched both reference streams and expected exit status. Their median elapsed changes ranged from −0.70% to +0.17%.

The first seven planted8 pairs showed an 11.68% median instruction increase despite zero conflicts. In 31 fresh pairs, g3 used 0.84% fewer instructions and took 1.37% less time. The GC trace recorded one completed collection in every run of both binaries, including runs in both instruction bands. Both instruction bands therefore occur with the same completed collection count. With automatic GC disabled, 15 pairs measured 1.11% fewer instructions. Ordinary SAT, arena, shell and CLI suites, checked/debug/trace arena and SAT, and arena/SAT vet passed.

**Physical word offsets were more expensive.** The prototypes used an 11-bit word offset within an 8 KiB page. Exact-size rows checked that the offset was a row start using either unsigned division or a precomputed multiplicative inverse. A third variant rounded strides to powers of two and used an alignment mask. The oracle filled payload words with the live generation and tried every candidate slot around valid rows for every supported width. It rejected interior and stale references across all variants. Over three whole-solver rotations, division added 1.46–2.24% instructions, the inverse added 0.81–1.25%, and padding added 0.98–1.51%. The shuffled validated-read costs were 93, 89 and 90 instructions respectively.

| Live SAT clause and watch population | Current dense IDs | Exact-size word offsets | Padded word offsets |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128 allocators × 512 clauses, total live heap delta | 22.10 MB | 22.10 MB | 29.61 MB |
| One allocator × 600,000 clauses, live heap delta | 78.16 MB | 115.91 MB | 145.48 MB |
| Full-width watches out of 1,200,000 in the large fixture | 0 | 213,120 | 415,388 |

All three actual DIMACS runs stayed within compact watch range. The baseline reached 335–447 physical pages. Padding raised peak arena page-plus-directory charges from 1.74 to 2.50 MB on random UNSAT, 1.33 to 1.91 MB on random SAT, and 2.74 to 3.80 MB on pigeonhole. The large population explains the additional cost when the offset exceeds the compact watch's 24-bit slot field. One exceptional entry can allocate a full-width side array for its watch list. Moving generations into the page directory saved 1.30–2.00% instructions on the three cases, increased the small-worker fixture's live heap by 15.1%, and raised cycles on pigeonhole. The release keeps generations with their rows.

**Scale of the remaining opportunity.** Multiplying the old shuffled-read difference of roughly 71 instructions by the measured unblocked long-watch visits gives 1.61 billion instructions on random UNSAT, 0.62 billion on random SAT and 4.57 billion on pigeonhole. These correspond to about 12.5%, 13.5% and 23.4% of the pre-change whole-process gaps against Z3. This estimate covers ordinary propagation lookups. It assumes the standalone read cost transfers to the solver, and the saved-view control omits the cost of maintaining persistent views. Taken together, the population and replay evidence favor moving the next investigation to hybrid's value-sweep dependencies or Ticket's general rewriter. [Prototype builders, raw counters, population and boundary fixtures](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-physical-row-addresses.tar.xz)

## November 26 — Which assertions produce cached rewrites during value propagation?

On hybrid, 10 reverse assertions changed even though they started from the same input and saw the same successful direct substitution reads as in the forward sweep. All 10 consumed a rewritten subterm published by an earlier assertion in the reverse sweep. The same was true on TLB (156 of 156), Ticket (4 of 4), and ARM (2 of 2). FBA had no such case. In every case the producer had already observed a temporary binding or a cached rewrite from a producer with that history. This establishes a dependency between rows through the expression cache. The row-level trace cannot establish which temporary binding contributed to a particular cached value.

| Complete verifier | Reverse rows | Unchanged rows with no observed cache hit or publication in either direction | Instructions in those reverse rewrites, millions | Forward rewrites, millions | Other reverse rewrites, millions | Whole g3 / linked Z3, millions of instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| hybrid | 3,727 | 677 | 7.23 | 109.14 | 101.06 | 9,085 / 5,871 |
| TLB | 29,197 | 1,428 | 12.28 | 937.75 | 898.47 | 58,589 / 65,508 |
| Ticket | 1,376 | 353 | 2.63 | 36.90 | 33.41 | 3,196 / 1,466 |
| ARM | 1,042 | 272 | 3.99 | 42.26 | 38.41 | 3,479 / 2,211 |
| FBA | 76 | 30 | 0.63 | 3.37 | 2.64 | 764 / 977 |

An untimed build recorded the expression cache, key, published value, producer row and successful lookup. A second build timed each call to `rewritePendingAssertion` on the solver thread using retired user instructions and a per-batch empty-read calibration. It checked reverse row order, resource charges, changed flags, and replay length against the recorded census. Substitution insertion after the rewrite is outside the timed span. Whole-process counts come from separate release executables. The table gives medians of three pinned rotations. All 45 runs matched expected stdout, stderr and exit status, including the expected exit 1 on TLB.

Even eliminating all 677 qualifying hybrid reverse rewrites for free would recover only **0.22% of the whole-verifier instruction gap**. For scale, the *entire* reverse rewrite phase costs about 3.4% of the gap. The qualifying rows on Ticket cost 0.15% of its gap. Selecting rows this way would also require accounting for failed cache probes, eviction, proofs and resource charging. Keep both sweeps and move the larger experiment to Ticket's per-instance rewriter, where matched visits already identify a roughly fourfold cost per step. [Observers, row classifications, paired verifier driver, reference outputs and raw counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-value-producers.tar.xz)

A separate overlay moved the ordinary validated fast return into `GetHash`, following `GetKind`. Across five paired runs at default GC it changed median paired instructions by −0.25% on hybrid, +0.46% on Ticket, −0.03% on ARM and +0.22% on FBA. Seven pairs with GC off saved 0.05–0.19% instructions on all four. Median paired cycles fell 0.40–1.01% across the two panels. The trial is archived for reference. Its instruction saving on Ticket is small relative to the measured gap.

To locate a larger target, a second analysis partitioned the earlier 24 Ticket g3 instruction profiles inside the quantifier queue’s theory rewrite. Application reduction accounts for **119 of 386** samples on check 127 and **128 of 476** on check 290. Expression-cache paths account for 51 and 66, and result ownership outside those two groups for 29 and 35. Categories use the archived script’s precedence when frames overlap. The Boolean AND/OR reducer `mkNFlatBody` was the most frequent reduction leaf across the two checks (26 samples), followed by declaration identity (19) and family lookup (15). The next experiment should count Boolean operand scans, repeated declaration lookups and actual simplifications per reduction on both engines. These samples are from the earlier matched replays and guide the choice of experiment; a current baseline is needed to quantify any saving.

### Frontend revision determines whether the Apple benchmark reaches g3

| Complete verification | GoIvy revision | Passed obligations | Released g3 median | Linked Z3 median |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary Raft (`raft_no_assume_test`) | 77f7733de | 419 | 2.663 s | 32.633 s |
| Apple `rfn2` | 07cdeec61 | 26 | 1.477 s | 9.276 s |
| Apple `dramc_nb2` | 07cdeec61 | 2,479 | 15.353 s | 18.347 s |

Each row used three alternating pairs on one pinned CPU with the same frontend, default GC and byte-identical transcripts. The older frontend was built from a source export with its local replacement pointing to the released solver. On GoIvy `77f7733de`, the current g3 and linked Z3 both reject `rfn2` during isolate construction. Stock g3 has the same diagnostic. The current Python Ivy checker also rejects it. The diagnostic identifies the call out to `rfn.abs.send[implement238]` from the hook at line 1958 of `ord_live.ivy` and its potential write to `rfn.abs.lastq`. No solver timing is available for this input on that frontend.

With g3 fixed at `1a65666db`, historical GoIvy `087c43b73` passed all 26 obligations. Its immediate successor `3dc52e26b` introduced the rejection. On the current frontend, a diagnostic overlay omitted assumed-invariant symbols only from the second symbol collection, which feeds the interference check. Both Apple isolates then reached all 26 and 2,479 successful obligations. Omitting them only from the first collection still produced the rejection, as did restoring only the old mixin membership predicate. The observer identified `rfn.abs.invar240` and `rfn.abs.invar241`, the assumptions at lines 1868–1869 which read `lastq`. Determining which assumed invariants should count as visible across this call requires an isolate-semantics decision. All performance comparisons above use stock frontend semantics. ## November 26 — Where the two Ticket CLI replays spend their instructions

Nine alternating pairs on one pinned CPU counted retired user instructions across SMT-LIB command boundaries. Each process received the original commands with echo acknowledgements inserted between groups. An empty acknowledgement cost about 5,000–7,000 instructions. Both engines returned unsat and matched decisions, conflicts, quantifier instantiations and resource counts on every run. The Go CLI used its default GC target of 400 and one P. Numbers below are median millions of instructions.

| Command | Ticket 127 g3 | Ticket 127 Z3 | Ticket 290 g3 | Ticket 290 Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| First sort declaration | 33.98 | 20.09 | 33.98 | 20.09 |
| First assertion | 11.36 | 14.34 | 10.13 | 13.67 |
| First push | 65.96 | 20.29 | 68.99 | 20.71 |
| Check | 153.48 | 54.61 | 173.85 | 56.73 |
| Complete process, including other commands | 277.94 | 119.12 | 298.63 | 120.26 |

The check explains 62% and 66% of the respective instruction gaps. First push explains 29% and 27%. On earlier Ticket 127 profiles, 577 of 804 g3 push samples went through the general rewriter. Across both inputs, 672 of 738 Go first-sort samples built the default strategy tree. GoIvy's incremental solver factory already defers this construction, which limits the relevance of CLI startup tuning to complete GoIvy verification.

Two overlays screened smaller opportunities. Borrowing the existing annotation views on quantifiers with at most one annotation of each kind saved 0.34M and 0.30M complete-process instructions. Using a native shift to form small BV sort bounds saved 0.72–0.76M first-sort instructions at GOGC=100 and changed power-cache population. Both trials stayed experimental. In a separate full-rate allocation profile, growing formula batches allocated 183,600 bytes on recorded Ticket 127 first-push stacks. Enode and fingerprint creation accounted for 383,184 and 342,432 allocated bytes on recorded check stacks. These figures measure allocation traffic and exclude caller stacks truncated before the phase marker.

A third overlay preallocated formula batches using the input count in the assertion passes and macro finder. In nine alternating pairs it saved just 69,000 and 71,000 first-push instructions (about 0.1% of push), with identical verdicts and all four search counters. The counts also overestimate required capacity when simplification discards rows. We kept the existing growth policy. The next experiment should target repeated work in the general rewriter reached by both push and check. ## November 26 — Theory rewriter application costs on Ticket

Across 24 matched runs of each Ticket replay, g3's theory rewriter during quantifier instantiation received 1,651 instruction samples and Z3's received 433. The innermost physical engine operation was application processing in 667 and 165 samples respectively. Application processing explains about **41% of the sampled rewriter gap** there. During first push the corresponding counts were 511 of 1,727 in Go and 212 of 536 in C++, about **25% of the gap**. These are physical-stack estimates with one sample per 1,000,003 user instructions. Inlining affects the method boundary. Every run matched the verdict and four search counters. All accepted profiles had zero lost or throttled records.

A second 12-round panel recorded the immediate physical callee of the application frame. During instantiation, 185 of 289 such Go samples entered the configured application reducer. In C++, 30 of 83 entered a visible reduce_app callee. During first push the counts were 158 of 267 and 62 of 117. Together with the earlier exact frame census, this points to cheaper dispatch and term access within each reduction. Changing how Go appends the 32-byte traversal frame alone moved complete replay instructions by at most 0.01%.

One case requires no reduction. When the ordinary theory rewriter visits a nullary uninterpreted application, the declaration has no theory operator and the ITE rules have no operands. If the proof register is empty, g3 now acquires the constant directly for the result stack. Substitutions still run first. A prior proof takes the regular path so its reference is released before the result is acquired. The new test exercises both register states and checks the exact reference counts through two visits and pops. [Rewriter](ast/rewriter/rewriter_engine.go) · [Ownership test](ast/rewriter/th_rewriter_test.go) · [Benchmark](ast/rewriter/theory_constant_benchmark_test.go)

| Ticket 127 complete process, median M instructions | 277.87 | 276.79 |
| Ticket 290 complete process, median M instructions | 298.64 | 297.45 |

The independent benchmark used eleven alternating pairs of 400,000 rewrites on a pinned CPU. Both cases had zero allocations. The command measurements used nine pairs at the ordinary CLI GC target of 400. On the complete runs below, the release-change column uses the median paired elapsed percentage across nine Go-vs-Go rotations. The engine comparison uses a separate five-pair panel with the same GoIvy revision (77f7733de), CPU 10, GOGC=100 and byte-identical verifier output.

| Complete verification | Release change, elapsed | g3 median | Linked Z3 median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket | −2.55% | 441 ms | 242 ms |
| Hybrid | −0.66% | 1,231 ms | 852 ms |
| ARM rules3 | −0.66% | 474 ms | 338 ms |
| FBA | −1.60% | 106 ms | 136 ms |

Complete-verifier instruction changes were −0.02% for Ticket, −0.15% for hybrid, −0.69% for ARM, and +0.24% for FBA. The 33% microbenchmark reduction applies only to an eligible constant. The whole-process effect depends on how much time that workload spends rewriting such leaves.

Eight alternative overlays remain experimental. Resetting the initial ten-cell activity table in place saved at most 0.03M whole-process instructions. Combining its first cells, queue and header in one allocation saved 0.17M. Only 165 of 1,491 and 149 of 1,710 constructed caches ever received an insertion. A single lookup for a quantifier's body and three counts saved 0.72–0.76M replay instructions, but default-GC Ticket over seven complete pairs used 1.12% more instructions, and FBA elapsed rose 10.16%. At GOGC=off their instruction changes were −0.11% and −0.04%. Reusing equality operands, combining declaration reads, dispatching on the original application's cached identity, and bypassing dispatch on unchanged nonconstant uninterpreted applications each saved 0.21–0.96M replay instructions. The nonconstant shortcut needs additional guards because binary applications can pull ITEs through their arguments.

The remaining Ticket gap spans several operations. Even erasing the entire sampled excess in queue application processing would recover about 10.5M instructions per replay on average (502 excess samples over 48 runs). The mean complete-process gap exceeds 160M. The existing phase profile places a further 16.5–23.6M excess instructions per check in queue clause assertion. Measure the two engines' literal internalizations, enode lookups, relevance registrations and clause insertions per asserted instance, including repeated inputs, before changing the rewriter again.
