The retained change is `05092af7a`. All six independent resource-limited SMT queries matched their original verdict and every collected integer search statistic in five pairs each. Complete ordinary Raft matched all 419 obligations and both output streams in three pairs, with median elapsed 2.634 s after and 2.644 s before. The ordinary rewriter, SMT core and API package tests passed, along with checked/debug/trace rewriter tests and rewriter vet.

## November 26 — Ticket quantified clause assertion and enode flag lifetime

Two instrumented CLIs counted work from entry to return of each quantifier instance assertion. Both returned unsat and reproduced decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. All fifteen logical counters matched after **every** assertion. Binding counts below examine operands of asserted root disjunctions after stripping at most one negation. Watch counts also cover gates created while processing those assertions.

| Work inside assertions | Ticket 127 | Ticket 290 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Assertions | 1,389 | 1,241 |
| Already-bound root OR operands / total | 4,858 / 6,310 | 4,417 / 5,416 |
| New Boolean variables | 1,929 | 3,076 |
| New enodes | 1,571 | 1,657 |
| Root clauses | 1,387 | 1,241 |
| OR watch ignored / immediately invoked / installed | 3,445 / 501 / 3,081 | 3,694 / 852 / 3,845 |
| Generic internalization calls, g3 / Z3 | 5,894 / 14,095 | 10,248 / 17,420 |

Sixteen alternating pairs sampled the uninstrumented binaries on CPU 12 with a period of 1,000,003 user instructions. Stacks containing both quantifier instantiation and the assertion routine accounted for 453 / 181 samples (g3 / Z3) on Ticket 127 and 610 / 148 on Ticket 290. This gives **17.0M and 28.9M estimated excess instructions per replay** inside that stack boundary. Clause construction appeared on 74 / 50 and 142 / 43 samples. Enode creation appeared on 90 / 24 and 88 / 5. The two engines expose different physical frames for Boolean publication and watch registration, so those fine-grained buckets are unsuitable for direct subtraction. The matched counts locate the gap in the work performed per assertion. Generic entry counts alone do not explain it.

Seven small trials tested an earlier enode lookup, conditional declaration flag reads, coallocated short enode argument storage, stack storage for short root ORs, short auxiliary clause sorting, hoisting assignment validation, and a cheaper negation accessor. None saved more than 0.22% of whole-process instructions on either input. We discarded all seven.

Commit `148eb53f7` removes an undo entry when the Boolean variable acquiring an enode was created at the current scope. Popping already retires that variable. A variable from an outer scope still needs its old flag restored. The regression exercises both lifetimes and repeats the push after popping. Before the fix the trail held both variables. Counting the entire replay through the final assertion found 1,630 and 1,635 same-scope appends and zero outer-scope appends. Both replays eliminated a 512-entry backing array, **2 KiB per solver**.

| 512-variable scoped benchmark | Baseline ns/op | Release ns/op | Trail capacity before / after | Paired instructions | Paired cycles |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All scoped | 229,778 | 212,857 | 2,048 / 0 bytes | −0.74% | −7.94% |
| Half survive | 189,193 | 178,096 | 2,048 / 1,024 bytes | −0.38% | −7.00% |

Elapsed medians used seven pairs of 100 iterations. Hardware counters used seven pairs of 1,000. The complete Ticket CLI processes moved by less than 0.005M instructions each. Four complete GoIvy controls matched both output streams and exit status. Across the first seven pairs, elapsed changed −0.36% on ARM, +6.77% on FBA, +0.54% on hybrid and +1.39% on Ticket. In seventeen additional pairs with the initial order reversed, FBA changed −0.65% and Ticket −3.35%. The scoped benchmark and trail footprint justify the change. Complete-verifier timings do not establish a repeatable speedup. Ordinary smtcore and API tests, focused checked/debug/trace tests and smtcore vet passed.

For the next experiment, measure clause insertion by arity and outcome, including binary auxiliary clauses emitted while building a formula gate. Ticket 290 shows the larger clause-construction difference. Count attempted clauses, literals simplified, units propagated and watch attachments before testing a direct binary insertion path against native ordering, proof creation and scope restoration. [Observers, profiles, trials and raw measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-ticket-clause-assertion.tar.xz) · [Scoped benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_flag_benchmark_test.go)

A second pair of instrumented CLIs counted attempted clauses by input width, final width and storage choice inside the same assertion boundary. All 87 nonempty rows matched exactly across engines. All attempts were auxiliary clauses. Each engine attempted 2,593 clauses on Ticket 127 and 6,829 on Ticket 290.

Both solvers pay for ordinary clause storage on most final pairs because the native compact representation has scope and level restrictions. A Go trial directly simplified distinct unassigned pairs into sorted order, then used the existing insertion path. Across nine pairs, total instructions fell just 0.046% and 0.113% on the two replays. Decisions, conflicts, instantiations, resource counts and verdicts matched throughout. In these two replays native chooses the same representation class at the same frequency. ## November 26 — Ordinary clause construction and Boolean negation costs

The matched clause census above showed both engines storing 2,548 simplified binary clauses as ordinary clauses on Ticket 290. Twelve earlier paired instruction profiles per input let us isolate construction within quantified assertion. Ticket 127 yielded 68 g3 samples and 33 native samples inside the clause routine. Ticket 290 yielded 131 and 28. Of the 199 Go samples, 28 included the clause object constructor. None exposed a separate watch insertion frame. Watch insertion can inline, so the profile alone gives no timing for attachment. In nine paired complete replay runs, allocating fresh short clauses in groups of sixteen reduced instructions by 0.087% and 0.180%. Reading the two already-selected literals directly for watch attachment saved 0.029% and 0.060%. Moving clause storage into a separate method allowed Go to open-code deferred scratch restoration and saved 0.121% and 0.236%. The split gave mixed complete-verifier results. We kept the existing storage and clause implementation.

The same profiles showed runtime defer handling in Boolean negation. The ordinary atom case previously checked NOT, fetched both canonical truth values, then queried the application identity separately for equality and equivalence. Release `474a4b0f8` dispatches on operand identity once. Only the equality case allocates and releases a temporary reference. The equality rewriter also now calls the theory value recognizer only when the other operand is an ITE, following the two short-circuit predicates in this fork's C++ bool_rewriter.cpp.

| Negation operand | Baseline ns/op | Release negation ns/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary atom, no reduction | 42.87 | 6.75 |
| Nested negation | 32.27 | 24.88 |
| True | 48.21 | 24.46 |

Seven rotating pairs used 500,000 iterations on CPU 14, with zero allocations in the measured loops. The negation-only variant saved 0.586% and 0.683% of whole-process replay instructions. The final source saved **0.688% and 0.864%** in eleven pairs against the release baseline. Verdict, decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource usage matched throughout. Six independent resource-limited queries also matched verdict and all collected integer search counters in five pairs each.

| Complete verifier | Release change in instructions | Release change in elapsed | g3 median | Linked Z3 median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

| Hybrid | −0.51% | −0.66% | 1,247 ms | 866 ms |
| ARM rules3 | +0.26% | −0.19% | 489 ms | 354 ms |
| FBA | −0.88% | −1.04% | 115 ms | 147 ms |

The changes are median paired percentages from nine complete before/after runs. The absolute medians are from a separate seven-pair comparison to linked Z3. Each panel used the same pinned core, frontend revision and normal GC. All runs matched the reference exit and both streams. Short verifier elapsed is variable. The negation-only Ticket trial initially measured +8.68% elapsed and then −0.58% in fifteen reverse-order pairs. The repeatable evidence for this release is the cheaper reducer and the two matched command replays. Ordinary rewriter, SMT core and API tests, full checked/debug/trace rewriter tests and rewriter vet passed.

A syntax scan identified 72 locations to inspect for unnecessary eager evaluation. Three macro-finder guards appeared capable of avoiding whole expression walks. Instrumentation found zero such opportunities on complete Ticket, hybrid and ARM and three on FBA. Those guards have low priority for this panel. For a larger Ticket improvement, profile repeated work by quantifier body and binding tuple across a complete search. ## November 26 — Quantifier subtree reuse and unary enode costs

Across complete Ticket verification the compiled substitution plans constructed 36,637 applications. Exact ordered operand handles and plan positions identified 12,086 repeat constructions among the 36,302 applications of arity eight or less. Every previous result was still live and the constructor returned the same handle. FBA had 9,777 repeats in 12,250 calls. Repeat frequency alone overstates the opportunity. In eleven alternating pairs on Ticket 127 and 290, bypassing construction saved only 0.546M and 0.229M instructions when both arms paid the same lookup cost. With lookup included, the experimental cache cost 2.376M and 1.242M more instructions than production. A cheaper trial remembering only the previous binding also failed to improve either replay.

Compiling a substitution plan on the second eligible call instead of the fourth saved 0.13–1.23% of complete verifier instructions across hybrid, Ticket, ARM and FBA in nine rotating triples. On Ticket the mean plan backing capacity observed at eligible calls rose from 4,903 to 11,215 bytes and the maximum rose from 20,480 to 29,088 bytes. The mean weights requests and measures only the plan arrays. First-use compilation reduced FBA instructions by 2.52% but increased its elapsed time by 1.87%. The release keeps fourth-use promotion.

A second observer followed the theory rewriter during instance materialization. It compared a frame's expression, depth limit and quantifier with completed frames from previous rewrites on that solver. On hybrid, 32 previously unchanged expressions subsequently rewrote to a different result, including 31 negations. In 28 cases both traversals took one step. A cache using those keys would change behavior. Eight alternating instruction-profile pairs attributed about 50M Ticket instructions and 90M hybrid instructions per verification to application processing under previously unchanged strict children. These estimates include bookkeeping and give the scale of the work before accounting for any safe lookup and maintenance costs.

The scoped enode benchmark exposed two allocations for ordinary binary nodes. Putting a node and both pointers in one allocation eliminated one allocation but whole-record initialization added write-barrier work. Allocating blocks of sixteen raised the width-2,048 fixture from about 433 KB to 495 KB per operation. A combined layout for unary and binary nodes added eight allocated bytes per unary node. We kept the existing layout. A separate change in `af7d977bc` reuses a registered unary operand through the ordinary term internalizer. It applies the same ownership and theory guards as the existing binary path. In complete Ticket, 679 of 679 eligible unary operands were already registered. The counts were 675/680 for hybrid, 1,337/1,340 for ARM and 39/40 for FBA.

| Unary scope width | Whole-process instructions | Benchmark elapsed per operation |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 | −9.43% | −11.44% |
| 256 | −9.82% | −11.64% |
| 2,048 | −7.37% | −11.83% |

Nine rotating triples measured each width. Allocation counts and bytes per operation matched baseline at each width. A regression discovered while testing this path also showed that registering a stale borrowed enode after slot reuse displaced its live replacement and cleared its relevance mark. Fix `71111321e` checks the borrowed owner's generation before publishing anything. Ordinary SMT core and API tests, focused checked/debug/trace tests, and SMT core vet passed. [Scoped benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_scope_batch_benchmark_test.go) · [Stale-registration regression](smtcore/smt_expression_setters_test.go)

Whole-verifier timing gives no repeatable Ticket gain. Six independent command holdouts matched verdicts and search counters in three pairs each.

## November 26 — Projection lifetime and finite-model function lookup

Three changes survived testing against solver baseline `af7d977bc`. All retain the existing arena and solver-local ownership.

### A completed projection kept its compiler alive

The quantified projector returned a pointer to the Boolean problem embedded in its compiler. In Go, that interior pointer kept the enclosing allocation reachable, including the term interning map, argument storage, source identities and gate-building scratch. Commit `97394ed5a` copies the result header before returning. The SAT consumer owns the same clause slice and sees the same variable count and work charge.

The regression benchmark holds sixteen completed projections of Apple `dramc_nb2` obligation 71 over one shared source AST. A collection before construction and another with all sixteen results live isolate what the results retain. Across nine rotating rounds the median fell from **873,477 to 73,777 live bytes per problem**, an **11.8× reduction**. This measures the handoff to SAT. The solver's other storage and the shared source AST are outside the delta. [Live-result benchmark](api/api_quantified_premises_test.go) · [Result ownership](api/internal/order/quantified_boolean.go)

Commit `c7f374a98` sizes the initial term table of a one-shot grounding from the parsed DAG and the remaining work budget, up to 2,048 entries. Tables kept for sibling goals still grow on demand. The fresh Apple projection fell from 2.17 to 2.04 ms and from 263 to 219 allocations. With a reusable parsed base it fell from **1.19 to 1.08 ms**, **1,072,120 to 886,056 B/op**, and **207 to 163 allocations**. These are nine-round medians, 25 projections per timed sample. Five whole-verifier allocation pairs also showed a reduction on hybrid, from 384.9 MB for the result-copy build to 379.9 MB with the bounded reservation. A trial reserving the full input size also saved allocations but could reserve more at once or keep spare capacity in the sibling-goal index. [Grounding implementation](api/internal/order/quantified_goal.go)

### How much time enode creation explains

| Workload | Paired profiles | Samples in g3 creation | Samples in Z3 creation | Share of whole-process instruction gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket 127 replay | 12 | 52 | 15 | 2.0% |
| Ticket 290 replay | 12 | 66 | 6 | 2.9% |
| Complete Ticket | 6 | 474 | 76 | 4.0% |
| Complete hybrid | 6 | 798 | 253 | 3.0% |

Each sample represents 1,000,003 retired user instructions. The percentage divides the excess creation samples by the excess samples across both whole processes. The call-tree anchors were g3's internal `mkEnode` and C++ `smt::context::mk_enode`. On complete Ticket, g3 had 270 construction samples, 69 in congruence insertion and 47 in registration. The respective construction and congruence counts in Z3 were 35 and 29. Some native registration is inline. These profiles include all newly created enodes and work below the creation routine. Operand internalization and variable binding before entry have separate call paths. Boolean nodes dominate the population, but even eliminating the measured excess inside creation would close only a small part of the gap. Sampling, inlining and stack unwinding limit the precision of these estimates.

### Scanning function interpretations in the candidate-model checker

In six complete hybrid profiles, calls through g3's quantifier manager to check a candidate model accounted for about **1.65 billion instructions per run**. The disjoint estimates included 629M in candidate-model generation, 479M elsewhere in auxiliary counterexample processing, 189M in finite-table compilation and 182M in the recursive table evaluator. These are g3 costs. The instruction saving available in each phase depends on the work native also does.

The evaluator copied each function row, including eight key integers, and tested the full key at every position. Commit `7562d9212` reads the row in place and compares the first two positions before checking the remainder of a wider key. The compiler zero-pads both keys. The first matching row determines the result, and the evaluator charges for every row through that match. A miss still charges for the full scan before evaluating the default interpretation. [Evaluator](smtcore/smt_model_table_check.go) · [Shared-prefix regression](smtcore/smt_model_table_diagram_test.go)

| 32-row function table | Before | Release |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unary, first hit | 26.99 ns | 12.38 ns |
| Unary, last hit | 347.7 ns | 42.54 ns |
| Binary, last hit | 350.0 ns | 47.94 ns |
| Eight arguments, last hit | 395.0 ns | 77.87 ns |
| Eight arguments, default | 386.1 ns | 80.18 ns |

Nine rotating triples used 250,000 calls per sample, with zero allocations per call. These benchmark keys differ in the first position. The shared-prefix regression also exercises keys that first differ in the third position. An independent evaluator compared the old and new implementations inside six complete verifications. All **277,403 root evaluations** agreed on value, remaining work and incomplete status, including 225,292 on hybrid and 17,506 on TLB. Both output streams and exit status matched on every workload. [Lookup benchmark](smtcore/smt_model_table_lookup_benchmark_test.go)

### Trials and the next measurement

- A row index preserved the original work charge but raised complete hybrid instructions by 0.26%. Memoizing finite terms that depend on at most two bindings raised hybrid instructions by 0.77%. An oracle checked value and budget preservation. The simpler row scan was cheaper.
- Storing a single resolved literal inside its unit justification saved just 0.03% and 0.09% on the two Ticket replays with GC off. Normal-GC results moved in opposite directions. The current justification still records every removed literal needed by assumption cores.
- Gating an ITE fold by arity, specializing theory traversal callbacks, and gating the one-bit equality rule by operand shape and sort each saved less than 0.45% of replay instructions with GC off. The sort trial improved the uninterpreted equality reducer from 154 to 123 ns, but the complete hybrid run took longer. Those variants remain experiments. [Reducer benchmark](ast/rewriter/th_rewriter_benchmark_test.go)
- **Next measure repeated function interpretation compilation within one candidate model.** Across 162 hybrid model-check calls the finite checker compiled 26,798 function tables. On 21,512 of those compilations it had already compiled the same declaration within that call. All 21,512 repeats had identical fallback handles and identical ordered argument and result handles, including 27,904 repeated rows. The census also found 19,024 empty tables among all compilations. Start by pricing empty and repeated tables separately. If they account for material work, test sharing the source rows during a single model-check call while preserving each quantified body's local value IDs, exact work charges and handling of nested function interpretations. Candidate-model generation itself took over three times as many samples as table compilation and warrants a direct native comparison before expanding the cache.

The evidence archive includes the release timings, allocation profiles, per-round instruction samples, per-tuple oracle counts, tested variants and reproduction drivers. [Measurements and scripts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-projection-lifetime-and-model-lookup.tar.xz)

### November 26 — Quantifier model adjustment on hybrid

Across six matched profiles of complete hybrid verification, candidate-model construction averaged **680 million retired user instructions in g3 and 420 million in linked Z3**. Quantifier model adjustment alone accounted for about **243 million excess instructions**, roughly 8% of the whole-process gap. Both implementations visit the ground applications of a function to build the instantiation set for each quantified variable in an argument position. On the Go side, ordinary map probes and the AES memory hash accounted for 407 of 1,895 samples inside adjustment. Native's most frequent individual leaf was the relevance test for an expression. [Phase counts by run](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-candidate-phases.csv) · [Profile reader](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/candidate_phases.py)

| Per complete hybrid run, estimated million instructions | g3 | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Quantifier model adjustment | 315.8 | 72.5 |
| Value generation | 178.8 | 322.0 |
| Partial function completion | 4.0 | 0.5 |
| Model cleanup | 100.2 | 18.3 |
| Other constructor work | 80.8 | 7.0 |

Each sample represents 1,000,003 instructions. The anchors are the Go kernel's candidate builder and native context's proto-model builder, across all callers. The earlier 629M g3 estimate covered the calls from model checking. Phase boundaries differ slightly. Native includes initialization and macro registration in its value generator. The Go profile attributes about 64M instructions for these two operations to other constructor work. The profiles were collected on g3 baseline `af7d977bc`. They measure aggregate work across a verification, including differences in the number of calls.

Commit `22b2eb3b3` scans each plain function argument position once per graph build. Merges precede population. The first scan inserts original ground arguments in context order, with their original generations. Later ordinary scans would only encounter existing entries. The mark belongs to the specific function and position, since two functions sharing the same root can supply different ground terms. Offset calculations and each resource-limit checkpoint still execute in their original order. Commit `6e13043d9` uses the node's already validated sort on a graph-index hit. Both indexes and the population marks expire at graph reset. [Implementation](smtcore/smt_model_finder_auf_graph.go) · [Shared-set and relevance tests](smtcore/smt_model_finder_auf_graph_test.go)

| Graph rebuild, median µs | Before | Scan once | Scan once and reuse sorts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 quantifiers, 32 ground arguments | 57.9 | 28.5 | 26.7 |
| 32 quantifiers, 32 ground arguments | 221.3 | 76.3 | 59.1 |
| 128 quantifiers, 32 ground arguments | 875.9 | 290.6 | 222.0 |
| 512 quantifiers, 32 ground arguments | 3,397.9 | 1,057.3 | 779.6 |
| 512 quantifiers, empty ground context | 1,077.6 | 1,059.4 | 786.0 |

Each quantifier mentions seven shared predicates and one private predicate. The populated fixture registers the same 32 distinct arguments for each shared predicate and checks the resulting set size. Nine rotating rounds measured 16 reset/build iterations per fixture on CPU 16. Run both benchmarks with `go test ./smtcore -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkSMTModelFinder(SharedGroundArguments|AUFGraph)$' -cpu=1 -benchtime=16x -count=9`. [Benchmark source](smtcore/smt_model_finder_auf_benchmark_test.go) · [All benchmark samples](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-graph-ground-arguments.csv)

The exact release ran seven rotating triples on CPU 12 with GoIvy `77f7733de`, ordinary GC, one Go processor and PGO off. Percentages are medians of the within-round change against `7562d9212`. Independent process-time medians appear in the next two columns. Every exit status and both output streams matched the reference, including three additional pairs on each of the expected-failure workloads TLB and test_liveness2.

| Complete verification | Release instructions | Release elapsed | g3 median, ms | Linked Z3 median, ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hybrid | −1.30% | −2.29% | 1,153 | 820 |
| Ticket | −0.42% | −2.26% | 423 | 234 |
| ARM rules3 | −0.35% | −1.11% | 462 | 329 |
| FBA | −0.76% | −2.46% | 106 | 137 |

Hybrid also saved 1.09% of instructions in the preceding nine-round trial. The other three workloads varied in sign between the trial and the release comparison. The shared-ground graph result and the hybrid instruction saving repeated. The ordinary SMT core and proto-model suites, model-finder tests under checked/debug/trace, and SMT core vet passed. [Complete release triples](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-graph-release.csv) · [Development triples](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-graph-trial.csv) · [Negative proof controls](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-graph-holdouts.csv)

The earlier 189M estimate covers the entire finite-table term compiler. In the baseline stacks, 63M occurred outside function compilation, 94M in function compilation outside its recursive fallback-term compilation, and 32M below the latter. A cache of interpreted functions has to rebuild or translate quantifier-local term and value IDs and account for the original work budget. The total time spent translating all terms is too broad an estimate of its potential payoff. [Reclassification](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/table_compile_phases.py) · [Counts by round](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-table-compile.csv)

A profiling-only build marked the first successful function build for each declaration within a single model check. On later local-cache misses it ran the same compiler under a separate stack frame. Six complete runs put **107M instructions** per verification under repeated builds. A second six-run observer split those calls by the previously completed table's row count. It measured **77M for repeated nonempty tables and 34M for repeated empty tables**. Nested calls are attributed to the innermost building function. All 12 transcripts matched, and the profiles had zero lost or throttled records. The markers add a lookup to the observer. These numbers include work such as compiling a fallback or assigning local IDs that reuse would still need to perform. Even removing the entire measured repeat cost would recover under 4% of the approximately 3B instruction gap. [Observer source, raw counts and replay scripts](perf/ivy_apple/model_finder/nov26-function-compilation-study.tar.xz)

A larger next experiment is to partition the entire remaining hybrid gap by verification obligation and compare the number of candidate builds, auxiliary checks and fallback queries in each engine on the highest-cost obligations. Agreement on the final verdict alone leaves room for substantially different search work. If model cleanup is pursued, native reuses its argument buffer through the traversal of one function fallback. Go currently allocates the argument slice inside the visit loop and reads the AST kind more than once. Price those two changes independently on model cleanup and on complete hybrid.

### November 26 — Where hybrid's quantifier searches diverge

Batch 35, goal 1 accounts for the largest concrete-check gap on hybrid reliable broadcast. The check took **336M instructions in g3 versus 51M in linked Z3**. The two engines queued 380 entries, rewrote 203 instances and asserted 203 lemmas before entering the first candidate-model check. The counts then diverged. In the first candidate both engines checked 64 quantifiers. g3 found nine falsifying tuples in the finite tables. Z3 made nine restricted auxiliary queries. g3 went on to check a second candidate, while native finished during the search following its first.

| Batch 35, goal 1 | g3 release | g3 with auxiliary witness selection | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Candidate checks | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| Quantifiers examined | 129 | 64 | 64 |
| Complete auxiliary queries | 2 | 10 | 64 |
| Restricted auxiliary queries | 0 | 9 | 9 |
| Queue entries before first candidate | 380 | 380 | 380 |
| Queue entries following first candidate, before any second | 2,591 | 2,121 | 1,307 |
| Queue entries following second candidate | 2,352 | 0 | 0 |
| Nontrivial lemmas across the check | 2,517 | 1,140 | 803 |

In a separate five-run counter measurement, entry to the first model check came after **35.7M g3 instructions versus 13.5M native**, a 2.65× difference with matching queue counts. This interval includes initial search, propagation and model construction. The queue accounted for approximately **199M g3 instructions and 19M native** on the release comparison. Descendants of lemma assertion accounted for about 82M versus 4M and theory rewriting for 64M versus 7M. Both the amount of work and its cost matter. Dividing inclusive queue cost by nontrivial lemmas gives about 79,000 instructions in g3 and 24,000 in native. These rates include work on entries that produce no lemma, and the two searches process different mixes of expressions. Gated profiles used four accepted runs per engine, with 1,000,003 instructions per Go sample and 500,009 per native sample. Runs with a lost or throttled record were discarded.

Batch 31, goal 34 shows why reducing the number of lemmas alone will not close the gap. g3 asserted **1,995 lemmas versus 2,597 in Z3**, and checked three candidate models in both engines. The concrete check still took **289M versus 177M instructions**. This pair and the matched initial counts on batch 35 provide two controls for investigating the cost of rewriting and asserting individual instances.

Five counterbalanced pairs covered all 839 obligations on GoIvy `77f7733de` and g3 `6e13043d9`. g3 discharged 305 before the concrete solver. Across a complete run, the median sum inside the remaining 534 concrete checks was 4.69B instructions, compared with 2.69B in Z3's 839 checks. The first physical pushes cost 1.64B versus 0.54B, and g3 spent another 0.66B on early proof attempts. First push can fall on a different sibling in the two engines. The largest first-push gaps were 72–77M per batch in batches 31–33. These are solver-thread measurements with the adjacent empty interval subtracted. Whole-process results include additional work and have a different denominator.

#### Witness selection experiments

Using finite tables only to certify satisfied quantifiers saved about **155M instructions on the concrete check at 35/1** across three rounds, but increased complete hybrid instructions by **18.3%** and elapsed by **21.9%** across five rotations. At 19/29 the same change cost 176M extra instructions on the concrete check. Across hybrid it raised complete auxiliary queries from 360 to 921, restricted queries from 62 to 976, and all candidate-model builds, including auxiliary models, from 301 to 1,624. Linked Z3 made 5,896 complete queries and 1,046 restricted ones. Disabling the table checker entirely increased complete hybrid instructions by 36.2%.

| Alternative | Complete hybrid instructions vs release | Independent result |
|---|---:|---|
| Delegate all table witnesses to the auxiliary solver | +18.30% | +67.57% on FBA |
| Delegate only when inverse generation exceeds zero | +10.17% | +31.42% on FBA |
| Delegate only when inverse generation exceeds two | +12.30% | +1.61% on FBA |
| Vary the outer binder fastest in scalar enumeration | +0.37% | −0.67% on ARM |
| Reverse the unbounded domain value order | +3.36% | −3.30% on ARM, +32.80% on FBA |
| Use ordinary inferred multi-patterns | +0.35% | +98.71% on FBA |

All alternatives reproduced the expected proof transcripts and exit codes. Restricting the generation of table witnesses was motivated by the 35/1 census, where eight of the fifteen recovered witnesses had positive maximum generation. Those thresholds predicted poorly across the full verification. The release keeps direct table witnesses, the current enumeration order and connected triggers.

#### Clause simplification buffer lifetime

While profiling assertion, the existing auxiliary-clause benchmark exposed repeated allocation after a tautology. The simplifier restored its solver-owned scratch slices only after the filtering loop. A true literal, a complementary literal or a satisfied auxiliary clause could return earlier, discarding any growth during that visit. Commit `9caff730a` restores the buffers on every exit. The active insertion keeps private ownership through callbacks, including nested insertions. Each solver can retain the peak capacity reached by an early-returning clause for reuse.

| Tautological auxiliary clause | Before | Release | Heap per operation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 8 variables | 229 ns | 138 ns | 56 B and 3 allocations → 0 |
| 32 variables | 675 ns | 374 ns | 248 B and 5 allocations → 0 |
| 32 variables, auxiliary lemma | 719 ns | 393 ns | 248 B and 5 allocations → 0 |

Nine rotations on CPU 16 measured 20,000 calls per sample, including the unchanged caller-data and empty solver-clause checks. Across complete Ticket, ARM and FBA, the preceding code recorded zero early returns with buffer growth. Hybrid recorded one. Seven rotating whole-verifier comparisons produced no consistent elapsed gain from this change. Hoisting the solver-open check also improved the synthetic case, but added branching with mixed complete-verifier timings. Only buffer restoration was retained. The ordinary SMT core suite, checked/debug/trace clause and justification tests, and SMT core vet passed. [Clause benchmark](smtcore/smt_clause_simplify_benchmark_test.go) · [Implementation](smtcore/smt_internalizer.go)

[Hybrid obligation measurements and scripts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-hybrid-obligation-costs.tar.xz)

### November 26 — Matched hybrid lemmas and the cost of internalizing their operands

On hybrid batch 35, goal 1, the ordered inputs to all 203 queue rewrites and the ordered inputs to all 203 assertions before the first candidate model check agree between engines. The comparison traversed application names and ordered children, variable indices, and quantifier kind, bound sorts and body. A single bijection across both streams reconciled eight generated symbol suffixes. This comparison covers expression shape. It omits declaration signatures, quantifier annotations and triggers. Raw AST hashes alone agreed at only 60 of 203 positions in each stream.

| Instructions over the matched prefix, median of five complete verifications | g3 | g3 with automatic GC disabled | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Rewrite instantiated input | 5,945,978 | 5,860,251 | 1,837,853 |
| Assert resulting lemma | 8,991,303 | 6,850,087 | 1,970,529 |
| Process OR operands and obtain literals | 4,834,876 | 4,631,215 | 1,438,652 |
| Create root clause | 464,271 | 447,412 | 135,186 |
| Register relevance watches | 443,004 | 409,651 | 123,127 |
| Mark parent relevant | 1,213,411 | 1,203,624 | 258,967 |

Each operation uses the solver thread’s user-mode retired-instruction counter on CPU 14, less the adjacent empty read interval. The last four rows come from separate instrumented binaries. Each cell is the median of five per-run sums. Independent stage medians need not add up to the median of the complete assertion. All 203 assertions took the OR branch. With ordinary GC, the g3 assertion total ranged from 7.08M to 12.75M. Disabling automatic GC narrowed that range to 6.85–6.90M and still left a 3.48× gap to Z3. The GC-off runs are diagnostic only.

Of 639 disjuncts, g3 reused an existing signed binding 380 times. Those probes cost 88,108 instructions in total with GC off. The other 259 operands spent 4,431,592 instructions inside recursive internalization, 36,874 on the initial probe interval and 63,212 obtaining their literal afterward. At those same 259 positions, Z3 spent 1,364,324 instructions in internalization and 8,257 obtaining literals. The 3.25× difference in recursive internalization accounts for 3.07M instructions on these operands alone. At the 380 positions with reusable Go bindings, native internalization plus literal lookup cost 57,478 instructions. Enlarging the short-literal buffer or shaving a few instructions off successful binding probes has little leverage here.

On batch 31, goal 34, g3 rewrote and asserted 1,995 lemmas across the entire check, versus 2,597 for linked Z3. Total rewrite instructions were 35.45M versus 13.79M and assertion instructions were 48.27M versus 13.99M. Even with 23% fewer calls, g3 spent 2.57× as many instructions rewriting and 3.45× asserting. The two searches differ here. Only the prefix on 35/1 received the ordered tree comparison.

Three release-build trials carried binary operands from lemma construction, used an eight-literal local buffer, or reused the sign of an already resolved positive disjunct during relevance registration. Individually, all three raised complete hybrid instructions by 0.04–0.37% over five rotating pairs. ARM rose 0.70–1.78%. The combined implementation changed hybrid instructions by +0.04% and Ticket by +0.77% over seven pairs. All complete runs included in these panels matched the reference stdout, stderr and exit code. None of the three trials entered the release. [Raw measurements, expression trees and reproduction scripts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-hybrid-matched-lemmas.tar.xz)

### November 26 — Where matched Boolean operand internalization spends its instructions

On hybrid batch 35, goal 1, the two engines created the same 602 Boolean variables, 410 enodes and 286 sets of gate constraints while internalizing the 259 matched operands. Both emitted 1,149 gate clauses and inserted 328 nodes into the congruence table. Gate construction explains the largest measured difference, followed by enode creation.

| Operation on the 259 operands | Calls per engine | g3 instructions | Linked Z3 instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Create Boolean variable | 602 | 367,186 | 241,970 |
| Create and register enode | 410 | 1,225,745 | 418,407 |
| Construct enode and attach parents, within creation | 410 | 475,243 | 124,143 |
| Congruence insertion, within creation | 328 | 163,473 | 59,980 |
| Emit gate constraints and install relevance watches | 286 | 2,285,052 | 627,786 |
| Emit gate clause, within gate construction | 1,149 | 1,591,249 | 482,452 |
| Register gate relevance watches | 286 | 321,371 | 102,787 |

Five complete verifications per observer used thread-local hardware instruction counts on CPU 14 with automatic Go GC disabled. Rows are medians of per-verification sums after adjacent empty-read subtraction. Some rows contain other measured operations and their probes. Use the independent whole-call totals from the preceding study for overall costs. Both transcript streams and the exit code matched. Each run also checked all 639 operand positions and 203 gates at the assertion root.

Of the 1,149 gate clauses, 646 ended during simplification. Both engines constructed 384 ordinary clauses and attached 768 clause watches. Go spent about 640K instructions entering and filtering gate clauses through the simplifier, including 363K on the early exits. The native auxiliary simplifier took 153K over all calls. Go's clause object constructor took 175K versus 61K in Z3, and attaching their watches took 176K versus 113K. Reading proof mode and computing a gate proof took only 69K in g3. Even a free clause constructor alone would recover only a fraction of this gap.

#### Declaration lookup during enode construction

Z3 short-circuits its commutativity query when an enode has any arity other than two. g3 was fetching the declaration flags first, even when it suppressed the arguments. Commit `52ea5fd9d` tests effective arity before reading the flags, with the same checked lookup for binary nodes. Across seven rotating pairs of 10,000 and 100,000 creation/deletion iterations, zero-argument nodes fell from 904 to 734 instructions per iteration, unary from 1,179 to 1,010 and ternary from 1,556 to 1,388. The binary control moved from 1,383 to 1,390. Median elapsed fell from 188 to 166 ns for zero arguments and from 222 to 202 ns for one. Allocations were unchanged.

Seven full-verifier pairs with normal GC changed instructions by −0.10% on hybrid, −0.17% on Ticket, −1.05% on FBA and +0.70% on ARM. ARM elapsed increased 0.93%. On the 203 matched hybrid assertions, the subsequent GC-off median was 6.81M instructions against the preceding 6.85M. The constructor and scoped population benchmarks are the appropriate tests for the local benefit. [Constructor benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_creation_benchmark_test.go) · [Scoped population](smtcore/smt_enode_scope_batch_benchmark_test.go)

#### In-place auxiliary clause simplification

Commit `bac000a7f` uses a single solver-local backing array to sort a private copy and retain surviving literals. The write index can never overtake the read index. The solver detaches that array until clause publication and any nested insertion finish. A negative control that left the buffer available to a nested insertion changed the outer lemma from literals [8, 10, 12] to [2, 4, 6]. The regression verifies both installed clauses and the caller's unchanged input.

Compaction alone reduced scratch space but raised the 203-assertion total from 6.810M to 6.961M instructions. Separating the filtering loop from clause publication let Go open-code the deferred buffer restoration. Inspection of the compiled filter showed the call to runtime.deferprocStack disappear. The combined release took **6.769M** instructions for the same assertions with GC off. Recognizing satisfied binary gates ahead of sorting saved only 4K on the matched prefix and increased complete Ticket instructions by 0.87%. Ordering binary pairs separately also failed to improve the verifier panel consistently. Both trials remain in the study archive.

| Tautological ordinary auxiliary clause | Before | Combined release | Retained scratch capacity in literals |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 3 variables | 72.1 ns | 44.1 ns | 8 → 4 |
| 8 variables | 133.8 ns | 91.3 ns | 20 → 12 |
| 32 variables | 386.4 ns | 369.5 ns | 68 → 36 |
| 64 variables | 579.0 ns | 596.6 ns | 136 → 72 |

The timed runs used nine rotating pairs at 20,000 iterations. Each width includes one additional complementary literal. All ran with zero steady-state heap allocations. Capacity counts the backing arrays used for sorting, filtering and removed false literals. At width 64 the saving is 256 bytes per solver in backing storage, in addition to removing one slice header from the solver. Whole-process CPU results were smaller and mixed. In nine complete-verifier rotations against the enode-only baseline, instructions changed −0.32% on hybrid, +0.85% on Ticket, −0.45% on ARM and −1.06% on FBA. Median paired elapsed changed +1.17%, −0.81%, −0.59% and −1.81% respectively.

| Complete verification on CPU 14, median of seven rotating pairs | g3 at bac000a7f | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hybrid | 1,207 ms | 849 ms |
| Ticket | 434 ms | 236 ms |
| ARM rules3 | 472 ms | 335 ms |
| FBA | 109 ms | 137 ms |

Every verifier run used GoIvy 77f7733de, normal GC, and the same expected stdout, stderr and exit status per case. The complete SMT core and API tests, checked/debug/trace clause, justification and scope restoration cases, and SMT core vet passed. The gate-clause instruction difference on the **matched prefix** is 1.11M. For scale, the previously measured excess on the **complete check** was 285M. Prioritize the later search divergence before spending more time on binary clause shortcuts. In particular, compare the first post-candidate witness, its generation and the resulting instantiation cascade at 35/1 against a control where delegating witnesses increased the cost. ### November 26 — Which model witnesses change hybrid search?

At hybrid batch 35, goal 1, both solvers assert the same first 203 lemmas. Their first candidate model then produces witnesses for the same nine quantified formulas in order. For the first formula, a universal binary predicate, g3 uses the same ground node for both variables. Z3 uses distinct nodes. Replacing only that witness reproduces Z3's first asserted instance and *increases* the total from 2,517 to 2,697. Each of the nine single-witness interventions either tied the baseline or increased the total.

| Hybrid 35/1 | Lemmas before first candidate | Lemmas after each candidate | Post-candidate decisions | Post-candidate conflicts |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| Linked Z3 | 203 | 600 | 641 | 11 |
| g3 baseline | 203 | 1,154 + 1,160 | 1,403 + 986 | 18 + 12 |
| Use auxiliary choice for witness 1 | 203 | 1,110 + 1,384 | 1,506 + 1,091 | 15 + 14 |
| Use auxiliary choices for all nine | 203 | 600 | 641 | 11 |
| Use auxiliary choices for 3, 6 and 9 | 203 | 395 | 455 | 9 |

The last two experiments used the ordinary g3 auxiliary solver after the finite checker had found a complete inverse binding. With all nine delegated, the counts match native, but only the first four post-candidate lemma trees and 38 signed decisions match in order under a consistent renaming of fresh symbols. In the triple, the earlier auxiliary call for witness 3 produced the original binding. The later calls changed the binding for 6 to a different quorum and the binding for 9 to a term built from the opposite quorum. In the default search, 3 and 6 repeat a binding, as do 4 and 9. Delegating 3 and 6 alone reduced the total to 940. These experiments identify an interaction between witness choices and auxiliary solver history.

With GC disabled, three rotating complete hybrid runs per variant measured **310.9M → 95.7M instructions** inside the 35/1 check for the triple. Delegating all nine took 130.9M. The independent control, batch 19, goal 29, had already diverged before its first candidate (31 versus 14 lemmas). Delegating every table witness there preserved the first six binding tuples and the subsequent 160 lemmas and 257 decisions, but increased the full g3 check from 412 to 997 lemmas and **85.1M → 247.9M instructions**. Ordinals are diagnostic interventions. Every run checked the complete hybrid transcript and exit status. The measured check counters use identical Go instrumentation across variants.

Staggering repeated-sort traversal, selecting the first or last available inverse value, delegating repeated-term tuples, trying several scalar witnesses, and delegating on nearby alternative witnesses each gave mixed or negative results in seven rotating runs across hybrid, Ticket, FBA and ARM. Taking multiple witnesses increased FBA instructions by 54.8%. Choosing the first or last inverse value increased FBA by 19.4% or 30.0%.

#### A bounded rule for repeated unary bindings

Commit `0aa2cee00` tries an alternative when a unary quantifier would reuse a positive-generation term from the last 32 pending instances. It considers the first eight inverse values in table order. Each alternative must belong to the same domain, falsify the body within the remaining evaluation budget, and recover a ground term absent from those recent unary bindings. The checker already has a valid fallback. Finite resource limits, flattened quantifiers with added declarations, and certification-only checks retain their original selection. All mutable state remains local to the solver.

| Concrete hybrid check, GC off | Earlier g3 | Released g3 | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 35/1 | 309.5M | **93.4M** | 50.9M |
| 19/29 | 84.9M | **75.0M** | 35.3M |
| 31/36 | 33.3M | **12.8M** | 14.7M |
| 11/5 | 39.0M | **70.1M** | 55.9M |
| 10/1 | 49.3M | **74.4M** | 37.9M |
| 31/34 | 266.0M | **269.3M** | 176.6M |

Five rotating runs on CPU 14 covered all 839 obligations. The median sum of instructions in concrete checks fell from **4.071B to 3.898B**, against 2.692B in Z3. The largest remaining check gap was 92.7M on 31/34, followed by 65.9M on 31/33. First pushes totaled **1.384B versus 0.543B**. Profile the full first-push paths across the 34 fresh solvers and rank their disjoint costs. For search improvements, compare 31/34 with 11/5, where the new choice made search longer.

| Ticket | 438 ms | 240 ms | −0.60% |

| FBA | 109 ms | 139 ms | −2.76% |

The panel used nine rotating triples on CPU 12. Hybrid's median paired elapsed change was −3.10%, with a 3 ms difference between independently computed medians. Three GC-off confirmation pairs on ten complete workloads put hybrid at −2.44% instructions and test_liveness2 at **+1.41%**. The other eight changed by at most 0.12% in either direction. The complete Apple rfn2 and dramc_nb2 baseline and release transcripts also matched in three pairs on the compatible frozen frontend. Their release medians were 1.49 s and 16.07 s respectively. The first attempted Apple run on frontend 77f7733de hit the previously documented visible-effect diagnostic before checking the proof. The timed Apple runs on both sides used 07cdeec61. ### November 26 — Disjoint costs of all hybrid first pushes

Two independent sets of solver-thread hardware counters bracketed the first physical push of each of 34 fresh solvers on all 839 hybrid obligations. The first set timed each invoked preprocessing pass. The second timed the enclosing kernel push, its call to internalize pending assertions, and the preprocessing inside that call. Each table entry is the median of seven summed runs, with GC disabled and the complete transcript checked. These Go counters include the quantifier field-read improvement in `0f3389d37`. Both engines used GoIvy 77f7733de.

| Disjoint part of first push | g3, M instructions | Linked Z3, M | Excess, M |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Value propagation | 217.9 | 69.0 | 148.9 |
| Macro finding and expansion | 322.1 | 186.3 | 135.8 |
| Pattern inference | 156.2 | 41.1 | 115.1 |
| Maximize bit-vector sharing, including ordinary reduction | 149.7 | 44.8 | 104.9 |
| NNF conversion | 104.5 | 34.4 | 70.1 |
| Explicit reductions | 91.3 | 51.1 | 40.2 |
| Refine injectivity | 4.5 | 0.7 | 3.8 |
| Whole push outside the named passes | 325.1 | 117.0 | 208.1 |

The independent nested brackets split most of the 208M remainder. **Installing and committing assertions after reduction accounted for 105.9M** (132.5M versus 26.6M). The rest of the kernel push accounted for 43.8M and work outside the kernel push for 57.0M. The nested observer measured 1.371B versus 0.544B for the full window. The pass observer measured 1.371B versus 0.544B independently. Small differences between sums include counter and reporting overhead. Batches 31–33 together cost 253.4M versus 98.8M. Value propagation is the largest individual gap. The six rotating whole-process stack profiles also put about 348M g3 instructions under quantifier frame processing during external pushes, including its reducer callbacks. That is an overlapping call tree and cannot be added to the table above.

#### Quantifier traversal and pattern-variable membership

Commit `0f3389d37` reads the quantifier body and three immutable counts from a single arena lookup whenever the rewriter resumes a quantifier. Both proof modes use the accessor. Seven samples of five million reads measured **23.31 → 7.21 ns** with zero allocations. In seven alternating stage-only pairs the median sum across the 34 first pushes fell from **1,383.8M to 1,370.1M instructions**. [Field-read benchmark](ast/ast_quantifier_update_benchmark_test.go)

Commit `8446c5998` stores membership for de Bruijn indices 0–63 in one word. A sparse map covers larger indices. Pattern inference uses the same completed set when recording a candidate and gives each growing multi-pattern independent membership storage. A regression exercises indices 63, 64 and 1,023 in a nested application and checks both the child and parent sets. In a fresh seven-pair measurement **pattern inference fell from 156.2M to 142.2M instructions**. The stage-only total for the first pushes fell from 1,370.3M to 1,356.4M. The other named passes were essentially flat. [Wide-index regression](ast/pattern/free_vars_test.go) · [Complete inference benchmark](ast/pattern/shared_applications_benchmark_test.go)

| Shared application width | Before → after, µs | Bytes/op | Allocs/op |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4 | 9.40 → 6.85 | 3,101 → 1,949 | 50 → 30 |
| 16 | 17.33 → 13.79 | 8,406 → 6,134 | 78 → 38 |
| 128 | 91.41 → 69.58 | 62,197 → 47,381 | 417 → 153 |
| 512 | 360.54 → 261.44 | 234,485 → 176,661 | 1,572 → 540 |

Seven alternating pairs ran 300 complete inference operations per sample. The benchmark verifies the two selected triggers and their order. With ordinary GC, adding the packed set to the field-read release saved 0.71% of complete TLB instructions in five pairs and 0.42% on hybrid in seven pairs. Ticket rose 0.44% in the latter panel. With GC disabled the two changes together saved 0.48% of complete hybrid instructions across five rotating groups. The local improvements account for only a small fraction of complete verification.

Two additional trial builds bypassed annotation deduplication when each list had at most one element, or returned an unchanged unannotated nonground quantifier when all binders had previously been proved used. The first saved 7.2M first-push instructions and had flat hybrid instructions in the normal-GC panel. The second saved 27.9M first-push instructions, but raised normal-GC FBA instructions by 1.75% and had mixed cycle results. Both remain experiments. The second also changes temporary reference acquisitions and would require independent resource-boundary coverage before release.

While testing the same reducer, a real allocation refusal constructing a merged quantifier returned success with the original quantifier. The fallback update had overwritten the error. Commit `363cfd63c` propagates the failure. Its regression proves that the previous code reported success, that the output retains its prior value on failure, and that retry successfully merges all 129 declarations. The AST, rewriter, pattern, SMT core and API suites and focused checked/debug/trace cases passed. [Quantifier merge regression](ast/rewriter/th_quantifier_merge_failure_test.go)

#### Can the fresh solvers reuse an identical base?

An observation build recorded the actual ordered formula/proof handle pairs entering each pass on all 34 first pushes. It retained the AST owner, slot and generation. All pushes used one AST owner, so literal identity could be compared across these solver instances. **None of the 34 value-propagation input batches repeated an earlier complete batch.** Of 2,558 input rows, 859 had appeared in an earlier batch. Only 80 fell within the longest identical ordered prefix of any earlier batch. Pattern inference had 289 previously seen rows out of 2,297. These comparisons do not establish equality of substitutions or macro state.

Seven additional complete runs timed each forward and reverse value-sweep row, including its substitution update. The rows in those 80 shared prefixes cost **1.79M instructions** across both sweeps. Previously seen rows outside the prefix cost 38.81M; rows new to batch history cost 108.69M. The ten most expensive rows accounted for only 0.86% of the measured row work. The reverse classification refers to the row's original slot in the forward input. Even perfect reuse of the identical prefixes would recover little of the roughly 149M value-propagation gap. Seven complete paired runs measured 134.65M g3 instructions for row rewrite and installation versus 45.68M in the native rewriter call. A separate seven-run g3 observer restricted to the rewriter dispatch counted 126.30M. This puts approximately 80.6M excess instructions inside traversal and 8.4M in the surrounding Go code. Substitution insertion used 15.82M versus 1.55M. The follow-up ordinary reduction used 59.85M versus 20.24M. These operation brackets exclude loop and scope cleanup costs. In six sampled runs the most frequent g3 leaf in the value-sweep rewriter was application processing (37 of 509 samples), followed by frame entry (20). Substitution lookup, cache operations and reference updates also recurred. The next comparison should count visits, reductions and cache hits on these same rows to distinguish extra work from a higher cost per visit.

Seven rotating normal-GC triples measured complete hybrid at 8.428B release instructions versus 8.458B in the preceding release and 5.829B for Z3. The median paired instruction change was −0.49% on hybrid, −0.29% on Ticket, +0.19% on ARM and −0.73% on FBA. The final panel ran during heavy host contention (one-minute load above 80 on 48 logical CPUs); paired elapsed changed +14.1% on hybrid. The GC-off control gave −0.68% hybrid elapsed and −0.48% instructions for the two performance changes together. The timed evidence supports an instruction and allocation reduction. After load subsided, 13 new alternating pairs on CPU 21 confirmed the instruction saving (−0.54%) but **cycles rose 2.37% and elapsed rose 2.40%**. Median elapsed was 1,151 ms before and 1,179 ms after. On this workload the local gains have yet to translate into a full-verifier speedup. [Raw profiles, stage counters, input census, trial variants and verification records](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-first-push-quantifier-traversal.tar.xz)

### November 26 — Matched value-sweep visits and linear clause traversal

Two independent complete hybrid runs per engine agreed on every one of the 5,116 value-sweep rows across 34 first pushes. Each row matched on visits, substitutions, application steps, reductions, constants and result releases. Across all rows both engines made 50,498 visits, tried 26,001 application reductions (25,831 misses), and hit 967 of their 17,914 visit-time cache probes. Native also made 16,947 frame-entry probes, all misses. The seven-run hardware counters from the preceding study put rewriter calls at 126.30M g3 instructions versus 45.68M native. Of the 80.62M excess, 55.56M came from the 3,608 rows that visited five to sixteen nodes. The largest single-row excess was 42,626 instructions. This workload isolates an instruction cost per traversal with virtually identical logical work.

Splitting the work **after** first-push reduction exposed a different issue. Before the two changes below, installing each reduced assertion cost 109.31M instructions in total, marking declarations forbidden cost 16.88M, and installing substitution bindings cost 6.22M. Z3 used 24.35M, 1.49M and 0.58M respectively. Samples in the installation loop led from model-finder quantifier registration to the clause-literal accessor. Accessing one literal validated every literal in its clause. Both the model finder and macro candidate collector repeated the validation for each index, giving a quadratic scan.

Commit `be10d443a` validates the clause once and gives the two consumers a borrowed view of its literals in their original order. The public single-element API continues to validate its input. Across five pinned repetitions of 100 scans, the medians below include validation and checking each returned handle. Both paths allocated zero bytes. | 8 | 1.67 µs | 0.255 µs | 6.6× |
| 64 | 77.5 µs | 2.19 µs | 35× |
| 512 | 4.84 ms | 18.3 µs | 264× |

The 64-root shared-DAG benchmark fell from 12.84 to 3.64 µs and from ten allocations to one. The 512-root case fell from 90.5 to 69.9 µs. #### Where the current hybrid searches first diverge

Five rotating GC-off release comparisons observed all 839 frontend obligations. The g3 frontend dispatched 534 concrete checks and the linked native frontend dispatched 839. The sum of per-check median solver-thread instructions was 3.888B for g3 versus 2.692B for native. Batch 31 goal 34 remained the largest single excess at **269.3M versus 176.6M**. Batch 31 goal 33 used 153.7M versus 87.8M. Batch 11 goal 5 used 70.1M versus 55.9M.

A separate observation build traced emitted lemma trees before and after each candidate on the complete proof. At 31/34 the first twelve trees matched in order under consistent renaming of generated symbols. Lemma thirteen already came from a different quantifier, before the first candidate. At that point g3 and native had chosen between terms later present on both sides. With generated names normalized independently within each tree, the thirteenth g3 shape occurred at native positions 23 and 25, and the thirteenth native shape occurred at g3 positions 20 and 43. The two pre-candidate sequences shared 48 tree shapes counting multiplicities out of 49 g3 and 66 native emissions. Each engine reached three candidate checks, with 2,093 versus 2,597 total emissions. The shape overlap allows separate symbol renamings per tree and cannot establish common ground-term identity across the sequence.

At 11/5 the ordered prefix had six trees. Only six of nine g3 and eight native pre-candidate emissions overlapped even under independent renaming. The mismatching seventh trees never appeared on the other side before the first candidate. This control reached six candidate checks in g3 and four in native. At 31/34, compare queued quantifiers, bindings, generation, cost and discovery order at emission thirteen. Check which entries both engines could select at that instant. The witness policy only takes effect later. [Paired solver counters and ordered lemma trees](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov26-sweep-census-and-clause-traversal.tar.xz)

### Boolean decisions precede the divergence in hybrid queue arrivals

Both solvers dispatched every pre-candidate offer in insertion order on 31/34 and 11/5. On 31/34 the first 24 offer shapes agreed, in batches of 16, 1 and 7. The fourth batch contained one offer in g3 and 17 in native. At lemma thirteen, neither solver had received the other solver's eventual choice. The corresponding shapes first arrived at offers 48 and 46 respectively. Changing the order within an eager batch cannot account for that emission.

The first two signed Boolean decisions agreed on both obligations. The third already differed. On 31/34, after 17 offers and ten lemmas, g3 assigned false to the disjunction of an equality and an acceptance predicate. Native assigned false to the acceptance predicate itself. On 11/5, after 16 offers and six lemmas, g3 chose a receive-initialization predicate and native chose a membership predicate. The first different offers came several decisions later on both inputs. The traces establish the sequence. They do not yet establish which choice caused a measurable cost difference. Compare candidate eligibility, assignment, activity and heap order immediately before the third decision, then measure a controlled decision substitution if both choices were available.

Both complete instrumented proofs matched their reference outputs. The decision observer preserved the previously recorded queue event stream. Cross-engine shapes normalize generated names independently per tree. The archive includes the observations and comparison scripts and uses the setup from the preceding paired-counter archive. [Queue and decision traces](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-hybrid-queue-arrivals.tar.xz)

#### Cost of substituting the native third decision

Both candidates were unassigned and present in the primary activity heap of both solvers. All shared Boolean IDs had the same assignment through the third decision on each check. The first three random-selection draws in each engine exceeded the random-branch threshold. The activity scores already differed before the first decision of the check, on 56 shared IDs at 31/34 and 20 at 11/5. At the third split on 31/34, g3 gave the disjunction 2.49048 and the acceptance predicate zero. Native gave them zero and five. At 11/5, g3 gave the receive predicate 1.16425 and the membership predicate zero. Native gave them one and two. Comparing scores by ID excludes the reserved true slot. The traces also identify both candidates by expression.

A temporary g3 build substituted the native choice only at those two splits. It took the usual random-selection draw, removed the eligible target from its primary heap, and used the normal phase selection and search. The control ran the same binary with substitution disabled. Five alternating pairs on CPU 14 with GC off matched both reference output streams across all 839 frontend obligations. The stage observer measured 534 concrete checks per run.

| Median solver-thread instructions | Ordinary selection | Native third choice | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 31/34 | 269.375M | 272.085M | +1.01% |
| 11/5 | 70.034M | 60.357M | −13.82% |
| All checks in batch 31 | 537.129M | 547.660M | +1.96% |
| All checks in batch 11 | 218.221M | 207.157M | −5.07% |
| All 534 concrete checks | 3.890B | 3.900B | +0.24% |
| All observed verifier stages | 5.849B | 5.858B | +0.15% |

The first visible decision difference does explain some excess work at 11/5. Copying that choice increased cost on the larger 31/34 gap. The two substitutions ran in one incremental proof, so the aggregate includes later checks that inherit search state. The observer measures solver-thread instructions inside stages. The trial provides no elapsed-time result. The next priority is repeated work where the engines perform the same search or rewrite operations, particularly the 80.62M instruction gap on matched value-sweep traversal. ### November 27 — Recycle AST references during unchanged rewrites

On 4,271 of the 5,116 matched first-push rows, neither engine hit a substitution or rewrite cache entry, or successfully reduced a nonconstant application. Their per-row medians sum to 110.54M instructions for g3 and 40.80M for Z3. These rows account for 69.73M of the measured excess. The counts describe the observed traversal. A shortcut that skips a row would also have to account for quantifier reductions, cache writes and resource checks.

Two proof-free application-frame prototypes consumed fewer instructions inside the sweep. Collapsing one or two shared child references directly into an unchanged result brought the seven-round median from 126.31M to 123.85M. Recognizing an unchanged uninterpreted application before theory dispatch brought it to 123.22M. The latter allowed the normal path for binary applications when cheap ITE pulling was enabled. Across the four complete default-GC verifiers, the first trial's instruction changes ranged from −0.75% to +0.81% and the second's from −1.93% to +0.47%. Both remain in the experiment archive.

Commit `571778234` improves a more widely used operation. A new owning AST reference can take a free slot and pin its validated node in one pass. Deleting a reference to a surviving node can validate the reference and decrement its node directly. Last owners, pending deletions, callbacks and exhausted generations still use the existing lifecycle. A stale-node regression failed on the initial prototype because it consumed a reference whose pointed-to generation disagreed. The release checks this generation. Recycling a slot also invalidates its previous owning handle. [Implementation](ast/ast_ref.go) · [Ownership regressions and benchmark](ast/ast_ref_reuse_test.go)

Across nine alternating one-million-operation benchmark pairs, the median cost per acquire/release pair fell from **46.86 to 22.02 ns** for a shared node and from **28.06 to 19.83 ns** for an empty reference. All four paths allocated zero bytes per pair. Seven paired hybrid stage measurements put the released value-sweep calls at **124.05M versus 126.31M** instructions. The enclosing instrumented first pushes fell from 1,371.41M to 1,346.45M. A shorter implementation that recycled only after entering the ordinary manager path used 124.82M and 1,357.19M respectively.

The four short cases also retired 0.32–1.04% fewer instructions over nine GC-off comparisons. Whole-proof elapsed time varied on the shared machine. All proof exit codes and both output streams matched the pinned references, including the two expected failures. Ordinary AST, rewriter, SMT core, API, shell and portcheck tests passed. Checked/debug/trace AST tests and AST vet passed. [Drivers, benchmarks and raw counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-rewriter-reference-cost.tar.xz)

Seven same-core pairs against linked Z3 gave the following absolute medians with the same GoIvy frontend and normal GC. Hybrid took **1,125 ms versus 813 ms** (1.38×) and Ticket **424 ms versus 230 ms** (1.84×). ARM took 465 ms versus 329 ms (1.42×). FBA took 106 ms versus 135 ms (0.79×). Matching the Z3 instruction count would require removing another 2.51B instructions on hybrid and 1.57B on Ticket in this panel.

#### Which matched operations account for the instruction gap?

Separate Go and in-tree C++ builds bracketed each operation on the pinned solver thread. All five call counts matched independently on **every row** in three complete proofs per engine. Each cell below is the median of the three sums after subtracting the row's mean empty-bracket cost. Nested brackets yielded to their outer operation. Go and C++ compile the observer differently, so very small differences carry less weight.

| Operation | Calls | g3 | Z3 | Excess |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nonconstant application reducer | 26,001 | 19.33M | 4.77M | **14.56M** |
| Substitution lookup | 50,498 | 9.74M | 3.00M | **6.74M** |
| Variable processing | 14,508 | 4.05M | 0.38M | **3.67M** |
| Quantifier reducer | 4,872 | 15.78M | 14.46M | **1.32M** |
| Constant processing | 4,036 | 0.66M | 0.27M | **0.39M** |

The quantifier reducer was the second most expensive measured operation in g3, yet the two engines performed it at similar cost. The application reducer used about **743 versus 183 instructions per call**. The 4,271 rows without hits or successful nonconstant reductions spent 15.72M g3 instructions there. Go's disjoint brackets also attributed 7.41M to cache insertion, 5.05M to shrinking owned root slices and 4.74M to scope exit outside the five operations above. These three measurements currently lack paired native brackets. [Per-row events and paired counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-rewriter-reference-cost.tar.xz)

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Equality or iff | 1,873 | 5.11M | 0.64M | **4.48M** |
| Negation | 6,627 | 4.21M | 0.97M | **3.24M** |
| Uninterpreted function | 10,856 | 3.12M | 0.72M | 2.40M |

Equality and negation together account for 7.72M excess instructions in these windows. Compare their operand shapes and failing rule paths on the matched Ticket replays before proposing a general fast path. Earlier experiments already tested an operand-sort guard for the one-bit equality rule. Even recovering the full 14.56M application-reducer excess here would cover less than 1% of the complete hybrid instruction gap. For a larger gain, measure the same operations during solver checks, where the same implementation handles many more instances, and price the rest of the frame loop separately.

### November 27 — Which arithmetic rewrites change on Toy consensus?

Across all 906 quantifier instances of Toy consensus check 18, g3 and Z3 agreed within every instance on the number of additions and inequalities that returned a result and the number that left their inputs unchanged. The following medians cover three CPU-pinned runs with GC off. The Go addition window covers polynomial normalization. The C++ addition window also includes its algebraic target check.

| Rewrite outcome | Calls in each engine | g3 instructions | Z3 instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Addition changed | 377 | 11.24M | 0.76M |
| Addition unchanged | 513 | 2.40M | 0.32M |
| Inequality changed | 328 | 14.46M | 2.37M |
| Inequality unchanged | 1,038 | 13.31M | 1.63M |

Go spent 10.59M instructions in the negative-polynomial comparison rule, 5.65M cancelling monomials, and 4.75M reconstructing coefficient products. A separate profile counted 12.32M instructions constructing numerals across arithmetic rewriter calls. These figures overlap. Constructing the numeral −1 alone took 10.69M instructions across 724 calls, compared with 0.76M across 434 native calls. Other negative numerals and nonnegative integers through 15 matched in aggregate count.

Z3's addition normalizer copies a singleton monomial into its output when the coefficient can be kept. A Go trial reused that input after grouping. It eliminated exactly 290 constructions of −1 and saved 4.28M instructions in those calls. The remaining 434 constructions cost 6.41M. The isolated replay saved 0.73% of instructions and 1.77% of cycles. Across three independent numeric incremental workloads the change was under 0.03% in marginal instructions. Complete Toy under default GC appeared to save 7.69% of instructions in five pairs, but under GC-off control the difference was 0.01% over nine pairs. Complete Ticket used 1.75% more instructions and took 1.42% longer in five default-GC pairs. We kept the trial as a benchmark.

A second trial passed the already assembled lexical declaration metadata directly to the numeral factory. It reduced marginal instructions by 1.11% on repeated Toy and 0.22–0.62% on the three numeric workloads. Complete Toy took 2.84% longer across seven default-GC pairs. Both trials matched the current solver's output on 7,408 arithmetic simplifications. The numeral trial passed the focused checked/debug/trace tests, but a new trace comparison found a concrete behavioral difference. The first construction of a pinned −1 produced one copied-rational allocation event versus two in the baseline. A second construction produced zero versus one. The release retains the original factory and its diagnostic behavior.

For the remaining 434 negative-one requests, distinguish time spent preparing declaration metadata from hashing, lookup and application registration before adding any cache. The complete Ticket and hybrid gaps also warrant measuring traversal costs outside operator reduction. [Benchmark scripts, trace control, per-instance counts and paired replay and verifier results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-arithmetic-normalization.tar.xz)

### November 27 — Two inline declaration parameters and the cost of constructing a live numeral

Commit `ea70c4287` stores the first two owned parameter handles inside each AST information record. A handle needs only the slot and generation within its manager. Wider declarations allocate storage for the remaining handles at their known final width. Both old and new records occupy **88 bytes** on amd64. An arithmetic numeral uses two parameters, so repeat construction now makes **zero Go heap allocations**, including on negative numbers outside the plugin cache. The commit also reuses the rational manager's existing admission checks for releasing inline integers and removes a duplicate cleanup preflight from the service.

On the previous Toy consensus experiment's **434 matched requests for −1**, constructing a declaration took 2.60M retired instructions inside g3's plugin factory versus 0.49M in the native factory. The application step cost 0.13M versus 0.14M. In separate Go windows, temporary declaration metadata construction cost 0.78M, disposal cost 0.52M, node hashing cost 0.51M, and table insertion cost 0.52M. The captured rational copy and its two cleanup calls accounted for another 0.96M and 1.05M. Each pair of runs agreed on all four search counters and request counts in every quantifier instance. These scoped costs come from the monomial-reuse diagnostic build described above. Production keeps the ordinary addition path.

In the pinned live-numeral microbenchmark, rational cleanup alone reduced repeated −1 construction from 1,638 to 1,474 ns and cached +1 construction from 355 to 285 ns. The baseline allocation profile attributed 99.86% of sampled objects to growing the parameter slice. A second alternating panel held the cleanup change constant to measure storage. Medians of five runs, one Go scheduler thread:

| Operation | Original storage, ns | Inline storage, ns | Heap bytes before → after | Allocations before → after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Reconstruct live −1 | 1,477 | 1,382 | 48 → 0 | 2 → 0 |
| Copy and release one declaration parameter | 100.9 | 55.5 | 16 → 0 | 1 → 0 |
| Two parameters | 198.0 | 78.9 | 48 → 0 | 2 → 0 |
| Three parameters | 242.4 | 154.8 | 112 → 32 | 3 → 2 |
| Eight parameters | 421.5 | 287.3 | 240 → 72 | 4 → 2 |
| Sixty-four parameters | 2,249 | 1,777 | 2,032 → 536 | 7 → 2 |

The release saved 0.33–0.94% of marginal instructions across three independent numeric workloads and 0.88% on repeated Toy consensus. All 7,408 simplifications matched, as did the first and repeated live-numeral trace (two copied-rational allocation events, then one). The full Go suite passed, as did the checked/debug/trace AST suite and focused numeric ownership controls.

Complete-verifier elapsed effects were mixed. In the eleven-pair panel after the full suite, Ticket, hybrid and ARM were within 0.2% of baseline and FBA took 0.68% longer. An earlier eleven-pair overlay run on a different CPU was 10.24% slower on ARM and 8.14% slower on FBA. Three-pair controls matched the complete Raft, Toy, TLB, liveness and both Apple transcripts. The two Apple paired elapsed medians improved 3.48% and 6.11%, while their instructions moved by −0.04% and +0.29%. These measurements support a storage and arithmetic improvement. Whole-verifier latency remains workload- and run-dependent.
