### Which Ticket obligations account for the current gap?

Across five complete runs per backend, the instrumented frontend reached 284 numbered final-condition goals in nine physical first-push batches. On the release, g3 spent 1.697B instructions in 252 concrete checks plus 145.72M in 41 early-proof attempts. Linked Z3 used 599.77M in 284 concrete checks. Physical first pushes added 360.44M versus 143.37M instructions. The rank uses the sum of each goal's median early-proof and concrete-check cost measured together per run. It excludes push, assertion, pop and frontend work.

**Two conjectures account for 305.90M excess instructions across eight checks**, or 24.63% of the 1.242B goal-level gap. We matched their exact check windows to the frontend's printed source lines 333 and 345 of `ticket_protocol.ivy`. Both concern the saved service ticket and split on program-counter cases. The four actions were `step12`, `step22`, `step23` and `step31`. On `step23`, line 333 cost 74.46M versus 13.94M. On `step12`, line 345 cost 84.89M versus 30.50M. The largest single excess was 66.40M at batch 7, goal 1. The 20 most expensive goal differences account for 51.95% of this gap.

Compare solver decisions, instantiations and assertion costs at the eight recurring goals in their original push/pop histories. This tests whether the same search or implementation difference recurs across actions. Seven paired whole runs measured g3/native instruction ratios of 2.06 on Ticket, 1.43 on hybrid, 1.54 on ARM and 0.78 on FBA. The corresponding median paired wall-time ratios were 2.21, 1.41, 1.52 and 0.71 on the shared host. [All goal rankings, action and line mappings, and exact-transcript measurement drivers](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-live-numeral.tar.xz)

### November 27 — Ticket search history and the cost of executing the same proof

The ordinary g3 solver and linked Z3 can follow the same search on all eight of Ticket’s most expensive recurring obligations. The release uses independent proofs before or after a physical push and therefore gives the concrete solver a different history. We measured the effect by replaying the **complete verifier** from startup and selectively bypassing those proofs. Every run matched the baseline exit code, stdout and stderr. No solver settings or proof rules changed between goals.

| Eight Ticket checks, summed | Released g3 | Ordinary g3 | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Offered quantifier instances | 14,862 | 14,597 | 14,597 |
| Asserted instance lemmas | 4,493 | 3,700 | 3,700 |
| Boolean decisions | 989 | 1,177 | 1,177 |
| Instructions inside the checks, millions | 475.42 | 421.45 | 169.30 |
| Batch 4, goal 55 alone, millions | 74.46 | 36.79 | 13.94 |

In the ordinary pair, every ordered offer (quantifier and binding trees) and asserted lemma tree matched within its check under a consistent renaming of generated suffixes in each event stream. Every signed decision tree also matched after allowing reversal of equality operands. These observers compare printed application names, ordered children, quantifier binder sorts and variable indices. No candidate-model check occurred in these windows. Rebuilding the native observer from this fork reproduced its complete selected event file byte for byte.

On batch 4, goal 55, the release issued 193 decisions and asserted 725 lemmas. Ordinary g3 and Z3 issued 45 decisions and asserted 356 lemmas. Other goals respond differently. On batch 2, goal 55, ordinary g3 did **more** work than the release (68.72M vs 49.34M). Across all eight, matching the history removes 53.97M of the 306.12M instruction gap. **82.4% remains with matched decisions, offers and assertions.** The instruction sums are medians across five complete runs per backend with GC off and event tracing disabled. Omitting the optional frontend goal simplification changed the ordinary eight-check sum by just 0.04M.

Instruction sampling in 15 additional alternating complete runs used the eight concrete-check intervals on their actual OS thread. Each interval was identified with CLOCK_MONOTONIC timestamps. The mean sampled totals of 420.40M and 168.59M are within 0.5% of the direct counts. The categories below partition samples inside the quantifier queue’s per-entry call. Each sample appears in one row.

| Sampled instructions across the eight checks, millions | Ordinary g3 | Z3 | Excess |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Assert rewritten lemma | 73.18 | 16.99 | 56.19 |
| Theory rewrite | 72.12 | 22.21 | 49.91 |
| Binding substitution | 51.38 | 21.94 | 29.44 |
| Candidate satisfaction test | 43.89 | 33.05 | 10.84 |
| Lemma assembly and other per-entry work | 44.42 | 9.23 | 35.19 |
| Outside the per-entry call | 135.41 | 65.17 | 70.24 |

Assertion and theory rewriting together account for about 42% of the matched gap. Within assertion, recursive formula internalization sampled about 25M instructions on g3 and 6M in the native formula-core path. In g3’s queue rewriter, application-frame processing appeared on about 63M instructions of stacks, while the theory application reducer itself appeared on only about 15M. These nested costs overlap. A useful next experiment is a compiled fast path for repeated application-frame traversal around the unchanged reducer. First count identical frame shapes and callbacks under different bindings. Compare cache writes, reference ownership, resource charges and the ordered lemma stream in addition to elapsed time.

**Scheduling controls.** Five rotating complete normal-GC runs on CPU 14 gave the following paired changes relative to released g3. Both variants run every goal in a physical scope. The post-push-only variant can still prove a goal through the independent proof batch after assertion.

| Verification | Post-push proofs only, instructions / elapsed | Ordinary solver only, instructions / elapsed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket | −7.26% / −7.74% | −10.66% / −10.74% |
| Hybrid | −5.75% / −6.25% | −1.99% / −0.98% |
| ARM | −1.54% / −1.78% | +14.95% / +13.70% |
| FBA | +3.30% / +1.61% | −0.79% / −0.34% |

Post-push-only completed all 419 Raft checks in a median 2.23 s versus 2.38 s for released g3 across three pairs. On the pinned Apple frontend it raised instructions from 11.53B to 25.13B on rfn2 and from 123.44B to 144.20B on dramc_nb2 in one complete pair each. These controls rule out removing either proof stage globally. Complete Ticket with ordinary g3 still took 380 ms versus 229 ms for linked Z3.

**Two general arena access experiments.** Returning an application's cached range sort directly and reusing already resolved operand slots in slice-application registration together saved 0.10–0.34% of instructions in three CLI replays across nine rotations. All decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts matched. In seven complete normal-GC verifier rotations, their combined effect ranged from 0.67% fewer instructions on hybrid to 1.84% more on FBA. Both remain experiments. The retained archive includes build scripts, source patches, paired measurements, ordered event trees and sampled stacks. [Ticket history controls and profiles](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-ticket-history.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Rewriter frames and lemma lifetime

The eight ordinary Ticket checks from the preceding study offer a matched search for comparing implementation cost. In g3, application-frame processing accounted for 63.4M inclusive sampled instructions and only 5.75M self instructions. Most of the cost on its stack occurs in callees. Three experiments tested whether repeated frame work or repeated lemmas could be avoided.

| Trial | Measurement | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check the parent declaration before reading the child reference count and associative flags | Alternating 32-deep unary chains fell from 4,908 to 3,982 ns/op. Same-declaration chains went from 4,847 to 4,881 ns/op. Both took zero allocations. Across nine complete-verifier pairs, instructions changed by +0.11% on Ticket, −0.31% on hybrid, +0.21% on ARM and −0.60% on FBA. | Retain the benchmark. Keep the release guard order. |
| Specialize proof-free theory visits | Saved 0.62%, 0.66% and 0.47% of replay instructions on Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and toy consensus. Complete Ticket saved 1.07% and ARM used 0.36% more. | Keep the shared visit implementation. |
| Retain the last 512 lemma ASTs across backtracks | Saved 0.33%, 0.39% and 0.59% of replay instructions against the zero-retention overlay. All three resource counts changed. | Keep current AST lifetimes. |

**Can one ground instance predict the next traversal?** Across 3,700 instances and 36,543 visits in the eight checks, a 128-entry recent-path predictor matched 264 complete callback paths under different ground roots. Those matches covered 2,125 visits (5.8%). An oracle choosing among the last 16 distinct paths per quantifier could cover 8,225 visits (22.5%) on complete matches, or 20,089 (55.0%) up to the first mismatch. These are coverage ceilings before guard costs. The signatures record visits, substitutions, cache behavior and reducer callbacks. Executing a matching path still requires correct results, cache effects, resource charges and references.

**Can the solver reuse the earlier assertion?** Of 3,700 lemma trees, 1,527 repeated an earlier tree in the same check. A separate observer recorded scope ancestry and physical membership of the earlier root clause in the live clause directory. Every repeat followed a backtrack out of the earlier assertion scope. Zero had a surviving earlier clause or the same earlier AST handle. Of those repeats, 1,117 stored a fresh root clause. A direct lookup for a live duplicate therefore misses every opportunity suggested by the syntactic count.

The CLI trials used nine rotating runs with GC off for the traversal variants and five for AST retention. The complete verifier trials used normal GC. Extending the existing literal shortcut to two-child disjunctions also had mixed results across seven complete pairs, including 0.83% more instructions on Ticket. No production variant was retained. The next measurement is the cost of new and previously internalized atoms in recursive formula internalization, which sampled about 25M instructions in g3 versus 6M in Z3 across these checks. [Benchmark](ast/rewriter/theory_frame_benchmark_test.go) · [Trial sources, raw measurements and compressed callback traces](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-frame-paths.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Fresh Boolean atoms in the matched Ticket search

Both solvers reached **2,404 fresh positive formulas and 1,546 negations of fresh operands** at the outermost formula call while asserting 3,700 quantified lemmas. The two engines took very different numbers of calls for already-bound operands. g3's assertion loop can directly reuse a signed literal. Its saving there leaves the cost of creating the fresh atoms clearly visible.

| Outermost formula entry | g3 calls | Z3 calls | g3 instructions | Z3 instructions |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Fresh positive | 2,404 | 2,404 | 12.67M | 3.30M |
| Negation of fresh operand | 1,546 | 1,546 | 12.25M | 3.13M |
| Already bound positive | 14 | 3,487 | 0.003M | 0.100M |
| Negation of bound operand | 28 | 11,350 | 0.021M | 1.376M |

Each cell is the median of five complete Ticket runs, summing the eight original incremental checks in each run. The timed intervals include recursive work. Nested intervals were disabled, and the adjacent empty counter read was subtracted. Entry classification was outside the bracket. An independent observer counting all depths found exactly 4,773 fresh formulas excluding stripped NOT gates in both engines, including 1,688 equalities. The frontend transcript and exit status matched for both observers.

The 15-round uninstrumented stack sample puts 9.23M instructions in Boolean enode attachment under g3’s outermost formula-core frame, 6.42M in recursive internalization, 4.68M in gate constraints and 2.41M in Boolean variable creation. The formula-core frame itself accounted for 0.80M. Native enode creation under the corresponding outer frame accounted for 2.41M. Differences in native inlining affect attribution between frames. These stack estimates overlap the hardware intervals above.

A second set of five complete runs timed the work *inside* those fresh formula calls after the registration change below. Go and native created exactly the same Boolean variables, enodes and gate clauses. Enode creation accounts for the largest measured excess within these calls. Both cost columns are calibrated instruction totals in millions.

| Operation inside fresh positive or negated formula | Calls g3 / Z3 | g3 | Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Create Boolean variable | 4,773 / 4,773 | 3.42 | 1.27 |
| Create enode | 4,336 / 4,336 | 11.63 | 3.17 |
| Congruence insertion, within enode creation | 4,332 / 4,332 | 2.20 | 0.62 |
| Generate gate constraints and relevance watches | 589 / 589 | 4.68 | 1.49 |
| Emit gate clause, within gate constraints | 1,828 / 1,828 | 2.42 | 0.66 |
| Recursive term internalization | 6,452 / 6,604 | 2.38 | 0.31 |

The enode interval includes congruence insertion and can occur inside a term call. Instrumentation inside a parent affects its measured total, so these rows should not be added. Only about 1.58M of the 8.45M enode gap came from congruence insertion. The earlier matched stacks put 5.35M g3 instructions in the node constructor under enode creation and 2.41M in registration, versus 1.74M inside the native constructor. Comparing child resolution, parent attachment and allocation inside those constructors is the next experiment.

Two experiments targeted enode construction. Passing already-resolved non-Boolean child pointers into unary and binary predicates saved 0.38%, 0.24% and 0.10% of standalone Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and toy consensus instructions. Across seven complete-verifier pairs it saved at most 0.12% and raised FBA instructions by 0.33%. That prototype remains in the archive.

**Commit `b98d8b1a3` resolves one expression page for enode registration.** Finding the prior enode, publishing the new one and recording relevance all use the same generation-checked slot. Public borrowed registrations still validate the AST handle before any page write. An owned registration preserves the atom’s prior relevance. A repeated public registration takes the caller’s explicit relevance value. The regression exercises both through their public entry points.

| Scoped construction and rollback | Width 32 | Width 2,048 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unary, paired instructions | −3.09% | −2.83% |
| Binary, paired instructions | −2.71% | −2.10% |

Seven alternating pairs used 1,000 iterations at width 32 and 50 at width 2,048. Allocation counts were identical. Nine complete normal-GC verifier pairs changed instructions by −0.54% on Ticket, −0.27% on hybrid, −0.47% on ARM and +0.03% on FBA. Paired elapsed changed by −0.18%, −1.19%, +0.70% and +4.07%, respectively. The repeatable gain is in scoped node construction. [Scoped benchmark](smtcore/smt_enode_scope_batch_benchmark_test.go) · [Registration regression](smtcore/smt_expression_setters_test.go) · [Sources, snapshots and measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-internalization-and-premises.tar.xz)

**Complete verification.** A seven-round confirmation after the native Go suite compared the new release, its parent and linked Z3. Median release / Z3 times were 425 / 236 ms on Ticket, 1,131 / 825 ms on hybrid, 462 / 331 ms on ARM and 106 / 137 ms on FBA. Relative to the parent, release instructions changed by −0.75%, +0.48%, +0.30% and −0.17%, respectively. The earlier FBA elapsed increase did not repeat. In five separate 419-check Raft pairs the release and its parent took 2.71 and 2.61 seconds; that panel overlapped the native suite. On the pinned Apple frontend, three pairs gave **1.47 vs 9.17 seconds on rfn2** and **15.39 vs 18.74 seconds on dramc_nb2**, release vs linked Z3. Every complete-verifier comparison matched stdout, stderr and exit status.

### Can a smaller premise set remove the expensive search?

A diagnostic native run named the positive conjuncts of the base and obtained an unsatisfiable core. Plain g3 and Z3 then solved each reduced input from scratch, keeping the complete original goal. The selected costs exclude the cost of learning the core. A refutation of a subset proves the original. A SAT or unknown result requires solving the original.

| g3 CLI, median millions of instructions | Premises selected / available | Original | All conjuncts regrouped | Selected | Selected, original let nesting |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket 127 | 36 / 120 | 268.60 | 268.38 | 138.22 | 142.86 |
| Ticket 290 | 36 / 92 | 287.41 | 287.13 | 216.59 | 219.42 |
| Toy consensus 18 | 51 / 78 | 651.26 | 1,185.55 | 1,905.42 | 2,389.24 |

The eight-rotation panel includes parsing, push, check and statistics. Z3 on the original inputs used 119.05M, 120.18M and 223.76M instructions. In particular, the 1.94× saving on Ticket 127 required an offline proof and still left g3 above native. On toy consensus, even regrouping every original conjunct changed the search. The smaller selected inputs gave more costly proofs in both engines.

**Prospective selection.** Exported snapshots of goals 55 and 56 from four successive Ticket actions have identical premises within each action. Fresh standalone replays exercise those logical inputs without the verifier's earlier learned clauses. In all four actions, the core learned on 55 gave **SAT** with goal 56 in both solvers. In a second trial, each action used the immediately preceding action's core for the *same* goal, plus every premise new to the destination action. Four of six subsequent goals still refuted, but only one ran faster. The six original g3 snapshots used 1.452B instructions. The selected attempts used 1.894B, and the two required retries cost another 0.415B. Total cost was **1.59× baseline before charging for core discovery**.

All five multi-obligation Ticket bases were satisfiable by themselves. The four unsatisfiable bases belonged to the terminal single-goal batches. Checking each base up front would add a satisfiability search to every multi-goal batch here. A separate symbol-frequency selector refuted Ticket 127 at two of twelve tolerance/depth settings and could select nothing from the constant goals on Ticket 290 and toy consensus. These measurements favor looking for cheaper construction of the fresh atoms shared across proofs and for work removable across complete workloads. They give no basis for adding a general premise-selection prepass. [Inputs and trial drivers](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-internalization-and-premises.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Enode construction, retired pointers and scope removal

Across the same eight Ticket checks, both solvers constructed 4,336 fresh enodes while asserting quantifier lemmas. Five alternating instrumented runs reproduced the reference transcripts. The table gives median retired instructions summed over all eight checks, in millions. The boundaries differ because Z3 attaches each child to its parent in the same loop that resolves it.

| Constructor work | g3 | Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Setup | 1.892 | 0.135 |
| Allocate and initialize fields | 2.181 | 0.332 |
| Resolve children and attach parent links | 3.499 | 0.446 |

Go spent 2.391M instructions resolving children and 1.108M appending parent links. The Z3 setup interval includes region reservation. The Go setup interval includes declaration inspection. Sampling without the interval probes attributed about 1.34M instructions each to slice allocation and node allocation beneath the Go constructor. Even eliminating the entire measured child-loop difference would recover only about 1.2% of the 252M-instruction gap across those checks.

### What happened when we reduced allocations

The allocation experiments used solver-local storage, preserved enode addresses, and left the AST arena in place. Each scope benchmark pushes, internalizes unary or binary applications, and pops. The retained-reference benchmark holds every 32nd node from a popped 2,048-node scope and measures live heap before and after releasing those 64 pointers.

| Storage | Bytes kept alive by the 64 pointers | Result |
|---|---:|---|
| Existing individual nodes | 13,312 | Exactly 64 × 208 bytes in this fixture |
| Blocks of eight nodes | 114,091 | Scope instructions rose in all four arity/width combinations |
| Blocks of 32 nodes | 431,915 | Scope instructions fell at width 32 and rose at width 2,048 |
| Two inline child pointers, with overflow storage | 13,312 | Roughly half the allocations, but complete Ticket, hybrid, ARM and FBA used 1.11%, 0.89%, 1.99% and 5.95% more instructions |

The inline variant with cached arity reduced peak live heap at width 2,048 from 583,691 to 552,971 bytes. A second design placed one or two trailing child pointers beside the node, retaining slice-based reads. It saved at most 0.06% of instructions on each of the three CLI replays. Neither layout justified changing production storage. Direct child lookup and cheaper declaration flag reads also failed to deliver a consistent improvement. The retired-pointer and congruence benchmarks are retained in commit `0839cb04e`.

### Duplicate probes during scope pop

The general Erase first finds a congruent node, then probes again to remove the representative by its current signature. A prototype that tried deleting the exact pointer first cut scope instructions by 2.3–4.2% across unary and binary applications at widths 32 and 2,048. Its extra lookup increased work on misses. Returning a slot from every short-table lookup also penalized ordered read probes. These tradeoffs motivated testing exact-pointer deletion only at scope teardown, where the caller already knows it is retiring a congruence root.

Raw rotations and external overlay generators are in the [enode study archive](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-enode-construction-and-erasure.tar.xz).

Restricting the exact-pointer shortcut to the scope-pop caller reduced paired instruction medians by 4.59% and 2.29% on unary scopes of widths 32 and 2,048, and by 4.19% and 3.89% on binary scopes. Nine alternating complete proofs per engine reproduced their reference outputs and exit status. Ticket used 1.08% more instructions, ARM 0.65% more, FBA 0.66% more and hybrid 0.61% fewer. The shared slot-returning variant saved instructions on the four complete runs but increased ordered read-probe instructions from 84.36M to 90.36M per 200,000 iterations including process setup. All three erasure variants remain experiments.

### Where Ticket spends time outside queue instantiation

A disjoint classification of the existing fifteen instruction-sampling rounds across eight matched checks assigns 24.36M excess instructions to conflict resolution, 16.19M to assertion internalization, 11.10M to E-matching, 13.11M to remaining propagation and 5.49M to all other work outside queue entries. Labels use the outer operation when one invokes another. These are sample estimates.

Within conflict resolution, the immediate scope-pop call accounted for 31.31M instructions in g3 and 9.90M in Z3. Relevancy rollback underneath those calls alone accounted for 10.31M versus 1.07M. The Go watch trail holds a reference to every registered source. Measure the existing held-reference decrement there, including the last-reference and retry paths. The underlying stack samples are in the [Ticket history archive](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-ticket-history.tar.xz).

The conflict stacks attribute 8.03M instructions to undoing the Go relevancy trail. Its immediate reference-release call accounts for 5.35M and the table unlink for 1.87M. Each handler or watch registration retains its source before appending the trail entry. Commit `ea1b41486` uses that ownership to call the existing held-reference decrement. Final references, manager callbacks, and checked builds still use the validated release path. The unconsumed-reference retry tests passed.

Across eleven alternating rounds of 1,000 scope pops, releasing 128 watches with surviving sources fell from 2,775 to 1,911 ns per scope (31%), with zero timed allocations. On nine paired fresh-process CLI replays with GC off, Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and Toy consensus 18 used 0.14%, 0.17% and 0.07% fewer instructions. Search counters agreed. Complete verifiers with normal GC had mixed paired instruction counts (Ticket +0.30%, hybrid +0.13%, ARM −0.62%, FBA +1.68%). All transcripts matched. These results establish the improvement in watch retirement; complete proof speedup remains unproven.

In a further seven paired complete runs per workload with collection disabled, instructions fell by 0.20% on Ticket, 0.06% on hybrid, 0.10% on ARM and 0.09% on FBA. Elapsed paired medians rose by 0.1–1.3%. The holdouts support keeping the small watch-specific improvement while directing further work toward larger costs.

## November 27 — Why Ticket spends more on relevance rollback

The ordinary Go solver and native Z3 ran the same eight Ticket verification conditions in the same incremental history. The observers counted the references immediately before each decrement, splitting by the owning structure. Both complete runs reproduced the reference stdout, stderr and exit status. Counts below cover the entire selected check, including any pops during it.

| Owner | g3 surviving | g3 final | Z3 surviving | Z3 final |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Positive watch source | 3,095 | 0 | 3,095 | 0 |
| Negative watch source | 4,494 | 0 | 4,494 | 0 |
| Asserted OR parent held by a watch | 0 | 2,601 | 0 | 0 |
| OR in the relevance-mark vector | 2,773 | 854 | 172 | 3,455 |
| Other expression in the relevance-mark vector | 5,211 | 26 | 5,205 | 32 |

Both engines retire 7,589 watch sources and perform **3,455 final OR releases**. The Go watch that first registers an asserted disjunction owns its parent so the handler can still run if the caller drops the last external reference. Z3's mark vector performs the final release in all 3,455 cases. Counting only the watch trail would incorrectly attribute 2,601 extra disjunction destructions to g3.

A second observer timed the final OR decrement, including child destruction, and checked the count at both owner sites in every check. Five alternating runs with GC disabled used per-thread userspace instruction counters, subtracting the cost of back-to-back reads. g3 used **6.515M instructions** (1.208M from marks and 5.307M from watches). Native used **0.915M**. This is approximately 1,886 versus 265 instructions per final root. The native mark observer sets each element to null in the original forward release order and then shrinks the cleared vector. The Go observer releases in that same order. The interval measures these instrumented release calls.

### Two changes tested against the same proofs

A temporary variant let later watches borrow sources from the first watch's retained parent. The first watch still owned its own source and released the parent last. The ordinary smtcore suite passed. On nine paired CLI runs the trial saved only 0.08%, 0.06% and 0.01% of instructions on Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and Toy consensus 18. Complete Ticket, hybrid, ARM and FBA saved at most 0.13% with GC disabled. The additional ownership mode remains a prototype.

Commit `738700434` removes duplicate handle validation from the common AST decrement. Individual and batched releases now share the same origin check and a single slot/generation check. Malformed zero-slot handles, foreign handles, retired generations and out-of-range slots still fail before changing counts. The canonical null handle still succeeds. Existing deletion code retains responsibility for reporting whether a failed destructor consumed its input.

| Four retains and four releases of a shared sort | Baseline ns/op | Patched ns/op | Paired change in instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Individual manager calls | 74.92 | 71.41 | −8.66% |
| Combined batch | 57.18 | 51.22 | −14.33% |

Nine alternating 500,000-iteration runs used one pinned CPU. Retired instructions include process setup. Both paths allocated zero bytes in the timed loop. All three replay instruction medians improved by 0.06–0.10%. In seven pairs of complete verifications without GC, instructions improved by 0.08% on Ticket, 0.11% on hybrid, 0.04% on ARM and 0.03% on FBA. Default-GC results were mixed across nine pairs (−0.04%, −0.48%, +0.69%, +0.83% respectively). The complete verifier timing data do not establish a general speedup. All proof transcripts matched. The [reproduction archive](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-relevance-rollback.tar.xz) includes per-round samples and both observer implementations.

A third observer counted every AST destroyed by those 3,455 final root releases. Both engines destroyed applications exclusively. Counts matched at every arity from two through ten. The only difference was 584 unary applications in g3 versus 578 in Z3. In particular, each engine destroyed 1,376 four-argument applications and 1,606 applications wider than g3's four inline argument slots. The six-node difference cannot explain the roughly sevenfold instruction ratio by itself. The raw arity histogram is in the archive.

Across the earlier fifteen sampled rounds for the entire eight checks, the Go deletion worklist body accounted for 11.51M instructions, including 7.23M attributed directly to the loop, 1.20M beneath table removal and 1.07M beneath child access. Native deletion accounted for 1.87M. The sampled region includes other deletions and uses an earlier solver revision. Next, measure the final-release loop separately at widths four, five and ten. Try reading a wide application's operand payload once per retiring node. Keep the arena allocation, ascending child decrements, reverse worklist order and partial-error behavior.

The baseline was solver commit `738700434`. Five alternating observer runs priced four operations inside each of the 4,039 Go and 4,033 native AST destructions reached from Ticket's 3,455 matched final OR releases. Each observer verified the destruction count **for every check and arity** against the independent census and reproduced the complete verifier transcript. | Visit the declaration and release child edges | 2.901 | 0.192 | 2.194 | 0.098 |
| Return storage | 0.764 | 0.141 | 0.601 | 0.056 |

Both engines destroyed exactly 1,606 applications wider than four operands. g3's indexed child reader rechecked the arena payload for each operand beyond the four inline slots. Each timed section subtracts an adjacent empty read on the same thread. The boundaries include some observer bookkeeping and exclude worklist entry, exit and manager-level setup. The section totals therefore differ from the separately timed complete release calls.

### Local benefit and whole-proof cost

Six prototypes retained the arena and tried different ways to consume the same operand references. The implementation committed for evaluation as `6a13b555a` read the inline prefix directly, resolved the arena payload once, then decoded the remaining references in place. A failed payload validation fell back to indexed reads so the first bad operand stopped deletion after all preceding decrements. The lifetime regression covers a repeated operand straddling the inline and wide portions and a worklist exceeding 16 entries. The full suite passed across 114 packages. Focused checked/debug/trace tests passed.

| 4 | 99.78 | 96.22 | −1.74% |
| 5 | 171.09 | 143.78 | −15.61% |
| 10 | 253.53 | 163.81 | −35.08% |

The benchmark builds 64 distinct disjunctions outside the timer, retaining the operands. Each timed batch releases all 64 roots. Counts and times come from nine alternating 500-iteration runs on CPU 16. Each timed batch allocated zero bytes. The matched Ticket release intervals fell from 6.515M to **5.204M instructions** across five pairs, a 20.1% saving. Nine full CLI replay pairs with collection off saved 0.24%, 0.15% and 0.18% of instructions on Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and Toy consensus 18, respectively; the answers and solver counters matched.

| Complete verification | Candidate / baseline elapsed change, CPU 14 (9 pairs) | CPU 11 (13 pairs) | Baseline g3 / linked Z3 median elapsed, CPU 14 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Ticket | +0.41% | +0.62% | 430.0 / 231.5 ms |
| Hybrid | +1.23% | +0.84% | 1,176.0 / 844.0 ms |
| ARM rules | +1.16% | +1.28% | 458.4 / 325.9 ms |
| FBA | +2.76% | +1.45% | 106.0 / 135.3 ms |

Complete runs used default GC and matched stdout, stderr and exit status. CPU 14 rotated baseline, candidate and linked Z3. CPU 11 rotated baseline and candidate. Candidate cycles also increased in all eight workload/CPU comparisons. The measurements establish a local improvement and an end-to-end regression in this panel. The cause of the regression remains open. The benchmark and lifetime test remain in git. The prior production loop was restored and the AST suite passed again. Two other implementations also had mixed whole-verifier results in nine normal-GC rotations. The tail-loop variant took 1.58% longer on FBA, and the wide-only variant took 1.49% longer on ARM. Neither replaced the baseline.

### Does Ticket's largest single-goal difference reflect a different search?

The retained ordinary, release-policy and linked native event observers all reached **319 signed decisions, 2,887 instance offers and 820 asserted lemmas** at batch 7, goal 1. The ordered term sequences matched under generated-name renaming. There were zero candidate-model events. These event observers are from the earlier Ticket-history study; five fresh untraced, stage-counted runs used the wide-deletion candidate for g3. The concrete check cost 91.66M instructions with the release proof policy and 91.54M with ordinary g3, versus 36.74M native. The unsuccessful early attempt added another 10.54M before the release-policy check.

Fifteen paired profiles sampled exactly the three concrete check intervals at batches 6, 7 and 8, goal 1. In the largest one (batch 7), ordinary g3 spent **20.61M versus 5.62M** on theory rewriting inside queue instantiation and **17.66M versus 4.95M** on instance assertion. Their combined 27.70M excess accounts for about half the directly measured 54.80M concrete-check gap. E-matching outside instantiation was 6.29M in both solvers. This independently identifies instance processing on a goal outside the previously profiled eight. A higher-leverage experiment is to measure which quantifiers account for both excesses and whether their ground Boolean bodies can be simplified during substitution before building intermediate applications. Preserve rewrite order, proof mode and the existing assertion/relevance semantics in any trial.

The [reproduction archive](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-wide-release-and-late-ticket.tar.xz) includes raw timing and instruction samples, variant patches, matched per-arity section counts, and the three new per-goal event traces and stack profiles.

## November 27 — What changes during Ticket instance rewriting?

Ticket batch 7, goal 1 spent **26.66M excess g3 instructions** inside instance rewriting and assertion, about 49% of the previously measured 54.80M whole-check gap. Both solvers rewrote 820 instances and asserted all 820. The same 519 raw bodies survived rewriting unchanged in both engines. Even those consumed 9.36M g3 rewrite instructions versus 2.55M native.

| Matched bodies | Instances | g3 rewrite | Z3 rewrite | g3 assert | Z3 assert |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Unchanged | 519 | 9.36M | 2.55M | 11.31M | 3.15M |
| Changed | 301 | 9.05M | 2.86M | 7.49M | 1.98M |
| All | 820 | 18.40M | 5.41M | 18.80M | 5.13M |

The figures are median solver-thread user instructions across five alternating pinned-core runs with GC disabled. Each observer read the same hardware counter twice before an operation and once after, subtracting the empty read interval. The Go rewrite interval includes fetching the rewritten handle. Separate tree-capture runs supplied the formulas. The exact output, error stream and exit code matched the complete Ticket reference on every run. The two engines agreed on the full sequence of quantifier IDs and per-instance change flags. IDs follow first appearance in the asserted lemmas and each lemma explicitly names its guarding quantifier. Two of 46 guard texts differed only in generated suffix numbers.

The most expensive quantifier (ID 6) relates the saved and current ticket relation under nested conditionals. Its 62 instances account for **4.81M excess instructions**, split between 2.54M in rewriting and 2.28M in assertion. Forty-eight of its bodies changed. The most frequent quantifier (ID 35) guarded a six-literal disjunction with two thread bindings. All 104 bodies came through unchanged, yet their combined rewrite and assertion gap was 2.71M. These results favor improvements shared across multiple quantifiers.

### Can Boolean simplification move into variable substitution?

A bottom-up prototype replayed the actual raw AST of each instance. It applied local rules for constants, equality, negation, conditionals, duplicate literals and complements. We scored exact ordered result trees, including child order. Three runs progressively supplied the state already available to the solver.

| Inputs to the offline prototype | Changed bodies reproduced exactly (of 301) | Unchanged bodies preserved (of 519) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Raw tree and local Boolean rules | 2 | 519 |
| Plus the current instance’s observed substitution hits | 165 | 519 |
| Plus its observed changed rewrite-cache hits | 301 | 519 |

The last row is an oracle for this trace. A production implementation must obtain each answer at the right traversal depth and cache scope, preserve cache writes, and charge the same resource steps. The replay assigns no cost to those operations. Direct observation found 373 substitution hits. Of these, 357 replaced a binding itself and 16 replaced an application built from variables in the quantifier. All **570 changed cache hits** replaced variable-dependent applications. That explains why collapsing constants and duplicates during construction reached so little of the measured work.

We also tried replacing bindings before building their parents, then applying the same captured lookups and Boolean rules. This changed the initial tree of 169 instances and affected 1,235 distinct application trees counted per instance. For 140 instances it changed the input to a previously observed enclosing lookup. In two cases (instances 20 and 212, guard 12) the result diverged from the solver. Both had a cached rewrite of the negated ticket-order predicate over conditional service and next-ticket arguments. An implementation that eagerly normalizes bindings needs to preserve the original parent lookup.

### Combined AST read under real verification

A separate Go overlay used one validated node read to answer both the substitution-miss question and the rewriter’s subsequent node-shape question. It checked manager identity, handle lifetime and the cached substitution table generation. In nine same-build-flag CLI pairs it saved **0.62%, 0.63% and 0.44%** of instructions on Ticket 127, Ticket 290 and Toy consensus 18. All outcomes, decisions, conflicts, quantifier instances and resource counts matched.

Nine rotating complete normal-GC pairs on each of CPUs 14 and 11 gave Ticket elapsed changes of **+2.01% and −0.09%**. Hybrid elapsed changed −1.34% and +0.12%, ARM −1.45% and −0.18%, and FBA −0.32% and −0.53%. The trial stays in the study archive. The next measurement is the price of constructing the raw variable-dependent applications that lead to changed cache hits, plus the cost of lookup and result propagation. Keep those intervals disjoint and compare against the same native instances before investing in a fused traversal. [Observers, prototypes, all 820 input/output trees, paired counters and verifier runs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-ticket-instance-cost.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Pricing Ticket cache hits and Boolean reductions

Constructing, looking up and publishing the 570 changed cache hits explains **0.212M of the 54.80M excess instructions** on Ticket batch 7, goal 1. All 820 per-instance sequences matched the in-tree C++ control on constructor count, matched key constructions, cache probes and hits. Of the 262 instances that consumed a changed cache hit, only 94 constructed any applications during variable substitution. The others already had their raw bodies. Hash-consing calls count as construction even when they return an existing AST.

| Operation | Calls per engine | g3 instructions | Native instructions | Excess |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| All application constructors during substitution | 2,667 | 2,988,211 | 1,434,538 | 1,553,673 |
| Constructors whose returned handle later supplied a changed cache hit in the same instance | 191 | 149,368 | 95,403 | 53,965 |
| Read a cached result that differs from its key | 570 | 118,852 | 15,099 | 103,753 |
| Push that result and mark the parent frame | 570 | 80,940 | 26,220 | 54,720 |
| All first-visit cache probes | 5,490 | 1,113,730 | 149,961 | 963,769 |

The last row comes from a separate observer and includes the changed-hit reads. Both engines hit 3,505 times. The constructor subset is included in the first row. The observer joined constructor returns to subsequent cache keys by live handle or pointer within each instance and charged each matching construction once. Publication ends when the visit installs the cached result on its stack. Later work in the parent frame has its own cost. Each figure is a median of five complete, alternating, CPU-pinned, GC-off runs with a calibrated user-instruction counter. All reference exit codes and both output streams matched. Call counts and costs cover this one goal.

Across 3,796 nonconstant application reductions on the same goal, five further pairs measured 4.52M g3 instructions and 0.90M native. The expensive operators differ from the most frequent ones.

| Operator | Calls per engine | g3 | Native | Excess |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Equality and Boolean equivalence | 519 | 1.293M | 0.148M | 1.145M |
| If-then-else | 448 | 1.139M | 0.115M | 1.024M |
| Disjunction | 955 | 1.265M | 0.470M | 0.796M |
| Negation | 801 | 0.515M | 0.111M | 0.404M |
| Uninterpreted application | 1,073 | 0.311M | 0.060M | 0.250M |

On the 3,751 ordinary failed-reduction frame completions, releasing the child results took 0.499M / 0.168M instructions (g3 / native), acquiring the result 0.266M / 0.154M, conditionally caching the frame result 1.134M / 0.351M, and clearing the temporary result register 0.296M / 0.056M. These windows measure individual operations inside application frames. They exclude child traversal and frame scheduling. The two engines agreed within each instance on all five operator counts and on the number of these completions.

### Three uninstrumented trials

- A direct activity-cache read saved 0.31–0.41% of instructions on three incremental CLI replays. Complete normal-GC Ticket elapsed improved 0.80%, while hybrid and FBA elapsed rose 0.25% and 0.38%. The upper bound from all first-visit reads is small on the matched goal.
- Reading equality operands once, checking one-bit equality shapes with one AST identity query, and deferring optional nested ITE checks saved 0.216M of the 18.40M instructions inside the goal’s instance rewrites. In nine paired normal-GC runs complete Ticket elapsed rose 2.36%. Hybrid and ARM also took longer.
- Recognizing distinct uninterpreted application handles in the Boolean equality and ITE rules lowered the existing equivalence benchmark from **196.7 to 72.55 ns** and uninterpreted equality from **157.3 to 92.29 ns**, with zero allocations. Different handles alone never establish disequality. The trial returns the rewriter’s unchanged status. On the matched goal, instance rewriting fell from 18.406M to 17.940M instructions. Across nine complete normal-GC verifier pairs on each of CPUs 11 and 14, Ticket elapsed changed −0.21% and +0.88%, hybrid +1.16% and +0.14%, ARM +0.07% and −0.61%, and FBA −0.41% and −0.23%. Both reducer trials passed the rewriter suite.

All three overlays remain experimental. Every timed CLI pair preserved the verdict, decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource counts. The isolated reducer gains supplied little of the whole-verifier time.

### Larger opportunity across the complete Ticket run

Reclassifying the previous five-rotation full-stage records by whether the *same* goal subsequently reached a concrete check identifies **nine early proof attempts that fell through**, one in each of nine batches. Their median combined cost was **109.75M instructions**. Another 32 early attempts proved the obligation for 35.77M combined. The nine failures represent 75.4% of the measured early-stage cost. Eliminating the entire early stage previously regressed the Apple holdouts. Measure the stages of these nine misses against successful early proofs in Ticket, Raft and Apple. In particular, distinguish eligibility checks, building the private problem, private search, and releasing an unsuccessful attempt. This can establish whether a general, solver-local rejection test has enough time to pay for itself. The 109.75M is an upper bound on the full Ticket opportunity from these misses, independent of the smaller cache and reducer costs on one check. [Measurement code, trials, per-instance counters and complete verifier controls](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-ticket-cache-prices.tar.xz)

## November 27 — When Ticket private proofs fail

Ticket spent 109.78M solver-thread instructions on nine unsuccessful pre-push proofs and 35.73M on its 32 successful ones. No individual stage dominates the misses. Private SMT checks used 16.91M, ground-premise refutation 14.63M, asserting translated premises 14.46M, Boolean checks 9.94M and adding observed instances during projection 9.86M. These are exclusive costs from a nested observer with GC disabled. The separate phase observer measured 109.67M on the same misses. The control workloads had 59 successes and 12 misses on Raft, 26 successes on rfn2 and 2,479 successes on dramc_nb2.

Four Ticket misses first found a model of the selected definitions, then exhausted the rare-premise search budget. A trial that proceeded directly to ordinary solving after the first model reduced the nine misses to 88.47M instructions. However, satisfiable definitions can have an inconsistent extension among the rare premises. Both a ground fact and a pair of complementary clauses produce a cheap private proof on the released solver. The trial missed both. Full solving still gave the right verdict. Raft also had a successful second search following an inconclusive first search. The regression exercises the private proof and independently checks the full solver. [Regression](api/api_verification_goal_test.go)

A second trial looked for a constant-predicate model of the actual selected premises before starting their private search. It found witnesses on four of ten short Ticket plans and reduced the nine misses to 90.79M instructions. Both new regression cases passed. The complete-run measurements below are median paired percentage changes with normal GC, alternating order, a pinned CPU and exact verification transcript checks. Negative values indicate less work or time.

| Workload | Pairs | Skip after satisfiable definitions, instructions / elapsed | Witness on selected premises, instructions / elapsed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket | 9 | −1.64% / −1.63% | −1.26% / −0.21% |
| Hybrid | 9 | −0.53% / −0.23% | −0.34% / +0.05% |
| ARM | 9 | −0.61% / −0.24% | +0.76% / +1.47% |
| FBA | 9 | −0.03% / +0.22% | +0.77% / +1.05% |
| Raft | 5 | +0.51% / −0.43% | +0.46% / −0.05% |
| Apple dramc_nb2 | 3 | −0.12% / +1.68% | +0.03% / −0.34% |
| Apple rfn2 | 3 | +0.90% / +0.54% | −0.59% / −1.54% |

Keep the existing scheduling. The first trial loses private proof coverage. The second scarcely changes whole-Ticket elapsed time and costs CPU on ARM and FBA.

Across five complete Ticket runs, the separate post-push observer found 132 unsuccessful private attempts costing 85.76M instructions and 111 successful attempts costing 11.77M. Observed-instance proving, Boolean input checks and quantified-premise projection accounted for 28.51M, 26.69M and 14.38M of the unsuccessful total. Even eliminating all the unsuccessful post-push work would recover only a fraction of the previously measured 1.08B check-stage gap. Prioritize the ordinary checks that contribute the most excess instructions. The archive includes both trial implementations, observer builders, raw counts, paired measurements and analysis scripts. ## November 27 — Ordinary Ticket checks and substitution across sibling goals

Across all 284 numbered checks, ordinary g3 has a 939M-instruction gap against linked Z3. The eight checks of lines 333 and 345 account for 248.02M. The three later checks in batches 6 through 8 account for 91.44M. The remaining **273 checks account for 599.16M**, more than the eleven previously profiled checks combined. These totals sum per-goal medians from five complete runs per backend. The ordinary configuration sends each goal to the general solver in its original incremental history. Among those checks the largest individual gaps are batch 7 goal 1 (54.80M), batch 2 goal 56 (41.05M) and batch 2 goal 55 (39.18M). The released configuration instead has its largest concrete-check gap at batch 4 goal 55 (60.21M). Search history affects the ranking.

Five further complete ordinary Ticket runs counted every call to ground substitution inside those 284 checks. Of 9,132 calls, 5,771 took the general traversal while waiting for the fourth use of a body and cost 145.46M instructions. The 3,361 compiled calls cost 74.05M, including plan construction on promotion. None fell back because of an unsupported body, a rejected binding, a live previous rewriter result or a resource limit. The two groups contain different bodies and bindings. Their mean costs cannot predict the savings from promoting a particular body.

A separate identity observer found that 5,039 of the cold calls had already seen the same body on an earlier sibling goal. They cost 125.99M instructions. A second observer compared the full ordered binding tuple and source body using owner, slot and generation. It checked liveness **before** reconstruction and compared each surviving result with the actual answer. Across 9,132 requests, 3,720 tuples were new, 5,353 had a retired result and only 59 could reuse a live answer. Those 59 cost just 0.71M instructions to reconstruct. An unbounded directory of weak result handles would have little to return here.

| Whole verifier | Toggle only the Boolean setting | Use cached flat-associative declaration flags | Keep small weak traversal plans | Retain up to 128 substitution tuples |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ticket | −0.70% / −1.14% | −1.13% / −0.80% | −1.31% / +2.27% | −0.79% / +0.15% |
| Hybrid | −0.20% / −0.50% | +0.02% / +0.34% | +0.34% / +2.46% | −0.59% / +0.24% |
| ARM | −0.09% / −0.44% | −0.63% / +0.08% | +0.02% / +0.63% | −0.43% / +0.97% |
| FBA | −0.06% / −0.38% | +0.31% / −0.04% | −1.24% / +0.28% | +0.42% / +1.20% |

Entries give median within-pair changes in process instructions / elapsed time with normal GC. The first two trials used nine alternating rounds per case and the last two used seven. Every completed process matched the reference exit and both output streams. The phase-only experiment assumes that all other settings remain current. The real API can append context parameters and apply them on the next phase change. Its small observed saving would need to cover invalidation and testing of that contract. The flat-associative trial carries cached flags to the existing arena constructor for variadic applications. Its four-workload results were mixed.

The weak plan trial discarded scratch and kept metadata across a search reset only with at most 32 body entries, 8 KiB of plan backing arrays and an active preceding substitution cache. The strong tuple trial retained the existing directory into another search only after growth and with at most 128 entries and 768 handles. It served 1,444 cross-search hits on released Ticket, 2,192 on hybrid, 1,892 on ARM and zero on FBA. Those counts include the complete verifier, while the identity observer above covers ordinary check windows. Retaining a root can keep its whole subgraph alive. The elapsed results give no reason to pay that memory cost for each worker.

Nine alternating sampling rounds per backend covered all 284 concrete check windows on CPU 14, with normal solver search and GC disabled. On the 273 other checks the sampled totals were 976.39M for ordinary g3 and 373.41M for Z3, within 0.7% of the direct 970.07M and 370.91M counts. The largest disjoint excesses were **104.87M in preprocessing** (excluding rewriter phase settings), **103.33M in instance substitution**, **91.52M in instance assertion** and **81.04M in instance rewriting**. Within preprocessing, the entire macro-finder invocation accounted for 41.86M excess and value propagation for 25.16M. These are sampled call paths. Counts by formula and pass are needed to separate extra passes from a higher cost per visit. Compare those two passes in the later physical scopes, including their inputs, outputs and the number of active definitions, before testing a shortcut for unchanged pending assertions. ## November 27 — What changes during Ticket macro discovery and value propagation

The two solvers made the **same 676 macro-finder calls** across 232 of the 273 ordinary Ticket checks outside the two earlier panels. The ordered sequences of input size, output size, unchanged positions and installed-definition counts matched on every check in all five repetitions. Both visited 1,993 input rows, produced 1,993 rows and preserved the expression and proof at 1,741 positions. Neither installed a new definition. Both still applied definitions from earlier scopes.

| Solver-thread intervals, millions of retired instructions | g3 | Linked Z3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Discover or expand, 522 calls returning the same rows | 15.34 | 8.34 |
| Publish and simplify those batches | 18.22 | 4.69 |
| Discover or expand, 154 calls changing the batch | 32.31 | 15.68 |
| Publish and simplify those batches | 9.05 | 2.23 |
| Rewrite individual value-propagation rows | 16.47 | 5.31 |
| Insert their temporary substitutions | 3.88 | 0.63 |

Macro timings split at the return from the finder, before copying its output and reducing the pending assertions. The Go publication interval ends before the finder output batch's deferred close. The row-rewrite intervals include result replacement. Go visits 1,316 value rows against 1,490 native. Only batch 1 goal 41 and batch 2 goal 41 differ in their row/change sequence. Across the other checks the positions and outcomes match. These observers count operations at matching frontend check boundaries, including any auxiliary solving inside them.

A second observer separated macro expansion from the theory normalization of its result. Both engines changed the same 252 rows in sequence and performed two expander traversals on each. Those rows used 15.34M versus 6.40M instructions in expansion and 15.29M versus 8.23M in normalization and cleanup. On the 1,741 unchanged rows the existing identity probe let Go do 368 full traversals versus 1,741 in native. This still cost 11.74M versus 8.36M instructions. The independent observations exclude the equality-counting loop from the reported operation intervals.

**Unchanged finder output does not imply that the subsequent reduction is redundant.** The reduction changed one of two rows at goals 34 and 35 in each of batches 3, 4 and 5, even though the finder returned its entire input unchanged. Both backends agreed. On the other 516 unchanged finder calls, publication and reduction preserved every row and cost 18.15M versus 4.67M instructions. After a changed finder result, reduction preserved the entire batch 144 times and changed it ten times.

The same cost appears on complete ordinary hybrid checks. Across three runs per backend, both made 1,951 finder calls. Discovery cost 119.8M versus 69.5M instructions, and publication and simplification cost 79.1M versus 23.3M. On ARM the corresponding costs across 324 calls were 59.9M versus 21.9M and 38.5M versus 9.8M. First pushes are a separate population. For example, the Go solver made 34 hybrid first-push finder calls versus 68 native.

### November 27 — Can an earlier rewrite predict a fixed point?

A diagnostic overlay recorded successful proof-free assertion rewrites by solver, complete generation-checked formula handle and eliminate-AND setting. One observer counted predictions whenever the current input had previously been returned as output. Another required the same substitution epoch as well. Insert, erase and reset each advanced the epoch before the operation. Both observers always ran the real simplifier and checked its output. The maps were diagnostic and held no AST references. Three GC-off repetitions per short workload measured user instructions on its pinned solver thread.

| Check workload | Earlier output matched, rows | Cost of correctly predicted rows, M instructions | Same epoch, rows | Same epoch cost, M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ticket | 1,706 | 15.66 | 1,136 | 12.52 |
| Hybrid | 4,423 | 40.83 | 2,589 | 21.68 |
| ARM | 593 | 24.58 | 368 | 15.40 |
| FBA | 106 | 3.69 | 106 | 3.69 |

All predictions on these four workloads agreed with the observed output. Four independent controls added TLB, alternating bit protocol, GCD and test_liveness2. **Six predictions failed on test_liveness2 even with the substitution epoch included.** In each of batches 8 and 10, goals 22, 27 and 28 supplied one earlier output that changed on the subsequent pass. All observer runs preserved exit status and both output streams. The narrower predicate that the last rewrite *of this input* returned the same input had zero observed mismatches on the eight cases. On hybrid, the same-epoch version of that predicate covered only 15.34M check instructions. Skipping those calls would also change traversal resource accounting and could omit cache publications used by later rows.

An optimistic solver-local prototype skipped the rewrite on an earlier output match, including matches across epochs. Seven alternating default-GC pairs put the complete instruction savings at 0.81% on Ticket, 0.06% on hybrid, 1.67% on ARM and 1.58% on FBA. Three pairs on TLB saved 0.85% of instructions and **increased elapsed time by 2.55%**. These five transcripts matched. The direct formula comparison on test_liveness2 rules out this prototype for release.

Two frame-loop experiments specialized the theory rewriter's per-step memory and resource checks. Storing the concrete configuration on the engine saved 0.14–0.44% of whole-verifier instructions over seven pairs per case, with mixed elapsed time. A local type assertion preserved the engine size but increased instructions on three workloads. A third experiment omitted empty binding slots during ordinary quantified theory rewrites. The retained benchmark rewrites a universal predicate that uses every declared variable. Seven paired 20,000-iteration runs took 813/792 ns at width one, 1,160/1,083 ns at eight and 3,916/3,542 ns at 64 (baseline/trial), all at zero allocations. Nine complete pairs per case increased instructions on ARM by 0.76% and FBA by 0.20%. None of these experiments changed the release. ### November 27 — SAT watch grouping and conflict trail scans

### November 27 — Flash goal width and the cost of a private proof miss

All 28 batches of examples/ivy/flash2.ivy ask the same second question. Can the current action violate the 23-clause `[aux]` invariant at the witness constants? All 28 answers were UNSAT. The first batch has 19 distinct positive top-level premise conjuncts, and the largest has 98. After expanding SMT-LIB lets, all 28 premise sets are distinct. Fourteen first goals were proved privately. In each of those batches g3 tried the second goal privately and then sent it to the concrete solver.

The private definition search capped a goal at five operands, but the outer unary Boolean application passed that test for a wrapped negation of a 23-way conjunction. The released check applies the same cap to a conjunction or disjunction beneath unary Boolean wrappers. It reuses the bounded arena traversal. A declined attempt falls through to the existing verification path with the original asserted formula. The regression exercises widths five and six. With the old code both received private proofs. The new code proves the first privately and the concrete solver proves both.

| Complete Flash, seven rotated runs per binary | Median instructions | Median elapsed |
|---|---:|---:|
| Previous g3 | 5.831B | 813 ms |
| g3 with bounded width check | 5.556B | 782 ms |
| Linked Z3 | 4.333B | 620 ms |

The median **paired** improvement over previous g3 was 4.11% in instructions and 4.32% elapsed. Flash remains 1.26× native elapsed. All 2,147 passes and 65 expected failures, exit status and both output streams agreed. The independent seven-pair panel saved 4.80% of instructions on Flash and 5.39% on CAV 2024 examp2. Two complete pairs on each of the 37 historical gaps matched linked Z3's transcript. Twelve-pair follow-ups on indexset_test, learning and test_liveness2 put instruction changes between +0.14% and +0.19%. Apple rfn2 and dramc_nb2 changed by +0.61% and less than 0.01% respectively across three pairs each. These small shifts do not establish speedups on those controls.

Three GC-off solver-thread profiles locate the saving. Across the second obligations private proof work fell from 196.0M to 20.3M instructions. Their physical first pushes took 408.0M before and 407.9M after. Concrete checks took 945.4M before and 945.5M after, against native's 374.9M. All 28 first pushes still occurred. Across all 2,212 obligations the sum of measured solver stages fell from 4.133B to 3.957B, versus 2.569B native. The larger remaining target on the second obligation is concrete checking.

**Contextual reduction experiment.** In six of the 14 private misses the existing universal-premise matcher could establish 22 of 23 conjuncts individually. A scratch bridge passed the concrete solver the negation of just the remaining conjunction under the same base. Seven complete pairs against the original g3 saved 9.32% of instructions and 9.02% elapsed on Flash. The private-only variant saved 5.34% and 5.01%. These comparisons use the same original baseline as the width change. They do not measure an additive saving. On the other Flash input, hybrid and Ticket the concrete variant changed median paired instructions by −0.24%, −0.19% and +0.52%.

A separate incremental replay used direct syntactic instances of whole asserted universal clauses. It removed 424 of 644 ground conjunct occurrences across the 28 captured bases. Across three rotations of 28 fresh CLI processes per variant, median summed instructions fell from 3.368B to 2.655B for g3 (21.2%) and from 1.529B to 1.251B for Z3 (18.2%). These totals include CLI startup, parsing and an explicit first push. The whole-verifier experiment measures the effect with shared frontend state. A production reduction must live within the exact active assertion scope and preserve proof, core, model and resource-limit semantics. The scratch bridge cannot establish those contracts. ### November 27 — Remove refuted literals when a scoped clause enters search

An incremental solver can assert a shorter ground disjunction if the committed premises already imply that some of its literals are false. The implementation uses the existing sort-checked universal-instance matcher on the kernel's committed prefix. It builds a temporary clause just before internalization, keeps the original formula in the assertion vector, and releases the temporary reference after search takes ownership. No index survives the call. The removed literals stay false for the lifetime of the scoped clause because every premise used was committed before the clause. Pending siblings cannot participate in the proof.

On Flash, an observer saw 24 affected disjunctions across the 28 second obligations. Preprocessing had already eliminated or changed some source conjuncts. At the search boundary the affected clauses contained 527 literals, of which **404 were refuted by committed premises**. Seven resulting clauses were empty. The production rule examines ground disjunctions of width 16–128, independent of predicate names and input paths. It is enabled in the incremental default backend when constructed without proof or core production. Explicit proof objects, tracing, resource limits and allocation injection retain their ordinary internalization behavior.

| Complete Flash, nine rotated runs per binary | Median instructions | Median elapsed |
|---|---:|---:|
| g3 at `b2c87f098` | 5.563B | 792 ms |
| g3 with scoped clause reduction | 4.816B | 683 ms |
| Linked Z3 | 4.332B | 622 ms |

Across paired runs g3 used **13.46% fewer instructions and 13.72% less elapsed time** than the committed width baseline. Its remaining ratios are 1.112× native instructions and 1.095× native elapsed. Both output streams and exit status matched on all runs, including the 65 expected failures.

| Solver-thread instructions, median of three default-strategy runs with GC off | Prior g3 | Current g3 | Linked Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Concrete checks on second obligations | 945.5M | 367.0M | 374.9M |
| All concrete checks | 2,863.0M | 2,224.7M | 2,084.8M |
| All 28 first pushes | 794.5M | 795.3M | 350.0M |
| All measured solver stages | 3,957.2M | 3,314.9M | 2,568.6M |

Moving the reduction into the public frontend simplifier was unnecessary. Against the committed width baseline, the first-push-only bridge prototype saved 8.45% of whole Flash instructions. Applying it before all concrete goals saved 13.64%; narrowing goals only within the private solver saved 3.33%. The kernel search boundary recovered the full concrete gain while retaining the original assertions. The regression covers an uncommitted premise, one surviving literal, original-assertion inspection, a model of the original query, an assumption core, allocation injection, cancellation, proof mode and popping the premise.

The width sweep compared 4, 8 and 16. At width 4 the independent examples/liveness/ticket.ivy spent 3.21% more instructions in a 12-pair confirmation. It removed only one literal from each of eight five-literal clauses. On TLB, 81 matches each removed just one literal. Starting at 16 kept the Flash gain. Among the 37 historical gap inputs, Flash alone exposed eligible clauses this wide to the observer. The other workloads establish compatibility and bound overhead. The seven-pair release controls changed instructions by +0.16% on test/flash2, −0.06% on the independent Ticket, +0.26% on hybrid and −0.33% on POPL18 Ticket. Raft changed by +0.18% across four pairs. Apple rfn2 and dramc_nb2 changed by +0.05% and −0.11% across three pairs each.

Every historical input matched its reference transcript in two release pairs. One historical reference for IBM cache recorded a missing ABC executable. A separate run with a working ABC beside all three binaries recovered the 314-line counterexample transcript, with identical output and expected exit 1. Seven pairs on that complete check changed instructions by −0.07%. The portable comparison driver now accepts a completed FAIL-only witness and rejects a missing model checker. ### November 27 — How much first-push work can subsequent verification batches reuse?

At g3 `3f776bda1`, four complete verification runs each used one GoIvy AST context across every observed physical action batch. The observer recorded the original base at the first concrete push in each batch, flattened conjunctions in source order and read context-owned AST IDs. It checked both output streams and exit status against linked Z3. The counts include duplicate conjunct occurrences and exclude goal rows and any separately asserted assumptions. An adjacent-common count is the multiset intersection with the previous base.

| Verifier | Physical batches | Base occurrences | Adjacent common | In identical leading positions before first mismatch |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Flash example | 28 | 2,948 | 1,560 | 119 |
| Hybrid | 34 | 2,882 | 1,870 | 853 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 9 | 837 | 486 | 0 |
| TLB | 41 | 26,665 | 20,015 | 480 |

A streaming replay ranked current conjuncts by frequency in *earlier* batches. Each worker could maintain this history locally. The replay kept a stack of groups and popped the suffix starting at the first group missing a premise in the new base. An independent control pushed the same groups in the same order anew for every action. Both engines returned UNSAT for all 28 Flash second goals in each of five rounds. At group width 8, submissions fell from 2,327 to 1,907 and pushes from 305 to 252. Median g3 instructions fell from 2.325B to 2.165B (7.01% paired), and native from 0.783B to 0.738B (5.79%). At width 32 g3 saved 6.52%. These are baseline CLI measurements on the captured second goals. The full frontend also performs private proof attempts, invokes SAT/model callbacks and processes sibling obligations.

**How often could an earlier UNSAT result discharge a later action outright?** Z3 produced a named-premise core for each of the 28 queries. g3 independently proved UNSAT on every extracted core with the original goal. Five later batches contained a previously extracted core. For a bound independent of core selection, we checked all 378 pairs using the intersection of their full premise sets and the shared goal. Z3 answered SAT on 369 and UNSAT on nine. g3 confirmed all nine UNSAT results. Only **six of the 28 batches** admitted such reuse (5, 11, 13, 21, 24 and 28). A satisfying assignment on the intersection also satisfies every subset of that intersection, so mining smaller cores from an individual preceding batch can recover at most one additional batch beyond the five observed hits. This bound applies to reuse of an unchanged premise subset and goal.

**First-push pass trials.** A separate Go overlay changed only the initial physical push in the verifier strategy. The four-round Flash screen found that omitting value propagation saved 1.03% of whole-example instructions but cost 16.90% on the independent test/flash2. Omitting NNF alone reproduced an AST release-continuation error on both hybrid and POPL18 Ticket. Their release runs complete. Skipping just the BV-sharing phase, including its follow-up ordinary reduction, saved 2.80%, 1.69% and 1.84% on Flash, hybrid and POPL18 Ticket in five paired rounds. Running the ordinary reduction alone saved 0.72%, 1.02% and 0.24%. The whole-phase trial changed Raft, rfn2 and dramc_nb2 instructions by −0.17%, +0.02% and −0.12% in three paired rounds. The timing and instruction controls use the release PGO profile, pinned cores and exact transcript checks. These measurements include later search costs. The release retains the existing schedule. The next full-frontend trial should target high-overlap action bases, especially TLB, and measure the cost of preserving model and callback lifetimes. ### November 27 — Whole-verifier action scopes and pattern-inference traversal

**Keep the original action scopes and private proof batch.** We ran every sibling goal, SAT callback and model path on four complete GoIvy inputs. At the first concrete push, the prototype moved to a physical solver containing the current premises and accumulated assumptions. It retained a shared prefix only after an action finished without returning a model. All four transcripts and exit statuses matched linked Z3. Compared with the prior release, three rotated pairs changed whole-verifier instructions by +46.17% on TLB, +6.77% on hybrid, +4.60% on Flash and −1.63% on POPL18 Ticket. Rebuilding the same split scopes each time cost +46.61% on TLB. The 7% saving in the earlier standalone replay covered one goal per action.

TLB exposed the reason. Replacing the private proof batch on the *same solver*, with the *same assertions*, cost 43.10% more instructions. Giving the replacement batch the original sibling count reduced the excess to 10.54%. Moving the original unsplit base to a fresh solver cost 43.46% with an unsized replacement batch. A second prototype kept the original pre-push prover alive for later goals and routed inconclusive cases to the separate concrete solver. With shared action scopes it cost 1.73% more instructions on TLB, 14.97% more on hybrid and 65.42% more on Flash relative to the prior release. The latter trial used the pattern change below in both physical solvers. An unsplit transfer with the same private prover also regressed Flash by 65.75%. These controls distinguish the value of sibling-aware proof state from ordering and sharing premises. The release keeps all solver state worker-local.

**Retained change in `a515ad5e8`.** During unbounded, proof-free verifier pattern inference, the only changes possible inside an application subtree come from binders and the generic rewriter's folding of constant-condition ITEs. The arena already propagated quantifier and label bits at application creation. Packing these into a byte also records ITE presence, preserving the application record layout. The traversal can return the original subtree on a negative test. The actual trigger-selection algorithm still sees the entire body of every quantifier it processes. A regression compares results with the ordinary traversal and forces two nested ITE folds under a negation. The initial quantifier-only prototype fails that regression.

**The next two first-push costs are now directly measured.** Flash value propagation costs 144.66M instructions versus 48.37M native. Its BV-sharing pass costs 117.08M versus 40.01M. On hybrid the corresponding figures are 196.85M versus 68.98M and 137.43M versus 44.77M. On TLB they are 2.221B versus 0.774B and 1.823B versus 0.594B. In a second observer, BV traversal itself cost 42.41M, 53.16M and 710.90M on the three Go runs respectively. Its following ordinary theory reduction cost 71.94M, 81.48M and 1,081.73M. Traversal changed zero of 2,207 Flash rows, 2,297 hybrid rows and 25,881 TLB rows before that reduction.

An experimental shortcut in the initially unconfigured BV rewriter reduced Flash and hybrid instructions by a further 1.24% and 1.19%. A two-scope witness explains why it stays experimental. The original traversal caches a shared four-argument addition as unchanged. After the first push enables associative rewriting, a second formula reuses that cached addition. Skipping the first visit makes the later traversal rebalance it into binary additions. Both are algebraically valid, but the solver now receives a different AST and reference history. Price changed rows and substitution/cache effects in the follow-up reduction before attempting whole-pass elimination. ## November 27 — First-push BV sharing and the 228-input verifier survey

The ordinary theory reduction immediately following BV sharing returned its input on all 48,567 assertion rows observed across 34 of the 37 verifier inputs screened. On TLB alone the rewriter visited 364,035 nodes. Across TLB, Flash, hybrid and POPL18 Ticket there were zero successful direct substitutions, changed cache hits or changed cache publications in this pass.

Commit `9a27a7fc0` keeps the BV sharing traversal, including its persistent cache. On the eligible initial verifier push, it skips the follow-up simplifier when the entire sharing batch preserves the input formulas and proofs in order. Any changed row triggers ordinary reduction on the entire batch. A regression with double negation in an earlier row and a simplifiable ITE in a later row failed when reduction was unconditionally omitted. The observation about unchanged roots applies to the measured workloads.

Five rotated runs per binary on a pinned core compared the preceding release, the new release and linked Z3. Percentages are median paired changes from the preceding g3 release. Times in the last three columns are independent process medians.

| Input | Instructions | Elapsed | Prior g3 ms | New g3 ms | Z3 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| TLB | −2.15% | −1.21% | 6,133.7 | 6,219.0 | 8,820.6 |
| Flash | −1.35% | +1.06% | 724.4 | 722.7 | 668.8 |
| Hybrid | −1.10% | +2.20% | 1,129.8 | 1,154.6 | 837.3 |
| POPL18 Ticket | −1.89% | −1.34% | 422.4 | 414.6 | 233.9 |

Two rounds on all 37 inputs matched the reference exit status and both output streams in all 148 runs. On the long controls the instruction changes were +0.09% on dramc_nb2, +0.18% on rfn2 and −0.36% on Raft. Elapsed results were mixed. The retained benefit is a measured reduction in work on the first-push workloads.

A separate overlay tested dropping either direction of value propagation and skipping the reverse sweep whenever the forward sweep changed nothing. On eight Flash batches the reverse sweep changed a row after an unchanged forward sweep. Against the release, forward-only saved 3.93% of instructions on POPL18 Ticket but cost 16.68% on independent Flash. The conditional reverse sweep cost 9.83% on independent Flash. Both sweeps remain in production.

One pinned pair on each of the historical 228 proof-producing inputs matched linked Z3 byte for byte, including exit status. g3 used fewer instructions on 203 and less elapsed time on 194. This screen ranks remaining opportunities. It cannot attribute improvements since the older inventory to this release alone. Hybrid led the remaining instruction deficits at 2.073 billion, followed by POPL18 Ticket at 1.398 billion, ARM at 0.971 billion, Ticket L2S at 0.892 billion and nested Ticket at 0.877 billion.
