## November 27 — Where the four Ticket verifiers spend their instructions

Three runs per engine counted user instructions on the solver thread with GC disabled. Both backends used the same GoIvy frontend. Every run matched the reference exit status and both output streams. The table shows g3 minus linked Z3, in millions. Translation includes the base and each final condition. The check window starts after the goal is asserted. Depending on the backend, it can include a post-push private proof or a general solver check.

| Complete input | Goal translation and base translation | First pushes | Pre-push proofs | Check calls | g3 / Z3 check calls |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| POPL18 Ticket | 2.8 | 165.9 | 142.2 | 995.1 | 252 / 284 |
| Nested Ticket | 1.9 | 185.1 | 207.4 | 558.2 | 278 / 413 |
| Ticket L2S auto | 3.4 | 163.7 | 126.5 | 804.3 | 255 / 297 |
| Ordinary Ticket | 2.3 | 117.3 | 152.0 | 232.5 | 157 / 239 |

The three largest Ticket deficits share a 2.36B-instruction excess in check calls. Moving the first push later can charge it to a different obligation on each engine. The isolated **check** gaps include 148M at nested Ticket batch 16 goal 1, 92M at L2S 12/8, and 56M at POPL18 4/55. Those values exclude their push costs.

### Matched proof replays

The native frontend saved the active assertions for ten high-cost obligations. Each was submitted to both CLIs with the default settings, either as one fresh query or with a push before the final assertion. This latter replay reconstructs the boundary but omits learned state from preceding siblings. On all twenty inputs both engines returned UNSAT with identical decisions, conflicts, quantifier instantiations and resource counts in each of three rounds. Summing the per-query median **whole-process instructions** gives 4.184B versus 1.726B on fresh queries and 2.297B versus 1.025B on incremental ones. The latter ratio is 2.24× even with the four search counters matched. These totals include parsing and startup.

One distinction changes where to optimize. In the nested 16/1 standalone incremental replay, sampling assigned about 263M g3 and 70M Z3 instructions to checking individual quantifiers against candidate models. In the complete nested verifier, g3 already has its finite-model table checker. The same category costs much less there. POPL18 4/55 and L2S 12/8 showed no samples in this category on incremental CLI replay. Whole-verifier and standalone profiles are archived separately.

### Policy and implementation trials

* Using ordinary phase caching instead of conservative phase caching reduced complete POPL18 instructions by 10.33%, nested Ticket by 4.00%, and L2S by 4.52% in five pinned pairs. It increased hybrid by 6.71% and Flash by 4.46%. Three additional pairs on 37 inputs put toy consensus 2 at +23.52%, ARM at +6.89% and POPL18 at −12.45%. All 222 screen runs matched their references. Changing only single-condition batches saved 6.72% on nested Ticket but added 1.04% on L2S. Keep the current general policy.
* In three incremental CLI runs of each fixture, phase caching cut nested 16/1 from 523M to 263M instructions, while raising L2S 12/8 from 264M to 329M. Disabling relevance tracking approximately doubled the ten-query total from 2.30B to 4.59B. The phase policy is sensitive to the surrounding proof history.
* Restricting the ordinary rewriter's ITE constant-fold probe to arity three saved at most 0.71% of instructions across the six full verifiers in seven pairs. Extending the private solver's true-body MBQI shortcut to full verification changed instructions by less than 0.7% on all six in five pairs. Neither trial establishes a material elapsed gain.
* Sending raw quantified instances directly to the internalizer diverged from the expected transcript on all four Ticket inputs and hybrid. On hybrid the internalizer stopped on an AST precondition. Flash completed but took 4.15% longer in three pairs. Any combined substitution and rewriting path must supply normalized lemmas to the internalizer.

* A single-pass prototype used the existing theory rewriter with de Bruijn bindings to substitute and simplify together. All six complete inputs matched their reference transcripts in five pairs. POPL18 saved 7.86% of instructions, but nested Ticket cost 4.19% more and L2S cost 7.78% more. All ten fresh and ten incremental standalone cases still returned UNSAT. Each differed from the released solver on at least one of the four recorded search counters. The ten incremental cases rose from 2.297B to 2.471B instructions. Retain separate substitution and normalization.

### Where the shared overhead remains

Three whole-process instruction profiles per engine and input used normal GC. Across POPL18, nested and L2S, the sampled quantifier queue spent 833M g3 versus 261M Z3 instructions asserting instances, 685M versus 282M rewriting them, and 658M versus 294M substituting bindings. The three disjoint differences sum to **1.34B**. Within g3's assertion samples, 408M were below formula internalization, 138M below relevance marking, 125M below root clause creation, and 83M below asserted-OR watch registration. Across the three full verifiers, checking individual quantified formulas against candidate models cost about **43M versus 157M**. The expensive model check on the standalone nested replay would be a misleading reason to prioritize MBQI for the full verifier.

Next, compare the numbers of instance operands, newly created Boolean variables and enodes, and clauses emitted on nested 14/44 and L2S 12/8. Charge the samples to those counts. A shared per-new-operand cost would justify optimizing construction and registration. A large count divergence would favor changing which lemmas the solver needs to internalize. Use POPL18 4/55 as a control with earlier matched-queue evidence. Profile classifications are approximate, depend on visible stack frames and cover the entire process. The separate pinned direct counts measure the check-stage gaps.

## November 27 — Instance assertion counts, per-operation cost and sibling history

An observer around quantified-lemma assertion counted work inside three actual GoIvy checks. Each engine ran the complete spec five times on the same pinned CPU with GC disabled and matched the reference exit and both output streams. The frontend used its released proof policy. Counts below are g3 / linked Z3. The enode and gate probes time operations within operand internalization. A root clause is an attempted root-clause addition.

| Check | Asserted instances | Root OR operands | Root clauses | New Boolean variables | New enodes | Gate clauses |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| POPL18 4/55 | 725 / 356 | 3,780 / 1,871 | 725 / 356 | 877 / 426 | 819 / 390 | 260 / 152 |
| Nested 14/44 | 718 / 588 | 3,364 / 2,724 | 718 / 588 | 895 / 741 | 751 / 634 | 481 / 355 |
| L2S 12/8 | 1,983 / 2,490 | 9,147 / 11,756 | 1,980 / 2,488 | 2,791 / 3,415 | 2,347 / 2,901 | 1,563 / 1,864 |

At L2S 12/8, g3 did less construction in every column. Creating an enode still cost 2,570 instructions versus 723, constructing a Boolean variable cost 728 versus 270, and emitting a gate clause cost 1,487 versus 406. Enode creation took 6.03M versus 2.10M in total on this check. The other two checks also had about 3.6× the per-enode cost. The counter builds use matching entry points with adjacent empty-read subtraction, and nested probes affect the parent intervals. These counts support investigating both cost per new node and what drives the number of instances.

### Which earlier proof changes the expensive check?

| Private-proof policy | POPL18 4/55 instances | Nested 14/44 instances | L2S 12/8 instances |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Released | 725 | 718 | 1,983 |
| Disable pre-push attempts | 725 | 718 | 1,983 |
| Disable post-push attempts | 422 | 572 | 1,316 |
| Disable both | 356 | 588 | 2,490 |
| Linked Z3 | 356 | 588 | 2,490 |

Individually changing initial push preprocessing, connected trigger selection, or finite-table model checking left all three measured instance counts at their release values. The experiment with both proof paths disabled also ran with those three options disabled and gave the same counts. These are counts on the selected goals. Each setting was measured twice with complete reference transcript checks.

A separate experiment chose **one previously privately proved, post-push sibling per run** and sent it to the ordinary solver. There were 21 eligible predecessors in POPL18, 20 in nested Ticket and one in L2S. Each intervention ran twice. On POPL18, forcing 4/17 reduced 4/55 from 725 instances to 442 and saved 53.5M summed check-window instructions across the spec. On nested Ticket, forcing 14/31 reduced 14/44 to 424 instances and saved 31.5M. On L2S, forcing 12/6 reduced 12/8 to 1,316 instances and saved 45.8M. These windows include observer overhead and do not measure whole-process elapsed time. The selected predecessor is known in hindsight.

Three general scheduling trials show why these results need held-out controls. Publishing the negation of each post-push privately refuted goal after popping it raised whole-process instructions by 6.6% on POPL18, 16.6% on nested, 14.7% on L2S and 15.5% on hybrid in three pairs. Sending all post-push goals to the ordinary solver saved 3.1% on POPL18 but cost 13.3% on nested. Sending only the next eight checks to it after the first concrete push saved 5.85% on POPL18 and 1.77% on L2S while adding 1.43% on nested, 1.70% on hybrid and 3.21% on Flash in five pairs. Keep the existing general schedule.

### Congruence table allocation

Commit `82a3d422c` creates the wide-signature map only on insertion of a term with more than two arguments. Declaration registration, reference ownership, table IDs and the small-signature table still follow the first lookup. Across five complete inputs, the solvers registered 2,383 declaration buckets and none received a wide insertion. Hybrid accounted for 1,348 of them. The existing ternary collision regression exercised actual wide insertion.

Across nine alternating runs of the 64-declaration benchmark, allocations fell from 162 to 98 per operation, bytes from 36,128 to 33,056 and median time from 23.07 to 20.78 μs. That saves one 48-byte allocation per narrow bucket on this runtime. Eleven same-binary pairs at normal GC changed complete verifier instructions between −0.16% and +0.16%. Median paired elapsed ranged from +0.02% to +2.58%. Seven separate-binary pairs also gave mixed instruction results and slower elapsed measurements. The demonstrated benefit is less allocation and faster declaration registration. Other scratch trials shared binary lemma operands, placed short root literals in a stack buffer, and reused the declaration cache on enode insertion. All gave small or mixed results across complete workloads.

### What carries over between private and ordinary proofs?

On two complete verifier runs per intervention, restoring the two cached Boolean phase bits for surviving variables after one ordinary proof left all five later instance counts unchanged. Restoring the generator's starting state often undid most of the benefit. A complementary experiment kept the original private proof and advanced just its solver's generator by the number of draws the ordinary proof had consumed. Four of five later checks then matched the ordinary predecessor's instance **and** OR-operand counts exactly.

| Earlier sibling → later check | Ordinary draws | Released instances | Ordinary predecessor | Ordinary, restore RNG | Private, advance RNG | Private, shift initial activities only | Private, shift other decisions only |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| POPL18 4/4 → 4/55 | 6 | 725 | 423 | 725 | 423 | 437 | 753 |
| POPL18 4/17 → 4/55 | 1 | 725 | 442 | 562 | 452 | 811 | 433 |
| Nested 14/31 → 14/44 | 8 | 718 | 424 | 718 | 424 | 424 | 683 |
| Nested 14/43 → 14/44 | 130 | 718 | 414 | 697 | 414 | 414 | 689 |
| L2S 12/6 → 12/8 | 16 | 1,983 | 1,316 | 1,983 | 1,316 | 1,219 | 1,138 |

The last two columns used parallel copies of the generator, advanced in lockstep on each call. Only the selected consumer saw the shifted stream. New Boolean variable priorities alone reproduced both nested results. On POPL18 4/17 either consumer alone gave a different result, and even shifting both left a difference from the ordinary predecessor. This experiment does not identify the remaining state on that sibling.

Advancing by one draw after **every** successful post-push private proof reduced whole-process instructions on 20 of 37 inputs and increased them on 17. Three paired rotations matched all 222 reference transcripts and exit statuses. The extremes were −4.95% on Ticket L2S and +5.49% on card2. With the verified solver's public `random_seed` set explicitly, three pairs per seed gave the following median instruction changes. Stock and trial used the same executable and CPU within each pair. Different seeds ran on different pinned CPUs. All 150 runs matched their reference outcomes.

| One extra draw after private proof | Seed 0 | Seed 1 | Seed 2 | Seed 3 | Seed 4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| POPL18 | −2.50% | −2.13% | +1.70% | +5.08% | −2.26% |
| Nested | −0.53% | +2.79% | +4.10% | −0.05% | −1.71% |
| L2S | −4.14% | −3.60% | +6.78% | −5.49% | +1.68% |
| Hybrid | +1.75% | −0.91% | −3.38% | +1.29% | +0.60% |
| Flash | −0.92% | +0.41% | +1.30% | −2.22% | −2.60% |

Initial activity policies that preserved RNG consumption also gave mixed results in four pairs. Zero activity saved 5.35% on POPL18 and 7.08% on L2S while adding 1.53% on nested. AST hash added 4.41% on nested and 4.08% on L2S. Slot hash added work on all five. No search-policy change was retained.

### Where to recover instructions independently of the search seed

In the earlier sampled complete-verifier stacks, installing pending assertions accounted for about 1,353M g3 instructions versus 594M Z3 across POPL18, nested and L2S. Most of the g3 window was assertion preprocessing (1,182M). The two largest named g3 passes were macro finding (362M versus 218M) and value propagation (302M versus 65M). These are sample estimates averaged over three runs per input and then summed. The install category excludes samples already assigned to instance creation or model checking. The archive includes a script that groups the original stacks by caller and callee. Parent and child rows overlap.

A second Go observer measured the two value sweeps in five complete verifiers. Three runs per input used normal solver logic, pinned execution and disabled GC. A separate complete run enabled visit counters. Elapsed and whole-verifier trials below used normal GC. In the table, rewrite costs are the median sum of row calls in millions of user instructions. Forward and reverse substitution updates are combined. The last column times the ordinary simplifier invoked once the sweep has changed a row.

| Input | Rows per direction | Changed forward / reverse | Forward rewrite | Reverse rewrite | Substitution updates | Post-change simplifier |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| POPL18 | 1,376 | 233 / 139 | 29.77M | 28.73M | 8.20M | 25.43M |
| Nested | 1,614 | 42 / 75 | 30.41M | 30.70M | 9.47M | 24.92M |
| L2S | 1,344 | 63 / 98 | 33.55M | 33.45M | 7.81M | 22.82M |

| Flash | 3,062 | 28 / 134 | 73.92M | 74.08M | 18.11M | 24.73M |

Across the three Ticket inputs, 801 of 75,255 substitution probes hit (1.06%). The rewriter returned a cached result different from its key on 39 of 22,609 cache lookups. Both directions changed formulas on every input. The final ordinary simplifier changed zero formulas and zero proofs on all 7,032 rows across the five inputs. Omitting it as an upper-bound experiment gave complete-verifier instruction changes of −0.53%, −0.69%, +0.41%, −0.39% and −0.27% respectively in three same-binary pairs. Eliding the unused proof output slot during proof-free preprocessing gave changes between −0.25% and +0.35% in five pairs. Neither trial was retained. The sweep measurements cover every invocation in these processes, including those outside the sampled installation stack.

Inside enode creation on L2S, separate calibrated intervals averaged 218 instructions for validation and reference acquisition, 1,150 for the constructor, 766 for interpretation or congruence handling, 265 for registration, 31 for trailing and equality propagation, and 26 for trace attachment per new enode (medians over five full runs). This places the largest Go interval in the constructor. Eliminating its entire cost on this goal would save only about 2.7M instructions. The forward and reverse rewriter together therefore warrant higher priority.

## November 27 — Wide unsigned order proofs on complete ring verifiers

Both leader-election verifiers now finish faster with g3 than with linked Z3. Their expensive obligations include trichotomy, transitivity and asymmetry of unsigned 64-bit values. In the extracted 186-byte trichotomy goal, both ordinary solvers used 440 decisions, 101 conflicts and 22,585 resource units. A word-level proof can settle it before any of those decisions.

Commit `afb546562` recognizes small conjunctions of comparisons in reusable verification batches. For example, assuming neither unsigned value is smaller gives both weak inequalities. Together they imply equality, contradicting the third trichotomy assumption. The implementation computes transitive closure on up to eight terms using one byte per row. It follows at most 32 Boolean nodes, respects polarity, and checks the width of the conflicting component. Arbitrary expressions can serve as endpoints. The rule has no dependency on a spec, symbol name, solver identity or check number. It preserves the existing resource and cancellation gates. Ordinary SMT-LIB checks still take the general path.

Eleven rotated triples on one pinned CPU used the same GoIvy frontend for previous g3, new g3 and linked Z3. The figures are medians for the complete process. All 99 exit codes and output streams matched, including each ring spec's expected counterexample.

| Complete input | Previous g3 ms | New g3 ms | Linked Z3 ms | Previous g3 M instructions | New g3 M instructions | Z3 M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| leader_election_ring | 91.56 | 38.20 | 78.19 | 504.65 | 92.00 | 409.82 |
| leader_election_ring_btw | 107.11 | 59.79 | 85.58 | 610.03 | 212.58 | 457.16 |
| arm_rules3 | 527.07 | 503.89 | 390.10 | 3,227.56 | 3,212.97 | 2,193.49 |

**Why the cutoff is 32 bits.** The initial all-width prototype settled six opening ARM obligations and increased complete ARM instructions by 37%. Moving those proofs changed downstream cost. The exact downstream solver state responsible remains unidentified. Varying only the bit width in the plain ring produced the following whole-run medians over five rotated triples. At 32 bits the shortcut first removed over half the work. With the production cutoff, instrumentation recorded exactly three early proofs on each ring and zero on ARM in each of three runs.

| Width | Previous g3 M instructions | All-width prototype M instructions |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 91.7 | 90.2 |
| 4 | 96.0 | 92.4 |
| 8 | 105.8 | 89.5 |
| 16 | 123.3 | 90.2 |
| 32 | 219.5 | 90.4 |
| 64 | 511.0 | 90.4 |
| 128 | 1,300.3 | 90.2 |

All 222 runs in the separate 37-input screen matched. The three largest unfavorable instruction changes received 15 additional pairs each. Those medians were +0.98% for PLDI16 learning switch, −0.51% for indexset and −0.89% for toma8. Three paired complete runs each on Raft, Apple rfn2 and Apple dramc_nb2 matched the reference, with median instruction changes of −0.36%, less than 0.01% and +0.07%, respectively. The two-bit regression checks 208 predicate triples against all 64 valuations. Separate tests cover compound endpoints, signedness, the 31/32 boundary and the verification API. The saved closure benchmark allocated zero bytes at widths 4, 64 and 256. [Measurements, drivers, fixtures and overlays](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-frame-cost-frontier-and-wide-order.tar.xz)

### What the remaining verifier gaps cost

* **Rewriter frames.** In Ticket 290 the engines visited the same 15,307 child operands. Operand fetch consumed 1.061M instructions in g3 and 0.061M in Z3. Child visits cost 8.866M and 2.379M, and the 8,227 unsuccessful reductions' frame completions cost 5.333M and 1.406M. The 188 actual rebuilds cost only 0.270M and 0.102M. Avoiding a redundant fold check cut the binary microbenchmark from 6.59 to 6.34 µs. Whole-verifier effects were mixed, including for direct operand reads and specialized visitors. Keep the benchmark and the existing implementation.
* **Private proofs and first pushes.** For the 36 historical inputs in the 228-input survey with excess time or instructions, three paired GC-off instrumented runs per input matched all 216 reference outcomes. Summing per-input medians gave 8.876B excess instructions inside checks, 4.391B in early private proof attempts, and 4.156B on first concrete pushes. Further instrumentation measured 2.941B on unsuccessful early attempts and 1.324B on unsuccessful attempts inside checks. The latter are already included in check cost. An experimental scheduler supplied with the actual unsuccessful positions from an earlier run saved 4.23–14.64% of total normal-GC release instructions on 12 inputs, across 240 exact runs. An online predictor using formula shape missed valuable proofs and increased instructions on Apple rfn2 by about 62% and dramc_nb2 by 13%. Keep the current scheduler. A promising next experiment is a cheap witness that a relaxed formula is satisfiable, validated against entire solver lifetimes.
* **Next matched-search cases.** ARM goals 6/5 and 6/6 matched Z3 on decisions, conflicts, instantiations and resource count, yet each cost g3 roughly three times as many instructions in fresh SMT-LIB replay. ARM 6/5 alone produced 4,967 instantiations. In sampled stacks on both fixtures, asserting generated instances was a larger source of excess instructions than rewriting them. On card3 goal 3/9 all four counters also matched, while the sampled excess concentrated in model-based quantifier checking. Split the cost of evaluating the quantified body, checking the auxiliary context and extracting witnesses before choosing an implementation change. Fresh replay and complete-verifier samples are recorded separately in the archive.

On the final paired card3 3/9 recording, 887 g3 samples under the quantifier checker fell inside auxiliary solver checks versus 226 in Z3. At 500,203 instructions per sample, the estimated difference was 331M instructions. Of these samples, installing pending assertions accounted for 465 versus 107 (about 179M excess), and bounded search accounted for 305 versus 82 (about 112M excess). The bins are disjoint. The absolute estimates are from a single matched pair and cover only this standalone replay. Compare the number and size of formulas installed per auxiliary check before changing model evaluation or allocating new scratch. The archive includes the per-child counts and classifier. To reproduce, run `held_profile.py` through its final pair and then run `card_children.py` against the retained recordings.

## November 27 — Finite model checks in mixed arithmetic verifiers

In card3 goal 3/9, g3 and Z3 checked 97 quantifiers and entered assertion installation 257 times. Both began those passes with 549 pending rows in total. **All 448 installed expression trees matched, in order**, comparing application names, arities and integer numeral values. The expanded trees contained 71,769 nodes. The observer retained the original answer and the four native search counters, including 616 decisions and 665 quantifier instantiations. In the earlier paired sampled stacks, preprocessing accounted for 401 of 465 g3 installation samples and 92 of 107 Z3 samples. The expensive part of installation here is processing the same data.

Disabling individual auxiliary passes changed later search. Omitting BV sharing saved roughly 11% of instructions on the extracted card3 goal, while adding 21% to complete card3 and 31% to card2. Disabling all preprocessing changed output on all four complete verifier controls. Skipping ITE traversals on unchanged ground or ITE-free expressions gave small, mixed results. These schedules remain unchanged.

Commit `6fe39ec40` removes a whole-context restriction on the existing finite-model checker. Previously an unrelated active arithmetic atom barred it from checking a quantified formula over Booleans or uninterpreted sorts. The table compiler already checks the sorts, operators and function interpretations used by the quantified formula. It can discharge the supported formula or find a concrete binding that falsifies it in the candidate model. Unsupported expressions still reach the auxiliary solver. In the new regression an active integer inequality coexists with a Boolean identity and an integer identity. The previous solver launched two auxiliary checks. The updated solver launches only the integer check.

The table shows complete process medians from 25 rotated triples on one CPU, with the same frontend, PGO configuration and native reference output. All 225 runs matched. Units are milliseconds. A separate eleven-triple run also placed g3 narrowly ahead on card3.

| Complete input | Previous g3 | Mixed-theory g3 | Linked Z3 | g3 instruction change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| card2 | 61.69 | 55.45 | 49.87 | −16.98% |
| card3 | 84.21 | 78.24 | 80.77 | −9.17% |
| toy_consensus2 | 145.87 | 134.60 | 128.39 | −11.18% |

An eleven-triple comparison also measured 4.8% fewer instructions on indexset. All **456 runs across 228 complete inputs** matched reference stdout, stderr and exit status. Seven additional pairs per input confirmed instruction savings of 4.8% and 5.4% on two other toy-consensus verifiers. The largest initial unfavorable percentage, 9.6% on ordered_set, became −1.5% on repetition. Three paired complete runs each on Raft, Apple rfn2 and dramc_nb2 matched, with median instruction changes of +0.10%, +0.26% and −0.16%. Saved measurements include raw runs, observer builds for Go and in-tree Z3, both assertion streams, release drivers and the rejected pass schedules. [Reproduction archive](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-cardinality-model-checks.tar.xz)

### Exact integer arithmetic over finite binding domains

Several quantified bodies in these inputs apply integer-valued functions to finite-domain variables. g3 can enumerate the binding tuples and evaluate the resulting integer expressions without launching a second SMT solver. The finite-model checker now interns small integer values, compares them exactly, and evaluates addition, subtraction, negation and multiplication with a 64-bit intermediate. It falls back if an intermediate leaves the signed 32-bit range, if the table needs more than 1,024 distinct integers, or if an operator or domain is unsupported. Integer-bound quantifiers still take the ordinary path. Tests cover concrete counterexamples, lookup with a computed integer key, equality, comparisons, arithmetic overflow and ordinary fallback.

Scheduling matters even for a correct local proof. The unrestricted prototype saved a further 34% of instructions on indexset, but cost 33–36% on the two other toy-consensus verifiers in the 228-input screen. Each of those regressions involved mixed integer expressions with one or two binders. Accepting only proofs of validity still added about 18%, and accepting only witnesses added about 62%. A trial with cutoffs of 8, 16, 32 and 64 binding assignments found that the lower two still cost over 20% on the two holdouts. The retained cutoff is **at least 64 assignments**, based on actual finite domain sizes. This recovered more of the indexset saving than the 32-assignment cutoff while preserving the toy holdouts. The existing schedule for tables without integer values continues to apply.

Twenty-five rotated triples on a pinned CPU gave the following complete process medians. All 300 results matched both native output streams and exit status. The baseline predates both mixed-theory changes.

| Input | Previous g3 ms | Final g3 ms | Linked Z3 ms | Previous g3 M instructions | Final g3 M instructions | Z3 M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| card2 | 71.03 | 61.20 | 56.85 | 261.85 | 195.30 | 198.29 |
| card3 | 95.40 | 83.71 | 90.03 | 426.48 | 353.45 | 437.56 |
| indexset_test | 130.13 | 98.92 | 100.88 | 657.40 | 443.58 | 505.97 |
| toy_consensus2 | 165.26 | 141.41 | 147.00 | 860.85 | 702.45 | 824.26 |

An independent 15-round four-build run included the intermediate mixed-theory commit. The two timing panels both placed g3 ahead on card3 and indexset. The elapsed winner on card2 and toy_consensus2 changed between panels, while g3 retired fewer instructions than Z3 on both in each panel. On doc/examples/toy_consensus and test/toy_consensus_mc the final build used 2.330B and 2.331B instructions, within 0.1% of the mixed-theory build. All 456 final-candidate and intermediate-baseline runs across the 228-input corpus matched. Nine additional pairs each on the 11 largest unfavorable percentage changes put the largest confirmed increase at about 2% on ordered_set and proving9. Three rotating production pairs per long control matched the reference. Whole-process instructions changed by −1.03% on Raft, +0.32% on Apple rfn2 and +0.05% on Apple dramc_nb2 versus the pre-study release. These process measurements include startup and GC. [Drivers, controls, fixtures and all raw runs](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-cardinality-model-checks.tar.xz)

**ARM remains open.** In the final 15-round panel g3 took 503 ms versus 355 ms for Z3. Three paired stack profiles on each of ARM's matched 6/5 and 6/6 replays attribute about 161M and 110M g3 instructions to recursively internalizing expressions from generated instances. Marking relevance cost about 33M and 20M. Adding root clauses cost about 7M and 4M. In Z3 the largest direct child on both replays was equality internalization. Sample categories depend on inlining. The next comparison should count equality operands, newly installed enodes and hits on existing enodes before optimizing watch insertion or root clauses.

## November 27 — Equality operands in ARM quantifier instances

The two ARM replays exercise the same search in g3 and the C++ fork. An observer at the recursive equality-operand call recorded the enclosing instance number, operand position, Boolean sort, declaration family, arity, existing enode and existing SAT variable. **The ordered records agree on all 26,072 visits.** These are operand visits within asserted quantifier instances. A single expression can occur more than once.

| ARM goal | Asserted instances | Existing enode | Missing non-Boolean enode | Missing Boolean enode, SAT variable exists | Missing both Boolean enode and SAT variable |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 6/5 | 4,967 | 7,441 | 462 | 62 | 6,637 |
| 6/6 | 4,280 | 5,377 | 422 | 93 | 5,578 |

Both answers were UNSAT. Decisions, conflicts, quantifier instantiations and resource counts matched the uninstrumented references on each goal. On 6/5 the missing Boolean enodes include 3,947 uninterpreted predicates and 2,752 basic applications. A shortcut for attaching an enode to an already bound Boolean variable would cover just 155 of the 12,370 missing Boolean enodes across the two goals. In the 6/6 stack profile, 480 samples under the core formula routine entered recursive child internalization and 28 entered Boolean enode attachment directly. Of 47 sampled sort-constraint calls in term internalization, 46 entered the datatype theory. Recursion makes these stack counts inclusive.

The first release prototype bypassed recursive internalization for a live non-Boolean equality operand whose declaration family had no registered theory. On ARM there were 4,367 and 3,024 already installed, non-Boolean, uninterpreted operands on the respective replays. Nine alternating pairs on each complete verifier yielded the following process medians. All 54 outputs and exit codes matched their native references.

| Complete verifier | Baseline ms | Shortcut ms | Baseline M instructions | Shortcut M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM | 478.12 | 468.09 | 3,200.01 | 3,219.26 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1,106.43 | 1,097.80 | 7,930.26 | 7,889.56 |
| card3 | 74.13 | 73.38 | 357.95 | 360.09 |

The shortcut cost 0.60% more instructions on its target and 0.60% more on card3. The single timing panel favored it by 0.8–2.1%. The release keeps the original path.

The second prototype sent a surviving Boolean equality to the existing IFF gate when the ordinary equality rewriter declined to simplify it. This changes the search. On 6/5, instances fell from 4,967 to 4,787 and decisions rose from 481 to 503. On 6/6, instances fell from 4,280 to 4,017 and decisions rose from 456 to 514. Both remained UNSAT. In nine standalone pairs with GC disabled, the median instruction savings were 4.7% and 2.4%. The complete verifier reversed the result.

| Complete verifier | Baseline ms | IFF ms | Baseline M instructions | IFF M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM | 461.13 | 550.23 | 3,221.14 | 3,912.57 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1,106.54 | 1,115.82 | 7,923.38 | 8,040.85 |
| card3 | 73.48 | 73.11 | 355.77 | 357.37 |

All 54 complete runs matched native stdout, stderr and exit status. General IFF lowering added 21.5% to ARM instructions and is excluded from the release. The two selected obligations predict the direction incorrectly for this transformation. Before another change to equality encoding, rank **all** ARM obligations under the two builds with their original incremental history, then compare search counters at the largest regressions. For a search-preserving optimization, measure the cost of installing the 12,215 fresh Boolean operands, splitting child traversal, SAT-variable creation and congruence registration on the matched search. [Fixtures, benchmark drivers, prototypes and raw measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-arm-equality-operands.tar.xz)

### Which incremental ARM checks account for the IFF regression?

Seven alternating pairs preserved the complete GoIvy run and profiled each stage on the solver thread, using the release PGO profile and normal GC. The median paired increase across measured stages was 698.87M instructions, close to the independently measured 691.43M whole-process increase. Ordinary checks added 734.60M, and early private-proof attempts saved 51.37M. Stage totals come from paired runs. Medians of individual rows need not sum to the median of their total.

| Incremental check | Baseline M instructions | IFF M instructions | Decisions, baseline → IFF | Instantiations, baseline → IFF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Batch 6, goal 25 | 77.41 | 548.16 | 736 → 4,686 | 383 → 1,000 |
| Batch 6, goal 5 | 231.84 | 495.81 | 2,199 → 3,103 | 720 → 1,249 |
| Batch 6, goal 6 | 187.02 | 158.55 | 734 → 554 | 646 → 525 |

The paired increases on 6/25 and 6/5 were 454.78M and 273.81M. In combination they exceed the whole-run increase because several other goals improved. IFF made 6/5 cheaper in isolation and more than twice as expensive after four earlier checks on its live solver. The incremental route changed in batch 5 as well. The baseline discharged goals 3 and 4 before the first push. IFF needed its first push at goal 3 and reached the ordinary solver for both goals. Per-mode stage sequences were stable in all seven runs, and all outputs and exit codes matched native. Separate counter builds read each solver's cumulative statistics immediately after each ordinary check. The table differences successive snapshots within a batch.

A separate release trial changed the initial SAT decision on an equality with no saved phase to true after honoring queue and theory preferences. It used the ordinary equality encoding and excluded the always-true and random modes from the override. In seven alternating pairs per input, median complete-process instructions rose from 3.202B to 5.070B on ARM (+58.3%), 7.901B to 8.008B on hybrid (+1.4%) and 360.31M to 400.17M on card3 (+11.1%). All 42 runs matched native output and status. The production decision policy stays in place.

### Installing fresh Boolean operands on the matched ARM search

Three matched standalone replays per engine and goal used counters around the first encounter with an equality operand lacking both a Boolean variable and an enode during instance assertion. All baseline decisions, conflicts, instances, resource counts and answers remained identical. The engines made exactly the same number of calls in each measured category. Counts below are median millions of retired user-mode instructions, inclusive for each named operation. An empty counter interval cost about 60 instructions in Go and 38 in C++. Figures include instrumentation overhead.

| Operation | 6/5 g3 | 6/5 Z3 | 6/6 g3 | 6/6 Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Complete fresh operand | 143.60 | 37.84 | 122.06 | 31.47 |
| Recursively internalize its children | 109.16 | 27.17 | 93.06 | 22.55 |
| Create its Boolean variable | 4.30 | 2.15 | 3.69 | 1.78 |
| Attach its Boolean enode | 13.44 | 3.19 | 11.47 | 2.69 |
| Install its gate constraints when applicable | 10.59 | 2.77 | 8.84 | 2.30 |

A second observer classified every immediate child by Boolean sort, declaration family, arity, existing enode and existing SAT variable. All category counts agree between engines. One category explains about four fifths of the recursive instruction difference. Fresh five-argument Boolean applications in the basic family cost 87.32M versus 21.39M instructions over 2,272 visits on 6/5 and 71.58M versus 16.89M over 1,856 visits on 6/6. Classification and logging sit outside the individual child counter interval. The outer totals from this second observer include the extra measurement work and are excluded from the table.

A third probe identified all 4,128 nodes as OR gates. In g3, recursive work on their five children took approximately 52.5M and 43.2M instructions on the two goals. Installing the gates’ own constraints took another 30.4M and 24.9M. None of the ORs needed an enode of its own. The six depth-three expression shapes on each goal all correspond to versions of the ARM event-ordering predicate. One child tests membership in four of five operation constructors. Another disjoins address equality with two operation tests on a different event.

A fourth trial registered OR relevance watches using the gate's existing signed literals, falling back to expression traversal on reserved literals. All 54 complete verifier runs matched native. The median paired instruction changes were +0.34% on ARM, −0.10% on hybrid and −0.01% on card3. The existing watch path stays in the release.

The finite-enumeration prototype rewrote an OR of distinct constructor equalities on a shared enum term when exactly one constructor was absent. The public simplifier reduced four of five values to inequality with the fifth. Mixed-term and duplicate controls preserved their meaning, including a satisfiable mixed-term witness. In nine complete-verifier pairs, median paired instructions changed by −1.44% on ARM, +0.22% on hybrid and +1.10% on card3. Both standalone goals kept the original four search counters and cost about 0.25% more instructions. A complementary input-level trial applied all 27 four-of-five rewrites in each recorded input before any preprocessing. Seven pairs per engine yielded these medians.

| Goal | g3 original → early M instructions | Z3 original → early M instructions | Instances in both engines, original → early |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 6/5 | 1,186.88 → 1,243.30 | 402.55 → 415.21 | 4,967 → 5,909 |
| 6/6 | 1,093.38 → 1,213.59 | 377.84 → 409.64 | 4,280 → 5,321 |

Both engines returned UNSAT in all 56 runs and agreed on all four counters for each input version. Early folding increased quantifier instantiations by 19% and 24%. The experiments favor keeping the current encoding. A candidate for the next search-preserving trial is the construction of the six gate clauses for each five-way OR. Measure simplification, retained clauses and relevance registration separately, then test bulk installation if repeated per-clause work is material. A separate algorithmic opportunity is to quantify how many instances come from expanding the event-ordering definition before changing its encoding again. ## November 27 — The live ARM verifier and the missing macro option

**Correction to the ARM priority.** The exported SMT-LIB assertions omit GoIvy’s solver parameter `smt.macro_finder=true`. The earlier standalone measurements correctly describe the two exported formulas with default options. They do not establish that their five-input disjunctions are expensive in the complete ARM verifier. Instrumenting that verifier with the same eligibility test counted **zero qualifying fresh Boolean equality operands and zero qualifying five-way ORs** across 5,274 asserted quantifier instances (5,239 during ordinary checks, 19 during private proofs and 16 during first pushes). Its native transcript and exit status matched. Checks 6/5 and 6/6 asserted 720 and 646 instances in their live incremental history.

On the original default-option replays, g3 and Z3 each emitted 13,632 and 11,136 clauses from the selected disjunctions on the respective goals. Both entered post-simplification storage 7,785 and 6,525 times. On 6/5 the sampled region around storage and its callees took about 9.15M counted instructions in Go and 2.93M in C++. OR relevance registration took 7.98M and 2.61M. These inclusive counts include probe overhead. The gates are a reproducible microbenchmark. Checking for an already satisfied binary gate clause before calling the generic emitter moved median whole-verifier instructions by +0.63% on ARM, −0.52% on hybrid and +0.61% on card3 in nine pairs. All 54 verdicts and transcripts matched. The release keeps the existing emitter.

### Why definition-head triggers looked promising in exported goals

The input-level experiment added a single explicit match pattern for an uninterpreted Boolean predicate applied to a permutation of all bound variables on one side of a universally quantified equality. Forty-four quantifiers qualified per input. A narrower diagnostic selected the 26 event-ordering definitions. Neither transformation changed the formulas’ logical meaning. Five pairs per engine gave these median instruction counts for the general rule.

| Replay and options | g3 original → explicit, M instructions | Z3 original → explicit, M instructions | Instances, original → explicit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 6/5, CLI defaults | 1,186.92 → 606.97 | 402.55 → 237.62 | 4,967 → 812 |
| 6/6, CLI defaults | 1,093.48 → 584.72 | 377.84 → 231.68 | 4,280 → 702 |
| 6/5, macro finder enabled | 605.71 → 608.82 | 246.17 → 248.53 | 660 → 660 |
| 6/6, macro finder enabled | 578.93 → 582.04 | 241.47 → 243.73 | 445 → 445 |

Restoring the solver option eliminates the apparent trigger advantage even on a fresh solver. With the complete frontend and its normal macro setting, constructing explicit head patterns increased median ARM instructions from 3.243B to 4.398B in nine pairs. Seven paired stage profiles put 723M extra instructions in batch 6 goal 25 and 401M in goal 26. The 6/5 and 6/6 CLI fixtures remain useful for experiments about default-option search. For ARM release decisions, verify the effective options and event counts in the live verifier before ranking a replay hotspot.

### What the live verifier spends on quantified instances

Three live runs timed each call to materialize and internalize an offered instance, grouping by the source quantifier body's declaration tree to depth four. The timer includes offers that finish as true. All per-shape call counts repeated exactly and all three verification transcripts matched native. Four prominent shapes were the load, acquire-load, store and release-store conjectures relating a conjunction of two event predicates to a conjunction of three event properties. The largest acquire-load shape cost 56.30M instructions over 335 calls. The corresponding release-store, store and load shapes added 27.11M, 24.95M and 22.05M. Other separately counted versions use different declarations for the event state. For comparison, the most frequent transitivity shape had 3,600 offers but only cost 7.78M.

Three full-verifier relevance-policy comparisons on each of ARM, hybrid, card3 and Ticket showed large variation by workload. On card3, level 1 reduced median instructions from 353.6M to 291.4M. On ARM it raised them from 3.178B to 4.007B. Level 0 raised ARM to 4.535B and Ticket from 1.610B to 3.046B. All 36 runs matched native. Keep the current policy.

Splitting a quantified equivalence between conjunctions into two directional implications reduced complete ARM instructions by a median paired 2.14% and elapsed time by 2.05% over 13 pairs toggled inside the same executable. A second CPU gave about 1.9% fewer instructions. Splitting each conjunct separately increased instructions. Both frontend variants matched the native transcripts and exit codes on 228 inputs each, after rerunning seven cases that required the companion ABC executable. In two longer pairs the directional split moved Raft instructions by −0.45%, Apple rfn2 by +1.27% and Apple dramc_nb2 by +0.16%. Placing the split in g3's first push gave −1.09% on ARM, −0.24% on hybrid and +1.85% on card3 across seven pairs each. Neither placement earned a release change. Combining explicit triggers with disabling the macro finder raised complete ARM instructions by about 133%.

### Where to look for a larger ARM improvement

Three pinned complete-verifier profiles per engine assigned each instruction sample to one category. Values below are millions of user instructions. The groups are approximate because native and Go inline different functions and use different stack unwinders.

| Phase | g3 | Linked Z3 | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Installing formulas | 551 | 167 | +384 |
| Search outside installation and the quantifier groups | 907 | 316 | +591 |
| Quantifier queue, instance assertion | 167 | 43 | +124 |
| Quantifier queue, rewriting | 130 | 50 | +80 |
| Quantifier queue, substitution, checking and other work | 174 | 72 | +102 |
| Model-based quantifier work | 162 | 297 | −135 |
| Remaining work | 1,142 | 1,257 | −115 |

Within inclusive stacks, g3's theory assignment propagation accounted for about 219M instructions versus 56M for native atom propagation. Conflict resolution accounted for 237M versus 81M. These stacks overlap other categories. g3 also spent about 177M in scope pop. Reusing the equality enode's two child pointers in the assignment path increased complete ARM instructions by about 0.6%. The next measurement should count propagated equalities, parent visits, conflicts and undone assignments per live check alongside these costs. A different number of events calls for a different change than a high cost at equal event counts.

### Reuse the congruence-table slot on deletion

Erase previously looked up a congruent representative, then searched the declaration table again to delete it. The updated short-arity path retains the slot from the first successful probe and applies the existing backward-shift deletion there. It still validates equality, tries reversed roots only where allowed, and falls back to the representative's current key if a merge changed its roots. The wide path hashes once and removes the matching member of the collision chain. The arena and per-solver ownership are unchanged.

| Exact release change against its parent | Pairs | Median paired change in process instructions |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ordered erase and reinsert, 200,000 iterations | 5 | −1.98% |
| Commuted erase and reinsert, 200,000 iterations | 5 | −3.17% |
| Erase miss | 5 | +0.39% |
| Read-only ordered hit / miss | 5 each | −0.10% / −0.07% |
| Merge and undo, both unrelated-class sizes | 7 | −1.57% |
| Scope-memory benchmark, all three widths | 7 | +0.12% |
| Complete ARM / hybrid / card3 | 7 each | +0.35% / +0.14% / −0.40% |

Nine paired latency runs showed ordered and commuted erase/reinsert taking 3.68% and 3.19% less time. Miss-only elapsed times were noisy, including a 13.35% increase in the unchanged read-only miss benchmark. All 42 complete runs matched linked Z3's exit status and both streams. Keeping the single-pass deletion improves successful removal and the higher-level merge/undo workload. It has no demonstrated whole-verifier speedup on these three controls. The earlier prototype's 5.82% instruction saving on erase misses did not carry through to the final build. ### What equality maintenance costs at matched volume

Separate observers measured instructions inside the three corresponding source functions, with a neighboring empty read for each call. They include callees and some instrumentation overhead. The independent uninstrumented stage panel supplies the end-to-end numbers above.

| Undo an equality merge | 5,537 | 2,517 | 810 | 9.46 |

The baseline short-arity table walked 64,027 occupied slots following 175,733 deletions and moved only 9,117 entries. Read probes visited 513,547 slots over 385,976 calls. These counts bound what changing the deletion policy alone could recover.

On 6/5 both engines entered core propagation 2,360 times and conflict resolution 161 times. The corresponding 6/6 counts were 882 and 148. Three separate observer builds timed search, propagation components and the quantifier manager. The intervals below include callees. Compare like rows across engines. We then instrumented the three instance operations themselves. On 6/5 both engines substituted, rewrote and asserted exactly 720 instances. On 6/6 both performed all three operations exactly 646 times. These live counts resolve the volume question even within the queue.

These measurements motivate comparing how both engines classify literals and traverse already-internalized expressions when installing the *live* lemmas, then testing a path that can reuse the prior rewrite or Boolean result for a whole subtree. Compare the ordered output, resource accounting and retained clauses before attempting to share or remove a traversal.

### Congruence changes tested on complete verifiers

The baseline was `4808f7da6`. Release builds used the same frontend and Go PGO profile. The table reports median paired differences in complete process instructions. Every measured transcript and exit status agreed with the stored native result.

| Prototype | Pairs per input | ARM | Hybrid | card3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

The new test exercises a distinct node at an obsolete key after a class split. All **228** complete-verifier corpus outputs and exit codes matched native with the release change. The single-pass insertion prototype duplicated table insertion logic for a narrow gain and saved only 0.07% in the merge-and-undo benchmark. ## November 27 — Installing live ARM lemmas and splitting datatype variables

Two places in the Go datatype theory were materializing every constructor of a sort. One needed only the number of constructors. The other often already had the recognizer it needed. The cost grew with the width of the datatype in both cases. Both changes preserve the order of recognizer selection and leave the arena and solver-local ownership model intact.

### Where the live assertion time went

These measurements use the GoIvy verifier with its macro finder enabled. On ARM goal 6/6, g3 and linked Z3 asserted the same 646 lemmas and visited the same 2,131 root OR operands. Both found 1,454 already bound, internalized 677 fresh operands and created 1,093 Boolean variables. On 6/5, both found 1,665 bound operands out of 2,326. The first operand was already bound in every observed root OR. A shortcut for finding bound literals would miss most of the cost.

| Live interval | g3, million instructions | Z3, million instructions |
|---|---:|---:|
| Process root OR operands, goal 6/6 | 9.69 | 2.15 |
| Simplify and store root clause, goal 6/6 | 1.40 | 0.37 |
| Attach root clause watches, goal 6/6 | 1.32 | 0.39 |
| Process root OR operands, all ARM checks | 115.06 | 25.40 |
| Install children of fresh Boolean equivalences, all checks | 69.72 | 13.20 |
| Install fresh equality operands within the child disjunctions, all checks | 41.33 | 6.22 |

The last two rows measure nested intervals in separate instrumented builds. Summing them would double-count work. Three independent runs per observer used solver-thread user instructions with adjacent empty reads. Nested probes can also charge instrumentation to their parent. Search diverges on some other checks, so the complete-input totals combine operation price and frequency.

The large recursive cost led to 417 fresh equalities between the result of an event-operation function and an enum constructor. In g3, registering the datatype variable and its recognizer called `DatatypeConstructors` to obtain a length. Native uses constructor-count metadata. With `db3d9261b`, the same 417 equalities cost **13.65M instructions, down from 31.35M**. Single-constructor reconstruction still obtains the declaration it needs, and conflicting recognizers resolve their own constructor directly.

The second change follows native's `theory_datatype::mk_split`. Once the preferred recognizer is false, examine the existing slots first. An already relevant, unassigned recognizer ends the scan. Only an empty slot requires looking up its constructor. The solver's existing datatype utility owns the cached declarations.

### Scaling with the number of constructors

Seven alternating baseline/candidate pairs per width, pinned to CPU 18 of a Ryzen Threadripper 3960X, Go 1.27.3, one Go execution thread. Each column reports median ns/op. The fresh-term benchmark uses 2,000 iterations per invocation and includes push, internalize and pop. The split benchmark uses 5,000 iterations, rules out the preferred constructor during setup, then revisits the still-unassigned second choice. Each baseline is the revision immediately preceding that change.

| Constructors | Fresh term before | Fresh term after | Split revisit before | Split revisit after |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 9,153 | 5,642 | 2,246 | 370 |
| 16 | 18,756 | 5,698 | 7,040 | 349 |
| 64 | 60,997 | 6,667 | 26,612 | 378 |

At width 64, process-wide user instructions including test startup fell from 1.232B to 96.93M in the fresh-term benchmark and from 1.428B to 42.71M in the split benchmark. Fresh terms went from 12 to 10 allocations/op. Split revisits went from one to zero. Reproduce both through the [checked-in Go benchmarks](smtcore/smt_datatype_enum_benchmark_test.go).

Eleven paired release runs used identical frontend, PGO and input. Constructor counting reduced complete ARM instructions by 2.27%. ARM elapsed changed by +0.40%. Hybrid broadcast and card3 instructions changed by +0.18% and +1.41%. The subsequent split change moved instructions by −0.03%, −0.05% and −0.57% on those three inputs respectively. The large split speedup is observable when the operation repeats. Its contribution to these complete inputs is small.

Both production revisions independently matched the exit code, stdout and stderr of the linked native verifier on all 228 complete inputs. The full Go suite passed after the count change, including the FMA cross-build test. The split change (`450b4dd06`) passed the affected smtcore and API packages, the checked/debug/trace datatype checks and smtcore vet.

The final same-frontend comparison alternated g3 and linked Z3 on CPU 16 for eleven rounds. Times include process launch. Concurrent work on the host makes small elapsed differences uncertain.

| Complete verifier input | g3 median ms | Z3 median ms | g3 median user instructions | Z3 median user instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM rules | 469 | 345 | 3.15B | 2.19B |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 1,135 | 846 | 7.91B | 5.82B |
| card3 | 72 | 81 | 361M | 439M |

### Other approaches tested

- A ground-clause encoding can avoid two intermediate OR gates for an equivalence between small disjunctions. The broad version triggered 956 times on ARM, generated 4,761 clauses and reduced new Boolean variables from 15,392 to 11,161. A same-binary comparison preserving the original fallback saved 2.69% of ARM instructions. The narrow binary-lemma version saved 3.26% against the initial baseline. The corpus eligibility census found **only ARM** triggered the broad rule among 228 inputs. Leave it experimental until a second real workload demonstrates value. Splitting only the outer equivalence increased ARM instructions by 10.31%.
- Deferring enum splits to the final theory check increased ARM instructions by 5.48% across nine same-binary pairs. Deferring all datatype splits increased them by 3.73%. Keep the current split timing.
- Registering watches directly from available signed literals changed complete ARM instructions by +0.46%, reusing gate arguments by +0.14% and specializing short sorts by −0.22%. None justified a production change.

Next, measure the original and rewritten lemma DAGs on matched ARM and Ticket checks. Distinguish mandatory visits from repeated visits to unchanged shared terms, and measure the cost of the repeat visits before introducing a cache. The earlier live measurements put the excess rewrite cost at about 86M instructions. The 4.156B excess first-push instructions across the separate 36-input survey remain a larger cross-workload opportunity.

## November 27 — First-push pass costs across the slower verifier inputs

Value propagation is the largest named first-push cost across the 36 inputs previously selected for excess elapsed time or instructions. On the current g3 revision (`450b4dd06`), it used **1.637B instructions versus 555M in linked Z3**, a 2.95× ratio. It was more expensive on 33 inputs. Two of the 36 emitted no first-push observations in either engine. All 216 complete runs matched the reference exit code and both output streams, including the expected model-checking failure.

| First-push pass | g3, M instructions | Z3, M instructions | Excess, M |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Value propagation | 1,637 | 555 | 1,082 |
| Pattern inference | 692 | 301 | 391 |
| NNF/CNF | 540 | 192 | 348 |
| Macro finding | 1,271 | 982 | 289 |
| Ordinary assertion reduction | 616 | 396 | 219 |
| BV sharing | 391 | 338 | 52 |
| Injectivity refinement | 36 | 6 | 30 |

Each entry sums per-input medians of three complete runs on pinned CPUs, measuring user instructions on the solver thread with GC off. The named pass boundaries correspond in the two implementations. Totals include the passes each engine actually ran, including differences in the number of physical pushes. The historical 4.156B deficit measured the frontend's first-push window with Go PGO disabled. This Go observer uses the release profile and starts inside the eligible kernel push. Comparing the two outer totals would confound code changes, compiler settings and measurement boundaries.

### Which assertions cost the time?

A second observer covered the ten inputs with the largest historical first-push deficits. They include hybrid broadcast, both Flash specifications, both alternating-bit inputs, CAV examp5, three Ticket variants and ARM. Across both value-propagation sweeps, 27,644 of 30,166 row rewrites returned the same formula. These unchanged rows consumed **612.05M** instructions, changed rows **73.43M**, and the subsequent substitution updates **85.66M**. A separate run classified the input before starting each row counter.

| Input to row rewrite | Unchanged rows | Unchanged cost, M | Changed rows | Changed cost, M |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Quantifier at the root | 17,696 | 504.11 | 873 | 46.94 |
| Ground application | 8,987 | 79.10 | 1,541 | 22.86 |
| Other nonground application | 961 | 29.03 | 108 | 3.63 |

The final ordinary reduction triggered by changes in either sweep cost another **268.54M** instructions over 139 calls. It lies outside the row intervals. A quantifier returning its original handle can still visit and cache its children or perform a successful substitution. The earlier forward/reverse dependency study observed changed descendants, resource costs and cache publications even when the root stayed unchanged.

Two release prototypes measured bookkeeping outside these traversals. Seven alternating pairs per input used normal GC, CPU 12, identical release profiles and the same frontend. All 112 runs matched the references. Omitting the unused proof output reference duplicated an earlier negative result. Instruction changes were −0.05% on hybrid, −0.18% on Flash, −0.22% on alternating bit and −0.29% on ARM. Creating the output formula batch only after the first changed row preserved the rewrite and cancellation checks. Its instruction changes were +0.11%, +0.05%, −0.09% and +0.78%, respectively. Both remain research overlays.

On those same 17,696 unchanged quantified rows, 18,447 calls to the theory quantifier reducer included nested binders. Preparing the updated quantifier used 26.47M instructions, acquiring the updated reference and eliminating unused variables used 14.04M, and reading and publishing the result used 15.20M before deferred cleanup. Their combined 55.71M is about **11%** of the independently measured 504.11M whole-row cost. This bounds the measured portion of binder finishing. The remainder includes child traversal, application reduction, generic frame/scope management, wrappers and cleanup. Its distribution still needs a direct measurement. The next experiment should measure application visits and frame completion *within these rows*, and compare their counts and prices with native on the same batches.

## November 27 — Matched traversal inside unchanged quantified assertions

Across the ten largest historical first-push gaps, **17,694 unchanged quantified assertions matched on batch, sweep position, assertion index, input root kind and change status**. The two engines matched on every row's four event counts. Both visited 218,642 expressions, ran 200,416 application-frame steps and attempted 109,055 nonconstant application reductions. All 109,055 returned failure to reduce. The preceding Go-only survey counted 17,696 unchanged quantified rows. This comparison excludes unmatched rows. Across all assertion kinds, 710 positions appeared in only one engine and 21 shared positions differed in classification.

Three complete instruction-count runs per engine and input priced the same selected rows on the solver thread with GC disabled. Counts below measure application children. They exclude initial root visits and children visited directly by the quantifier frame. Frame completion begins after selecting the resulting expression and ends after updating the result stack, cache, frame stack and temporary result reference.

| Operation | g3 calls | Native calls | g3, M instructions | Native, M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Load child operand | 182,503 | 182,503 | 10.77 | 0.73 |
| Visit child | 182,503 | 182,503 | 99.94 | 29.07 |
| Prepare reducer argument view | 109,055 | 109,055 | 6.98 | 2.29 |
| Rebuild after a child changed | 355 | 355 | 0.31 | 0.20 |
| Complete frame after reduction failed | 109,055 | 109,055 | 71.98 | 18.38 |
| Test for short-circuit folding | 61,807 | 182,503 | 5.17 | 7.46 |
| Enter quantifier cache scope | 18,445 | 18,445 | 5.86 | 2.38 |
| Leave quantifier cache scope | 18,445 | 18,445 | 18.19 | 7.46 |

Each entry sums the per-input median of calibrated intervals. Quantifier scope measurements used independent builds. The 355 rebuilds on rows whose *root* stayed unchanged illustrate why a root-handle comparison cannot justify eliminating internal work. Go already restricts the short-circuit fold test to positions where it can fire.

**Child visitation and failed-frame completion together explain 124.47M excess instructions** on these rows. Across these ten complete inputs, the operand load itself offers at most 10.04M excess instructions. Reusing a prepared accessor cannot recover the full visit cost. On hybrid alone, joining the earlier three-run reducer profiles by row and checking every application-reduction count yielded 15.69M versus 3.76M instructions on the same 21,414 unsuccessful reductions. Earlier Ticket measurements found that an identical failed reducer request could later succeed on the same ordered arguments. A global negative-result cache would require a stronger correctness condition.

A release trial used the arena's existing subtree metadata to reject binary cheap-ITE pulling when neither operand could have an ITE root. Across seven alternating complete pairs per input, instruction changes were +0.11% on hybrid, −0.27% on Flash, −0.26% on alternating bit and −0.79% on ARM. Elapsed changes ranged from −1.09% to +3.33%. The shortcut remains experimental.

### Reading ITE value trees

In `src/ast/rewriter/th_rewriter.cpp`, `is_ite_value_tree` tests the operator, then retrieves only branches 1 and 2 when it decides to descend. In g3, the old helper loaded the condition and both branches even when its caller only wanted to know whether the term was an ITE. The revised traversal uses the arena's existing `AppIdentity` lookup, checks arity for a positive match and reads each needed branch during descent. Both solvers descend through nested ITEs only while they have a single reference. A test holds, shares and releases the same nested ITE to exercise that boundary.

| Depth of value tree | Before, ns | After, ns | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 (ordinary Boolean value) | 16.20 | 6.83 | 2.37× |
| 1 | 140.4 | 65.8 | 2.13× |
| 16 | 1,549 | 688.5 | 2.25× |
| 128 | 13,816 | 5,042 | 2.74× |

Seven alternating pinned pairs at 3,000 iterations per depth. Both builds allocated zero bytes per operation. An earlier version fetched the entire AST node header. That trial improved long chains but increased the ordinary leaf check from 15.86 to 23.69 ns, which motivated testing the smaller identity read. [Depth benchmark and shared-branch test](ast/rewriter/theory_ite_value_tree_test.go)

Commit `24ac46553` retains the identity-read version. Across seven paired runs per input, complete-verifier instruction changes were −0.01% on hybrid, −0.11% on Flash, −0.26% on alternating bit and −0.62% on ARM. The local benchmark is where the improvement is established. All 228 complete reference transcripts matched, including expected exits. The rewriter and smtcore packages, checked/debug/trace ITE tests and rewriter vet passed.

Eleven alternating runs on CPU 16 compared the final production build directly to linked Z3. ARM took 489.6 versus 345.6 ms, hybrid 1,115.6 versus 831.4 ms, and card3 73.8 versus 81.2 ms (g3 first). The corresponding median process instructions were 3.187B versus 2.192B, 7.893B versus 5.823B, and 353M versus 437M. These are whole-verifier results, including startup. A complete verifier can spend three times as many instructions on the same rewriter operation and still gain little from optimizing that operation alone. We measured the proofless theory rewrite of each generated instance in three complete GoIvy verifiers. Each measurement ran three times per engine with GC off, a pinned solver thread and a thread-local userspace instruction counter. We subtracted the cost of an empty measurement inside each instance. A second set of builds split child visits and unsuccessful non-macro application completion into smaller operations. Both sets reproduced the reference exit status, stdout and stderr in all 36 runs. The argument-view experiments below used ordinary release builds with GC on.

| Complete input | Rewritten instances, g3 / Z3 | Child visits, g3 / Z3 (M instructions) | Failed frame completion, g3 / Z3 (M) | Combined excess (M) | Whole-process release gap (M) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM rules3 | 5,274 / 5,851 | 33.95 / 12.39 | 21.45 / 6.67 | 36.34 | 958.94 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 14,647 / 13,113 | 71.23 / 18.66 | 40.04 / 10.38 | 82.23 | 1,424.27 |
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 18,586 / 28,798 | 85.00 / 40.73 | 53.24 / 22.77 | 74.73 | 2,096.47 |

The combined differences amount to roughly 3.8%, 5.8% and 3.6% of the respective release gaps. These are comparisons of scale across different builds and GC settings. The release denominator is the difference of whole-process medians from five alternating g3/Z3 pairs. Different instance counts contribute to the aggregate differences. The matched stages below isolate the cost of performing comparable work.

| Check | Instances in each engine | Child visits, g3 / Z3 (M) | Failed frame completion, g3 / Z3 (M) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM 6/5 | 720 | 4.81 / 1.58 | 3.00 / 0.87 |
| ARM 6/6 | 646 | 6.00 / 1.93 | 3.74 / 1.06 |
| Ticket 7/1 | 820 | 4.66 / 1.34 | 2.53 / 0.70 |

On each of these stages the engines matched instance by instance on operand fetch, visit, frame preparation, changed-application rebuild and failed completion counts. On ARM 6/6, querying the configured substitution took 2.38M instructions in Go and 0.78M in C++. Testing whether a term needed caching took 0.71M / 0.18M, and probing the result cache took 0.89M / 0.10M. At completion, replacing the stack arguments with the result cost 1.04M / 0.41M, the conditional cache publication cost 1.74M / 0.59M, and frame removal with result-reference cleanup cost 0.67M / 0.11M. The same three completion measurements on Ticket were 0.76M / 0.30M, 1.05M / 0.35M and 0.50M / 0.08M. These inner measurements come from separate binaries and omit surrounding control flow.

### Borrowed argument views

The normal Go view carries a slice, an application handle and owner, and the information needed to validate a borrowed literal-vector span. We measured three alternatives at the public accessor and through complete proofs. The 64-byte layout moved the span descriptor behind a pointer. The 40-byte layout also moved the application owner and handle into a separately allocated record. The direct-read trial kept the 72-byte representation and read a slice directly in the exported accessor. All three preserved the checked fallback for application and literal-vector operands.

| Implementation | Bytes/view | Read slice (ns) | Read borrowed application (ns) | Construct and read application view (ns) | Allocations per construction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Current | 72 | 8.63 | 12.88 | 40.95 | 0 |
| Span behind pointer | 64 | 5.62 | 12.90 | 29.21 | 0 |
| Application or span behind pointer | 40 | 11.98 | 17.63 | 62.80 | 1 (64 bytes) |
| Direct slice read | 72 | 8.51 | 14.08 | 43.82 | 0 |

Seven samples of one million operations each, with a non-inlined consumer passing the view by value, on Go 1.27.3 linux/amd64. The benchmark verifies the returned child on every iteration. The direct-read microbenchmark ran in a separate series on the same pinned CPU.

| Whole-verifier instructions, median paired change over seven pairs | ARM | Ticket | Hybrid | card3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64-byte view | −0.78% | −0.43% | −0.13% | +1.70% |
| 40-byte view | +0.90% | +0.15% | +0.25% | +0.95% |
| Direct slice read | +0.14% | −0.79% | −0.31% | −0.24% |

The direct-read candidate finished 0.5–3.0% sooner across the independent 13-input panel, but that result did not reproduce with the release-quality source. A fresh build of the baseline was byte-identical to the earlier binary. We built the gofmt-formatted candidate and compared it to the baseline and a byte-for-byte copy of the baseline, on one CPU with all six execution orders represented twice. On ARM the candidate used 0.76% more instructions, 0.54% more cycles and 0.48% more elapsed time. On Ticket the changes were +0.16%, −0.10% and −0.01%. Hybrid elapsed improved 0.98%, while the identical copy improved 0.59%. The largest absolute elapsed shift for the identical copy across six verifiers was 0.82%. All 228 reference transcripts and exits matched the formatted candidate. These results do not establish a repeatable benefit large enough to change the accessor. All three trials remain experimental. ### Where the most expensive early proof misses spend their instructions

The earlier 36-input survey ranked hybrid, test/flash2 and CAV 2024 examp5 highest by the total cost of unsuccessful early private attempts. Together they accounted for 934.55M of 2.941B instructions on that revision. We profiled the three on the current revision, including the successful attempts, then selected misses for the table. Each of four nested-instrumentation builds ran every verifier three times and reproduced its exit status and both output streams. Counts are solver-thread instructions with GC disabled, summed across the misses on each input and rounded to millions.

| Input | Misses / attempts | Total miss cost | Private SMT Check | Translate premise roots | Assert translated roots, including first-use construction | Cold solver factory | Parameter validation / application |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hybrid | 34 / 339 | 333.7 | 97.9 | 9.0 | 56.3 | 38.4 | 6.8 / 4.3 |
| test/flash2 | 29 / 124 | 295.2 | 91.7 | 10.1 | 57.6 | 41.3 | 5.5 / 3.4 |
| CAV examp5 | 28 / 132 | 280.8 | 93.6 | 10.1 | 50.1 | 34.4 | 4.7 / 3.0 |

The columns come from successively finer probes. Construction and parameter handling sit inside other calls, so adding all columns would double count. Across the three inputs, searching the private solver cost 283.1M instructions. Translating the selected roots cost 29.3M. The solver factory cost 114.0M during cold initialization. Once cold setup was charged separately, asserting the translated roots cost just 6.7–8.0M per input. The private batch reuses an AST manager across plans but resets the child solver after each plan. Its first assertion calls the solver factory and validates and applies the handle's explicit parameters.

We also recorded each plan’s ordered source roots, with origin, slot and generation, across complete private-manager lifetimes. Of 58 adjacent short-plan pairs in the same manager, only two had any common prefix. They shared three roots in total. Hybrid had zero across 28 adjacent pairs. All three transcripts matched. A reusable ordered premise prefix offers little here. The next experiment is to break the 114M factory instructions down by constructor and measure how much of each constructed solver is used before reset. The 283M spent in private search is the larger target. Attribute it by plan and by SAT, UNSAT or budget exhaustion before changing search scheduling.
