## November 27 — Repeated Ticket substitutions and the size of a sufficient ground proof

**What survives backtracking.** Three solver-thread observations per workload tracked generation-checked arena handles, the quantifier instance registry and the identity of the previous regular auxiliary clause. The table counts one execution of each check. The other two gave the same counts. “Same charge” compares the actual resource-counter delta of the two rewrites. Both POPL18 and Hybrid were included as transcript controls but their selected windows yielded no repeat events for this comparison.

| Workload and check | Repeated substitutions | Prior rewritten AST still live | Live and same charge | Prior finished lemma live | Prior auxiliary clause still installed / observed | Already bound arguments |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Automatic Ticket 12/8 | 1,526 | 1,155 | 995 | 0 | 0 / 1,017 | 5,301 / 7,045 |
| Automatic Ticket 14/8 | 755 | 608 | 495 | 0 | 0 / 516 | 2,571 / 3,441 |
| Automatic Ticket 16/1 | 712 | 653 | 516 | 0 | 0 / 472 | 2,665 / 3,212 |
| Nested Ticket 16/1 | 284 | 101 | 78 | 0 | 0 / 207 | 873 / 1,154 |

On 12/8 the actual charge changed on 225 repeats, including 160 whose previous rewritten AST survived. A 4,096-entry solver-local prototype reused the previous charge on a live-result hit. On eight complete workloads, three rotated runs per mode matched all 72 golden transcripts. On automatic Ticket the identity-only prototype saved 2.3% of median process instructions and the unrestricted prototype saved 1.2%. Across the seven controls, unrestricted changes ranged from a 1.4% saving to a 0.02% increase. The changed resource charges rule out shipping this shortcut. Reusing the completed lemma after backtracking would also require rebuilding its solver state.

On 12/8 repeated OR assertions, setup and lookups for bound operands cost 2.40M instructions, internalization and literal lookup for missing operands cost **13.82M**, root-clause insertion cost 3.48M and relevance setup cost 4.29M. Missing operands also cost 7.47M on 14/8 and 10.75M on 16/1. These disjoint windows exclude diagnostic printing. The earlier 31.22M inclusive assertion figure covers all repeated instances. This gives a narrower internalizer target if the proof-search experiment below falls short.

**Can a smaller search settle the expensive checks?** We captured 35 original automatic Ticket obligations whose g3 verification calls exceeded 5M instructions. Among 40 pairs with identical let-expanded goals in different captured batches, 37 common-premise intersections were SAT in native. Three intersections proved UNSAT in both engines, covering only 14/20 and 15/20. For 12/8, selecting an offline native core cut the fresh flat input from 118 to 33 premises and from 878 to 209 instantiations in both shells. On 14/8, 12 of 119 premises sufficed and the count dropped from 584 to 62. These fresh flat counts differ from the pushed replay and the original verifier.

In a separate experiment we Skolemized the inputs, checked that every remaining universal occurred positively, and replaced each universal with a conjunction of selected ground instances. An UNSAT result on this weakening suffices for the original. Constants alone yielded SAT on all five full inputs, even when every declared non-Boolean constant was available. Grounding once more with applications of fresh witness functions, seeded by fresh constants and constants from atomic facts, proved **all five**. Both shells verified every successful ground proof. The initial expansions occupied 4.0–8.0 MB. Greedy deletion in two orders followed by native core extraction identified much smaller sufficient inputs.

| Automatic Ticket check | Initial terms | Retained terms | Ground assertions in extracted core | Original pushed g3, M instructions | Ground core g3, M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 12/8 | 42 | 6 | 36 | 264.1 | 91.7 |
| 13/8 | 36 | 7 | 32 | 190.1 | 88.3 |
| 14/8 | 36 | 6 | 22 | 229.2 | 87.2 |
| 15/8 | 42 | 5 | 31 | 175.3 | 88.3 |
| 16/1 | 34 | 13 | 67 | 283.4 | 121.9 |

These are single whole-shell instruction measurements, including startup and parsing. The ground column prices checking an already discovered proof. It excludes normalization, term selection, core extraction and original incremental solver setup. The reducer needed 45–110 probes per input and order. These figures establish proof size and a replay target. They do not establish a verifier speedup.

**Which cheap selectors worked?** Exposing the goal's top-level conjuncts in order changed aggregate g3 instructions by less than 0.1% across 34 eligible pushed replays. Adding just the ground conjuncts increased them by 0.2%, and reversing the order increased them by 1.2%. Feeding both normalized assertions back to ordinary quantified search increased aggregate g3 instructions 29.9% across all 35 inputs, even excluding normalization time. Using only constants from the normalized goal plus one witness-function expansion proved zero of five. Adding atomic facts proved one. Including all fresh constants with the goal seeds proved three, and including both sources proved all five. Restricting each universal binder group to one distinct term per sort proved 15/8 and 16/1. Allowing two also proved 12/8 and 13/8. The 14/8 input still required a wider group in this experiment.

**Next experiment.** Start with the narrow substitutions on 15/8 and 16/1. Use ground assignments and predicate occurrences to select the next violated quantified rule and its bindings. Measure candidates visited, terms built and discovery instructions against the original incremental check. Keep 14/8 as the control that needs more than two distinct terms in a binder group. Bound a speculative attempt and measure its misses on complete workloads before considering a solver change. [Captures, five standalone ground proofs, verifier overlays, trials and raw counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-repeated-lemmas.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Finding the finite Ticket proofs and paying for misses

**A model can find the terms without a proof oracle.** The prototype starts with ground facts and weakenings of the normalized rules. After each SAT result it groups candidate terms by their value in the current model. It visits representative bindings, adds consequences falsified by that model, and checks again. A positive universal can contribute any instances, a false conjunction can contribute a false conjunct, and a false disjunction must retain a consequence from every branch. Only an UNSAT result discharges the original. The existing nested-scope solver supplies the fallback. With up to eight violated bindings per binder visit, the prototype found all five proofs. All successful ground inputs also proved UNSAT independently in g3 and native.

| Automatic Ticket check | Maximum distinct bindings per sort in one binder group | Refinements | Candidate bindings visited | Ground rows added |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 12/8 | 2 | 13 | 32,020 | 164 |
| 13/8 | 2 | 16 | 52,273 | 200 |
| 14/8 | unrestricted | 12 | 29,852 | 144 |
| 15/8 | 1 | 16 | 33,507 | 147 |
| 16/1 | 1 | 20 | 24,245 | 179 |

The Python/native-model reference took 1.4–3.2 seconds for these successes. At width two, 14/8 exhausted the candidates. Using g3's ordinary model-based search with E-matching disabled proved all 35 original pushed obligations but cost 8.68× default instructions, versus 6.24× for native. Disabling model-based search left three UNKNOWN in each engine. A separate purely syntactic restriction of same-sort binders proved 18 of 35 at width one and 32 at width two. Successful width-two replays together took 2% more instructions than their renamed controls. These transformations alone offer poor admission criteria.

**Which reasoning actually closes the ground checks?** Propositional abstraction made all five extracted ground cores SAT, even after substituting direct constant equalities. Adding congruence clauses for observed applications differing in one argument made four UNSAT. The 22-row core for 14/8 also needed explicit equality transitivity under this encoding. For the larger sets of rows found by the model-guided procedure, single-argument congruence sufficed for all five. Unit propagation alone closed none of the five extracted cores. That motivated a standalone Go prototype which compiles the positive universals directly to CNF, includes selected congruence implications, propagates units, eliminates pure literals and invokes g3's existing SAT solver in the same process.

| Check | Cheapest successful Go configuration tested | Ground, reduce and solve, M instructions | Original live g3 check, M | Original linked Z3 check, M |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 12/8 | Width 2, all source seeds, functions applied to fresh constants | 288.8 | 175.2 | 87.0 |
| 13/8 | Same as 12/8 | 262.1 | 87.5 | 37.6 |
| 14/8 | Width 3, full pool | 416.2 | 100.7 | 36.4 |
| 15/8 | Width 1, fresh constants and their applications, unary congruence | **33.8** | **51.8** | **21.4** |
| 16/1 | Width 1, full pool, unary congruence | 110.2 | 98.1 | 44.1 |

The table uses the polarity-aware encoder and three solver-thread counter readings per configuration. The minimum is selected retrospectively for each input. The Go interval starts from a decoded, normalized DAG, ends after closing the SAT solver, and includes the SAT solver's setup and cleanup. It excludes Skolemization and parsing. A second Go encoder that propagated universally asserted units before generating other rules reduced 13/8 to 226.9M but raised 15/8 to 36.5M. The 35 original queries shared seven distinct base formulas. Even making all CNF construction free across siblings would leave substantial speculative SAT work.

**What happens inside the complete verifier?** The inexpensive 15/8 policy proved eight of 35 captured expensive obligations and returned inconclusive on 27. All ten independently SAT common-premise inputs remained SAT in the abstraction. Both SAT shells reproduced all 45 abstract results. Attempting the 35 inputs cost 1,225M instructions before normalization, including 505M inside SAT construction, search and cleanup. Their eight successes replaced only 277M original check instructions. A benchmark-only GoIvy overlay loaded the saved normalized DAG at each selected original verification point and ran the actual Go proof procedure. It continued ordinary incremental search on every miss. Seven rotated runs per policy matched the reference exit status and both output streams.

| Complete automatic Ticket | Median instructions | Median elapsed |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same binary, ordinary verification | 2.766B | 403.83 ms |
| Try all 35 eligible captures | 4.389B | 569.98 ms |
| Try only the eight known successes | 2.865B | 406.09 ms |
| Try only 15/8 | 2.693B | 393.06 ms |

The verifier measurements include reading the prepared inputs, constructing clauses, solving, cleanup and effects on later siblings. The source-to-DAG conversion was performed offline. The eight-success and 15/8-only schedules use information unavailable to an online solver. A production optimization needs an inexpensive predictor of *net savings*, since selecting every eventual success still increased complete instructions by 3.6%.

**Two solver-cost controls.** Deferring model-finder analysis until the first candidate model saved 2.05% of complete automatic Ticket instructions in three rotated pairs but changes cancellation and resource accounting. Reusing existing term children while constructing predicates and looking up previously bound positive literals directly produced mixed results across ten complete workloads. Individually they changed median instructions between a 1.05% saving and a 1.23% increase. All 180 complete control runs matched the references. None of the scheduling or operand experiments entered the release. [Go benchmarks, proof-search prototypes, 45 replayable DAGs and measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-ticket-ground-discovery.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Which small premise selections pay for a private solver?

**The expensive part was checking selected rows.** In three solver-thread profiles of the examples alternating-bit verifier, relevant-premise proofs took 132.8M instructions before the first concrete push, including 102.4M inside the proof-plan check. Building the premise and definition indexes took 12.9M and 15.6M, and selecting definition rows took 1.25M. On the POPL18 alternating-bit example, proof-plan checks took 45.3M of 57.4M. On nested Ticket they took 65.3M of 84.5M, and on Hybrid 136.9M of 191.2M. Nested observer intervals include their children. All four complete workloads matched their reference transcripts.

**Raft is the counterexample to dropping this pass.** Across 228 complete reference runs the narrow definition selector proved 43 of 285 nonempty selections. The rare-symbol selector proved 36 of 226. No wide selection reached a nonempty check on this corpus. The wide selector has its own positive API regressions. Among the 38 later selections contained in the immediately preceding subset, only 37 already had evidence of satisfiability, so those 37 bound the opportunity for avoiding repeated searches by this test. On the two alternating-bit examples, every one of the 28 observed nonempty selections failed. Removing the whole pass saved 7.4% and 3.2% of complete instructions on the examples and POPL18 versions in a three-pair confirmation. It raised ordinary Raft by 20.3% and raftok by 29.1%. Omitting only the rare-symbol pass reproduced those Raft regressions. In both Raft inputs that selector succeeded with 10 of 39 base rows.

**Release rule.** In a sized proof batch eligible for private context reuse, when the base contains more than 64 rows, try a narrow or rare-symbol selection if it contains at least one eighth of the base. A wider definition search retains its existing admission test. Skipped attempts proceed through the verification batch's regular fallback. The cutoffs govern speculative search cost. They impose no restriction on the underlying logic. The comparison included skipping only narrow checks, applying the fraction only above 128 rows, and removing each pass individually.

| Complete verifier | Prior, M instructions | Release, M instructions | Change | Prior / release median ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Examples alternating bit | 2,637.0 | 2,555.0 | −3.11% | 409.15 / 399.09 |
| POPL18 alternating bit | 2,512.6 | 2,479.5 | −1.32% | 389.67 / 382.60 |
| Nested Ticket | 2,416.4 | 2,376.9 | −1.63% | 352.57 / 346.70 |
| Hybrid | 6,862.4 | 6,726.2 | −1.98% | 982.53 / 960.61 |
| ARM rules3 | 3,132.1 | 3,060.8 | −2.28% | 482.14 / 478.29 |
| test_liveness2 | 1,731.1 | 1,718.3 | −0.74% | 284.39 / 278.58 |

These are seven rotated pairs from the release binaries, with normal GC. Automatic Ticket and POPL18 Ticket changed by +0.01% and +0.10% of median instructions. Cardinality initially rose 2.41% on seven pairs. A separate 15-pair confirmation measured 183.45M before and 182.42M after, with median elapsed 50.42 and 50.77 ms. The 228-input event inventory saw zero nonempty selections on this cardinality example. Every reference exit status and both output streams matched for both binaries in the 228-input release comparison. In three additional rotated pairs, median instructions in billions were 15.850 / 15.796 on ordinary Raft, 11.207 / 11.182 on Apple rfn2 and 119.952 / 119.223 on Apple dramc_nb2. These small differences are holdout checks. [Profiles, admission prototypes, complete corpus comparisons and holdout measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-private-premise-pricing.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Pricing first-push NNF conversion and the following theory rewrite

On Hybrid, both solvers normalized **2,144 formulas across 34 fresh solvers**, introduced zero definitions, and changed the same 52 formulas in the ensuing theory rewrite. The Go theory rewriter took 28,827 steps and linked Z3 took 28,821. The extra six iterations, spread across five rows, leave the difference in cost per step as the principal target. The theory rewrite, cancellation check and transfer of the result into the output vector together consumed **57.56M Go instructions versus 22.19M native**. NNF conversion itself accounted for a further 17.19M excess instructions.

| Complete verifier, first pushes | Matched rows | NNF conversion, g3 / Z3 (M instructions) | Theory rewrite and output, g3 / Z3 (M) | Rewriter steps, g3 / Z3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Hybrid reliable broadcast | 2,144 | 28.39 / 11.20 | 57.56 / 22.19 | 28,827 / 28,821 |
| Nested Ticket | 913 | 2.51 / 0.89 | 17.13 / 6.42 | 7,968 / 7,968 |
| POPL18 alternating bit | 1,507 | 3.81 / 1.33 | 27.60 / 9.66 | 12,444 / 12,444 |
| Examples alternating bit | 1,906 | 3.52 / 1.31 | 27.01 / 9.49 | 11,440 / 11,440 |

Each cell is the median sum of three complete pinned runs with GC disabled. Each backend read the solver-thread hardware counter around its own conversion and main-row rewrite. The conversion observer also counted Go visits. It adds some instructions to the Go totals. All transcripts matched. Rows were paired by solver batch and position. Every pair agreed on both transformation identities and the number of definitions. Nested Ticket had one additional native first push with 24 formulas, excluded from the table. On Hybrid, the 1,675 rows that survived both operations unchanged still cost about 36M instructions in Go's rewrite and output alone.

**Reuse across fresh solvers has a low ceiling here.** The input handle, including manager origin and generation, had appeared in a previous Hybrid batch for 601 rows. Their entire conversions consumed 3.34M instructions, or 0.05% of the 6.73B-instruction verifier. Their entire subsequent rewrites cost another 7.68M. Only 222 of the 601 repeated inputs passed NNF unchanged with zero resource charge. A cache keyed by input alone would have to account for Skolem freshness, substitutions, cache effects and cancellation. Even a free hit on every repeated conversion would recover little of the whole-verifier gap.

**Four production-path prototypes.** Five pinned frame-pointer profiles with normal GC yielded 887 samples whose stacks included the NNF rewrite-and-output call. Of these, 513 included application processing, 193 included quantifier processing, and 47 included output assertion insertion. These inclusive counts overlap. The profiles cover all invocations of this call during complete Hybrid verification. The following trials used uninstrumented binaries with the release PGO profile, normal GC, alternating execution order and exact transcript comparison.

| Experiment | Cases × pairs | Median change across case instruction medians | Smallest to largest change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Preserve the existing quantifier pattern array when no Skolem pattern is removed | 4 × 5 | +0.23% | −0.04% to +1.17% |
| Test root/atom cache ineligibility before configuration dispatch | 12 × 5 | −0.10% | −0.73% to +1.11% |
| Read the possible-substitution-key bit with the AST shape on theory traversal | 12 × 3 | −0.51% | −1.65% to +1.09% |
| Bypass failed theory reduction on eligible unchanged uninterpreted applications | 12 × 3 | −0.48% | −0.98% to +1.27% |

Eleven more rotated pairs for the combined substitution and shape read measured **−0.66% on Hybrid, −0.77% on POPL18 Ticket, +0.33% on nested Ticket and −0.14% on liveness Ticket**. The prototype could also bypass substitution-owner validation on a negative key. A production version would need to preserve validation when a previously attached substitution has been released. The small mixed effects do not justify adding these paths to the release. Driving just these two first-push windows to native instruction cost would save about 52.6M instructions, or **0.78% of complete Hybrid**. The more promising target is shared work across complete solver checks. [Benchmark drivers, observed rows, stack samples, reference transcripts and trial results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-nnf-row-comparison.tar.xz)

### Where a larger saving could change whole-verifier performance

A fresh set of three complete, alternating g3/native runs per input used the same frontend workload, CPU and solver-thread counter with GC disabled. The four inputs had the largest excess instructions in a comparison of the latest 228-case release screen with the archived native processes. That older process comparison serves only to select inputs. The stage measurements below come from the fresh binaries. Push includes all physical pushes on each backend. Check includes calls that reached the ordinary solver. An early private proof can avoid such a call in g3, so these totals include the benefit of checks it skipped.

| Complete workload | Push, g3 / Z3 (M instructions) | Ordinary checks, g3 / Z3 (M) | Excess in ordinary checks (M) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Hybrid | 1,125.62 / 545.56 | 3,006.44 / 2,691.59 | 314.85 |
| ARM rules3 | 279.65 / 113.99 | 1,484.22 / 909.43 | 574.79 |
| Automatic Ticket | 326.95 / 164.26 | 1,345.28 / 594.35 | 750.93 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 310.96 / 144.40 | 929.08 / 599.77 | 329.31 |

The largest measured group is ordinary checking on automatic Ticket. Its three largest paired check gaps are 88.27M at batch 12 goal 8, 64.27M at 14/8, and 53.87M at 16/1. Together these explain 27.5% of the net check gap. ARM 6/5 and 6/6 are a second concentrated target with 227.63M instructions between them. For the next experiment, measure the first solver decision or quantifier instantiation that contributes to the eventual conflict on these checks, and how much search each engine performs before that event. Earlier measurements already price the small finite proofs and show the cost of discovering them online. A cheaper way to reach an existing conflict through the ordinary search could benefit both workloads without paying for a second solver.

## November 27 — Conflict-level reads and the cost of a Ticket decision across sibling checks

The resolver copied the assignment level of **every live Boolean variable** before analyzing each conflict. Z3 reads the levels of the variables it encounters from their Boolean records. g3 now does the same during conflict resolution and unsat-core extraction. The public maximum-level queries still accept explicit level arrays. This removes a solver-local backing array and a full pass over unrelated variables. The benchmark resolves the same two-literal base conflict with increasing numbers of unrelated internalized variables.

| Boolean variables | Before, median ns/op | Direct level reads, median ns/op |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 | 133.5 | 57.54 |
| 1,024 | 1,456 | 56.84 |
| 8,192 | 8,461 | 56.91 |

Five samples per binary, 30,000 resolutions per sample, zero allocations per operation after rounding. [Retained benchmark](smtcore/smt_conflict_levels_benchmark_test.go)

| Complete verification, ordinary check calls | Conflicts | Variable records previously scanned | Resolver instructions before / after |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ARM rules3 | 1,269 | 1,004,193 | 34.32M / 20.56M |
| Automatic Ticket | 479 | 130,483 | 4.92M / 3.13M |
| Hybrid | 860 | 185,352 | 6.28M / 3.70M |
| POPL18 Ticket | 353 | 85,481 | 4.40M / 3.24M |

These are median sums over three pinned complete runs per build with GC disabled. The matched conflict counts and live variable counts were identical. The windows cover the call to the resolver, excluding backtracking and installation of the learned clause. The twelve-case normal-GC whole-verifier screen of the initial implementation showed mixed effects (−1.75% to +1.62%). The case for the change is the measured removal of work as solver size grows. The final release matched all 228 reference transcripts plus ordinary Raft and both long Apple isolates. The smtcore and API tests, focused checked/debug/trace conflict tests and smtcore vet passed.

**Search ordering.** On ARM 6/5 and 6/6, the complete streams matched by event kind, signed decision variable ID, emitted quantifier generation, and learned literal set with its levels. At 6/6, all 734 signed decision expressions, 646 normalized instance shapes and 147 learned clauses also matched. On 6/5, all 720 normalized instances matched, but some identically numbered decisions denoted different terms. Automatic Ticket diverged at decisions 10, 111 and 58 on 12/8, 14/8 and 16/1. These comparisons normalize fresh numeric suffixes by first appearance and canonicalize equality operand order. They locate divergence without establishing which lemmas are ancestors of the final contradiction.

**Causal experiment.** Selecting the first differing native variable once on 12/8 reduced that check from 175.25M to 119.33M instructions. Its sibling 12/16 then cost 58.42M extra. The total across all ordinary checks fell only 4.24M. Selecting the native variable on 14/8 had little effect, while the substitution on 16/1 cost another 10.85M. All selected variables were eligible and received their normal solver phase. These diagnostic substitutions use goal ordinals and were excluded from production.

A separate five-round replay on the direct-level build retained the 12/8 choice and restored only the solver's 32-bit random generator state at the start of 12/16. The latter check dropped from 139.04M to 110.04M; the unmodified search took 80.73M. Replacing the seed in the opposite direction increased 12/16 from 80.73M to 102.13M. Restoring the baseline seed for every subsequent check in the batch gave almost the same result as restoring it on 12/16 alone. This isolates one way a local search improvement shifts work into a sibling. About 29M of 12/16's penalty remained after restoring the seed. A useful next comparison is the set of persistent learned clauses, cached phases and variable activities at entry to 12/16. [Events, benchmark drivers and raw measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-conflict-levels-and-ticket-search.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Activity carryover between Ticket checks and sparse conflict marks

**Activity scores and the priority queue explain the remaining Ticket 12/16 penalty.** At entry to 12/16 the two runs had the same 176 Boolean expressions in the same slots and the same 90 variables in the decision heap. After intervening on decision ten at 12/8, 28 scores differed and 83 heap positions had changed. The activity increment was 8.84 versus 16.25 in the baseline. Neither run retained an explicit learned clause at this boundary. All 41 auxiliary clauses had the same literal sets, although 11 had different literal order. Binary watch lists were identical.

Five rotations measured one state substitution at a time. Every row below the baseline made the same 12/8 decision change and restored the baseline random seed at entry to 12/16. All runs matched the reference exit status, stdout and stderr. The solver-thread counters exclude the diagnostic state inspection and substitution window.

| State restored at 12/16 | Check 12/16, M instructions | All ordinary checks, M instructions |
|---|---:|---:|
| Baseline, original decision and search history | 80.76 | 1,343.59 |
| Random seed only | 110.06 | 1,311.82 |
| Also restore cached phases and the phase counter | 110.07 | 1,311.86 |
| Also restore clause and watch order | 110.11 | 1,311.76 |
| Also restore scores and their increment | 82.69 | 1,297.25 |
| Reinsert the old heap order under the changed scores | 173.72 | 1,373.98 |
| Restore both scores and heap order | 80.74 | 1,290.17 |

We tested whether a general user-scope policy could turn the diagnostic result into an optimization. The prototype saved state when a scope opened and restored it when the scope closed. Across twelve complete verifications and three rotated pairs against the control, score-and-heap restoration ranged from −1.78% to +1.74% in median instructions. Adding random-state restoration improved POPL18 Ticket by 3.19%, but increased ARM by 27.75% and nested Ticket by 10.49%. All 144 transcripts matched. Keep the existing public-scope behavior. The diagnostic can restore a good counterfactual state for a particular sibling; ordinary push/pop has access only to the parent's actual state.

**Which instances appear in conflict analysis?** A solver-local observer attributed explicit clause records to the quantifier instance installing them and recorded direct visits during first-UIP analysis, minimization and the terminal conflict lookup. On 12/8, 1,393 of 1,983 instances installed explicit records. The resolver directly visited records from 22 instances, including root clauses from 12. The corresponding counts on 14/8 were 794 of 1,087 and 16 contributors; on 16/1 they were 742 of 958 and 21 contributors. These are lower bounds. Propagation, compact binary reasons, units and dependencies carried through earlier learned clauses can all matter to the contradiction. Promoting every future instance of a quantifier as soon as one of its clauses was visited would have flagged 745 instances on 12/8 and covered nine of the 22 directly observed contributors. That signal alone offers little selectivity.

**Result-capture ceiling.** Within the instrumented verifier stages, saving literal results cost 11.56M instructions on Hybrid, 5.84M on ARM, 3.90M on automatic Ticket and 5.60M on POPL18 Ticket. A cheaper assignment-first scan and a diagnostic build omitting unheld snapshots both had mixed whole-process results. Neither entered the release.

**Retained solver change.** On a successful first-UIP resolution, g3 already unmarks each visited current-level variable, each temporary minimization mark and the remaining lemma variables. It now clears the entire scratch array only if resolution returns an error. The error-retry regression marks a variable before encountering an invalid antecedent and then reuses the resolver twice. Removing error cleanup caused the retry to report a missing marked assignment at level 2.

| Variables for the same two-literal learned conflict | Before, median ns/op | After, median ns/op |
|---|---:|---:|
| 64 | 216.3 | 220.0 |
| 1,024 | 216.8 | 214.1 |
| 8,192 | 284.3 | 226.0 |
| 65,536 | 776.0 | 347.8 |

Five alternating pinned benchmark pairs used 40,000 resolutions per sample. The 2.23× result at 65,536 measures resolution of a sparse conflict. The final production build matched all 228 corpus transcripts and the Raft, rfn2 and dramc_nb2 holdouts. The SMT and API suites, focused checked/debug/trace tests and smtcore vet passed. [Retained benchmark](smtcore/smt_conflict_levels_benchmark_test.go) · [State snapshots, interventions, benchmark drivers and raw results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-sibling-activity-and-conflict-marks.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Replaying the terminal conflict on Ticket and ARM

How much of each proof can the solver use at the start of search? We traced the final conflict through assignment reasons, compact binary clauses, equality explanations and earlier learned clauses. We then rebuilt each original scoped obligation, including its preceding checks. The two traced verifications matched the native frontend transcripts. Removing the new dependency records from the logs reproduced all 5,603 previous Ticket events and all 4,610 ARM events exactly.

| Check | Instances emitted | Candidate instances | Last candidate ordinal | Attributed conflicts / all | Candidates installed at search entry | Check instructions, ordinary → early hints |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ticket 12/8 | 1,983 | 42 | 1,977 | 21 / 41 | 31 | 175.0M → 37.1M |
| Ticket 14/8 | 1,087 | 16 | 1,086 | 10 / 36 | 12 | 100.5M → 58.1M |
| Ticket 16/1 | 958 | 61 | 956 | 27 / 34 | 47 | 97.9M → 95.2M |
| ARM 6/5 | 720 | 25 | 704 | 142 / 161 | 25 | 188.9M → 207.5M |
| ARM 6/6 | 646 | 36 | 645 | 121 / 148 | 36 | 174.6M → 219.0M |

The early-hint column uses the target's own later proof to select instances. At entry to bounded search, the diagnostic matches registered quantifiers and existing ground enodes by expression shape, skips ambiguous matches, checks binding sorts, and rebuilds the guarded lemmas with the ordinary instantiator. Each timed check includes this lookup. All 18 complete-verifier controls and hint-transfer runs matched native stdout, stderr and exit status. These single hardware-counter readings measure one solver thread. They do not establish a production speedup.

**Sufficiency.** On ARM, installing the 25 or 36 bindings at entry still proved the scoped obligation with subsequent ordinary quantifier publications suppressed. Empty controls exceeded the process deadline. Applying the filter later, when ordinary matching emitted a candidate lemma, proved only ARM 6/6. On Ticket, all three early-hint sets required additional search with ordinary publications enabled. Restricting later publication to the observed candidate shapes also gave three inconclusive results. Allowing every recorded shape reproduced the baseline emission counts and all five proofs. Conflict ancestry alone omits work that creates terms or makes bindings reachable. Candidate counts can also include multiple origins for identical binary clauses. The experiment establishes replay sufficiency only for the successful runs.

**Transfer and subsequent checks.** The 137.8M saving at Ticket 12/8 became a 108.5M saving across all measured solver stages of the complete workload. The corresponding whole-workload savings for its two other same-check hint sets were 38.5M and 3.6M. Across the three earlier-to-later Ticket pairs, zero complete bindings transferred, even after normalizing generated numeric suffixes and skipping ambiguous matches. ARM 6/5 supplied all 25 bindings to 6/6, but stage instructions across the complete ARM verifier rose from 1.860B to 2.615B. Normalizing suffixes installed 24 and still raised the total to 2.126B. Reusing a previous conflict's bindings as a general policy failed this screen. [Benchmark drivers, proof traces, selected bindings and raw counters](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-terminal-conflict-replay.tar.xz)

**One binding explains most of the Ticket 12/8 saving.** In 11 complete runs, we removed groups of the 42 candidates while retaining both a sub-60M target check and a complete solver-stage total within 30M of the full hint set. An empty set cost 176.0M instructions at 12/8 and 1.783B across stages. A single guarded instance of the positive unary fact `forall x. __l2s_g_1(x)`, using the existing thread constant `T:ticket_protocol.thread!42`, cost 53.4M and 1.646B. These complete transcripts all matched. The singleton saved more across the workload than the original 31 installed instances, even though the latter proved 12/8 sooner. This identifies a candidate rule using only syntax available to the solver.

**Removing the oracle.** A second prototype scans live registered quantifiers for a positive uninterpreted unary predicate applied to its sole bound variable. It tries existing uninterpreted constants of the binder sort, in deterministic AST slot order, through normal guarded instantiation. It uses no case names, saved expressions or conflict records. Applying this rule to all matching constants at entry to **12/8 alone** cut the check to 54.8M instructions. The previously measured linked Z3 control used 87.0M. Applying it on every check of automatic Ticket cut 12/8 to 38.8M and the complete solver-stage sum from 1.782B to 1.617B, still above linked Z3's 0.779B stage sum. Picking only the first or last constant at 12/8 increased the total across Ticket despite reducing the target check. The all-constant rule also raised the complete solver-stage totals on nested Ticket, Hybrid and test_liveness2. The general workload screen is decisive for release.

**Can assignment, scope or conflict count predict when to use this rule?** Requiring an active quantifier cut the 12/8 candidates from 46 to 22 and the check to 47.3M. Applied everywhere this still added 15.1% to nested Ticket. Requiring a constant introduced above the user base selected zero at 12/8. Waiting for one conflict saved 5.7% across automatic Ticket and cost 12.8% across nested Ticket. Waiting for four narrowed those figures to a 2.1% saving and a 0.5% increase, but cost Hybrid 2.3%. Waiting for sixteen increased automatic Ticket by 1.1%. The positive unary fact is a substantial opportunity on an individual check. None of the measured admission rules earned a production change. [Saved drivers and per-workload results](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-terminal-conflict-replay.tar.xz)

Across transfer, subset removal, unary-policy and admission experiments, all 144 complete runs matched the reference exit codes and transcripts, including cases with expected failed checks. The packaged observer was rebuilt in fresh private storage and reproduced both full event logs byte for byte after decompression. Publication-suppression runs are reported separately in the archive because they intentionally change the search and can return inconclusive.

## November 27 — Why a unary Ticket witness helps and why its cost changes a later solver

**Automatic Ticket 12/8.** At the start of bounded search the solver had 22 eligible bindings of two active unary universals. None of the 22 predicate applications had a Boolean variable. The proposed binary-watch and near-unit-clause test therefore selected zero. The successful binding's thread constant already existed at level zero, had two enode parents, and was outside the relevance set.

In ordinary search the solver first assigned the predicate on that constant **false** after 356 decisions and 14 conflicts, at scope 49. Unit resolution on `P(x) ⇒ Q(x)` and a false `Q(t)` supplied the reason. That negative assignment propagated through another implication and conflicted with `∀x. P(x)` before another decision. Supplying the singleton made `P(t)` true at scope 1 before the first decision. The same implication then propagated `Q(t)` in the forward direction. Here `P` is `__l2s_g_1`, `Q` is `__m_l2s_g_1`, and `t` is `T:ticket_protocol.thread!42`.

| Intervention at entry to 12/8 | Target instructions | Solver-stage sum, complete automatic Ticket |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ordinary | 175.0M | 1.782B |
| Construct and release the ground AST | 175.2M | 1.782B |
| Internalize the ground atom | 159.5M | 1.771B |
| Instantiate the universal at that same term | 51.9M | 1.645B |
| Internalize an unrelated fresh Boolean | 159.4M | 1.802B |

Testing all 22 bindings individually gave 50.0M–226.6M instructions with guarded instantiation. Internalizing the atom alone gave 159.3M–159.8M. The truth of the chosen instance explains most of the target saving, while introducing one Boolean also changes search order. Forcing both a fact and a matching unary implication saved 7.3% across automatic Ticket's measured stages but added 6.5% on nested Ticket. Resolving unary facts and implications into guarded universal consequences before grounding also had mixed results. No admission rule from this group entered the solver.

**Nested Ticket 16/1.** Enabling the unary hints throughout verification added 191M solver-stage instructions. Of that, 137M appeared on 16/1. With hints enabled only on 16/1 the check used 78.9M instructions versus 78.3M ordinary. With hints only in the preceding batches it rose to **291.8M**. The frontend creates a new solver for the batch using the same AST manager. At the start of bounded search, the two histories had identical Boolean assignments, activity scores, phases, heap, compact watches and 330 auxiliary clauses. All 335 Boolean expression shapes and 59 registered quantifiers matched after consistently renaming fresh suffixes. AST IDs differed on 300 Boolean expressions. Both runs contained the same 203 normalized enode shapes; 164 positions differed when traversing their storage by slot.

**Isolating fresh names and hashes.** Earlier hints had consumed three fewer fresh suffixes. The diagnostic advanced the shared counter by three at the start of batch 16. All 861 decision, instance and conflict events then matched the baseline, despite the earlier hints. A separate control changed only the spelling used to compute the stored hash of newly interned symbols ending in a numeric suffix. Actual names, uniqueness and equality were preserved in that arm. The following single-run counts include the entry snapshot. An independent build from the saved archive reproduced all eight native transcripts and both the slow and fast paths.

| Earlier hints | Advance suffix counter | Offset applied only to stored symbol hash | 16/1 instructions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| None | 0 | 0 | 89.1M |
| None | 3 | 0 | 284.5M |
| None | 3 | −3 | 87.9M |
| Earlier batches | 0 | 0 | 302.1M |
| Earlier batches | 0 | +3 | 87.1M |
| Earlier batches | 3 | 0 | 88.7M |

The stored hash changes model-finder iteration and subsequent witness selection. In the slower history only the first inverse-map input matched before terms appeared in a different order. The two auxiliary universe restrictions matched. The ordered instantiation-set restrictions and the negated candidate-model body differed. The first 654 normalized search events still agreed. The fast run eventually emitted 515 instances and made 323 decisions, the slow run emitted 2,241 and made 1,251. Sorting allowed values alone left the slow check at 302M. Sorting inverse inputs by printed term reduced it to 243M. Sorting all three measured traversals put both histories near 276M. A consistent order by itself can consistently choose a costly proof.

**Which counterexample caused the loss?** The first different binding changed from `ticket_protocol.sk1` to `__l2s_s_9`, two representatives of the same model value. Replacing this binding alone reduced the instrumented slow check from 302.5M to 240.9M. Replacing only the **third** binding tuple reduced it to **94.9M**. The same intervention in reverse raised the fast check from 88.8M to 240.4M. This third quantifier was binary. The faster history supplied the same ticket for both binders. The slower history supplied two distinct tickets. The experiment looked up live, unambiguous, sort-checked terms and pinned the resulting actual quantifier instances. All 14 complete counterfactual runs matched native. [Drivers, traces, counterfactual tuples and measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-unary-demand-and-fresh-symbols.tar.xz)

**Retained change.** When the finite-table path finds a binary counterexample it cannot enqueue, the auxiliary solver can still return a pair of distinct values. On the last available instance, g3 tries the second value in both positions if the binders have the same sort and both inverse maps identify the same ground term. It evaluates the original quantified body on that pair and accepts it only when the result is false. The instance carries the maximum generation of the two retained representatives. The opportunity is restricted to unbounded checks with at least two earlier instances, the most recent of them binary. These scheduling conditions reflect the measured workload; the validity of the witness comes from the model evaluation. [Implementation](smtcore/smt_model_checker_repeated_binding.go) · [Regression](smtcore/smt_model_checker_repeated_binding_test.go)

The robustness benchmark independently advanced the fresh-name counter by offsets 0 through 23 before nested Ticket batch 16. Each arm ran the complete verifier. The input, solver configuration and starting assertion order were identical within each pair. All 48 runs matched the reference transcript.

| Solver-thread instructions across 24 histories | Previous median | New median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Check 16/1 | 273.55M | 83.31M |
| Sum of measured stages in nested Ticket | 1,442.50M | 1,252.06M |

Sixteen histories benefited. The other eight already selected a cheap proof. The widest observed check cost fell from 292.67M to 83.42M instructions. The default naming history was already near 78M, so its end-to-end benchmark measures the overhead on an already fast run.

Three order-rotated pairs per workload used ordinary GC, optimized binaries and whole-process instruction counters. All 90 timed runs matched native output and exit status. Default nested Ticket used 2.367B → 2.375B instructions (+0.32%). Among the 12 regular workloads, the median changes ranged from −1.18% to +0.32%. Raft used 15.820B → 15.794B, Apple rfn2 used 11.241B → 11.198B, and Apple dramc_nb2 used 119.173B → 119.079B. The reason to keep this change is its reduction in expensive proof searches across fresh-name histories. The ordinary holdouts show little movement.

Three fresh runs with the same frontend linked to Z3 gave a median of 121.18M solver-thread instructions on nested Ticket 16/1. Every one of the 24 g3 histories tested finished this check in fewer instructions. Across all measured stages the linked Z3 median was 1,049.46M, so g3's new 1,252.06M median still leaves a 19.3% aggregate gap. These comparisons measure retired instructions with GC disabled. [Control driver and raw measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-unary-demand-and-fresh-symbols.tar.xz)

The release candidate also matched exit status, stdout and stderr on all 228 compatibility inputs, including the seven that invoke ABC. The ordinary smtcore and api suites, the focused model-checker regression in the checked/debug/trace build, and go vet on smtcore passed.

## November 27 — Where nested Ticket still loses after stabilizing check 16/1

At `14a4f46e1`, g3's concrete checks on ordinary nested Ticket used **118.69M fewer instructions** than linked Z3. Pushes consumed **184.61M more**, and the pre-push proof attempts consumed 131.57M. Z3 checks those conditions through its ordinary solver. Subtracting both engines' total measured stages leaves a **197.48M deficit**. A successful pre-push proof can postpone g3's first physical push to a different obligation, so push costs are compared by solver batch. Comparing individual push ordinals would overstate several gaps.

| Input | g3 measured stages, M | Linked Z3, M | Push excess, M | Concrete check excess, M |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Nested Ticket | 1,247 | 1,049 | 185 | −119 |
| Automatic Ticket | 1,782 | 759 | 163 | 749 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 1,322 | 744 | 167 | 329 |
| ARM | 1,859 | 1,023 | 166 | 561 |
| Hybrid broadcast | 4,339 | 3,237 | 580 | 313 |
| Ordinary Raft | 13,123 | 23,349 | 195 | −10,618 |

Each cell uses three complete pinned runs per engine with the same frontend and GC disabled. The measured stages are the timed push, early-proof and check calls. Frontend work, construction, assertion and pop are outside these counters. Individual phase medians can differ slightly from the median of their sum.

**How often is there another valid repeated binding?** A prototype retained the unbounded, proof-path and last-instance guards and tried the second model value in both positions on any eligible restricted binary result. It preserved the sort, inverse-representative and model-falsification checks. Three extra ground tuples were selected on Hybrid, one each at 24/33, 25/34 and 34/33. No extra tuple was selected on the other five inputs. Total measured Hybrid stages increased by 4.89M instructions. The check with the largest improvement among those three saved only 35K instructions. The broader scheduling rule stays out of production.

**What runs inside push?** Three instruction-sampling runs each yielded 2,095 nested Ticket and 7,677 Hybrid samples whose stacks contained `internalizePushBase`. The general rewriter appeared on 63.4% and 66.7% of these stacks. On nested Ticket, value propagation accounted for 26.6% and macro finding for 23.6%. On Hybrid, macro finding accounted for 34.2%, including 26.8% inside macro expansion. These percentages are inclusive and overlap with rewriting. Sampling uses frame pointers, so these shares apply to recovered stacks. Hybrid batch 32 alone had a 39M push gap. It gives a stronger preprocessing target than widening the binary witness rule.

The baseline-path observer evaluated the second-value alternative and restored the original binding and generation. Across the six default inputs, 21 auxiliary results already had the same value in both positions, nine had different sorts, four failed the body test and three passed it. All 28 outcomes outside Hybrid belonged to Raft or nested Ticket. A separate arm tried the first model value in both positions. It selected four tuples on Hybrid and reduced the complete measured stages there by 1.28M out of 4.34B (0.03%). Neither direction merits general adoption from this evidence. The downstream costs explain why: after Hybrid 34/33, repeating the second value added 5.31M instructions over the rest of the batch. The first-value policy saved 1.76M over that interval, including another substitution at 34/34. This last saving is attributable to the policy over the batch; the two interventions were not isolated.

**Would caching macro substitutions recover the push gap?** A separate diagnostic measured the complete substitution path after a declaration lookup succeeded. A repeat required the same manager, application handle and defining quantifier within a single physical push. Counts and instructions are medians of three complete runs per input.

| Input | First / repeat calls | First / repeat instructions, M |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Hybrid | 399 / 651 | 9.08 / 14.66 |
| ARM | 64 / 317 | 3.02 / 19.15 |
| Nested Ticket | 105 / 57 | 1.64 / 0.65 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 72 / 16 | 1.34 / 0.28 |
| Automatic Ticket | 63 / 35 | 1.00 / 0.41 |
| Ordinary Raft | 111 / 138 | 2.94 / 1.64 |

Even eliminating all measured repeat substitution work on Hybrid would cover only about 2.5% of its 580M push deficit. ARM has the best ceiling at 19.15M against a 166M push deficit. A real cache would still have to pin the replacement, propagate dependencies and retire entries. There is no production cache from this trial. The six-workload measurements, both witness alternatives, passive acceptance census, post-goal costs and push profiles are preserved together. [Benchmark drivers and raw measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-binary-witness-and-push-costs.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Replaying live macro expansions with a proof-free application walker

On Hybrid, 1,674 of 2,009 full macro-expansion steps in the measured pushes could use a bounded application walker. Of these, 888 changed the expression. The remaining 335 used the general rewriter. This population starts after the existing small-term identity probe. It includes each fixed-point iteration and excludes subsequent theory normalization.

The first prototype walked the input recursively, looked up macro applications before visiting their arguments, and used the existing substitution routine at each matched declaration. It rebuilt changed applications and quantifier bodies. It kept separate visited-node tables under binders and left quantifier patterns alone. It declined ITEs, applications with more than 16 children and walks exceeding 512 visits. A second prototype compiled a whole traversal plan before performing substitutions. It also declined definitions carrying dependencies. A rejected plan could therefore fall back before changing the AST or charging substitution work.

For each comparison, the prototype and the ordinary traversal processed the same incoming root in sequence. The observer checked the resulting AST handle and the resource count charged by the traversal, including substitutions. The ordinary traversal supplied the solver's output. Across 228 reference inputs the preflight plan completed 11,136 steps on 89 inputs, including 5,509 that changed the root. It declined 3,979 steps. Every accepted result and resource count agreed, and all verifier exit codes and transcripts matched. This corpus measures ordinary proof-free runs. It does not establish error recovery, bounded cancellation or proof-generation behavior.

| Input | Accepted / declined per run | Changed among accepted | Push instructions saved by applying the plan, M |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Hybrid | 1,674 / 335 | 888 | 29.54 |
| Hybrid batches 31–33 only | 322 / 109 | 184 | 5.66 |
| Nested Ticket | 292 / 67 | 142 | 3.67 |
| POPL18 Ticket | 102 / 142 | 61 | 0.96 |
| Automatic Ticket | 202 / 42 | 92 | 3.41 |
| ARM | 56 / 177 | 52 | 0.20 |
| Ordinary Raft | 413 / 55 | 204 | 8.17 |

Values are differences of three-run medians, summing physical push intervals on the solver thread with GC disabled. On Hybrid the ordinary traversal used 87.6M instructions for accepted steps. The recursive walker used 44.8M for this work. Building and executing the preflight plan took 55.7M, and compiling declined plans took another 1.36M. The walker timings end before temporary-reference release, so the full push comparison is the better estimate of the saving. Hybrid's 29.54M improvement covers about 5% of the previously measured 580M push gap.

**Whole verifier under ordinary GC.** Three release variants used a dense plan, a dense plan with small local buffers, or a sparse plan containing only the ancestors of possible substitutions. Across 12 inputs and three rotations, Hybrid instruction changes were −0.72%, −0.91% and −0.45% respectively. All three gave mixed results across inputs. A fourth version reused plan storage within each solver's macro manager and constructed the general traversal only after a decline. A separate 228-input run applied that version and matched every native transcript and exit status.

Seven alternating pairs in a single optimized executable isolated the scratch-reuse policy from code-layout differences. The median paired change on Hybrid was −1.17% (seven pairs improved), but on ARM it was +1.39% (six pairs regressed). An adaptive variant stopped trying after at least eight declines outnumbered acceptances in the current push. This put ARM at −0.45% and Hybrid at −0.85%. Its other median changes ranged from −0.87% on POPL18 to +0.18% on test_liveness2. Each adaptive workload had seven pairs. The larger phase-level saving shrinks to under 1% on the complete Hybrid verifier under that policy. Given the extra traversal implementation, workspace per macro manager and untested failure paths, the prototypes remain benchmarks. [Drivers, exact overlays, corpus checks and measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-macro-expansion-walkers.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Which unary search wins survive the binary-witness fix?

The narrow binary-witness change removed most of the nested Ticket penalty that previously ruled out early unary instantiation. Three rotations per combination changed only the binary witness implementation and the unary policy. Each run used the complete input and verified native output. The unit rule instantiates an existing universally quantified positive unary fact at existing constants of its sort. The active variant requires the universal to be true and relevant. The check pays for discovering and installing its own instances.

| Input and policy | Earlier binary rule, M stage instructions | Shipped binary rule, M |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Nested Ticket, ordinary search | 1,247 | 1,247 |
| Nested Ticket, active unary facts | 1,435 | 1,299 |
| Nested Ticket, all unary facts | 1,597 | 1,380 |
| Automatic Ticket, ordinary search | 1,782 | 1,782 |
| Automatic Ticket, active unary facts | 1,675 | 1,675 |
| Automatic Ticket, all unary facts | 1,617 | 1,617 |

With the active rule, nested Ticket 16/1 itself now costs 78.57M instructions versus 215.50M on the earlier binary implementation. Other checks still add about 51M to the full stage sum. Unconditionally trying every unary fact also adds about 145M instructions on Hybrid. These effects are large relative to counter noise.

**How much can better ground-term selection recover?** Requiring the constant to be outside the relevance set and to have at least two enode-class parents reduced automatic Ticket's stage cost by about 11.3%, with 326 attempts. Requiring the source predicate to appear as the antecedent of an active positive unary implication eliminated every attempt on nested Ticket. The cost of finding these candidates still added about 7M instructions there. The positive-tail rule made 2,460 attempts on TLB and added about 1.04B instructions.

Limiting each source predicate to its two eligible constants with the fewest enode-class parents gave the best automatic Ticket result among the immediate policies. Measured stages fell from 1.782B to 1.539B and check 12/8 fell from 175M to 44M. On TLB the same policy made 820 attempts and increased the measured stage sum by about 2.7%. Choosing just the first eligible constant still added about 2.4% there. A per-source cap controls the number of instances but does not predict their downstream cost.

**What if the solver waits for evidence of demand?** Selecting one low-parent-count witness after one conflict saved 2.9% of automatic Ticket stages but added 1.14% on TLB. Waiting for four conflicts saved 0.49% on TLB and cost 2.37% on automatic Ticket. Restricting instantiation to the birth of an actual unary Boolean variable also had mixed results. Watching the source predicate made just seven attempts across automatic Ticket, reducing its measured stages by 2.77%. On TLB it made 73 attempts and added 0.55%. Watching both source and positive implication-tail occurrences increased measured stages on both inputs.

The birth trace explains the limit on reactive strategies. On automatic Ticket 12/8, neither the source predicate nor the implication tail on the useful thread had a Boolean variable before decision 356, conflict 14 and scope 49. Both appeared at that same point. The earlier birth on another thread occurred at decision 303. A callback on the useful predicate or its implication tail cannot select that ground witness at search entry.

**How much of the TLB regression comes from lookup?** Three rotated runs separated ordinary search, discovering the same two prospective witnesses without installing them, and actually installing them. On TLB the median stage sums were 27.457B, 27.999B and 28.195B. Candidate discovery alone therefore cost 542M instructions. Of 13,358 concrete checks, 410 received candidates in the applied arm. Summing per-check medians, those 410 checks accounted for 519M of the discovery overhead. The largest individual end-to-end check penalties were 25.3M at 43/70 and 25.1M at 54/80. Only about 1.3M of each came from discovery. TLB 60/1 went the other way, saving 189M. Sibling search history matters on both sides.

On automatic Ticket the corresponding stage sums were 1.782B, 1.791B and 1.539B. The added search rule helped well beyond what its 9.5M lookup cost can explain. Check 12/8 saved 131M, 13/8 saved 64M, 12/16 saved 31M and 16/1 saved 28M. These figures compare each complete policy with its own ordinary-search control. Crediting a single binding with the entire change would require a separate intervention.

**How much can the solver save by indexing the same rule?** Registering unary facts and implications as quantifiers enter and leave the solver reduced TLB discovery overhead from 551M to 106M instructions in the same executable. Scanning the existing dense enode stack and breaking equal-parent-count ties by AST slot reduced discovery overhead to 18.6M in a separate executable. Both recompute assignment and relevance from live solver state. Each executable had its own baseline and three rotated runs per input.

| Complete input | Ordinary stages, M instructions | Dense discovery alone, M | Dense discovery and instantiation, M | Applied change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TLB | 27,459.63 | 27,478.18 | 27,677.52 | +0.79% |
| Automatic Ticket | 1,781.85 | 1,782.89 | 1,530.75 | −14.09% |
| Nested Ticket | 1,247.26 | 1,247.58 | 1,247.42 | +0.01% |
| test_liveness2 | 919.89 | 920.25 | 923.34 | +0.38% |

The dense version made 226 attempts on automatic Ticket and cut check 12/8 from 174.98M to 43.49M instructions. On TLB it made 820 attempts. About 199M of its 218M instruction penalty arose after enabling instantiation. Checks 43/70 and 54/80 each made two attempts and cost an extra 23.9M and 23.8M. Check 60/1 saved 189.9M with zero attempts in that check. An intervention restricted to the target check and a complementary one restricted to earlier checks would distinguish the local proof effect from inherited search history. These are solver-stage instruction measurements with GC disabled. The benchmarks preserve the indexed implementation for that experiment. [Drivers, overlays, transcripts comparison results and per-stage counts](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-unary-witness-eligibility.tar.xz)

## November 27 — Which earlier checks change TLB and Ticket witness search?

The three-rotation replay enabled the dense unary-witness rule only at specified checks of the complete input. Each batch creates a fresh solver, and sibling checks within that batch use push and pop. A separate linked-Z3 binary ran the same inputs three times on a pinned core. The table gives median solver-thread instructions in millions with GC disabled. Each column draws its local and earlier-only rows from interventions targeted at that particular check.

| Where g3 installs witnesses | TLB 43/70 | TLB 54/80 | TLB 60/1 | Automatic Ticket 12/8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary search | 79.17 | 43.29 | 1,092.55 | 174.98 |
| Every eligible check | 103.16 | 67.09 | 902.69 | 43.49 |
| This check alone | 80.24 | 44.56 | 1,093.16 | 54.08 |
| All checks before this one | 102.74 | 66.07 | 902.16 | 149.76 |
| Earlier siblings in this batch alone | 104.86 | 63.81 | — | 149.76 |
| All earlier batches alone | 76.95 | 43.31 | 902.16 | 174.96 |
| Linked Z3 | 40.01 | 11.96 | 387.68 | 87.01 |

The local interventions made two attempts on each of the two losing TLB checks and four on Ticket 12/8. TLB's large penalties come primarily from changed search on the same incremental solver. On Ticket, the local intervention alone saved 120.90M instructions in the target check, but just 28.20M across all measured stages in the complete verifier. Later checks absorb much of the local saving. Ordinary g3 still beats linked Z3 across the full set of **TLB solver stages** (27.46B versus 42.48B), while automatic Ticket still costs 1.782B versus 0.759B. These figures exclude frontend work outside the measured stages.

**Why a fresh TLB solver changes.** Enabling witnesses only over batches 40 through goal 69 of batch 43 reduced TLB 60/1 from 1,092.56M to 796.43M. Earlier siblings confined to batch 43 left 60/1 at 1,092.61M. In a separate executable the first fresh-function declaration in batch 60 saw counter 407 after ordinary search and 408 after enabling witnesses through batch 42. Advancing only the ordinary run's counter to 408 reproduced the roughly 296M saving. The all-witness history also arrived at 408 but cost 903M. The counter suffices to reproduce the fast prefix result and does not explain the entire difference between histories.

The ordinary and all-witness traces make the same first 684 semantic decisions, including polarity, and learn the same first 12 recorded conflicts. They emit the same first 1,416 normalized quantified lemmas. The first differing burst follows 594 decisions and 12 conflicts. Each run emits ten lemmas there and six coincide as a multiset. The next burst after decision 595 contains 1,086 emissions in each run, of which 971 coincide. Over the whole check the ordinary run emits 19,943 quantified lemmas and the all-witness run emits 15,038. Their numbers of distinct raw printed lemma expressions are much closer at 5,477 and 5,428. Printed expression identity is a diagnostic count and does not establish that a previous clause remains installed after backtracking.

An independent queue observer identified the first changed binding. Ordinal 1,415 came from pattern matching in both histories. The next eight came from model-based instantiation. At 1,417 the slow history bound the binary quantifier to a fresh processor and the constant `tlb.sk0`. The other history used its corresponding fresh processor and a conditional term that can select `tlb.sk0` or `__l2s_s_28`. The following two unary instances changed their processor binding in the same way. This puts model-value representative selection upstream of the first large E-matching expansion. It leaves open which individual replacement changes the final cost.

For eight adjacent starting counters, 407 through 414, ordinary 60/1 took **1,093, 797, 1,007, 797, 1,007, 797, 1,093 and 797M** instructions respectively. Setting the counter to 10,000 at the first declaration of the batch put all three histories within 1M of 1,093M. Setting it to 10,001 put them within 1.4M of 1,007M. A performance change on this check needs a distribution of fresh-name histories and a same-binary control.

**Can stable ordering recover the saving?** Two repetitions at each of four starting counters compared five solver-local policies, each restricted to 60/1 and paired with ordinary search in its own executable. The first two changed which root wins an equal-size congruence-class merge. The next two changed the inverse term selected for a model value among terms of equal generation. The last changed how the unrestricted context maps a model value back to a ground term. The table rounds within-counter medians to millions of instructions.

| Policy | 407 | 408 | 409 | 410 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Ordinary | 1,093 | 797 | 1,007 | 797 |
| Merge into lower-slot root | 858 | 896 | 972 | 896 |
| Merge into root with more parents | 892 | 863 | 947 | 863 |
| Lower-slot inverse representative | 917 | 917 | 917 | 917 |
| Prefer conditional inverse representative, then lower slot | 917 | 917 | 917 | 917 |
| Prefer conditional unrestricted context representative, then lower slot | 1,093 | 797 | 1,007 | 797 |

The inverse tie-break removed almost all sensitivity across these four counters and sacrificed about 120M instructions on the two faster histories. Changing the unrestricted context representative had negligible effect. The class-merge policies also slowed both faster histories. These trials remain in the benchmark. The direct follow-up is to replace individual bindings in the first differing model round, then observe the amplified burst and final proof. [Replay drivers, raw event streams, linked control and measurements](perf/ivy_apple/holdouts/nov27-tlb-witness-history.tar.xz)

The auxiliary model checker needs the keys of an inverse map when it restricts a Skolem constant to values of the candidate model. It copied every complete hash-table entry into a slice, then copied each key into the result. Reading the keys directly in table order removes one allocation without changing the selected values or their order.

| Distinct values | Earlier median ns/op | Direct median ns/op | Allocated bytes/op, earlier → direct |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 56.28 | 24.49 | 80 → 16 |
| 8 | 165.5 | 61.52 | 640 → 128 |
| 64 | 942.5 | 326.5 | 5,120 → 1,024 |

Five alternating pairs per size used optimized benchmark binaries on one pinned core. Each lookup now allocates once. Three complete release pairs per input under ordinary GC matched all reference outputs on automatic Ticket, nested Ticket and TLB. The full verifier changes were under 0.4% on each input.
